#6483. The Gifts Chefs and Bartenders Actually Want This Year

Streetwear cooking shoes, a perfect pepper mill, and more

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

This is not your average “gifts for foodies” round-up. We know that you’ve probably been given a few too many wine glasses and cookbooks. “As a professional, I don’t want to be gifted introductory-level items that will ultimately go unused,” says Storm Brunni, private dining director at Barolo Grill in Denver. That’s why, for our guide, we’ve consulted you, the hospitality pros, about what you actually would like to receive this year.

New shoes for service. “I’m getting all of my favorite people the new high-top kitchen shoes by Chuck Taylor in leather anti-slip. They’re cool enough to complete your streetwear look, functional enough to wear in the dining room, kitchen, or work, and comfy enough to wear as a commuter.” —Jonathon Sawyer, chef at Kindling in Chicago

An industry-favorite hand cream. “Between constant handwashing, citrus, chiles, and hot pans, hospitality hands take a beating. Add a heated neck massager to use on the couch after a midnight close, and you’ve basically given someone a spa day.” —Antelmo Ambrosio, executive chef at Casa Oaxaca in New York City

Something for the coffee nerds. “It’s definitely a splurge, but I buy myself the Onyx Coffee Advent Calendar every year. A lot of hospitality pros nerd out about coffee, and Onyx is one of the best roasters. They fill the calendar with individual portions of beans (enough for two people) with different origins, roasts, and processes every day. Everything is roasted on a schedule so that when you’re brewing each one, the coffee is at its peak that day. The calendar has some of their signature coffees, alongside one-offs that you’ll never be able to get again, and I’ve tried some of the best coffees of my life in past calendars.” —Katie Renshaw, owner of Bar Bambi in Chicago

An upgrade for kitchen organization. “I love this automatic tape dispenser. Gift it with a nice fresh box of Sharpies.” —Kevin Beary, beverage director of Gus’ Sip & Dip, Kitty’s Cosmopolitan Club, Three Dots and a Dash in Chicago

The gift of longer-lasting produce. “Vejibag is a family-owned business, run by a small team of women who create 100 percent organic cotton bags designed to keep produce fresher for longer at home. They genuinely work and are an amazing addition to any kitchen.” —Lauren DeSteno, executive chef at Ai Fiori in New York City

A tool for operators who know there’s always something that needs fixing. “I was given a precision screwdriver from HOTO Tools and now I’m obsessed with the brand and their design aesthetic. So many things in the restaurants need little fixes all the time and the 3.6V Electric Screwdriver Kit Pro has all the bits you could need. I also love their rotary drill for polishing plateware with chips/scratches for work.” —Zach Engel, chef at Galit and Cafe Yaya in Chicago

Gifts with a personal touch. “As a general manager some of the top staff requests I’ve received are for nice wine keys (it’s an even nicer touch if they’re engraved) and custom server books.” —John Schneekloth, general manager at Toro in Chicago

Nice dishware is worthwhile at home, too. “I’d love to receive items from Ivo Angel, a beautiful ceramics company out of Italy. I am a huge fan of the splatter design and always want a pinch bowl; I can’t have too many. Also the olive bowl with an attached vessel for pits is perfect for hosting.” —Julia Jaksoc, chef and owner of Bar Roza, Cafe Roze and Roze Pony in Nashville

The pepper mill that chefs swear by. “It’s one of those tools that gets used constantly, makes a real difference, and is something every cook or bartender would appreciate having.” —Marco Torres, Chef at Brass and The Tusk Bar in New York City

Fun socks. “Being locked down in heavy black pants, unforgiving non-slip shoe leathers, and a stiff chef coat means you have to find your personality somewhere. A pair of loud, ridiculous socks underneath always makes me feel a little more human. I’ll never forget getting this pair of bright yellow Spam socks as a Christmas gift one year. Honestly, it’s one of the best presents I’ve ever unwrapped, and it brings a little joy each time I slip them on.” —Soo Ahn, chef/partner at Adalina Prime, Arla and Adalina Italian in Chicago

Something to take the edge off. “For the industry pro who enjoys a little puff puff and a good nap (especially after a Saturday morning shift with lines out the door), you can’t go wrong with Tokin’ Jew rolling papers. We sell them at the deli because, come on, but they’re also a fantastic gift. And for the pipe people, their pickle pipes are another way to keep it kosher.” —Jake Schneider, chef and co-owner of Schneider Deli in Chicago

A beautiful book for recipe writing. “I would gift this brown leather journal cover from Shinola along with this 12-pack of pens. I think the notebook is a worthwhile splurge, and while I know the idea of a more expensive and elegant pen is both compelling and sexy, it is also impractical for when you’re on the go or as prone to losing nice pens as I am. These ones write fluidly and beautifully.” —Róbert LeBlanc, creative director and founder of LeBlanc + Smith in New Orleans

The kitchen fit of your dreams. “I could wear this jumpsuit 24/7! It’s comfortable, easy to move around in, and perfect for those long days in the kitchen when I’m constantly running around and want something that looks as good as it feels.” —Andrea Belfiore, chef and founder of EVÈNTO in New York City

A tool for foraging. “I love my ARS pruning shears. I take them pretty much everywhere when I’m out foraging, and they’re great for everything from cutting herbs to collecting branches and other ingredients for drinks. They’re one of those tools I use all the time.” —Danny Childs, co-owner of Field Day in Philadelphia

A trio of pastry chef staples. “On any given day, a pastry professional will produce dozens of recipes, and we need tools to measure mass/weight, time, and temperature. Even when we have our own, backups or better ones are always welcome! My top picks include: this scale, which has a pull-out screen when you’re scaling on to sheet trays or large bowls; this kitchen timer has four color-coded channels for timing multiple projects at once; and this thermometer, which is fast-reading, accurate, and has a magnet on the back for easy access on any magnetic surface.” —Orlando Soto, executive pastry chef of Le Bernardin in New York City

The perfect vessel for an industry-favorite amaro (or 50/50 shot). “Some of the best hospitality happens in an ounce and a half: a pour of Cynar for a regular who had a long week, a welcome taste for someone new at the bar. I’d recommend these little ceramic artichoke shot glasses to make that moment feel even more considered.” —Steven Waters, owner and operator of Fino in Denver

Many knife options. Patrick Dooley of Harry’s Bar in Paris recommends Le Grand Tradi, which is sized between a paring and chef’s knife, making it a great workhorse option, while Nancy Santiago, beverage director at NYC’s IGC Hospitality, recommends a Japanese petty knife “for precise citrus work and garnish prep.” Amir Babayoff of Ophelia Lounge in NYC is partial to Tojiro’s chef knives.

And knife storage and upkeep options. Schneekloth of Toro recommends a knife backpack, while Devin Denzer, chef at Atsumeru in Chicago, recommends a whetstone and ceramic sharpening rod, especially for newer line cooks.

A thoughtful gift card. “Here are a few gifts that I have received that stood out to me: a hefty gift card to a sought-after restaurant with guaranteed reservations on a night off, which is such a good way to give someone a night out; a gift card to a shoe store that carries high-quality work shoes, like Red Wings, Dansko, or Blundstones; and a gift card to something wellness-related—my business partner Jesse got me three sessions at a body-stretching spa downtown.” —Phila Lorn, chef and co-owner of Mawn and Sao in Philadelphia

A new positioning technology could make autonomous vehicles and robotaxis more reliable at recharging themselves.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Researchers in Japan have developed a new technology that could enable electric vehicles (EVs) to charge "simply by parking".

Wireless charging is still relatively nascent in the EV market, but scientists hope that integrating more wireless charging devices into roads and parking spaces will move the EV industry away from bulky plug-in infrastructure. It uses the same wireless power transfer technology found in modern smartphones and consumer electronics: a transmitter coil inside in a ground pad generates an oscillating magnetic field, which induces an electric current in a receiver coil underneath the vehicle. This current recharges the EV's battery cells.

However, small misalignments between the two coils can affect how quickly and efficiently the battery recharges. This new system uses short-range radio signals to determine the position of the vehicle's magnetic charging coil relative to the charging device in the ground, including its distance and angle. This helps the EV and its driver get into the optimal position for efficient charging.

The technology could be particularly useful for driverless "robotaxis" and other autonomous vehicles that need to be able to recharge quickly and efficiently without human assistance, the researchers said. They detailed their findings in a study published Aug. 26 in the IEEE Open Journal of Vehicular Technology.

"We hope this research will lead to a future where EVs charge simply by parking, much like smartphones placed on wireless chargers," Ryotaro Hada, first author of the study and a master's student at the University of Osaka's Graduate School of Information Science and Technology, said in a statement.

Existing methods for aligning an EV's charging coil with a wireless charging pad use magnetic sensors or cameras. Magnetic systems work best when the coil is close to the pad, while cameras can struggle in rain, poor lighting or when dirt obscures the pad, the researchers explained.

This new system uses four ultra-wideband radio devices mounted around the vehicle's charging coil to communicate with four antennas around the charging pad.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

By measuring how long radio waves take to travel between the ultra-wideband devices and the antennas, as well as detecting tiny differences in how the signals arrive at each of the vehicle's sensors, the system can pinpoint the position and angle of the EV's charging coil relative to the ground pad.

The same technology is used in some digital car keys. They use short radio pulses to detect when the driver is close by, allowing the driver to unlock their vehicle without requiring a physical key.

In laboratory experiments using a scaled-down vehicle model, the system worked out where the vehicle's charging coil was to within 0.09 inches (2.32 millimeters) of its actual position and which direction it was facing to within 0.25 degrees. Correcting for distortions in the radio signals reduced the positioning error by around fivefold, the team said.

The researchers noted that the system still needs to be tested outdoors, on full-size EVs and under real charging conditions.

#6480. Scientists May Have Finally Found What’s Driving the Universe Apart

The same fundamental physics that holds atomic nuclei together may also help explain why the Universe is expanding at an accelerating rate. Researchers at the University of British Columbia (UBC) and the University of Sheffield have developed a theoretical model that connects dark energy to the strong nuclear force, potentially explaining cosmic acceleration without introducing undiscovered particles or new fundamental fields.

Dark energy accounts for approximately 70 percent of the Universe’s total energy budget, yet its physical origin has remained unknown since scientists discovered cosmic acceleration nearly three decades ago. Many proposed explanations rely on hypothetical particles or fields that have never been detected. The new research, published in The Astrophysical Journal, instead draws on established principles of the Standard Model of particle physics.

The proposed explanation centers on Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD), the theory describing the strong nuclear force that binds quarks inside protons and neutrons. According to QCD, even apparently empty space contains quantum fields with complex properties. The researchers suggest that the vacuum’s underlying structure could produce a small energy shift as the Universe expands, potentially accounting for the acceleration observed across cosmic distances.

A key feature of the model involves the vacuum’s topological properties, which describe aspects of its quantum structure that can influence physics over large distances. The researchers propose that this structure responds to cosmic expansion in a way that generates an effective dark energy contribution through its interaction with gravity.

“Our theoretical framework suggests no new particles may be required at all,” says Professor Ariel Zhitnitsky of UBC’s Department of Physics and Astronomy, whose earlier theoretical work provided the foundation for the study. “The characteristic energy scale predicted from the QCD vacuum and gravity comes out close to the observed dark-energy scale today without having to introduce an ad-hoc new field nor new parameter.”

Rather than introducing an adjustable parameter to reproduce the observed strength of dark energy, the framework derives its characteristic energy scale from established physical constants.

“The most striking result is that the observed dark-energy scale emerges naturally from known physical constants, without the need for any additional fitting parameters,” says UBC Professor Ludovic Van Waerbeke.

The researchers also investigated whether the framework could reproduce measurements of the Universe’s expansion history. Using astronomical observations, including light from distant exploding stars (supernovae) and radiation left over from the early Universe, they found that the model performed comparably to standard cosmological models in fitting the data.

“The idea that the quantum vacuum as described by QCD could have the right properties to account for the accelerated expansion of the universe is very intriguing,” says Dong Ha Lee, a PhD researcher at the University of Sheffield and lead author of the paper.

The analysis also indicates that the framework can reproduce the changing dark energy behavior suggested by current cosmological observations. Unlike a simple cosmological constant, which maintains a constant energy density over time, evolving dark energy models allow that density to change as the Universe expands.

“It raises the possibility that dark energy could be connected to the established theory of the strong nuclear force, without introducing new fundamental fields. Testing models based on this idea against cosmological data is an essential step. Our analysis shows that such a model can reproduce the evolving dark energy behavior suggested by current observations. This motivates further theoretical work to better understand how the QCD vacuum responds to cosmic expansion and to develop predictions that can be tested with future observations.”

Although the model agrees with existing astronomical measurements, that agreement does not establish that the QCD vacuum is responsible for dark energy. Further theoretical work is needed to clarify how its quantum structure interacts with cosmic expansion and whether the framework produces predictions that distinguish it from competing explanations.

The team plans to refine its calculations and compare the results with upcoming observations from next-generation space telescopes. More precise measurements of how the Universe has expanded over billions of years could help determine whether dark energy is connected to the same quantum physics that governs matter inside atomic nuclei.

Reference: “Evolving Dark Energy Is Vacuum Energy After All” by Dong Ha Lee, Carsten van de Bruck, Eleonora Di Valentino, Ludovic Van Waerbeke and Ariel Zhitnitsky, 20 November 2026, The Astrophysical Journal. DOI: 10.3847/1538-4357/aeb9cc

Linking cosmic dark energy directly to the quantum vacuum structure of the strong nuclear force (the QCD vacuum) shows how deeply subatomic topology and large-scale spatial evolution can be connected without inventing an extra exotic field. Viewed through a Torsion Hill lens, tying microscopic vacuum structure to macroscopic expansion offers an intriguing parallel for how active tension and boundary interactions across regimes drive structural reorganization across scales. By inserting human genes into lab mice, scientists were able to study the underlying mechanics of a disease that's been notoriously difficult to research.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists have unraveled the workings of a rare disease by putting a large chunk of human DNA into a lab mouse.

The incurable disorder, called X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism (XDP), mostly affects men of Filipino descent and leads to early death. The new mouse studies revealed previously unknown aspects of the disease's biology that could point to new avenues for treatment.

The condition has long been thought of as a disease of neurons, as it triggers neuron death in a part of the brain that's key to controlling movement. But the new findings highlight an unsung role of neurons' support cells, called glial cells.

"This had never been described in this disease before," study co-author Shane Liddelow, an associate professor in the Institute for Translational Neuroscience at the NYU Grossman School of Medicine, said of the new findings. "It really sort of upended this idea of the disease" as primarily affecting neurons.

The two studies, published Thursday (Nov. 19) in the journal Cell, not only shed new light on this rare disease but also showcase a powerful technique for mimicking human conditions in laboratory animals. Known as "SwAP-In," it enables researchers to rewrite large portions of an organism's genetic code by inserting big chunks of synthetic DNA. In this case, the approach was used to insert a human gene into lab mice.

"It is kind of a generic method that can be used to make extensively humanized mice," said study co-author Jef Boeke, director of the Institute for Systems Genetics at the NYU Grossman School of Medicine and a lead developer of the SwAP-In technique.

Liddelow anticipates that this new method for humanizing mice, or tweaking their biology to more closely match that of humans, will prove useful for studying a wide range of diseases, from common conditions like Alzheimer's to "orphan" diseases like XDP, which are rare, underresearched and lacking effective treatments.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

XDP is a neurodegenerative condition that particularly impacts the striatum, part of the brain that's crucial for movement. The disease causes symptoms such as slowed movements, tremors, muscle stiffness and involuntary muscle contractions.

On average, symptoms emerge around age 39 and patients live for 13 to 16 years after their symptoms appear. In late stages of the disease, problems with breathing and swallowing can lead to deadly complications such as malnutrition, aspiration pneumonia and respiratory failure. Historically, XDP has also carried a lot of social stigma, which has contributed to high rates of depression and suicide among those with the condition.

"Patients get sort of shunned and hidden away," Liddelow said. That, among other factors, made XDP difficult to study.

XDP shows an X-linked recessive inheritance pattern (depicted above).

Although XDP isn't fully understood, its underlying genetic cause is known. It stems from a mutation in TAF1, a gene on the X chromosome that helps translate DNA sequences into new proteins. Because males carry only one X chromosome — and thus have no backup copy of the gene — the condition affects far more males than females.

The mutation first appeared in a person on Panay, an island in the Philippines. Due to a phenomenon called the "founder effect," it has risen in prevalence among people of Filipino ancestry but is not seen in other demographics, Boeke explained. Studies suggest there are about 5.7 cases per 100,000 people in the Philippines.

XDP's rarity and associated stigma have made the condition difficult to study, but there's another layer of complexity: The mutation in TAF1 was originally caused by a "jumping gene" ‪—‬ a bit of DNA that changed its position within the genome. In this instance, the DNA happened to jump into the middle of TAF1 and disrupted its function, Boeke said.

But the jumping gene in question is found only in primates. Ideally, if you wanted to study the disease in lab mice, you'd have to insert that jumping gene into their DNA — and that's exactly what the researchers did in the first of their two new studies.

Using SwAP-In, the team inserted 78,000 "letters" of human DNA code into mouse embryonic stem cells. This code included part of the human version of the TAF1 gene and the relevant jumping gene that causes XDP. In both lab dishes and living mice, this gene insertion triggered the telltale signs of XDP: low levels of the TAF1 protein, cell death and holes in the brain, especially in the striatum.

One big difference between mice and humans is that the mouse version of XDP progresses very quickly, with symptoms appearing in just 1.5 months, whereas the human disease takes years to show up. That may be because human bodies have safeguards to help offset the jumping gene's effects — at least for a while — while mice lack this safety net, the study authors theorized.

That difference in disease progression is actually a "huge advantage" for researchers, Boeke noted. "Because it's so sped up, it's possible to do experiments on therapeutics," he said. For instance, if an experimental drug is successfully fighting the disease, that should be obvious in the mice, whose condition would otherwise progress very quickly.

I think that is, one, interesting from a biological standpoint, but two, profoundly important for how you might develop therapies to help these patients.

In the second of the team's new studies, they took a closer look at the new mice with XDP, to see how the disorder affected their brain cells. Through a battery of tests, they realized that glial cells known as oligodendrocytes showed dramatic changes in both their overall numbers and their gene activity.

These cells would normally make a fatty insulating material called myelin, which wraps around the outgoing wires of neurons to help them send signals. To see how the cells were faring in the XDP mice, study co-author Priya Prakash, a postdoctoral scholar in Liddelow's lab, used a blue stain to label the cells within the mouse brain tissue.

"Where you would normally see this beautiful blue brain, full of lipid, full of myelin, you essentially see a white brain, with none of this lipid there," Liddelow said. This was especially apparent in the striatum and the prefrontal cortex.

Further experiments revealed that the mutation was preventing oligodendrocytes from fully maturing, and that reduced the amount of myelin made in these parts of the brain. They backed up these findings in brains of people with XDP that had been donated after death.

The researchers think this extensive loss of insulation may leave neurons vulnerable to dying early, Liddelow said. In short, "this is a neurodegenerative disease that may not first be manifesting in neurons themselves," he emphasized. "I think that is, one, interesting from a biological standpoint, but two, profoundly important for how you might develop therapies to help these patients."

Together, the studies raise several ideas for treating XDP. One treatment could involve cranking up the activity of the TAF1 gene to boost the levels of its related protein. This idea showed promise in experiments with mouse cells in the team's first paper. The second paper points to oligodendrocytes as potential targets for future therapies, and myelin loss as a potential early sign of the disease that might be useful for diagnosis.

There's still much more to learn about the biology of XDP and what types of treatments might reverse the drivers of the disease, Liddelow and Boeke emphasized. But now, other scientists have access to a brand-new mouse model that can help them solve the disease's remaining mysteries.

Don’t show up empty-handed or with a cheap bottle of wine — bring status cocktail cherries, a beeswax candle, or a painterly placemat

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

A good host is always thinking of others, whether it’s by making guests feel welcome, accommodating everyone’s diets, or setting an Instagram-worthy tablescape to make the night feel extra special. But the holiday season is an opportunity to flip the script and show the host you’re thinking of them, too. Bringing them a gift is the cardinal way to thank the host for all their thoughtful work. The only question remains: what to give?

For those who delight in trotting out their special dinnerware for guests, there’s a world of creative and whimsical gifts out there, even if it seems like they already have the entire CB2 catalog. And if that is the case, this just means you, as the gift-giver, can allow them to indulge in the things they typically would not. Take, for instance, some unique vintage shot glasses, intricately carved chopsticks, and pearl cocktail picks. Not only do these playful takes on essentials inspire joy, but they’re also sure to be conversation starters for future gatherings. And, as the bestower of the new treasured piece, you just might secure yourself the invite for the next one.

You can never have enough serving utensils if you love to host. That moment when you toss your pasta salad, plate everyone’s green beans, or dole out your main dish is an opportunity to flex some of your more decorative yet functional kitchen tools. This ethereal stainless steel set from Leif boasts pewter star-shaped handles with sea glass.

Even Diaspora Spice Co.’s everyday spices come in bold, ready-to-gift packaging, but the equitable spice company’s new holiday spice sampler gift box is an extra colorful treat for the senses. The bundle includes samples of its beloved Nandini coriander, a rare Ceylon cinnamon, a Himalayan foothills-sourced pink garlic powder, and several more spices to inspire your host.

When it comes to gift-giving, we believe in working smarter, not harder. Case in point: Buy a set of nice-looking vintage glasses — these are labeled shot glasses by the seller, but they’re just as nice for sipping cordials — and rather than giving one lovely host a set of eight, split them up into pairs or fours and use them for multiple gifting situations. There’s always a use for little glasses like this (and they’re pretty enough to display, too).

It’s pretty fun to use a posh plaid napkin when you’re digging into some quiche or sipping on mulled wine.

It’s always fun to kick off an evening of cocktails with a caviar bump, which is what makes this Imperia Caviar bundle such a gift for the avid party host. The 30-gram tin of royal ossetra comes with a mother-of-pearl spoon and a caviar tin opener in a velvet bag, and the bundle’s compact size means you can simply slide it into your purse or jacket on the way to the function (unlike a heavy bottle of wine or olive oil, which would likely need their owns bags).

It really has been the year of the dirty martini. For those who are building a bar cart (or want to start), getting a couple of sets of proper cocktail picks can be a game-changer. Nothing wrong with a traditional wood toothpick, of course, but it really does add a lot of pizzazz to a martini to bite the olives off a pearl-emblazoned skewer.

Swooning will abound once people get a look at these beautiful walnut chopsticks featuring inlaid geometric designs. Another great example of “practical, but nicer to look at than what you might get for yourself.” Plus, you can grab a set of five on sale right now for under $20.

When it comes to cocktail cherries, one brand truly reigns supreme: Luxardo, which has been making candied cherries soaked in marasca syrup for 120 years. A classic for a reason!

Jonathan Adler is another designer to keep tabs on when it comes to playful but elevated home decor. This set of Matisse-esque coasters also has a slight lip to keep condensation from spilling, and would be prime for serving up lychee martinis the next time you gather with friends. Snag them while they’re 40% off for Black Friday.

Halen Môn is a salt nerd’s dream. The organic, hand-harvested sea salt hails from the tides of the Isle of Anglesey in Wales (Halen is Welsh for salt; Môn is Welsh for Anglesey), and has earned numerous awards for its subtle crunch and crisp mineral flavor. Any host would be thrilled to receive a bag of the stuff, but this gift set combines the salt with a charming ceramic cellar and spoon.

Matches are always a solid host gift, and a small but useful present that’s made all the better with cool packaging. The lifestyle brand State the Label, for example, has housed its matches in a folk art-inspired cottage (the striker paper is on the bottom of the house).

Those who like to entertain likely appreciate a good placemat. This set of two block-printed placemats from West Elm puts a romantic spin on the dining-table staple with painterly tones and bright hues. Who wouldn’t love to receive these dreamy accents?

Is your host a lover of ice-cold martinis? Perfect gift incoming: Quincy’s fabulous olives, which have superb flavor and are ratioed with drink-perfect brine to make exactly 14 dirty martinis per jar.

Scents are tricky. Unless you really know your host, refrain from gifting them scented candles, and opt for a beeswax pillar candle instead; they can light it sans candelabra (unless you’re sure that they own one and prefer tapers) by simply placing it on a small plate. Above all, beeswax candles make a wonderful dining companion, because they don’t emit the same stuffy, paraffin wax-based smoke as non-beeswax candles.

Sometimes, brevity is wit. Give it to someone who means business, or orders the business women special.

We all love a little Le Creuset in our kitchens, but a Dutch oven isn’t in the price range for what we’d consider an easy host gift. Enter the butter dish, a fabulous little thing to present and say “I brought you something,” presented with a kiss on the cheek and maybe a bouquet of flowers or bottle of wine.

#6477. Scientists Successfully Grow Potatoes in Simulated Moon Soil

Successful potato harvests in simulated lunar soil suggest that future astronauts could recycle their food scraps to help grow their next meal.

A future in which humans live on the Moon and grow their own food may be a little closer to reality thanks to one of Earth’s most familiar crops. Researchers at Oregon State University have successfully grown edible potatoes in simulated lunar soil, achieving growth and yields comparable to those produced on Earth by adding compost made with the help of earthworms.

The findings support NASA’s Artemis program, which aims to establish a sustained human presence on the Moon. Producing food locally would reduce dependence on costly resupply missions from Earth and help make long-term lunar exploration more sustainable. Potatoes are particularly appealing because they provide substantial nutritional value and produce more calories per unit of land than many other crops.

“We found that potatoes can complete their entire life cycle in simulated lunar soil when supplemented with organic matter,” said Aymeric Goyer of Oregon State University’s Department of Botany and Plant Pathology. “That’s an important step toward developing reliable food production systems that could support long-term human exploration of the Moon.”

One of the biggest agricultural challenges on the Moon lies directly beneath astronauts’ feet. Most of the lunar surface is covered in regolith, a layer of loose rock and dust containing very little organic matter.

In a study published in npj Microgravity, Goyer and his colleagues tested whether adding different amounts of vermicompost, a nutrient-rich material produced when earthworms break down organic matter, could make simulated lunar soil suitable for growing potatoes.

Because the composition of lunar regolith varies across the Moon, the team tested five simulants representing both the Moon’s darker plains, known as lunar maria, and its highland regions. For comparison, they included soil from Hermiston, Oregon, a region known for producing some of the highest potato yields in the world.

Potato plants grown in simulated lunar soil without compost were severely stunted and developed poorly formed roots. Adding between 5% and 15% vermicompost led to only partial recovery. However, plants grown with 30% vermicompost matched the growth and development of those cultivated in Earth soils.

Lunar regolith also contains elevated levels of heavy metals that can damage plant roots and interfere with growth.

“We believe the compost helps balance some of the toxicity we see in lunar regolith by reducing plant exposure to harmful compounds,” said David Handy, a postdoctoral researcher in Goyer’s lab.

The researchers suspect that organic matter binds to heavy metals, making them less available to plants and limiting their harmful effects.

Growing potatoes successfully would mean little if astronauts could not safely eat them. Encouragingly, potatoes produced in the lunar soil simulants maintained their nutritional quality and showed no statistically significant increase in glycoalkaloids, naturally occurring potato toxins often associated with green discoloration beneath the skin. The findings indicate that the potatoes were safe to eat under the conditions tested.

Future lunar explorers could potentially bring a small supply of organic matter from Earth and gradually produce more by recycling food scraps and plant waste. Such a system could turn everyday waste into valuable growing material while reducing the supplies astronauts would need to transport from Earth.

The research team is now investigating which potatoes might be best suited for lunar agriculture. A forthcoming paper will report results from experiments involving 10 potato varieties grown in simulated lunar soil.

Reference: “Growth and molecular responses of potato to lunar regolith simulants” by David Handy, Anika Loeffler, Medora Knudson, Sydney Campbell, Pankaj Jaiswal, Jeffrey C. Anderson and Aymeric Goyer, 19 November 2026, npj Microgravity. DOI: 10.1038/s41526-026-00668-z

#6475. Three Ancient Cosmic Collisions May Explain Why the Moon Has Two Faces

Scientists have narrowed down when three massive collisions reshaped the Moon, bringing them closer to understanding why its Earth-facing side looks so different from its far side.

Billions of years ago, a collision powerful enough to melt enormous quantities of lunar rock created the Moon’s largest impact basin. Subsequent collisions broke apart and scattered some of that ancient material across the surface, leaving behind a geological record that scientists are now piecing together.

Located on the Moon’s far side, the South Pole-Aitken (SPA) basin is one of the oldest and largest impact structures in the solar system. Understanding its history could help explain why the Moon’s near and far sides are so different, what lies beneath its surface, and when major collisions occurred during its early evolution.

An international research team led by Professor Guochun Zhao, Mok Sau-King, a professor in the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences (DEPS) at the University of Hong Kong (HKU), and Dr. Yuqi Qian, the study’s first author, has identified two types of magnesium-rich rocks with remarkably different origins. Published in Science Advances, the research also establishes a clearer timeline of the major impacts that shaped the region.

For decades, the basin remained largely unexplored. That changed in 2019, when Chang’e-4 completed the first successful landing on the Moon’s far side, followed in 2024 by Chang’e-6, which brought the first rock samples from this largely unexplored region back to Earth.

Using Chang’e-6 samples allocated to HKU DEPS and surface measurements from both missions, the researchers obtained the first direct geological evidence from the two landing sites for reconstructing the basin’s impact history. Satellite observations and numerical simulations helped them trace the origins of rocks across the wider basin.

One group of rocks, known as moderately magnesium-rich norites, formed in the aftermath of the original SPA collision. The impact generated a thick sheet of molten rock that gradually cooled, with different minerals crystallizing at different stages. Later collisions exposed these ancient rocks at the central peaks of large craters. Some were eventually blasted toward the Chang’e-4 landing site in Von Kármán crater by the impact that formed Finsen crater.

The second group contained considerably more magnesium and likely formed through a separate process called magnesium-suite magmatism, a type of magma activity associated with the original SPA impact. These rocks were exposed along the western ring of mountain peaks within the Apollo basin before the Chaffee S impact scattered some of them toward the Chang’e-6 landing site.

Earlier research by the HKU-led team had already uncovered evidence of prolonged volcanic activity and previously unrecognized magma activity in the region. Those studies also suggested that underground accumulations of titanium-rich minerals, known as ilmenite-bearing cumulates, helped account for the contrasting volcanic histories of the Moon’s two sides.

The latest findings suggest that the South Pole-Aitken basin formed approximately 4.34 billion years ago. Another major collision created the Apollo basin around 4.2 billion years ago, followed by the formation of the Orientale basin approximately 3.87 billion years ago. Together, these three events reveal how successive collisions reshaped the Moon’s largest impact basin over hundreds of millions of years.

Reference: “Postimpact evolution of the South Pole–Aitken basin revealed by Chang’e-4 and Chang’e-6” by Yuqi Qian, Wenlei Song, James Head, Mingyu Tian, Zhuang Guo, Harald Hiesinger, Carolyn H. van der Bogert, Le Zhang, Jingyou Chen, Wanfeng Zhang, Ziqing Li, Lingzhi Sun, Xiangsong Wang, Wei-Ran Li, Jiacheng Liu, Nicolas Dauphas, Yi-Gang Xu and Guochun Zhao, 18 November 2026, Science Advances. DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aeh9798

#6474. Comet Encke's Shape and Heat Revealed in Thermal Glow

Comets are time capsules of the origins of the solar system, containing materials that have existed for billions of years. While comets primarily orbit in the farthest reaches of the solar system, specifically the Kuiper Belt or Oort Cloud, some make their way closer to the Sun. When this happens, the increased heat cause cometary icy material to evaporate, producing a spectacular tail while also revealing the rocky material underneath, known as a cometâs nucleus. But how well can astronomers use telescopic observations to study the composition and temperatures of a cometary nucleus?

Now, a team of researchers from Japan might be one step closer to scientists better understanding comets, specifically a cometâs nucleus. Through findings recently published in The Astronomical Journal, the researchers presented new analyses regarding the shape and temperature of a comateâs nucleus, providing researchers with key observations that could be used to understand both the formation and evolution of comets and the solar system.

For the study, the researchers analyzed archival data on Comet 2P/Encke originally obtained from the Cooled Mid-Infrared Camera and Spectrometer (COMICS) on the Subaru Telescope in November 2003. During this time, Comet 2P/Encke traveled as close as 0.26 astronomical units (AU) from Earth, or about 37 million kilometers (26 million miles), enabling several ground-based telescopes, including the Subaru Telescope, to conduct mid-infrared observations of Comet 2P/Encke. This distance from Earth also put Comet 2P/Encke about 1.09 AU from the Sun, or about 163 million kilometers (101 million miles). Unfortunately, COMICS was retired from Subaru in 2020, leaving Subaru without a mid-infrared instrument, thus limiting its studies to archival data.

The primary goal of the study was to ascertain the composition of Comet 2P/Enckeâs nucleus while isolating its signal from the surrounding ice, gas, and dust that envelopes the comet and becomes larger and denser as the increased Sunâs heat evaporates it. In the end, the researchers found the nucleus of Comet 2P/Encke measured about 7 kilometers by 3 kilometers (4.3 miles by 1.9 miles) while its surface temperature is estimated to be about 328 Kelvin (55 degrees Celsius/131 degrees Fahrenheit).

"Our study of Comet Encke showed that mid-infrared observations can directly capture thermal emission from the nucleus itself," said Dr. Takafumi Ootsubo, who is assistant professor in the Department of Basic Sciences at the School of Medicine at the University of Occupational and Environmental Health in Japan, and lead author of the study. Despite COMICS retiring in 2020, Dr. Ootsubo is actively working to restart the program. "By restarting COMICS, we hope to study the shapes, temperatures, and surface materials of many more cometary nuclei in detail and get closer to revealing their true faces."

As noted, comets originate from the far reaches of the solar system, specifically the Kuiper Belt and Oort Cloud, with Comet 2P/Encke originating from the former. However, some comets periodically migrate inward and become whatâs known as a Jupiter-family comet, which is what happened to Comet 2P/Encke. This means Comet 2P/Enckeâs orbit has been both captured and reshaped by Jupiterâs massive gravity, resulting in its orbit becoming significantly shorter than traditional comets at only 3.3 years. This is in stark contrast to traditional comets, which can take anywhere from decades to millions of years to travel from the outer solar system to the inner solar system and potentially be observed from Earth.

While its orbit is only 3.3 years, this doesnât mean it encounters Earth every 3.3 years. Instead, Comet 2P/Enckeâs orbit is constantly reshaping, meaning it has only had a limited few encounters with Earth in the last few decades. Along with the November 2003 encounter, Comet 2P/Encke came within only about 0.19 AU (28.5 million kilometers/17.7 million miles) from Earth in July 1997 and is slated to come within 0.62 AU (93 million kilometers/58 million miles) from Earth in February 2027.

What new insights into Comet Encke and other comets in our solar system will researchers make in the coming years and decades? Only time will tell, and this is why we science!

As always, keep doing science & keep looking up!

Live Science spoke with marine biologist Annie Mercier about her role as a science adviser for Netflix's show "Below."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In Netflix's new series "Below," an ancient, squid-like creature known as "Mudder" threatens a small coastal community in Newfoundland, Canada, arriving around the same time as a mysterious iceberg that starts causing dangerous hallucinations in the town's residents.

The series blends marine science, horror and environmental themes, harking back to Newfoundland's long-standing connections with giant squid (Architeuthis dux), with the first sightings going back to the 1870s.

Annie Mercier, a marine biologist in the Department of Ocean Sciences at Memorial University in Newfoundland and Labrador, was brought on as a science adviser in 2025 just before Netflix began shooting "Below." Mercier's research focuses on deep sea organisms, studying their behavior, interactions and how they respond to environmental stressors like climate change.

Mercier's lab at the Ocean Sciences Center was used as a filming location, and she met with actor Mackenzie Davis, who plays the research scientist Dr. Fonda Howander, to guide the character. Live Science spoke with Mercier about how she helped bring Mudder — and the scientific endeavour to unravel its mystery — to life.

Annie Mercier is a professor in the Department of Ocean Sciences at Memorial University inNewfoundland and Labrador, Canada. She studies marine animals and their response to environmental conditions, conducting research on the behaviors and interactions of diverse invertebrate species from Arctic and deep-sea environments.

Kenna Hughes-Castleberry: How did you end up getting involved with "Below" as a scientific adviser?

Annie Mercier: Early in 2025, when they were just about to start filming or were finalizing the scripts, I heard that Jesse Mckeown [the director] was looking for a scientific adviser, preferably someone here in Newfoundland. We heard about it through Memorial University's communications team. They mentioned that there would be something about an ancient cephalopod in the series.

I'm not an expert in cephalopods … But I do have a broad background in marine biology, and I'm here at the Ocean Sciences Centre. I sent back my reply, and they eventually contacted me to ask more about what I was doing and what I'd worked on in the past. My research is centered around strange creatures and trying to understand them through curiosity-driven research, so I guess that resonated with them.

Another factor was that I'd previously worked as a consultant on documentaries and television series. I'd done a little work with the BBC, helping explain video sequences, as well as fiction series back in Quebec. I also write popular articles and books for general audiences, so I'm familiar with navigating between science and fiction and with trying to convey something wonderful about science in language that general audiences can understand. I guess that played a role as well, and they eventually asked me to be the adviser.

A view of the Ocean Sciences Center where Mercier works.

KHC: What did the advising process look like?

This article is part of a series called "Science Behind the Camera," which focuses on the role of science advisers in popular science and films . From helping to create engaging stories to designing sets and advising on scripts, these experts shape some of the most compelling narratives on screen.

AM: There were two phases. The main thing was that they wanted to share the scripts early on. That's when I was brought in.

Jesse told me they would send scripts at regular intervals, in sequence, starting with the first episode, then the second, and so forth. They would securely send me each script. We had some preliminary discussions to establish exactly what they wanted, because that was my question: How much detail or what kind of feedback were they looking for?

They told me that whatever came to mind, I should suggest it. Of course, I knew they couldn't take everything into account, but I think they wanted to know how far-fetched or how close to reality some of the things were. They asked me to focus mostly on the scientific aspects.

That included the squid, but also how they portrayed the scientific work and the character involved in it. They had climate change, icebergs, ocean currents and a number of other scientific elements in the story.

I went through every script and provided feedback on all sorts of things. Sometimes it was something as simple as the timing of an event. I pointed out things related to the migrations of marine animals and other details that I knew were a little different from reality.

I provided written feedback and sometimes links to additional information. I'd send it back, and occasionally there would be a follow-up meeting or a remote conversation about certain elements. It depended on the situation.

When they started filming, Jesse wanted to schedule a time for me to go behind the scenes and chat with the crew. It was difficult to coordinate because they were filming on three or more sets around Newfoundland, and I was working. Eventually, I managed to visit on a Saturday when they were filming at the Ocean Sciences Centre. I spent some time in the control room, met Mackenzie [Davis] and got to see what they were doing on-site.

Of course, when you're asked about giant squids and you know it's a fictional show, all sorts of things come to mind.

KHC: How much feedback did you end up giving on Mudder, the giant, squid-like creature? What aspects did you think were accurate, and where did the show take creative liberties?

AM: Of course, when you're asked about giant squids and you know it's a fictional show, all sorts of things come to mind. I was hoping they wouldn't go the route of having the arms come out and a giant squid jump onto a boat, or something like "20,000 Leagues Under the Sea." You see those kinds of things in some of the drawings from the 1800s, too. So I had some fears about that.

But when I read the scripts, I could see they were trying to make it as close to reality as possible. Obviously, they had some freedom because it's portrayed as an ancient, social type of cephalopod — more like a squid but with some octopus-like behaviors as well.

I focused my feedback on biology. For example, the eye was very large. It's well known that existing giant squids have one of the biggest, if not the biggest, eyes in the animal kingdom. So that was definitely something that made sense.

A drawing of a giant squid from the Connecticut Academy of Sciences dating to between 1879 and 1881. The drawing shows the large eye of the giant squid.

I also cautioned them about how giant squids move. Sometimes, in movies, you see their arms portrayed as very muscular, reaching far out of the water. These are mollusks [cephalopods belong to the phylum Mollusca], and in the water, they have quite a bit of strength. But outside the water, they don't have bones that attach muscles to support that kind of movement. It's a very different type of movement.

I drew their attention to the very few cephalopods that actually go out of the water. There's an octopus you can see on certain reefs, and I sent them some images of it. I explained that its movement is very fluid, the way it's able to advance across reefs outside the water.

I also mentioned the kinds of scars they could leave when interacting with sperm whales, for example.

I was quite happy to see that they kept the creature rather mysterious instead of trying to show too much. I was worried it might look completely funny, but I thought they made good use of keeping the mystery alive for a long time.

I also explained that cephalopods in the ocean have no way of detecting prey on the shore. They can't see it or sense it. So if you're going in that direction, you need to be a little careful. Obviously, that's where we're getting into fiction.

But I think they handled it pretty well. An audience expects some fearsome interactions, and if you don't include those at all, you'll disappoint people. Overall, I thought it was pretty good.

There's a lot of lore surrounding giant squids in Newfoundland. They definitely go together ‪—‬ not just in fiction but also because there have been remains, sightings and other encounters. I think this physical place played a role in the inspiration for the show's topic.

KHC: Did you advise on the hallucinogenic properties of the creature's mucus?

AM: No, we didn't specifically exchange information about that. A lot of marine animals have toxins. That's well known, and it's not just cephalopods; all sorts of marine animals have them. Now, how something like that could become airborne, or how it could be associated with melting icebergs and then ingested through the ice, is definitely fictional.

I'm aware of toxic substances, but I'm not aware of any that produce hallucinations, per se. And again, I'm no expert in that area.

KHC: Overall, do you think the series did a good job portraying science? Was there anything you would have changed?

AM: As I said, I had some fears at first. One downside of being an adviser was that I knew everything about the show before watching it, which was a first for me. It was a little different because I would watch and think, "Oh, OK; they did that. They adjusted this. Oh, they went all out with this one."

I discovered what they had taken into consideration and what they had discarded. It was fun to watch, and I think they did a pretty good job overall.

I always think about this when I watch series about different professions. When you see lawyers or police officers portrayed, I imagine they're probably laughing about how simple things seem. Maybe everything is compressed in time, or maybe it's not quite how it happens in reality. This time, it was my turn to see how they would portray my profession.

Mackenzie Davis, as Dr. Fonda Howander, conveys much of the science around giant squids in "Below."

I think they avoided some of the common clichés. In movies and television, when you go into a laboratory, you often see colorful tubes and bubbling Erlenmeyer flasks just to tell you that you're in a lab. The fact that they filmed here at the Ocean Sciences Centre, in real laboratories, contributed to the sense of reality. Our labs are eclectic. You have nets, tanks, microscopes and all sorts of things around. They're not perfectly ordered, and I think that helped.

I also appreciated that they were careful about how they portrayed scientists. When you're a marine scientist, you're a marine scientist. You're not all-knowing about everything in science. Sometimes shows portray scientists as knowing everything about everything.

For example, when it came to the substance in the show and its effects on health, I explained that a marine scientist might know how to make a diagnosis about something, but that doesn't mean they can necessarily provide a medical assessment. I think the character even says, "I'm not a medical doctor."

I also thought they did a good job portraying scientific uncertainty. In science, you follow lines of inquiry, but you're not necessarily sure what the answer is. You need confirmation and further investigation.

They also did what they could with the squid to make it fearsome but also lovable, without going too far from what a squid might actually do. And when they took creative liberties, they kept things mysterious enough that everything wasn't spelled out exactly.

I also thought they did a great job portraying Newfoundland. They captured the landscapes, the environments and the spirit of the people. The atmosphere was really well done. I think they aimed to make Newfoundland almost a character in the series, and they did that quite well.

Altogether, I thought the Ocean Sciences Centre and the labs were portrayed very nicely. Some of the students here were around during filming in 2025, and they've had showings of the episodes at the university. It's nice for them to see the labs where they work every day portrayed on screen.

Josh Harnett's character Calvin Penney relies on Mackenzie Davis's character Dr. Fonda Howander to learn more about the science of giant squids.

KHC: Beyond the creature itself, were there other scientific details in the scripts that you helped the writers get right?

AM: Yes. I provided feedback on a lot of smaller issues, including the use of scientific tools and how different analyses work.

For example, they were trying to date a block of ice. The process was a little different in the original script, and I explained that these analyses take time. You don't just do something in a lab and immediately get an answer. You sometimes have to collaborate with other people to establish things.

I also cautioned against making one microscope tell you everything about something you're looking at. A microscope is there to provide good magnification. It doesn't give you chemical signatures or anything like that. So I tried to caution them against making one instrument do more than it actually does in reality.

I thought they treated the laboratory work quite well overall. One thing they kept ‪—‬ and I can't blame them for it ‪—‬ was the very nice, almost magical tool they use to check the quality of icebergs. You just stick it into the iceberg, get a reading, and it tells you whether it's a good-quality iceberg.

Obviously, when I saw that, I thought it would be nice if it worked that way! But when you want to know the quality of ice or water, there are a number of different analyses you need to do, and you need to know what you're looking for.

In movies and television, it's often the case that you put something into a machine and it spits out exactly what you want to know. But in real science, you have to ask the right question. You have to know what you're looking for so the instrument can tell you whether something has a particular property or not.

I understood that they sometimes needed to take creative liberties to move the plot along. There were a number of comments I made about basic science and what was or wasn't realistic.

One feature of the Ocean Sciences Centre that they took into the fictional realm was the basement, where you go through a door and there's an ocean or water behind it. Obviously, don't look for that here! That's just about the only thing that isn't real. The rest is pretty close to reality.

Editor's note: This interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.

#6471. Experimental Drug Shrinks Tumors in Two of the Hardest-To-Treat Cancers

A single experimental drug designed to block signals from several cancer-driving mutations has shown encouraging early results, raising the possibility of treating multiple hard-to-treat cancers.

When pancreatic or lung cancer continues to grow despite several treatments, doctors can find themselves with few remaining options. In some patients, the difficulty lies in genetic mutations that keep cancer cells growing and have historically been difficult to target with drugs. An experimental cancer drug called ERAS-0015 has shown promising results in an early clinical trial, shrinking tumors in patients who had already undergone other forms of treatment.

The drug targets RAS, a family of genes that provide instructions for making proteins involved in controlling cell growth and division. In healthy cells, RAS proteins act like molecular switches, turning on when cells receive signals to grow and turning off when those signals are no longer needed. Certain genetic mutations can leave these switches stuck in the “on” position, continuously instructing cells to grow and helping sustain cancer.

For years, scientists struggled to develop drugs capable of interfering with these faulty proteins. ERAS-0015 takes an approach known as a pan-RAS molecular glue. It works by bringing proteins together at the molecular level and is designed to bind to RAS while the switch is active, blocking growth signals associated with several different cancer-driving RAS mutations.

“The overall goal of precision oncology is to match a patient’s mutation, or the ‘Achilles Heel’ of a specific individual’s cancer, to a drug that directly targets that mutation. This is what we are attempting to do by studying the effectiveness of ERAS-0015 in patients with RAS alterations,” said Dr. Judy Wang, a medical oncologist at Florida Cancer Specialists and Research Institute in Sarasota, Florida.

Wang presented findings from 148 patients participating in the phase I AURORAS-1 clinical trial on November 19, 2026, at the 38th EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium on Molecular Targets and Cancer Therapeutics in Barcelona, Spain.

The trial began in June 2025 and is evaluating ERAS-0015 both alone and in combination with other anticancer therapies. Participants include people with pancreatic cancer, colorectal (bowel) cancer, non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) that has spread beyond the original tumor site, and other solid tumors driven by RAS mutations. The results presented at the symposium included 83 patients with pancreatic cancer and 37 with NSCLC. The trial is continuing to enroll patients.

“AURORAS-1 has enrolled patients that have tried a number of other treatments for their cancer. In this context, ERAS-0015 treatment caused a 44% response rate in patients with RAS-mutant pancreatic cancer and a 60% response rate in patients with RAS-mutant lung cancer. A ‘response’ means the patients experienced considerable tumor shrinkage, and these response rates are important as they show clinically meaningful activity from ERAS-0015 treatment in patient groups that have few if any therapeutic options to address their cancer. In addition to this, ERAS-0015 was well tolerated with few severe side effects,” Wang told the symposium.

These response rates came from relatively small groups of patients receiving a 32 mg dose of the drug. Tumors shrank in 11 of 25 patients with pancreatic cancer who had previously received chemotherapy and in three of five patients with lung cancer who had previously been treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors, drugs that help the immune system recognize and attack cancer, or platinum-based chemotherapy.

Researchers gradually increased doses of ERAS-0015 from 2 mg to 40 mg to evaluate how well patients tolerated the drug. After a median follow-up of just over four months, there was no indication that the maximum tolerated dose had been reached.

At doses of 16 to 32 mg, the most common side effects, affecting at least 10% of patients, were rash, diarrhea, nausea, and inflammation of the lining of the mouth. Twelve patients (9.8%) experienced severe treatment-related side effects, classified as grade 3 or higher. No dose-limiting side effects were reported.

“We are encouraged by the preliminary clinical activity and tolerability of ERAS-0015 in patients that have tried a number of other treatments for RAS-driven lung and pancreatic cancer,” said Wang.

“Our goal is to give clinicians new, better options for treating their patients with RAS-driven cancers. Early results suggest ERAS-0015 has the potential to be one of these options.”

Phase I clinical trials involve relatively small numbers of patients and are primarily designed to evaluate safety and determine appropriate doses. Although the tumor shrinkage observed in this trial provides an early indication of the drug’s potential, larger phase II and phase III clinical trials will be necessary to confirm its safety and effectiveness.

“If these early results are confirmed, ERAS-0015 could offer patients with RAS-driven cancers a new option. Clinical development of ERAS-0015 would be impossible without the patients, caregivers, investigators and participating trial centers that put their trust in us to take part in our study. We are deeply grateful for their contribution to AURORAS-1,” Wang concluded.

Professor Elena Garralda, chair of the EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium and co-director of the Vall d’Hebron Institute of Oncology’s clinical research program, was not involved in the study. She commented: “This is the first presentation of these preliminary results from the AURORAS-1 clinical trial and they have been eagerly awaited. They show that the RAS inhibitor, ERAS-0015, has encouraging anti-tumor activity in cancers that are hard to treat successfully and for which there are few treatment options available. We look forward to further results from larger clinical trials, which are investigating whether ERAS-0015 can help a broader group of patients.

“This is one of several studies being presented at the EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium that are beginning to show it is possible to design drugs that target cancers driven by RAS mutations, which was not thought possible until recently.”

#6470. A New Discovery is Re-Drawing the Map of the Milky Way

Star formation is a galaxy's foundational process. Astronomers study how star-forming gas moves around in a galaxy, where it's compressed, and in which parts of a galaxy stars form. In a barred spiral galaxy like the Milky Way, star formation is mostly concentrated in the spiral arms. In the central bar, star formation is more sluggish.

Recent research shows that though the central bar contains many stars, star formation there is mostly concentrated in the bar ends. Shear forces, streaming motions, and overpowering shocks that make the gas in the bars turbulent all combine to to inhibit star formation.

The Milky Way is a typical barred spiral galaxy, and astronomers have studied it intently to understand where star formation is concentrated. There's ongoing scientific debate about what happens in a barred spiral galaxy's central bar. Observations of other spiral barred galaxies show that star formation suppression there isn't necessarily universal. Part of the difficulty in understanding our own galaxy is observing the region. Since we're embedded in the galaxy, it's difficult to observe the bar. In many ways, astronomers have an easier time observing other galaxies.

Researchers from Australia and Sweden have found an unusual structure in the Milky Way's center that appears to set it apart from many other barred spiral galaxies. It's a vast collection of rotating stars in the central bar that's generating powerful and large shock fronts in the gas. These shock fronts are triggering star formation in the structure, which goes against the idea that stars can't form there.

The results are in new research titled "The nature of the Norma arm as a bar-driven star-forming shock front," and it's published in Nature Astronomy. The lead author is Dr. Hilary Davis from the University of Sydneyâs School of Physics and Sydney Institute for Astronomy. The research is casting doubt on the existence of one of the Milky Way's spiral arms, the Norma arm.

This illustration shows the Milky Way's major and minor spiral arms, as well as its central bar. The Norma arm is close to the galaxy's center. Image Credit: NASA.

"The Milky Way is commonly depicted as having four main spiral arms, including the Normaâouter arm, and a central stellar bar whose properties remain debated," the authors write. In past work, researchers have used astrophysical masers, which are coherent microwave emissions from young massive stars, to trace part of the Norma arm that extends from the central bar. So those results suggest that the masers reside along the Norma spiral arm.

But the Milky Way's bar is tricky to study. âThe Galactic bar cannot be easily observed because of a combination of our position in the Galaxy and dust obscuring our view,â Dr Davis said. âAs a result, the barâs properties have been highly debated.â

This new research, based on observations and massive astrophysical simulations suggests that what those masers really trace is the shock front or dust lane in its bar. Since stars form along shock fronts where gas is compressed, star formation is at the heart of this work. "This implies that the bar dust lane is star-forming, shedding new light on our understanding of star formation processes in the Milky Way," the authors explain.

This graphic shows modelling of the Milky Way with the Norma arm overlapping the bar shock front in the Milky Way. It's based on observations of masers from young stars. Previous research suggested those masers and young stars were in the Norma arm, but this work shows they're tracing star formation along a shock front in the Milky Way's central bar. Image Credit: Hillary Davis/University of Sydney

âAt its heart, star formation is a process we understand from everyday physics. Forces set matter in motion. In this case gas is compressed, and that compression can create the conditions for new stars to be born on a massive scale,â lead author Davis said.

Modern telescopes give us clear views of other galaxies on a regular basis. Observations of other spiral galaxies show that star formation is abundant in their spiral arms, where gas is compressed by density waves.

âIn most similar galaxies, star formation very commonly occurs along spiral arms. Whatâs extraordinary is seeing this happen in a different region of our Galaxy, where shocks are usually so strong that star formation is often suppressed,â said Davis.

The researchers used large-scale astrophysical models run on powerful computers to try to understand the masers and what they meant for star formation, and what part of the Milky Way's structure they traced. They found that the masers indicated star formation along a shock front in the bar, not in the Norma arm. Observational challenges made it seem like those masers were in the Norma arm.

âWe believe that the Milky Wayâs bar has star formation occurring along its shock front, which is uncommon for most bars in nearby galaxies,â Dr Davis said.

This figure from the research shows how what appears to be a spiral arm with star formation is actually the shock front from the central bar where stars are forming. "The red scatter points with black borders are the Norma masers," the authors write, but they actually line up with the shock front and may not be a spiral bar at all. Image Credit: Davis, H., Bland-Hawthorn, J., Tepper-GarcÃ­a, T. et al. The nature of the Norma arm as a bar-driven star-forming shock front. Nat Astron (2026).

"The Norma masers trace very young (âª1âMyr) star-forming regions that are still close to the gas clouds in which they formed because they have not had sufficient time to migrate away. Hence, the association of Norma masers with the Galactic bar shock front suggests that SF is occurring along the Galactic bar dust lane," the authors explain.

The result is that part of the Norma arm may have lost its status as a spiral arm.

âWe found that masers previously associated with the Norma arm closely align with the shock front predicted by our simulations,â Dr Davis said. âThis suggests that at least part of the so-called Norma arm may not be a spiral arm at all, but a region of star formation along the leading edge of the Galactic bar."

These results show that stars can more readily form in the central bar, something that seemed prohibitive. âThis raises questions about the Galaxyâs spiral structure, and the bar region of the Milky Way, which needs further investigation,â she said.

Astronomers have studied the Milky Way's central bar and argued about its nature for decades. There's been plenty of uncertainty about its properties and its role in star formation, and these results are shaping our understanding of the bar. âOur findings place further constraints on the size, angle and rotation speed of this central bar,â Dr Davis said.

"By associating the masers with the simulated shock front, we determine the parameters of the bar to be: a â 4.3 Â± 0.2 kpc, b â 2.3 Â± 0.2 kpc, Ï = 20(+5/-2)âand Î©p â² 40 km sâ1 kpcâ1, representing the semimajor and semiminor half-lengths of the bar, the inclination angle and the pattern speed, respectively," the authors write.

In plain language, they're saying that the bar's full, end-to-end length is about 28,000 light years, its width is about 15,000 light years, and it's tilted about 20 degrees from our line of sight. It also takes about 154 million years to complete one rotation.

For comparison, prior estimates of the bar's length range from 3,000 to 16,000 light years, and its width has been estimated between 8,000 and 16,000 light years. Measurements of its time to complete one rotation range from 102 to 246 million years. So these results are inside existing ranges.

The wide ranges for its size and rotation speed illustrate how difficult studying the bar is. The wide ranges may seem absurd, but astronomers have had limited observations to work with. Overall, these results add new constraints on the bar's properties, and they carry more weight based on how the researchers arrived at them.

âBy comparing a new generation of large-scale computerised galaxy simulations, evolving over billions of years, against a more limited set of observations, we now have a stronger understanding of the bar and star formation processes in the Milky Way,â Dr Davis said.

The main finding is that the bar has the ability to form stars, and that may mean the Milky Way is different from many other barred spirals.

"This raises questions about the Milky Wayâs spiral structure and suggests that the Galactic bar is long, slow and star-forming," the authors write.

#6468. Using Lunar Craters as Free Radiation Shields for Moon Base Nuclear Reactors

Powering any future lunar base is a massive engineering challenge. The two-week lunar night can drain batteries charged by solar panels during the two-week day, if the batteries themselves can even withstand the freezing temperatures that go along with it. So, for decades at this point, engineers have planned to use a nuclear reactor to at least partially power any future human settlement on the Moon. A new paper from researchers at Los Alamos, NASA Glenn, Oak Ridge, Idaho National Lab, and Lockheed Martin, and presented at the American Nuclear Societyâs Nuclear and Emerging Technologies for Space (NETS) conference back in April, offers a simple solution to one major problem for any such future nuclear reactor - shielding.

Currently, space-based nuclear power is advancing under a NASA program known as the Space Power and Reactor Capabilities (SPARC) program. One crucial constraint in this plan to build a 40-kilowatt nuclear reactor on the Moon is its weight limit. Any system has to be under 6,000 kg in order to fit on a mobile rover on the lunar surface.

Thatâs not a lot of weight to work with for a nuclear reactor, especially one of that size. And in addition to being one of the most important health and safety parts of a reactor, shielding is also one of the heaviest. To lower the weight of their systems, space reactor designers have historically relied on directional âshadow shields.â Instead of encompassing an entire reactor with an absorbent material like lead or concrete, they use lightweight hydrogen-rich materials like lithium hydride combined with dense metal positioned in a specific direction to protect highly sensitive parts of the reactor itself, such as the control electronics.

Fraser talks in detail about the Kilopower reactor.

Directional shields mean the rest of the area around the reactor is left unprotected, which isnât great if part of that area is zoned for human habitation. Even 1 km away from the reactor site, the amount of radiation if left unprotected would be deadly. But bringing up even more shielding from Earth to protect any such habitation zone is extraordinarily expensive.

To solve this problem, the research team, led by Los Alamos researcher Alex Levinsky, turned to a simple solution â use natural lunar terrainâlike a crater depression or a dirt hillâto block the direct line of sight, and thereby most of the radiation from reaching the habitation area. Since building a mockup lunar nuclear reactor and procuring hundreds of tons of lunar regolith presumably wasnât in the budget for this research, the team turned to computer simulations instead.

They used a software called Monte Carlo N-Particle to simulate millions of subatomic particles emanating from the nuclear reactor core. Placing it 1.5 m off the ground allowed them to simulate its positioning on the back of a wheeled rover. They then started modeling what different kinds of barricades would look like between the reactor and the habitation space.

Fraser talks about lunar base site selection and why it needs a fission reactor.

First, their simulations focused on arbitrary landscapes, such as a three-meter-deep crater or a gently sloping three-meter-high dirt hill. Both effectively blocked almost all of the radiation coming from the reactor, knocking it down to roughly one-tenth of a rem per yearâabout fifty times lower than the five-rem-per-year limit set for reactor radiation above the Moon's natural background.

With that success in mind, the next task was to model an actual environment. The research team chose Connecting Ridge, a mountain ridge near Shackleton Crater at the Lunar South Pole. This is an ideal site for future crewed missions, as it combines two of the most sought-after features of the lunar landscape. Some of the ridges are in almost permanent sunlight, being lit 80-90% of the time, while also being right next to Permanently Shadowed Regions that never see the Sun at all and are home to deposits of water ice that is crucial to life support and rocketry in any future permanent colony.

When placing the reactor in this environment, the research team made sure to respect the limitations of the rover (no slopes more than 18 degrees), but managed to find a natural depression that could be separated from a simulated base camp by a 120-m-high crater wall. With that barrier in place, the radiation hitting the habitat from the reactor dropped to near zeroâonly about four-hundredths of a rem per yearâallowing the reactor's onboard shadow shield to focus solely on protecting nearby electronics.

Fraser talks about finding water ice in the Moon's Permanently Shadowed Craters.

One nice feature about the airless Moon in this context is the engineers donât have to deal with âskyshineâ â a phenomenon where radiation shot into the sky bounces off air particles there and bounces back down onto the habitat. Since the Moon has no atmosphere, there is nothing for the radiation to bounce off of, solving one of the problems with reactors on Earth.

However, there is one major catch. While placing regolith between the reactor and the habitat protects the habitat itself, inside the crater or operational space of the reactor is a death zone. Astronauts would immediately develop radiation poisoning if entering the area while the reactor is in operation. And since regolith actually reflects neutrons pretty well, many of those neutrons are reflected directly into space, meaning no spacecraft or landers could fly directly over it.

So while we might be able to save thousands of kilograms of launch cost by building our own radiation shields on the Moon, we might also create a no-fly exclusion zone on one particular part of the Moon, just to ensure that astronauts have light and heat during the long, cold lunar nights. That is likely a tradeoff many space enthusiasts will be willing to make. And this study will bring the dream of reliable, continuous nuclear power on our nearest celestial neighbor one step closer to reality.
