#6467. What 8 Cool Food People Outsource for Thanksgiving

﻿Laila Gohar, Deb Perelman, and others share their top tips

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

A few Novembers ago, I had a mild crash out over puff pastry. I was planning to meet my partner’s extended family for the first time over Thanksgiving, and volunteered to bring a holiday staple a few weeks prior (in what was one of the most helpful, albeit intimidating Excel sign-up sheets I’ve ever seen). What could be easier than apple pie? The ingredients for the recipe I found weren’t fussy, and it hardly called for fancy technical skills. Plus, I could make it ahead of time knowing that it would travel well.

Then I remembered the puff pastry. For some reason, I attached a moral imperative to the idea of making the whole pie from scratch, and spent the next two weeks poring over puff pastry recipes that felt like casual guides to wizard-tier alchemy. I loved to cook, but I simply wasn’t a big baker. (I also didn’t own a food processor, unless you counted my Magic Bullet.) My mother eventually brought me down to Earth. “Just buy it,” she told me over the phone, undoubtedly rolling her eyes. “Everyone knows it’s a pain in the butt.” Even the Barefoot Contessa herself, she reminded me, famously avoids the time-consuming task (“Nobody wants to make puff pastry!”).

Those words set me free. Once I realized that I could outsource my puff pastry, and the source of my Thanksgiving stress, I was finally able to relax and enjoy the holiday. Folks take pride in their Turkey Day dishes, as they should, but there’s nothing wrong with accepting a little help.

In the hopes of encouraging you to lighten your load, my colleague Bettina Makalintal and I asked some of the coolest people we know in the food industry what they prefer to outsource for Thanksgiving, from smoked hams to appetizers, in order to keep their holiday stress-free.

“There is a single premade item that I purchase for Thanksgiving: a smallish in-house smoked ham from The Meat Hook. It’s a sort of whatever part of the Thursday meal — I make a banging turkey, which commands most of the attention. But! The ham has become a key player during what my family calls Leftover Sandwich Weekend. Having an extra piece of protein mitigates any concerns about not having enough turkey left over. More importantly, a thin slice or two adds a salty, fatty, sweet, and smoky layer to the sandwich architecture. Much needed, very appreciated. Ham: I can’t imagine a turkey sandwich without it.” — Carla Lalli, cookbook author of books including Food is a Feeling

“I outsource pies because I don’t especially enjoy making them… or eating them!”— Laila Gohar, food-based conceptual designer, artist, and co-founder of Gohar World

“I almost always outsource appetizers and/or a cheese plate. If I’m making the big stuff (turkey, stuffing, sides, desserts… okay, I’m also a control freak with more time to cook than most), I feel absolutely overwhelmed if I am also making small things. So while I have a couple really simple apps I’ll put out if there are no volunteers, I much prefer having a friend or family member bring their favorite wedge of cheese and crackers, or [crossing fingers] bacon-wrapped dates. Here is one of my simple go-tos (it’s also in my Smitten Kitchen Every Day cookbook): herb-and-garlic baked Camembert. I’d still prefer if someone else can prep it; I don’t mind heating it up.” — Deb Perelman, cookbook author and recipe developer behind Smitten Kitchen

“We outsource lumpia from Chuck’s mom. We love having them for the holiday but don’t like frying at home when we have everything else cooking that day. She always has a couple hundred in her freezer ready and waiting to be fried for special occasions.” — Hailee Catalano and Chuck Cruz, cookbook authors and recipe developers behind @2peoplecooking

“I usually get a roast duck from Hay Hay Roasted in Chinatown, because they’ve got it down. It’s consistently delicious and not everyone eats turkey in our family.” — Camari Mick, chef and founder of Calabash

“I always outsource the pre-dinner snacks to the grocery store. I have so much respect for people who can construct elaborate cheese boards or spend the morning filling puff pastries, but that’s just not me. I like to set out a few bowls with tamari almonds, Castelvetrano olives, and — this is the most important one — Nacho Cheese Doritos. They’re the perfect mix of salty, crunchy little snacks to have with a drink before dinner is ready. The Doritos always get cleaned out first, so keep a backup bowl waiting in the kitchen.” — Casey Elsass, columnist at Cup of Jo and author of What Can I Bring?

“Last year for Friendsgiving, we collectively decided to skip the hassle of making the turkey and instead ordered Popeyes’ Cajun-Style Turkey. It’s rubbed with a blend of Louisiana-style Cajun spices and comes fully cooked, so all you have to do is thaw, heat, and serve it. It really set the tone for a very unserious dinner, which I think is what you want at a Friendsgiving. We’ll be ordering it again this year.” — Anna Archibald and Kevin Serai, content creators and recipe developers behind Cabagges.World

“We’re fairly relaxed about Thanksgiving, but if we do end up making food on that day, I usually outsource pie dough! I’m happy to buy organic frozen pie dough because usually it tastes fine and it saves me a little bit of time. I realized I prefer to spend my energy on the other parts of the meal, and I prefer not to add on to my own mental load by also making pie dough. I know it’s quick and easy; I’d just rather not! But I do make my own fillings.” — Ifrah F. Ahmed, author of Soomaaliya

#6466. An Overlooked Metabolic Byproduct Could Help Repair a Damaged Heart

A substance often treated as waste may be vital to the heart during a crisis, offering a potential target for treating heart failure and heart attacks.

The heart has to keep beating whether the body has plenty of energy available or is running low. Maintaining that constant supply of energy is a complicated process, and when it breaks down, it can contribute to serious cardiovascular conditions such as heart failure. Researchers at University of Utah Health have now uncovered an unusual feature of heart muscle cells that helps them stay fueled during periods of stress and could point toward new ways to treat a damaged heart.

Scientists previously knew that the heart could draw energy from two carbohydrate sources at once: glucose, a sugar, and lactate, a substance produced when cells break down glucose. In most human tissues, increasing the use of one fuel makes it harder to use the other. Heart muscle somehow avoids this competition.

In a study published in Nature, researchers discovered that heart muscle cells process these fuels in separate parts of the cell. Glucose is broken down in the cytosol, the fluid that surrounds structures inside the cell, while lactate is used inside mitochondria, which produce much of the cell’s usable energy. Keeping these processes separate allows the heart to draw energy from both sources simultaneously.

The system depends on a molecule called MCT1, which transports lactate into the mitochondria. The researchers found that genetic mutations affecting MCT1 prevented lactate from entering the mitochondria and disrupted the heart’s energy balance. Although the heart could largely function without this pathway under everyday conditions, losing it when the heart was under stress led to heart failure.

“This appears to be a critical backup system for heart function,” says Gregory Ducker, PhD, assistant professor of biochemistry at University of Utah Health and senior author of the study. “In an emergency, we would really, really rely on this.”

The discovery identifies a previously unrecognized role for lactate in sustaining injured heart muscle and gives researchers a potential target for developing treatments that restore its energy supply.

“Our findings help point to new areas in which we could target the heart muscle to benefit and repair itself by allowing it to use lactate better,” Ducker says. “That’s the long-term goal: to help the heart muscle heal.”

Whether enhancing this energy pathway can improve heart function in patients remains to be established, though the researchers see potential applications beyond heart failure.

“Rather than simply releasing lactate into the bloodstream as a waste product, we may be able to enhance the heart’s ability to use it as a valuable source of energy,” says Stavros Drakos, MD, PhD, professor of medicine at University of Utah Health and co-senior author of the study. “By optimizing this process, we could potentially improve heart muscle function in patients suffering from heart failure or heart attacks.”

Reference: “MCT1-dependent mitochondrial lactate import sustains cardiac metabolism” by Ahmad A. Cluntun, Joseph R. Visker, Jesse N. Velasco-Silva, James Carrington, Luis Cedeño-Rosario, Giulia C. Napoli, Ji Eon Kim, Thirupura S. Shankar, Marisa J. Brothwell, Rana Hamouche, Álvaro J. Narbona-Pérez, Jing Ling, Ashish G. Toshniwal, Hayden K. Low, Corey N. Cunningham, David R. Eberhardt, Jing Li, Claire E. Stanley, Queren A. Alcantara, Tarun Yadav, Ryan L. Maves, Wojciech I. Swiatek, Nicholas A. Offei, Bhavya Blaze, Sumangala P. Shetty, Dipayan Chaudhuri, Tingting Hong, Jeffery D. Rothstein, Deborah M. Muoio, Joao A. Paulo, Steven P. Gygi, Eleni Tseliou, Sutip Navankasattusas, James E. Cox, Katsuhiko Funai, Stavros G. Drakos, Jared Rutter and Gregory S. Ducker, 28 October 2026, Nature. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11182-3

All the must-see supermoons, meteor showers, star clusters, constellations and deep sky objects this winter — and the gear you need to see them.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Winter is an incredible time for stargazing. With the long hours of darkness and an impressive variety of celestial objects on display, it's easy to fall in love with the night sky during the winter. Whether you have binoculars, a telescope, a smart telescope or are just observing with your eyes, there's something for everyone to enjoy over the coming months.

We've listed all the best sights to see this winter, including the supermoons, star clusters, galaxies and deep-sky nebulae that are best placed in the sky in December, January and February. We see the return of Orion and the Pleiades, with Jupiter and Saturn also making their way back into the night sky, while December also has one of the best and brightest meteor showers of the entire year — the Geminids.

This is by no means an exhaustive list of everything you can see — we'd be here until July — but just a collection of some of our favorite winter sights. Some, like the supermoons and planets, are specific to 2026/2027 timings, but the constellations and deep sky objects we see over the winter are something stargazers look forward to all year. Something to get us through the cold, dreary weather, and a reassuring sign that we made it through another year.

A composite photo of a full supermoon rising into the sky.

This winter is host to three consecutive supermoons (in addition to the full Beaver Supermoon on Nov. 24, making four in a row). The first, and the most festive, is the Christmas Eve supermoon, peaking on December 24, 2026, at 01:28 UTC (which works out as late evening on the 23rd in North America). This last moon of the year is traditionally called the Cold Moon, and this supermoon will look up to 14% larger and 30% brighter than a normal full moon.

The first full moon of 2027, known as the Wolf Moon, peaks on January 22, 2027 at 12:17 UTC. Finally, the super Snow Moon peaks on February 20, 2027 at 23:24 UTC, coinciding with a penumbral lunar eclipse. This is when the sun, moon and Earth line up loosely during a full moon, causing the moon to pass through the Earth's faint outer shadow — the penumbra. During this type of eclipse, the moon only dims slightly, so it won't be nearly as dramatic as a blood moon eclipse.

A photo of an annular, or "ring of fire", solar eclipse.

Observers in South America and Africa will witness an annular solar eclipse on February 6, 2027, peaking at around 16:00 UTC. It will appear as a "ring of fire" in the sky, as an annular solar eclipse happens when the moon passes between Earth and the sun when the moon is near or at its farthest from Earth, known as apogee. Unlike a total solar eclipse, the sun isn't totally blocked, and the sky doesn't turn dark.

A photo of a bright planet glowing in the evening sky.

Since Saturn made its return to the evening sky in the fall, it rises earlier and earlier over the winter months, making this a great time to observe Saturn at a reasonable hour. There are still a few years before we will see the rings at full tilt again, but in 2026/2027 we can start to see more details in the rings after the planet appeared edge-on last year.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

To get a good glimpse of Saturn this winter, you'll need a telescope with at least 4 or 5 inches of aperture and a good eyepiece that gives you at least 100x magnification. Smart telescopes and binoculars don't have the reach, so this is a job for an observational telescope. But that's all right; the hill we'll die on is that there's nothing that'll take your breath away quite like seeing Saturn's rings with your own eyes.

Jupiter will reach opposition on the night of February 10-11, 2027, when it will be at its brightest and closest to Earth, making it appear its largest in the sky. This is the perfect time to observe it with your telescope to see the bands and the Great Red Spot, as well as its four Galilean moons. You'll be able to see the moons with a pair of big astronomy binoculars (we can see them with our 15x70’s), but you'll need a telescope to make out any of the finer details on the planet itself.

After almost a year of absence, Mars made its return to the evening sky in November (albeit quite late in the evening) and will reach opposition on February 19, 2027. Despite being one of our closest neighboring planets, Mars is notoriously difficult to get any meaningful observations with via a telescope, so its opposition is the best chance you'll have.

You'd be forgiven for thinking that because Mars is technically closer to Earth than Jupiter, Saturn and deep-sky objects like the Andromeda Galaxy or the Orion Nebula, viewing it through a telescope would be a breeze, but that's not the case. Mars is very small, with low-contrast features, and only comes observably close to Earth for a few months at a time around every 26-27 months, so it demands quite a lot from a telescope. Even with larger telescopes, it'll only show up as a fuzzy orange dot most of the time.

If you want to try viewing Mars with a telescope this opposition, you'll need 4-6 inches of aperture minimum, depending on what kind of telescope you have. However, for Mars, it's arguably more important to have good seeing (unfortunate with the nearly full moon on this day), excellent quality optics, a stable (preferably motorized) mount, a good focuser and an eyepiece with good eye relief that gives 100x magnification or more to observe any of the planet's finer details.

Alternatively, if you're more of a beginner and are just starting your stargazing hobby, you can head outside with just your eyes and go "Hey look, there's Mars. Cool!" and be done with it.

The Geminids meteor shower is active from December 4-20, peaking on the night of December 13-14, 2026. The waxing crescent moon sets early, leaving dark skies after around 9 pm for prime meteor viewing, and this is one of the few meteor showers that very kindly peaks before midnight.

The Geminids are one of the strongest meteor showers of the year, and this year’s show is expected to have around 120 to 150 meteors per hour under clear, dark skies — making it an exciting opportunity for astrophotography.

Unlike most meteor showers, which come from icy comets, the Geminids originate from a rocky asteroid called 3200 Phaethon. The debris from this asteroid is much denser than the dust from comets, making it able to survive deeper into the atmosphere before burning up. This results in brighter, stronger and more colorful fireballs than the other meteor showers.

If the Geminids left you hooked on meteor showers, you'll only have a few weeks to wait until the Ursids peak on December 22-23, 2026.

However, there are a couple of hurdles here. First, the activity rate is usually quite low — between 5 and 10 meteors per hour. Second, the nearly full moon will hinder visibility and limit sightings to only the brightest meteors. However, as they originate from Ursa Minor, which is circumpolar, the peak viewing time of 21:00-22:00 UTC is much friendlier than the showers that peak in the middle of the night, so it won't require an unreasonable amount of commitment if you do want to catch them.

The first meteor shower of 2027, the Quadrantids, is active between December 28, 2026 and January 28, 2027, peaking on the night of January 3-4, 2027. The thin waning crescent moon won't interfere with viewing conditions, and we could see up to 100-120 meteors per hour. The best time to view will be from midnight through to the pre-dawn hours, when the radiant point, Bootes, is highest in the sky.

Canis Major (the "Greater Dog") is visible over the winter months through until spring, and is easily recognisable by Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky. It's one of the closest stars to our solar system, sitting 8.6 light-years away, and due to its distance and apparent magnitude, its twinkling and flashes of color are particularly noticeable. This is known as scintillation, where turbulence in Earth's atmosphere bends starlight as it passes through different layers of air. It's especially noticeable when Sirius is low in the sky, as the light has more atmosphere to pass through.

You don't need any specialist gear to spot Sirius — it's easily visible with the naked eye. However, if you do have a pair of binoculars, you can even try to spot it in the daytime at certain times of the year.

Look above Canis Major, and you'll find Canis Minor — the "Little Dog". It primarily consists of two bright stars: Procyon and Gomeisa, the former making up a key part of the Winter Triangle and Winter Hexagon. Canis Minor is a fairly faint constellation, but a pair of binoculars will give you a better view.

Canis Minor and Canis Major are most famously known as the loyal hunting dogs of Orion, who spent seven years pursuing the Pleiades sisters to no avail. He should have just led with the fact that he had two dogs.

Speaking of Orion, one of the most recognizable sights in the night sky is Orion's belt, consisting of three bright stars in a straight line: Alnitak, Alnilam and Mintaka. Because of its prominence in the winter sky, Orion's belt has served as a universal celestial marker for navigation, timekeeping and mythologies across human history. The entire Orion constellation is a favorite among stargazers because there's so much to see, both with the naked eye and through binoculars or a telescope.

Another prominent feature of the Orion constellation is Betelgeuse. This red supergiant is easily visible to the naked eye, and astronomers expect it to explode as a supernova within the next 100,000 years. When that eventually happens, it will become visible in broad daylight and shine as brightly as the full moon for a few months. Betelgeuse, Sirius (Canis Major) and Procyon (Canis Minor) make up the Winter Triangle.

There's also Rigel, the brightest star in the constellation, which marks the hunter's foot, and Orion's Sword, a hanging line of stars just below the belt, which contains the Orion Nebula (more on that later).

Although Taurus returned to the evening sky in the fall, winter offers the best viewing time because it sits higher earlier in the evening. The brightest star in the constellation, Aldebaran, is easily recognizable as an orange-red star that marks the bull's eye.

With a pair of binoculars, you'll be able to see two beautiful star clusters — the Pleiades (M45) and the Hyades. The former is a bright open star cluster consisting of seven stars (also known as the Seven Sisters) that you can just about see with the naked eye under very dark skies, and the latter is a V-shaped open cluster that forms the face and head of the bull.

The Pleiades is an ideal first target if you're thinking of buying an entry-level smart telescope, and it's also easy to pick out in wide-field iPhone photos of the night sky.

Auriga is a pentagon-shaped constellation high in the sky between Taurus and Gemini, and is home to a few star clusters to observe this winter.

M36, the Pinwheel Cluster, contains around 60 to 100 stars and is located north of the star El Nath in Auriga. M38, known as the Starfish Cluster, contains over 100 stars, with its brightest forming an X shape, giving it a starfish-like appearance. Finally, M37, known as the Salt and Pepper Cluster, is the brightest and richest cluster in the constellation and contains over 500 stars.

Not only is Gemini the radiant point of the Geminids meteor shower, but its two most prominent stars, Pollux and Castor, are a very recognizable winter target in the night sky. Pollux is an orange giant star and the constellation's brightest point, while Castor appears blue. Although Castor looks like one star to the naked eye, it's actually a complex multiple star system, consisting of three distinct binary pairs: Castor A, Castor B and Castor C. With a small telescope, you can split Castor into its two main pairs, Castor Aa and Castor Ba.

Gemini also contains M35, a large open cluster also known as the Shoe Buckle Cluster, which you can easily view with binoculars.

It’s not an official constellation, but the Winter Hexagon (also known as the Winter Circle) is a recognizable pattern of prominent stars in the winter sky. It consists of Rigel (Orion), Aldebaran (Taurus), Capella (Auriga), Pollux (Gemini), Procyon (Canis Minor) and Sirius (Canis Major).

Once you spot all of the stars that make up the Winter Hexagon, it provides an easy way to navigate your way around the night sky with your binoculars or telescope.

Probably everyone's favorite nebula, largely because it's very easy to spot. It's located in Orion's sword, just below Orion's belt, and when conditions are dark enough, you can even see it with the naked eye and identify it in smartphone photos. Binoculars reveal it as a faint smudge, while telescopes give you a better view of the bright, glowing gas. It's also a wonderful target for smart telescopes with a wide field of view.

While you're there, you can find the Running Man Nebula, a bright reflection nebula complex located just north of the Orion Nebula — and it can be captured in the same frame if you're photographing it. If nebulas are your thing, Orion is absolutely packed with them, including the Casper the Friendly Ghost Nebula (M78), the Monkey Head Nebula (NGC 2174) and the Witch Head Nebula (IC 2118), although many of Orion's nebulas are quite faint and tricky to capture, requiring long integration times.

A photo of the Horsehead and Flame Nebulas

The Horsehead and Flame Nebula in Orion is another popular target for smart telescopes, as it takes up a big portion of the frame and doesn't need a super-long integration time to get a decent, web-ready image (although we'd always recommend shooting for as long as you can).

The Flame and Horsehead are technically two separate entities, but are often paired together due to their close apparent proximity, often fitting inside the same frame. The Flame Nebula is a bright, vibrant emission nebula that gets its name from its fiery network of dark, dense dust lanes. The Horsehead Nebula, on the other hand, is a dark nebula. It's composed of a dense cloud of molecular dust and gas that blocks the light from the emission nebula and stars around it. As the name suggests, this dark nebula takes on the form of a horse's head and neck.

The Rosette Nebula is a vast, star-forming region in the constellation of Monoceros and is a fantastic astrophotography target. Its large, flower-like appearance comes from stellar winds and radiation from the central cluster of young stars. The best time to view and photograph the Rosette Nebula is from January, when Monoceros climbs higher and higher in the evening sky.

The California Nebula lives in the constellation Perseus and gets its name from its resemblance to the U.S. state. This famous emission nebula is made up of ionized gas from the nearby Xi Persei, giving it its vibrant red and pink appearance. It has an apparent size of approximately 2.5 degrees, making it a great target for astrophotography and smart telescopes, as it appears quite large in the frame. Peak visibility of the California Nebula is from now until February.

12,000 light-years away, in the constellation Auriga, you'll find the Tadpole Nebula — a beautiful emission nebula and active stellar nursery. It spans 100 light-years across and makes for a stunning smart telescope target. It gets its name from the distinct, prominent gas and dust pillars that resemble cosmic tadpoles swimming through space — only these tadpoles are around 10 light-years long.

If you're using a smart telescope or astrophotography camera, you'll typically need an integration time of 2-3 hours to bring out more structure in the nebulosity, although longer sessions will yield better results.

Also in Auriga is the Flaming Star Nebula, although this nebula is much closer to Earth — around 1,500 light-years away — and spans about 5 light-years across. Despite being "smaller" than other targets, it appears quite big in the frame of a smart telescope due to its distance from Earth. It's best seen throughout late autumn and winter when Auriga is climbing high in the sky.

The Flaming Star Nebula is an emission and reflection nebula, with each type of nebulosity responding to different filters. In this instance, capturing two sets of data to stack in astrophotography software can help reveal more detail and colors. Broadband filter exposures capture the full range of visible light, including the blue light reflected by dust, as well as natural star colors. Narrowband or dual-band filters isolate specific emission wavelengths, such as hydrogen-alpha (Ha) and oxygen-III (OIII). By using these filters for separate sessions, your final image will show the red glow from the emission nebula and the blue tones from the reflective dust.

Kimberley Lane, E-commerce writer for Live Science, has tested a wide range of optical equipment, reviewing camera gear from Sony, Canon, OM System and more. With over 6 years of photography experience, her skills span across landscape and seascape photography, wildlife, astrophotography and portrait work. Her photos have been featured in a number of national magazines, including Digital Camera World and Cosmopolitan. She has also contributed to our sister site Space.com and Tech Radar, and she regularly uses binoculars and telescopes to stargaze in the dark skies of South Wales.

#6464. ALMA Reveals a Dying Star's Final Breath, Encoded In a Giant Ring of Gas

Stars transition through different stages as they evolve. Sun-like stars with low to intermediate masses (about 0.8 to 8 solar masses) begin as main-sequence stars, then transition sequentially to red giants, asymptotic giant branch (AGB) stars, then post-AGB stars. By the end, they leave behind only a planetary nebula. Each of those transitions are detailed and complicated, and astrophysicists crave a more complete understanding of them.

Stars in their AGB phase have an important job. They spread heavy elements into the surrounding interstellar medium (ISM) and those elements are taken up in subsequent star and planet formation. As they transition from AGB phase to post-AGB phase, they experience thermal pulses that expel material. These events are like brief snapshots in the long life of a star, and catching one in the act is challenging.

Astronomers working with the Atacama Large Millimeter Array (ALMA) have caught a star after what seems to be its final thermal pulse, leaving behing a planetary nebula. This is a rare opportunity to study this transition in detail.

âWeâve caught, for the first time, a starâs final nuclear heartbeat, frozen in gas.â - Raghvendra Sahai, NASA/JPL.

Their observations are in new research titled "The Last Gasps of a Dying Star: ALMA Observations of the Preplanetary Nebula IRAS 06530â0213." It's published in The Astrophysical Journal, and the lead author is Raghvendra Sahai, senior research scientist at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

IRAS 06530â0213 is a preplanetary nebula (PPN) about 12,000 light years away. Astronomers have been watching it for years as it takes shape. They know that the preplanetary nebula phase is a critical evolutionary stage in a star's transition from the asymptotic giant branch (AGB) stage to the planetary nebula (PN) stage. PPN structures contain critical insights that aren't available in any other way.

"These data show the presence of an extended circular ringâfirst evidence of the last thermal pulse preceding the post-asymptotic giant branch (AGB) phase in a carbon starâand a central bipolar nebula (CBN) and torus," the authors write. The outer ring came from the last thermal pulse about 6500 years ago, and is the first direct evidence of this type of thermal pulse that's emitted before a star like this begins its final phase.

This snapshot is all about the mass-loss stars experience as they die, and the authors explain that the AGB progenitor's mass-loss rate "decreased immediately after the thermal pulse, then rose again just before the post-AGB phase."

The mass-loss dropped off for about 2,000 years, then for about 1,000 years after that, it rose again. The filamentary structures around around the CBN are evidence of the star emitting a thick and lumpy shell of gas. An hourglass-shaped nebula with a torus is inside the filamentary arc region.

This ALMA image of IRAS 06530 show the PPN's structure. The outer molecular ring is from its progenitor star's final thermal pulse. The CBN is the central bipolar nebula, and the FAR is the filamentary arc region. The FAR is evidence of the progenitor's mass loss rate dropping immediately after the thermal pulse, then rising again just before the star's post-AGB phase. Image Credit: ALMA (ESO/NAOJ/NRAO); Sahai et al. (2026)

Based on the expansion ages of the torus and the CBN, Sahai and his co-researchers determined that the progenitor star transitioned to a post-AGB star around only 700 yrs ago, maybe a little less than that. That is a remarkably short amount of time to have lapsed since its transition, considering stellar ages.

In 2003 it was first identified as a carbon-rich PPN, and its envelope expansion velocity was measured. Subsequent research identified its s-process enrichment, where elements heavier than iron are synthesized. Then in 2025, this paper identified the PPN's spherical halo and central barrel-shaped torus.

Luck might not describe these most recent observations, because those prior observations were the primer, but good fortune might. The kind of good fortune that finds its way to people who spend their lives watching stars.

âMost of us think of stars as unchanging points of light, but this is a real-time snapshot of a starâs death throes,â said lead author Sahai, author and co-author of more than 140 published papers. âItâs the brief, violent transition between a bloated red giant and a glowing planetary nebula, frozen mid-action.â

There is something puzzling in this PPN and its filamentary arc region that still needs an explanation. "The arc stuctures are likely part of a 3D Archimedean spiral structure generally attributed to the presence of a binary companion," the authors write.

This image shows the central region of IRAS 06530, showing filamentary arc structures with dashed green, cyan, and white arcs. These arcs are typical signatures of a binary companion, but the researchers didn't fine one. Image Credit: ALMA (ESO/NAOJ/NRAO); Sahai et al. (2026)

Dying stars with companions not only have spiral structures, but they're normally found inside compact dust disks. The disks are evidence of mass-transfer with a close binary companion. The mass-transfer is usually the cause of the hourglass-shapes. But the researchers didn't find a dusty disk, the usual signature of a companion.

"However, we do not find a compact continuum source at the location of IRAS 06530âs central star, such as that associated with the compact dusty disks typically found in disk-prominent post-AGB objects known to have binary companions," the researchers explain.

âDying stars so often have hidden companions that reshape their ejected material into intricate, bipolar or multipolar forms instead of simple spheres,â said Sahai. âIRAS 06530 shows that the story is more complicated than the tidy explanation weâve been using.â

IRAS 06530 also has a chemical composition that's challenging to understand. It's significantly enriched in 13C, 17O, and modestly enriched in 15N.

"Compared with solar values, the torus of IRAS 06530 appears to be significantly (modestly) enriched in 13C and 17O (15N), as wellâa pattern of rare-isotope enrichment inconsistent with standard nucleosynthesis models," the authors write.

Â¹Â³C and Â¹â·O are expected, but Â¹âµN isn't. It should be destroyed and depleted to solar levels. Again, a binary companion could be one explanation for this anomaly, and future observations might find one. It's also possible that atypical bursts of nuclear burning are responsible, but that's beyond the scope of this work.

Finding the first direct evidence of a dying star's thermal pulse, something indicated by theory, is the kind of progress astrophysicists hope to make.

âItâs essentially a physical snapshot of an event that, until now, weâve mostly inferred from theoretical models,â said Sahai. âWeâve caught, for the first time, a starâs final nuclear heartbeat, frozen in gas.â

#6463. Hidden Viruses in the Human Gut Offer New Clues to a Disorder Affecting Millions

Many gut viruses were found at lower levels in people with irritable bowel syndrome, offering new clues to a poorly understood condition that affects roughly one in ten people.

Scientists have identified more than 116,000 groups of viruses living in the human gut, over 99% of which had no close match in the largest existing catalog of gut viruses. These largely unexplored microbes could offer new clues to how the digestive system functions and why it changes in people with conditions such as irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).

Research into the gut microbiome has traditionally focused on bacteria, leaving much less understood about bacteriophages, viruses that infect bacteria. Scientists from King’s College London, Helmholtz Munich, and the University of Nottingham are now filling that gap with two studies published on November 17, 2026, in Nature Communications and Gut.

Professor Ana Valdes and Dr. Afroditi Kouraki from the University of Nottingham said, “For a long time the viral part of the gut microbiome has been a kind of dark matter: we knew it was there but couldn’t see it. Advances in sequencing and computational methods mean we can now start to map it properly, and this study shows just how much has been hidden.”

For the Nature Communications study, researchers analyzed genetic material from stool samples collected from more than 1,000 participants in TwinsUK, the largest twin registry in the United Kingdom. Using data on gut bacteria, health measurements, and diet, they examined how populations of viruses and bacteria varied together. Certain viruses were consistently more abundant alongside particular bacteria, while others showed the opposite pattern.

Dr. Panayiotis Louca, a research associate at King’s College London who led the study, said, “Gut viruses are difficult to study, so most of what we found simply isn’t in existing catalogs. What stands out is how closely they track with gut bacteria and with the chemicals those bacteria produce. We can’t yet say whether the viruses are driving that, and testing it is our next step.”

Studying twins also allowed researchers to estimate how much genetics and the environment shape the gut’s viral community. Genetic factors accounted for an estimated 47% of the variation in overall viral diversity, although most individual viral populations appeared to be influenced primarily by environmental factors.

The researchers also discovered a small group of viruses carrying genes linked to harmful bacterial behavior. These viruses were more commonly found alongside bacteria that can sometimes cause infections and less commonly alongside bacteria that break down dietary fiber.

Such relationships could be relevant to IBS, a condition that affects around 10% of the population and can significantly disrupt daily life. Its underlying causes remain poorly understood.

In the second study, published in Gut, researchers used TwinsUK data to identify 50 viral groups associated with IBS, most of which were less abundant in people with the condition. Relationships between bacteria and viruses also differed, with many viruses infecting bacteria previously linked to IBS. This suggests that the condition may involve changes across the wider microbial community rather than in bacteria alone.

Senior author Dr. Cristina Menni, who leads the metabolomics research group at the Department of Twin Research, Ageing and Genomic Epidemiology at King’s College London, said, “Our research highlights that to fully understand the gut microbiome and its links to health and disease, we need to look beyond bacteria and consider the viruses that live alongside them. We reveal a fascinating and largely unexplored dimension of the gut microbiome—discovering that viruses are not only closely associated with bacterial communities, but also with the metabolites that connect the microbiome to our health. This opens exciting new avenues for understanding how the gut ecosystem works.”

Future research will examine whether gut viruses actively influence bacterial metabolism and how these interactions change in health and disease. Understanding these relationships could eventually help researchers develop better biological markers and treatments for IBS, as well as more personalized approaches to gut health.

Dr. Louca added: “The study is observational, so it cannot show that the viruses cause these effects, but it provides greater understanding of a largely unexplored area of the human gut. It would also be beneficial to replicate the study on a more diverse cohort, as participants were mostly older women of European ancestry.”

“Population-level characterization of the human gut phageome and its association with microbial metabolites” by Panayiotis Louca, Mohammadali Khan Mirzaei, Afroditi Kouraki, Erfan Khamespanah, Yu Lin, Xue Peng, Robert Pope, Alessia Visconti, Francesco Asnicar, Daniel Kirk, Ricardo Costeira, Nicola Segata, Mario Falchi, Jordana T. Bell, Tim D. Spector, Lindsey A. Edwards, Li Deng, Ana M. Valdes and Cristina Menni, 17 November 2026, Nature Communications. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-79230-0

“Large-scale shotgun metagenomic analysis of gut bacteria–phage interactions in IBS” by Daniel Kirk, Erfan Khamespanah, Panayiotis Louca, Alessia Visconti, Robert Pope, Francesco Asnicar, Sarah E Berry, Jonathan Wolf, Nicola Segata, Tim D Spector, Mario Falchi, Frances M K Williams, Mohammadali Khan Mirzaei, Li Deng and Cristina Menni, 16 November 2026, Gut. DOI: 10.1136/gutjnl-2026-338807

This research was funded by the Chronic Disease Research Foundation (CDRF) and in part by the Wellcome and Medical Research Council (MRC).

#6462. The Physics Wall Facing Orbital AI Data Centers

Basing entire business plans on back-of-the-envelope calculations might not seem like the best idea. However, according to a new paper available in preprint on arXiv by Dr. Slava Turyshev of NASAâs Jet Propulsion Laboratory, that is precisely what the companies touting orbital AI data centers are doing. While on paper, the math looks good, the physical constraints of actually utilizing all the processing power and free energy of the Sun that orbit provides is prohibitive in a number of ways - and it will be a long time before we have the technology to truly capitalize on the advantages of space-based AI.

First, letâs dig into what the back-of-the-envelope calculations say. Research from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory suggests that U.S.-based data centers could consume 580 terawatt-hours of electricity over a five-year window, an increase of around 17-46 gigawatts compared to modern levels. But land-based data centers are running into plenty of bottlenecks, from newly elected hostile politicians to hard caps on the electrical gridâs ability to supply all that additional power.

So the solution seems obvious - launch the data centers into orbit, where they will be beyond any individual NIMBY protesters, have access to essentially unlimited free solar power, and not have to deal with water cooling systems. Sounds pretty good. Until the actual physics of what that means comes into play.

Fraser addresses the idea of data centers in space.

There are three main physics hurdles that all culminate into a giant economic one facing data centers, and it all comes down to scale. Size and weight are the first major obstacle. Dr. Turyshev uses a baseline 1-megawatt orbital processing facility as an example. It would hold roughly the processing power of a small commercial server room. But in space it would require 5,640 square meters of deployed solar panels, even in a âdawn-duskâ orbit designed to minimize the time it spends in Earthâs shadow. Thatâs roughly the size of an American football field.

On top of that, the spacecraft would need around 2,500 square meters of radiator panels to stop the electronics from frying themselves. Combining the power generation and cooling equipment required would already bring a spacecraft up to 30 metric tons. Adding in structural trusses, control thrusters, and radiation shielding brings the total mass of 1 MW of orbital data capacity is likely between 34 and 59 metric tons.

For the purposes of practicality, Dr. Turyshev then drops down to a 100 kW center, since a 1 MW data center would not even fit in many modern rocket fairings. Arguably, since each 100 kW data center wouldnât be exactly 10% of the weight of a 1 MW data center, he uses a rough estimate of around 5 metric tons for a single spacecraft of that size. The problem is, to keep up with demand, we would need to launch between 170,000 and 461,000 of them over the course of five years. And each Falcon 9 can only launch at most four of them. That would require almost 9,000 Falcon 9 launches over the next five years - or roughly 33 of them per week.

Fraser talks about turning the Moon into a data center.

Even if we had the launch capacity for that sheer scale, there is another bottleneck to contend with - getting the data back to Earth. As we reported earlier this week, weâve made great strides in high-speed optical communications down from orbit lately. However, the headline number of 200 gigabits per second is a single point in time. These âhigh speedâ links realistically deliver around 13 to 26 gigabits per second continuously, in part because they require a direct line of sight to the ground station theyâre communicating with, and they also canât communicate through clouds. Even if we flooded major parts of the Earthâs surface with ground stations, those speeds would severely hobble any interactive cloud apps or data-heavy training runs that require continual syncing with anything on the ground.

But even if we solved the communications problem, thereâs still the problem of that omnipresent menace in space - radiation. Cosmic rays are famous for flipping single bits in computer memory, constantly forcing processors to run error-checking algorithms, and thereby eating into usable computer time. According to the paper, over a five-year mission, the cumulative radiation damage and micrometeoroid impacts would continually degrade both the electronics and solar panels, driving up the cost of every calculation completed.

With all that in mind, the economic hurdle becomes very clear. On Earth, a high-end AI data center costs between $10,000 and $40,000 per kilowatt of computing capacity. In order for a 40-kilogram per kilowatt orbital satellite to match that pricing, it would need combined launch and manufacturing costs of between $250 and $1,000 per kilogram. For comparison, current dedicated Falcon 9 launches work out to roughly $3,360 per kilogram. So the launch cost alone is three to thirteen times more expensive than the entire combined launch and manufacturing cost of a single data center.

Video from Astraveo arguing the same physics as what Dr. Turyshev talks about in the paper. Credit - Astraveo YouTube Channel

With all that said, there are some niche applications for orbital computing in the near future, according to the paper. The first is space-native processing, where satellites crunch the raw imagery for Earth-observation satellites or sensor data before broadcasting high-value insights back down to Earth. Another is communications-based edge computing, where processors piggyback on existing constellations like Starlink that already pay for solar arrays, lasers, and ground stations.

But ultimately, despite this paper, various organizations are moving forward with their plans for data centers in orbit. Even today (November 25th) the FCC approved SpaceXâs application to launch one million âStarmindâ orbital data centers by 2040. Earlier this month, Google booked a flight on a Blue Origin rocket for a test of its Project Suncatcher computing constellation. Until the real economics of the situation catch up with them, it might be a while before these efforts realize what hard physical limits theyâre going up against.

S. G. Turyshev - Orbital Data Centers: Spacecraft Constraints and Economic Viability

#6460. Semiconductor Breakthrough Cracks a Longstanding Solar Energy Problem

An unusual material could help us make better use of the sun’s energy, offering new possibilities for more efficient solar power and fuel production.

Generating more electricity from sunlight does not necessarily mean installing more solar panels. Finding ways to extract more energy from the light that already reaches them could make solar power a more practical source of electricity. Part of the challenge lies in what happens inside a solar cell in the moments after it absorbs sunlight.

Solar cells contain materials called semiconductors, which use the energy from sunlight to free negatively charged electrons, leaving behind positively charged gaps known as holes. Both charges must be collected to generate electricity. If an electron and a hole meet and cancel each other out, a process known as recombination, the energy they carry is lost. Unfortunately, materials that are particularly good at absorbing sunlight also tend to lose these charges more quickly.

A study led by the University of Oxford has identified a promising exception in a semiconductor called bismuth sulfide. Published October 28, 2026, in Nature, the research examined how the material’s unusual electronic structure could help overcome this longstanding limitation in solar energy technology.

To investigate how long electrical charges survive in bismuth sulfide, the researchers exposed thin films of the material to extremely short laser pulses. They then tracked how quickly the charges disappeared using a technique called ultrafast terahertz spectroscopy, conducting measurements at temperatures ranging from room temperature to just above absolute zero.

“One of the longstanding challenges in developing efficient solar-energy materials is that the properties which make a semiconductor very good at absorbing sunlight also tend to make the resulting electrical charges disappear quickly,” said corresponding author Professor Laura Herz (Department of Physics, University of Oxford). “Our work shows that this trade-off is not inevitable. By uncovering how an unusual electronic structure can combine strong light absorption with much slower recombination, we have identified a new principle for designing semiconductors that could help us harvest solar energy more efficiently.”

Electronic structure calculations by Professor Marina Filip’s group in Oxford’s Department of Physics helped explain why bismuth sulfide behaves differently. The material has two closely spaced routes through which electrons can move between energy levels. One allows the material to absorb light strongly, while the other sits at a slightly lower energy and allows charges to disappear much more slowly. Because the two are so close together, charges spend much of their time in the lower-energy states, which effectively serve as a temporary storage reservoir.

Cooling the material provided further evidence for this explanation. In most semiconductors, electrical charges disappear faster as temperatures drop. In bismuth sulfide, more charges settled into the reservoir as the material cooled, allowing them to survive longer. The results matched the team’s model of what physicists call a pseudo-direct semiconductor.

Even at room temperature, the researchers estimate that this arrangement reduces the rate of charge loss by about 75% compared with conventional semiconductors that absorb light equally well.

Giving electrical charges more time to be collected could improve the efficiency of solar panels without compromising their ability to capture sunlight. The benefits could also extend beyond electricity generation. Longer-lived charges could provide more time for the chemical reactions needed to produce fuels using sunlight.

“What makes this discovery particularly exciting is that we are not simply improving an existing semiconductor property but identifying a different way in which semiconductors can behave,” said Professor Herz. “Understanding this mechanism gives us a roadmap for discovering and potentially engineering other materials with similarly advantageous properties.”

The team’s calculations suggest that researchers could search existing materials databases for semiconductors with similar properties or engineer new ones. However, the study demonstrates the underlying physical mechanism rather than the performance of a finished solar cell. Further research will be needed to determine how these properties can be put to use in solar energy technologies.

Reference: “Delayed electron–hole recombination in a pseudo-direct semiconductor” by Marcello Righetto, Debalina Banerjee, Zhenglin Jia, Joshua R. S. Lilly, Vincent J. -Y. Lim, Snigdha Lal, Siyu Yan, Jae Eun Lee, Jay B. Patel, Michael B. Johnston, Qianqian Lin, Marina R. Filip and Laura M. Herz, 28 October 2026, Nature. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11223-x

#6459. The Event Horizon Telescope Views the Dynamics and Geometry of a Black Hole Jet in Extreme Detail

The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT), a massive international collaboration of scientists and radio observatories, is like the gift that keeps on giving. In 2019, the EHT Collaboration gave us the first image of a black hole: the supermassive black hole (SMBH) at the heart of the M87 galaxy (M87*). In 2022, it provided the first image of Sagittarius A*, the SMBH at the center of the Milky Way. Between 2024 and 2026, the international array also produced detailed images of the relativistic jet emanating from 3C 84 and M87*.

Meanwhile, EHT observations in 2021 also resolved the innermost jet region of the blazar 3C 279 in unprecedented detail. These efforts, described in a paper that appeared in Astronomy & Astrophysics, revealed the jet's dynamics and geometry at sub-parsec scales, suggesting it bends toward Earth-based instruments on these scales. Combined with earlier EHT campaigns and multifrequency data, the EHT team's latest results are helping astronomers identify its nature and the mechanisms driving it.

By definition, blazars are bright galaxies with an SMBH at their centers - Active Galactic Nuclei (AGNs) - that have relativistic jets of ionized matter directed straight toward Earth. Located approximately 538 million light-years away, the jet coming from its center is powered by an SMBH with an estimated mass of about 800 million solar masses (by comparison, Sagittarius A* is about 4.3 million solar masses). Because of its brightness, 3C 279 is considered a prime target for Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) and is frequently used for calibration.

An image of the core region of Messier 87, a supermassive black hole, processed from an array of radio telescopes known as the EHT with colours indicating brightness temperature (Credit: Event Horizon Telescope)

The 2021 campaign represents the largest EHT array configuration published to date, with the addition of two new sites. These were the 12-m telescope at the Kitt Peak Observatory in Arizona and the Northern Extended Millimeter Array (NOEMA) interferometer in the French Alps. These additions provided crucial intermediate baselines that significantly improved coverage, especially at intermediate scales, enabling constraints on specific angular scales. These constraints were essential for probing both compact and extended structures in the jet.

Hendrik MÃ¼ller, a staff scientist in the Data Management and Software (DMS) group at the National Radio Astronomy Observatory (NRAO) and a former researcher with the Max-Planck-Institut fÃ¼r Radioastronomie, was the lead author of the paper that appeared in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics. As he told Universe Today via email, the EHT is continuously growing and adding more telescopes every year, including the Greenland Telescope in 2018. But as he noted, the Kitt Peak and NOEMA observatories were especially important to these observations:

The physical baseline between two antennas in the array determines the spatial scale that this baseline can resolve. That is, for example, the reason why the Very Large Array (VLA) in New Mexico is built on railway tracks: When you move the antennas closer to each other, you zoom out of the image and see the larger field of view.

If you move them closer to each other, you zoom into the image, achieve higher resolution, but see only a small view of the sky. The locations of the radio telescopes in the EHT could of course not be changed, but Kitt Peak and NOEMA were important because they are relatively close to other telescopes in the array (NOEMA in the French Alpes to Pico Veleta close to Granada, Spain. They added information that was not available to us in previous years.

To process the volumes of data gathered by the EHT arrays, the team relied on Comrade, DoG-HiT, kine, and Difmap imaging software, a strategy similar to the one used to reconstruct the famous M87 black hole image in 2019. As MÃ¼ller explained, the team used different software packages that make different assumptions about the image to build confidence in the result by checking for consistency across methods. Beyond imaging, many more collaborators and software were used during early data-processing steps, like correlation or calibration.

Illustration of the multiwavelength 3C 279 jet structure in April 2017. The observing epochs, arrays, and wavelengths are noted in each panel. Credit: J.Y. Kim/MPIfR/VLBA and GMVA/EHT

The results, as noted, suggest that the jet curves so that one section of it points closer to Earth. While the jet is already oriented towards our instruments, MÃ¼ller explained how this small change can have two visible effects:

Because the plasma is moving close to the speed of light, its radiation is concentrated in the direction it's traveling. When that direction lines up more closely with Earth, we see brighter emission. At the same time, features in the jet are moving more nearly straight toward us, so they can appear to move more slowly across the sky. Think of a car coming almost head-on: it can be moving fast while barely shifting left or right in your field of view.

That's what makes the bend a useful explanation for 3C 279. Farther along the inner jet, we see brighter emission and slower apparent motion. Both can result from a change in direction, even if the plasma keeps moving just as fast. That also means the brightest spot in the image can be downstream from the black hole, where the jet points most directly at us.

What's more, the EHT images show that the direction of the inner jet changes over time, providing clues as to what is driving the jet. From the images, the team also noticed features that appeared to move more slowly along a farther, particularly bright stretch of the jet. The bending towards Earth could explain both effects, as the flow can keep moving just as fast while looking brighter and shifting less laterally. Said MÃ¼ller:

We also found a clue about where the jet picks up speed. Even close to the apparent base of the jet, some features are already moving across the sky at apparent speeds comparable to those much farther downstream. If those features travel with the plasma, that suggests the jet gains much of its speed over a short distance near its base. As the fast flow narrows again, it may form a shock that adds to the brightness we see near the bend.

While 3C 279 is one of the best-studied quasars in radio astronomy, the mechanisms driving its central jet are still a mystery, and future observations could reveal behaviors that have not yet been seen. Astronomers have decades' worth of observations on how its jet behaves on larger scales, but only a few images on how it behaves at the sub-parsec level. Nevertheless, the EHT Collaboration is extremely useful because it enables deep surveys and high resolution, allowing astronomers to detect details in the jet's innermost region that weren't available before. Said MÃ¼ller:

This paper is just the beginning. We have EHT observations from several years, as well as observations at other frequencies that we scheduled around the same time, that are currently [being] analyzed. Observing at different frequencies lets us see different parts of the jet. Taking those observations close together helps us tell which differences come from the frequency we're using and which come from the jet itself changing.

We expect a series of results from these data over the next few years. Very few quasars have been studied in this much detail. That makes 3C 279 one of our best opportunities to understand how a black hole launches a jet and how that jet gets up to nearly the speed of light, and the current manuscript is just the beginning of that journey.

Further Reading: Astronomy & Astrophysics

#6458. 2026 Was the Year Restaurants Went Full Midwest

It’s a giardinera- and tavern-style-stuffed, totally welcoming time in hospitality

At Kyle Knall’s Milwaukee restaurant Cassis, the showstopper dish is ravioli Dauphiné, a sheet of 24 tiny squares stuffed with the Wisconsin cheese Pleasant Ridge Reserve. Topped with glazed seasonal veggies, kernels of sweet corn in summer and sliced honeynut squash in late fall, it speaks to Knall’s Midwestern-meets-French approach—one of the reasons why his restaurant earned a slot on Eater’s 2026 list of the Best New Restaurants in America.

The Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, feature serious Midwest representation. The Best New Restaurants list includes Chicago’s Creepies, which also digs into that Midwest-French mashup, and Kansas City’s Akoya Omakase, which brings a distinct viewpoint to the omakase experience. Meanwhile, the pickled walleye cheeks at Rosy in Cleveland and the puffed grain toast at All Well in Chicago are among the Restaurant Dishes of the Year, and Chicago’s Bad Butter, a place best-known for its croissant take on a Chicago-style hot dog, is one of the Best New Bakeries. It even includes drinks—Culebra, a Puerto Rican spot that draws on the Latinx influences of its Chicago neighborhood, is on Punch’s Best New Bars list. Between these accolades and other national recognition, all eyes are on the Midwest right now. And that’s even before we get into the impact of the Chicago-set show The Bear, which put Italian beef on everyone’s radar, and the rise of tavern-style pizza around the country.

The Midwest has always had great restaurants, of course, but it’s undeniable that something has shifted. “People are flying into these cities rather than flying over them,” says Vinnie Cimino, the Cleveland chef who co-owns Rosy and Cordelia. “I think that word is getting out about these smaller pockets of culture and cuisine.” Some of this is attributable to diners being more willing to explore outside big coastal cities, but it’s also due to chefs returning home to the region. “Post-pandemic, a lot of folks moved out of larger cities and back home,” says Cimino. “Now they’re setting up shop and creating great things in the spaces that they grew up in.” David Posey, chef and co-owner of Creepies and Elske in Chicago, agrees, adding: “For a long time, it felt like we were playing catch-up with trends on the coasts. Now I think we’re less quick to follow trends and are more confident in having our own voice of what the Midwest is.”

One of those chefs who left New York is Knall, a Birmingham, Alabama, native who cooked at Gramercy Tavern in New York before moving to his wife’s hometown of Milwaukee in 2020. Another is Peter Hoang, who worked at his father’s Kansas City, Missouri, sushi restaurant before gaining experience in Chicago and New York restaurants. When he returned to open Akoya Omakase, he crafted menus with the audience in mind, with two omakases, priced more affordably than many at $85 and $165, as well as an à la carte menu. “My sushi is honed by Japanese techniques and sourcing,” he says. “But I interpret what I think is best for the fish, whether that’s highlighting the textures and flavors through different garnishes or using aging or salting techniques.”

It’s not simply that these are good restaurants located in the Midwest—these restaurants are deeply Midwestern in ethos. In Chicago, David and Anna Posey, who run the Michelin-starred Elske, wanted to open a French bistro for their second venture. But as they developed Creepies with chef de cuisine Tayler Ploshehanski, David Posey says they began expanding its focus: “We started taking flavors and adapting them to things that we’re a little more familiar with.” This means dishes that draw on the traditions of Michigan, Wisconsin, and Illinois—think tarte flambée on a tavern-style pizza crust and mussels with giardiniera. And it’s not just the food at Creepies that reflects the Midwest: “We told our designer that our inspiration board was a Midwest basement with wood paneling and low ceilings meets a bistro in the French countryside.”

At Cordelia, Cimino leans into the traditional cuisine of Northeast Ohio, with offerings like raw-beef cannibal sandwiches and kielbasa with cabbage salad. “It’s the familiar flavors that we grew up eating, rethought into this more modern light,” he says. Meanwhile, Rosy “is a deeper dive into the culture of our region” and features dishes like Balkan cevapi and Italian cotechino cooked over live fire. The approach is drawing a wide range of Cleveland diners, from 20-somethings there for the cool, candlelit vibe to grandparents there to taste the food they grew up with. “I think that’s what the Midwest is,” Cimino says. “Being able to be that transgenerational space everybody feels welcome in.”

That welcoming community sensibility is a key component of Midwestern restaurants. Knall counts several farmers and shoppers at the West Allis Farmers Market, where he sources for Cassis, as some of his regulars. “To me, it shows that’s really what Midwest food is: supporting those communities,” he says.

Perhaps more than anything, it’s hospitality that sets these spots apart. “Hospitality is our biggest focus between both restaurants and maybe even more of a focus than the food,” Knall says. “To me, the way that our team makes you feel in the restaurants is such a Midwest thing.” And at Cordelia, where the slogan is “Midwest Nice,” Cimino says: “It’s welcoming you into our proverbial home.”

#6457. Physicists Discover a Strange New Form of Magnetism in a Simple Metal

Electronics can use more than electrical charge, and evidence of unusual magnetism in europium silicide could help researchers explore how to put electron spin to work.

At very low temperatures, a simple metal made from europium and silicon develops a spiral pattern of magnetism that leaves it with no overall magnetization. Its electrons nevertheless appear to favor opposite spin orientations when they travel in opposite directions, an unusual relationship that could offer researchers new ways to explore and control electronic behavior.

An international team has found compelling evidence for this state, called p-wave magnetism, in europium silicide, or EuSi. The findings, published in Nature, provide an experimental foothold in a field where suitable materials have been difficult to find.

Spin is a quantum property that gives electrons a magnetic character, somewhat like tiny compass needles. In a conventional ferromagnet, spins tend to align in the same direction, producing net magnetization. In EuSi, between approximately 33 and 62 kelvin, or about −400 to −348 °F, the magnetic moments of europium atoms instead form an ordered spiral. The individual moments are substantial, but their contributions cancel overall.

The predicted relationship between opposite directions of electron motion and opposite spin polarizations is known as an odd-parity spin texture. Finding a material in which researchers can investigate it has been challenging. Previous candidates include electrical insulators and metals that develop magnetic order only at very low temperatures or have additional symmetry complications. EuSi combines a fixed chemical composition with a spiral magnetic phase that has the required symmetry, and researchers can grow high-quality single crystals for experiments.

Dr. Erjian Cheng grew those crystals approximately three years ago at the Max Planck Institute for Chemical Physics of Solids (MPI CPfS) in Dresden. Initial photoemission experiments, which use light to eject electrons and examine their properties, showed that magnetism had an unusually large influence on EuSi’s electronic band structure, the pattern of energies electrons can occupy inside the material. That raised the possibility that its magnetic order might link spin to the direction of electron motion.

The investigation brought together 38 researchers from 19 institutions, including ShanghaiTech University, the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, the Max Planck Institute for the Physics of Complex Systems, and Oak Ridge National Laboratory.

Combining theoretical calculations with several experimental techniques, the researchers examined both the atomic magnetic arrangement and its effects on electrons. Neutron diffraction revealed the spiral of europium magnetic moments and confirmed that its symmetry met the conditions for p-wave magnetism. Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, which maps electron energies and momenta, showed that magnetism substantially reshaped the electronic structure, producing energy separations exceeding 100 millielectronvolts.

Measurements that also resolved electron spin supplied a more specific test. The spin polarization changed sign across successive magnetic Brillouin zones, repeating regions in a map of electron momentum defined by the magnetic order. It also weakened sharply near regions where the predicted p-wave spin texture should vanish. Together, these observations provided spectroscopic evidence consistent with the theoretical state.

“When we first measured the electronic structure of EuSi, we were surprised by the exceptionally large effect of magnetism on the electrons,” explains Cheng. “That observation led us to investigate whether this simple compound could host a much more unusual magnetic state. The combination of crystal growth, neutron scattering and spin-resolved spectroscopy now provides compelling evidence for p-wave magnetism.”

The proposed spin pattern arises predominantly from magnetic exchange interactions, which influence how spins arrange themselves, and from the symmetry of the magnetic spiral. That distinguishes it from familiar spin-splitting effects driven mainly by spin-orbit coupling, an interaction between an electron’s spin and its motion.

The spiral also introduces handedness, or chirality. EuSi’s underlying crystal structure is centrosymmetric, meaning that it looks the same when inverted through its center. Its magnetic spiral, however, can twist in either of two opposite senses. Using magnetic force microscopy and spatially resolved photoemission spectroscopy, the researchers identified magnetic domains approximately ten micrometers across.

When examined with circularly polarized light, domains with opposite magnetic handedness showed distinct electronic responses. The results demonstrated that the spiral’s handedness is coupled to the electronic structure, connecting the organization of the atomic magnetic moments with the behavior of the electrons.

“What makes EuSi particularly exciting is that an unconventional electronic spin structure emerges from the magnetic order of a chemically simple metal,” says Prof. Claudia Felser, Director at MPI CPfS. “This demonstrates how the discovery of new materials can reveal entirely new electronic phenomena. EuSi now gives us an experimental platform to investigate how magnetic symmetry and chirality can be used to control electronic properties, with potential implications for future spintronics and unconventional superconductivity.”

Spintronics uses electron spin as well as electrical charge in electronic devices. The findings could inform that field, along with research on topological quantum materials and unconventional superconductivity. They also illustrate how a solid’s properties depend on its magnetic order and electronic quantum states, alongside its chemical composition and crystal structure.

Reference: “Evidence for p-wave magnetism in electronic band structure of metallic EuSi” by Erjian Cheng, Yixing Yang, Yifan Gao, Jan Priessnitz, Yiqing Hao, Jieyi Liu, Rui Lou, Alexander Fedorov, Mengyu Yao, Yuri Prots, Houke Chen, Ralf Koban, Xuemin Shi, Ying-Ting Chan, Ulrich Burkhardt, Berit H. Goodge, Walter Schnelle, Vicky Hasse, Jaafar Ansari, Zhuocheng Lu, Peter Bencok, Gerrit van der Laan, Makoto Hashimoto, Donghui Lu, Jacek Osiecki, Zhanfeng Liu, Shengtao Cui, Jaime Sánchez-Barriga, Oliver Rader, Yulin Chen, Hua Wang, Jiadong Zang, Leila Noohinejad, Weida Wu, Libor Šmejkal, Junwei Liu, Zhongkai Liu and Claudia Felser, 18 November 2026, Nature. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11295-9

#6456. Study Finds Artemis Astronauts Will Enjoy Moon-Grown Potatoes

By now, references to Mark Watney and how he grew potatoes in Martian soil have become a tired clichÃ©. Nevertheless, one can't help but recall the scene whenever news breaks about the latest experiment that examines the potential of growing plants in extraterrestrial soils. The latest comes from Oregon State University (OSU), where researchers have shown that potatoes grown in lunar soil simulant (amended with organic matter) are safe to eat and grow just as well as those produced on Earth.

This is good news for space agencies like NASA that are actively planning to send astronauts back to the Moon, and this time, to stay. Through the Artemis Program, crews will land around the South Pole-Aitken Basin and begin constructing a permanent base that will enable regular missions in the future (about one per year). China's National Space Agency (CNSA) and Roscosmos also plan on building a base - the International Lunar Research Station (ILRS) - in the same region by the end of the decade.

To support long-term missions far from Earth, where opportunities for resupply will be fewer and farther between, a degree of self-sufficiency is required. Whereas the International Space Station (ISS) is resupplied regularly and emergency supplies can be dispatched within hours, missions to the Moon will take at least three days to arrive. As such, any sustained program of exploration on the Moon must rely on In-Situ Resource Utilization(ISRU) as much as possible - i.e., using local resources for building materials and providing astronauts with water and food.

Research in the past few decades has led to methods for 3D printing habitats and other facilities using lunar regolith. This can be combined with a bonding agent to create "lunacrete," or sintered with microwaves to create molten ceramic. Either material is then deposited layer by layer by construction robots to form walls and other structural elements. While hydroponics remain a viable way to grow plants (as astronauts do aboard the ISS), the real question is whether Earth plants can be grown in lunar regolith and other extraterrestrial soils.

Led by Aymeric Goyer, a professor with OSU's Department of Botany and Plant Pathology, the Oregon team used lunar regolith simulants with different levels of vermicompost, a nutrient-rich organic soil produced when earthworms break down organic matter. With support from NASA's Johnson Space Center Simulant Development Lab, the team produced healthy potatoes with yields comparable to crops grown by farmers in Oregon (the 4th largest potato producer in the U.S.).

Goyer and his teams specifically selected potatoes because they produce more calories per square meter of soil than many other crops. They also offer substantial nutritional value: one medium skin-on potato (148 g/5.3 oz) provides roughly 110 calories, 26 g of carbohydrates, 3 g of protein, and 2 g of fiber. They are also naturally fat-free, gluten-free, cholesterol-free, and are therefore considered a practical staple food for long-duration space missions.

Since lunar regolith varies across the Moon, the researchers tested five simulants representing lunar mare (fine-grained basaltic soil) and lunar highland (feldspar-rich volcanic soil) regions. They also included soil from Hermiston, Oregon, which produces the world's highest potato yield. The results showed that potato plants grown in simulants containing 30% vermicompost grew as well as those cultivated in Earth soils. In other samples, plants grown without vermicompost were severely stunted and had underdeveloped root systems.

The "Moon Village" concept, conceived by MIT in collaboration with the ESA and Skidmore, Owings & Merrill. Credit: ESA/Skidmore, Owings & Merrill

Lastly, those grown with 5% to 15% vermicompost showed only partial growth. As Goyer said in an OSU press release:

We found that potatoes can complete their entire life cycle in simulated lunar soil when supplemented with organic matter. That's an important step toward developing reliable food production systems that could support long-term human exploration of the Moon.

The results also showed that the potatoes grown in lunar regolith simulants maintained their nutritional quality, with no statistically significant increase in naturally occurring potato toxins (glycoalkaloids) often associated with green discoloration. Lunar regolith still presents many challenges for plant growth, which include extremely fine-grained dust and elevated levels of heavy metals.

But the researchers are confident that adding organic matter helps bind heavy metals, preventing them from damaging roots, interfering with growth, or leaching into the potatoes themselves. In the future, astronauts could bring compost to the Moon, along with Earth worms, to create their own fertilizer, augmenting soil collected during surface trips to grow their food.

"We believe the compost helps balance some of the toxicity we see in lunar regolith by reducing plant exposure to harmful compounds," said David Handy, a postdoctoral researcher in Goyer's lab. Their results are reported in a paper, "Growth and molecular responses of potato to lunar regolith simulants," that appeared in npj Microgravity. Another paper, which reports the results of experiments involving 10 potato varieties to identify which grow best in lunar soil, will be released.
