#6444. Robots, Not Astronauts, Will Have to Fix Space Data Centers

Yesterday we explored some of the difficulties facing orbital data centers in our look at the bottleneck of launching enough solar panels and radiative cooling systems to power the AI computing boom in space. JPL physicist Dr. Slava Turyshev, who wrote the paper at the center of that article, also published a follow-up study in August, available in preprint on arXiv, about how getting the hardware off the ground is only half the battle. Once all that equipment is up there, someone, or something, is going to have to maintain it.

Modern hardware powering Artificial Intelligence even on Earth has an obsolescence problem. The computer chips and memory that power AI data centers become obsolete every 3-5 years. If a company builds an orbital data center, its processing power is effectively useless for training the latest AI models in less than half a decade. So, in their business plans, the solution is to build intentionally disposable satellites.

Unfortunately, that means throwing away literal tons of still-useful solar panels and heat radiators just to discard some obsolete computer hardware. Given that those bulkier pieces of equipment pose their own challenge for launches, as we saw yesterday, that seems a bit of a waste. So, Dr. Turyshev suggests that orbital data centers must be designed with hardware replacement in mind.

Fraser talks about a NASA project designed to assemble large-scale structures in space.

On Earth, replacement of data server racks involves a human technician walking down an air-conditioned aisle, pulling some cables, and pressing pins before replacing a standardized blade. In orbit, that would require a pressurized housing with airlocks, life support and fire suppression systems, while still having the problem of cooling all of those heat-producing microchips in the vacuum of space. According to Dr. Turyshev, that means the entire data center architecture should be based around plug-and-play âorbital replacement unitsâ (ORUs).

He assigns each of those ORUs into one of three main replaceable component tiers (alongside replacing an entire 100 kW satellite node if it suffers catastrophic damage). One is a 5 kW âcomputeâ module that holds the memory, storage and optical transceivers necessary to actually perform calculations. These are designed to be rapidly swappable, and are intended to be the most replaced part of the whole satellite.

Another ORU category is the âsubsystemsâ â the power converters, batteries, pumps, and manifolds meant to keep the whole system running but that are settled enough technologically to not require regular replacement. In the paperâs architecture, these can be swapped out by specialized 6 or 7 degree-of-freedom robotic arms, as compared to the automated cartridge changers that handle replacing the compute modules.

Fraser talks about the difficulties repairing missions at L2, like JWST.

The third group of ORUs consists of the solar arrays and radiator panels themselves. Making them modular has the added advantage of not needing to replace the entire cooling or power generation system if one part happens to be struck by a micrometeoroid, which will undoubtedly happen often even in Low Earth Orbit. Despite the fact these modules make up the bulk of the weight and surface area of the spacecraft, they will not have to be repaired as frequently as the compute modules, as random failures caused by cosmic rays will brick compute modules fairly frequently..

Unfortunately, replacing these systems isnât as easy as it would be on Earth. Each 5 kW processor will heat up nearly half a degree Celsius every second, triggering a thermal overload in a little less than a minute if left uncooled. And the power capacitors riding along to maintain power to the system have the capability of producing an arc strong enough to weld a robotic gripper to a maintenance touch point, so they must be bled off before a robot can start interacting with the satelliteâs hardware.

And then, there is once again the sense of scale. For a standardized 1 MW cluster, comprising ten 100 kW sized systems, a collection of 3-4 robots specialized assigned to each 1MW cluster would have to perform around four hundred standardized swaps per year â more than one a day. This would include replacing broken or damaged parts, as well as upgrading to the server hardware itself.

Hubble has already been repaired by a crewed mission. NASA wants to do it again, Great Space expliains. Credit - Great Space YouTube Channel

Scaling that up once again to a 1 GW computer cluster, comparable to a major modern AI campus here on Earth, the number becomes staggering. There would have to be 400,000 automated replacement tasks every year. And supplying the parts to do that would require launching up to 25 metric tons of replacement cargo every day.

To put it bluntly, we donât have that kind of launch capacity yet. Nor would sending humans up help manage such a drastic workload. The paper estimates that housing and feeding a crew of 4-6 technicians to actively manage a data center constellation would require $500 million to $1.5 billion per year. Until we get to the scale of several hundred megawatts to a gigawatt-level system, that is not economically feasible.

Thatâs not to say we couldnât launch specialized crewed repair missions occasionally. But at the scales needed to make a dent in the AI infrastructure we have down here on Earth, it would be hard to keep up with the overall maintenance workload using humans. And unfortunately, the entire concept of maintenance is another area that the back-of-the-envelope calculations of the companies that want to build orbital data centers seem to ignore.

Their solution is simply to add some extra hardware to account for the inevitable damage/failure that comes with operating in space. While that might work for a little while, if the plan is to have a long-term data center presence in orbit, it's better to design for at least the possibility of continual operation rather than burning up tens of thousands of satellites in fireballs across the world every year. It remains to be seen if that message will get across to the people designing these systems, though.

Frame TVs are one of the more interesting home theater innovations in recent years, mostly because they prioritize “form” as much as “function.” They take a two-pronged approach: offering high-definition 4K entertainment and decor in one fell swoop. In other words, you can finally get use out of your TV, even when you’re not, well, using it. That’s where the art function comes in.

#6442. Ancient Bison Hunting Site in Texas Challenges Decades of Archaeological Assumptions

Evidence of communal bison hunts spanning 3,000 years in Texas offers a fascinating glimpse into the enduring knowledge and ingenuity of ancient Indigenous hunter-gatherers.

For Indigenous hunter-gatherers in the Southern Plains, a successful large-scale bison hunt likely depended on people performing different jobs across the landscape. Some hunters located herds and guided them toward grazing areas near a cliff, while others waited in hiding to drive the animals over the edge, where the fall would kill or incapacitate them. Additional teams would have killed injured bison and processed the meat, hides, and other materials.

Archaeologists have now uncovered evidence that generations of Indigenous communities carried out such hunts at the same location in the Texas Panhandle over approximately 3,000 years. Known as Nighthawk, the site lies within Caprock Canyons State Park and is only the second scientifically verified example of a bison jump in Texas. For decades, archaeologists had questioned whether this sophisticated hunting technique, widely documented in the northern Great Plains, was also practiced farther south.

The findings, published in the journal American Antiquity, come from a collaborative investigation involving the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department, Texas Tech University, Plains Archeological Research, and other research partners. Rice University adjunct lecturer August “Gus” Costa served as a principal investigator and is the study’s lead author.

“Bison jumping is exciting because it’s a community activity,” Costa said. “Large-scale bison harvests (like jumps) are exciting because they require a large group of people working together to be successful.”

These gatherings likely fulfilled needs beyond securing food and other resources. Costa believes the hunts provided opportunities for communities to trade, hold ceremonies, celebrate, and strengthen social relationships.

Initially, stone spear and arrow points recovered at Nighthawk suggested that at least two hunts had taken place there. Radiocarbon dating of bison bones revealed a much longer history, identifying evidence of at least seven separate hunting events spanning approximately three millennia.

During that time, hunting technology shifted from stone-tipped spears to bows and arrows, pottery was introduced, and the surrounding landscape underwent substantial changes. Erosion alone moved the cliff’s jump-off point roughly the length of a football field.

“Returning to the same place over and over again over 3,000 years shows that people had a significant connection to the Nighthawk hunting facility,” Costa said.

The shape of the landscape also presents an intriguing problem. At many northern Plains bison jumps, the terrain may have concealed the cliff edge from approaching animals. Nighthawk, however, sits on a projecting cliff, meaning the bison could likely see the danger ahead. How hunters adapted their methods to overcome this difficulty remains unknown.

“We don’t know exactly how they managed herding the bison, but the setting is different from the typical northern Plains jump,” Costa said.

Before Nighthawk was documented, Bonfire Shelter, identified more than 60 years ago, was the only scientifically verified bison jump in Texas. Costa and his colleagues have since identified eight additional potential sites in and around Caprock Canyons, suggesting that the practice may have been considerably more widespread.

Part of the difficulty in finding these sites lies in where archaeologists traditionally look. Investigations often concentrate on former living areas, where people left tools and other traces of daily life. Steep slopes beneath cliffs would have made poor campsites and consequently received less attention. Erosion and limited access to private property have further complicated the search.

“The jump was hidden in plain sight,” Costa said.

With fieldwork at Nighthawk complete, the researchers are searching for additional sites across the Southern Plains. They are also examining ancient bison DNA and the chemical composition of bones and teeth to reconstruct herd migrations, understand past environmental conditions, and investigate possible connections to the bison living in Caprock Canyons State Park today.

“For a long time when it comes to Indigenous bison hunting culture, the Southern Plains hasn’t received much respect, at least when compared to the north,” Costa said.

For Costa, the discovery illustrates the danger of judging ancient societies solely by the evidence that happens to survive. Gaps in the archaeological record can obscure generations of accumulated knowledge, ingenuity, and cultural practices.

“It’s about respect,” Costa said. “Bison jumping is a complicated community effort, and getting that incorporated into the story of Southern Plains people is important.”

Reference: “The Nighthawk Bison Jump: New Evidence for Recurrent Late Holocene Bison Jumping in the Southern Plains” by August G. Costa, Brett A. Houk, Anthony S. Lyle, Leland Bement, Christopher Lintz, Ken L. Lawrence, Charles D. Frederick and Brendan J. Culleton, 9 November 2026, American Antiquity. DOI: 10.1017/aaq.2026.10229

First the wolves skirt around edges of the bison herd, building tension, restricting movement, fomenting internal strife, preventing herd coalescence. Then, when the wolves sense the moment is right, they launch a series of targeted attacks, skirmishes if you will, to provoke the herd to panic. A stunning new image from the Gemini North telescope captures two spiral galaxies caught in each other's gravity, helping to trigger the birth of new stars.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

What it is: NGC 7253 (also called Arp 278), a pair of interacting spiral galaxies

Where it is: 200 million light-years away, in the constellation Pegasus

Picture a spiral galaxy, and you'll probably imagine a swirl of stars. But some galaxies appear to be the complete opposite. One is NGC 7253, which looks more like a bizarre balloon animal than a cosmic coil. In reality, it's two spiral galaxies caught in each other's gravity. As shown in this recent image from the Gemini North telescope on Mauna Kea in Hawaii, the galaxies' once-ordered shapes are being disturbed and disrupted as their mutual gravitational pull stretches and distorts their spiral arms into a tangled arrangement of stars, gas and dust. It sounds and looks chaotic and destructive, but encounters between galaxies don't mean stars are physically colliding; the distances between individual stars are too great. Instead, something extraordinarily productive can happen.

Spiral galaxies contain huge clouds of cold gas and dust, particularly within their arms. When galaxies interact, gravitational forces can disturb and compress those clouds. If enough material is squeezed together and becomes dense enough to collapse under its own gravity, it can produce bursts of new star formation.

Evidence of just that can be seen in this image. Scattered through the galaxies are concentrations of bright pink light. These are H II regions — enormous clouds of hydrogen gas energized by intense ultraviolet radiation from hot, young stars.

The gravitational encounter is rearranging two structures containing billions of stars while simultaneously helping to create new ones. These interactions radically alter the shapes of the galaxies involved and, in time, can ultimately cause them to merge into a single galaxy. For now, NGC 7253 is listed as Arp 278 in the Atlas of Peculiar Galaxies, a catalog of galaxies that are neither perfectly symmetrical spirals nor smooth, spherical ellipticals.

The new image has another story much closer to Earth. It's just been given the Hawaiian name Nā 'Uhane Māhoe Huki Pū i ke Ola, meaning "The Twin Spirits Pulling Together Creating Life." Hawaii high school students participating in the 2026 Project Hōkūlani internship program chose the name. One reason was its position within Ka Lupe o Kawelo, the Hawaiian constellation corresponding to Pegasus.

The "twin spirits" represent both the two galaxies and the twin telescopes of the Gemini Observatory — one in Hawaii and the other in Chile.

#6440. Detection of Vaporized Rock Reveals the Birth of a Solar System

Astronomers have detected titanium oxide in gas form for the first time around a young, massive star. The detection offers a rare glimpse into the very earliest stages of solar system formation, before the formation of planets and asteroids.

The detection was made around a young protostar called Orion Source I, which lies some 1500 light-years from Earth. Orion Source I has not yet reached the main sequence phase of a starâs life cycle â it continues to accrete material from its surrounding molecular cloud.

Models of solar system formation have long held that certain rocky molecules, ones which are stable at high temperatures, act as the âseedsâ that make up the dust in a protoplanetary disk, and later form the basis for rocky planets like Earth and Mars. This includes elements like calcium, aluminum, and titanium. Only later do materials that vaporize easily â volatiles like water, for example â accrete to young solar system objects.

But itâs not exactly clear where these seeds form. Samples collected from our own solar system suggest that they form under high-temperature conditions. They are, as far as we can tell, the oldest solids ever formed in our solar system.

Now, for the first time, this detection of titanium oxide around Orion Source I is providing astronomers more direct evidence of vaporized rock at the dawn of a new star system.

âWe're in a unique situation with this object, Orion Source I,â said Adam Ginsburg, Associate Professor at the University of Florida and a co-author on the paper announcing the discovery. âThis object has a luminous enough star that it's evaporating the rock. We're seeing the rock evaporate from solid into gas, and so we can do the spectroscopy now and figure out what the rock is made of.â

Ginsberg and his coauthors are getting the first real glimpses at the formation environments of these rocky dust-seeding materials, which complements knowledge gathered from our own solar system.

âThe exciting thing is we're seeing the titanium oxide; we can measure how much there is, and we can start comparing our measurements to how our own solar system formed,â Ginsburg said. âIn our solar system, we can measure the ratios between different types of rocks, different elements, because we can grab those rocks and bring them into a lab.â

This isnât the first time Orion Source I has provided valuable insights into solar system formation. In 2019, salty compounds were similarly detected in the protoplanetary disk.

While the salt was found mainly in the outer disk around the star, the titanium oxide was found closer in, at the base of the starâs outflow of material: a hotter, more extreme region where the material could be vaporized. Understanding the origin of this material is an important discovery for researchers trying to piece together exactly how a new solar system comes together, and offers a glimpse into the past of our own star and rocky neighbourhood.

The detection was published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters in 2026.

#6438. AI Helps Three Powerful Supercomputers Simulate The Milky Way In Extraordinary Detail

In the early days, astronomers kept sketchbooks close at hand when they looked through their telescopes. They drew what they saw and shared their drawings. Modern astronomy, with its enormous segmented lenses, gigabyte cameras, and cryogenically-cooled infrared space observatories, makes those days seem more distant than they really are. But one of the latest efforts in astronomy makes astronomy's sketch-pad days seem so far in the past, they're almost red-shifted.

In an impressive technological maneuver, astronomers have harnessed three different supercomputers together to simulate the Milky Way at a level of detail never before achieved. They used the supercomputers and AI together to simulate the Milky Way down to the level of individual stars. Up until now, the smallest level of detail in simulations, called particles, was clusters of stars with the mass of about 100 Suns. The behaviour of individual stars was averaged out in those simulations (Auriga, FIRE, etc.)

These results are in a paper titled "Architecture-Agnostic Exascale Star-by-Star Simulation of Our Galaxy," from the SC26: International Conference for High Performance Computing, Networking, Storage and Analysis. The lead author is Keiya Hirashima, from RIKEN in Japan.

In simulations, achieving a level of individual stars means that individually simulated particles have one solar mass. So it's like a proxy for the population of stars. But regardless of that important distinction, the new simulations are extraordinary.

"Our highest-resolution Milky Way simulation used 5.4 trillion particles, â¼ 10, 000Ã those in the state-of-the-art simulations," the authors write.

âWe expect better simulations as computational power increases, but this still requires work on improving resolutions, and for a Milky Way-sized galaxy, itâs not straightforward,â said Professor Michiko Fujii from the Department of Astronomy at the University of Tokyo. âWhen we look at smaller regions in detail, we encounter areas where the gas is denser and changes rapidly. This means the simulation needs to take much shorter steps in time, which greatly increases the amount of calculation required."

This figure from the paper shows different structures of disk galaxies at different scales, emphasizing the complexity necessary for accurate simulations. Top left and middle: NGC 4414, a disk galaxy similar to the Milky Way Galaxy, taken with the Hubble Space Telescope. Top right: NGC628, a disk galaxy with spiral arms and bubble structures taken with the JWST. Bottom left: Carina star forming region taken with the JWST. Bottom middle: Cassiopeia A supernova remnant taken with the JWST. Bottom right: turbulent innterstellar gas around Cassiopeia A taken with Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer. Image Credit: Hirashima et al. 2026. SC2026.

To achieve this fine particle resolution, simulations need ever shorter time steps, and time steps are like simulation currency; the shorter they are, the more computing resources they demand. To supply the resources for that, the researchers harnessed the power of three exascale supercomputers together: Aurora, Frontier, and JUPITER. Each one ran the same software on different hardware: Intel, NVIDIA, and AMD graphic processing units (GPUs) and central processing units (CPUs).

But linking three supercomputers was only part of the solution.

"We overcame this problem by using an AI model to predict how gas around supernova explosions evolves," said Fujii. "This allowed us to carry out the simulation more efficiently and achieve a level of detail where individual stars can be represented."

By using this model, the larger simulation was able to skip over many small timesteps. It's called PHEASANT, and it was developed by postdoctoral researcher Keiya Hirashima from RIKEN. Supernovae are complex and require their own detailed simulations with very small timesteps. By plugging PHEASANT into the larger simulation, it relieved that simulation of a lot of work.

"With trillions of particles, we resolve individual stars and model their SN feedback self-consistently within a galactic-scale simulation," the authors write. "Such a simulation reveals how individual stars, such as the Sun, contribute to the overall structure of the MW through multiple physical processes."

This image from PHEASANT shows the Milky Way's disk. Galaxies are complex structures, with different types of structures at different scales. They have thin and thick disks, bulges, halos, spiral arms, star clusters, nebulae, and individual stars and gas clouds. In this work, the researchers divided the galaxy into smaller regions that could be processed by different parts of a supercomputer. Â©2026 PHEASANT/Hirashima/Fujii CC-BY-ND

âOne of my parts was to develop an AI model that predicts how the gas surrounding a supernova explosion changes over time. If we calculate this process directly, we need time steps of around 100 years,â said Hirashima. âMy model predicts gas distribution after 100,000 years. This means that, rather than having to calculate every small step, we can use a much longer time step for the entire galaxy simulation. Making this work efficiently on different supercomputers was a challenge because each system uses different AMD, Intel, or NVIDIA CPUs and GPUs. Achieving good performance across all three systems required some specific optimizations.â

These panels are snapshots from PHEASANT. The panel on the left shows the distribution and temperature of gas across a model galaxy. The panel on the right is a close-up view, where individual stars are visible as dots. Image Credit: Â©2026 PHEASANT/Hirashima/Fujii CC-BY-ND

We can't understand the Milky Way, or galaxies in general, without a detailed understanding of how its gas and stars behave. Stars are born, drift away from their clusters, and evolve. Depending on their masses, they can remain on the main sequence for trillions of years, leave the main sequence after a few billion years and then linger as white dwarf cinders, or exhaust their fuel rapidly and explode as supernovae.

Gas is also complex. It collects in clouds where stars form, can be funnelled into the galactic center and "recycled" by supermassive black holes, or blasted away by explosions. Stars and gas are linked, and there's an extraordinary amount of detail involved.

Supernovae are among the most complicated events. In some regions, the massive young stars that eventually explode as supernova are born in the same region. When they exhaust their fuel, they explode and carve massive bubbles in the interstellar medium. That can drive gas away to form more new stars elsewhere. They can even propel gas outside of the galaxy. It's all part of the life of the Milky Way, and simulations that struggle to recreate all of the detail in supernova explosions can lead astronomers astray.

This is LHA 120-N44 (N44) in the Large Magellanic Cloud, imaged by the ESO's Very Large Telescope. It features a massive bubble excavated in the interstellar medium by exploding young stars in its center. Some of the stars are still there, and they're still expanding the bubble with their powerful winds. Simulating all of the complexity involved is an enormous challenge. Image Credit: ESO/Manu Mejias

âSomething we want to understand is how events on the scale of individual stars connect to the larger structure of the Milky Way,â said Fujii. âWith this simulation, we can investigate how individual supernovae affect the number of stars that form, the size of these giant gas bubbles and the material that flows out of the galaxy. We can also study how groups of stars form and how they may eventually develop into star clusters.â

The PHEASANT AI surrogate model plays a critical role in this work, and that's part of a broader trend in science.

"The surrogate modeling approach can also be generalized beyond astrophysical problems to other research fields," the authors write.

"AI surrogate modeling accelerates simulations and bridges wider physical scales, opening new pathways in various real-world applications, including climate modeling, space forecasting, and low-temperature plasma," the authors conclude.

#6437. Alzheimer’s Breakthrough? Experimental Nose Drops Restore Youthful Memory in Mice

Experimental nose drops helped mice with signs of Alzheimer’s hold on to their memory, even though the treatment left the brain’s telltale protein clumps in place.

What if some of the memory loss associated with aging could be reversed with something as simple as nose drops?

Scientists at the University of Sydney have taken a promising step toward that possibility, developing an experimental treatment that restored learning and memory performance in older mice to levels comparable to those of younger animals. The same approach also protected mice genetically predisposed to Alzheimer’s-like disease from cognitive decline.

Both experiments centered on brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), a protein that helps nerve cells survive and adjust their connections as memories form. Lower levels of BDNF are associated with aging and Alzheimer’s disease. Supplying the brain with more of the protein poses a familiar problem. The blood-brain barrier keeps many medicines in the bloodstream from reaching brain tissue. Connections between the nasal cavity and the brain offer another way in, without surgery or injections into the brain or spinal cord.

“If we can proceed quickly to clinical trials in humans, this approach could represent a world-first non-invasive delivery system to treat Alzheimer’s that bypasses the blood-brain barrier,” said Professor Greg Neely, whose lab at the university’s Charles Perkins Centre led the study.

The researchers adapted the clinically validated design of the messenger RNA (mRNA) used in BioNTech’s COVID-19 vaccine, where it carries instructions that prompt an immune response. For the nose drops, the team packaged mRNA carrying instructions for BDNF in tiny particles made of fats, called lipid nanoparticles (LNPs). As the researchers reported in Advanced Science, cells in the nose read those instructions and made the protein, which could then reach the brain.

“The success of mRNA vaccines showed these systems can safely deliver genetic instructions to cells,” said first author Dr. Maria Bergamasco of the university’s School of Life and Environmental Sciences. “We wanted to see whether we could adapt that technology to deliver beneficial proteins to the brain in a completely non-invasive way.”

To compare older and younger mice, the researchers used standardized behavioral tests that measured how well the animals could hold information in mind briefly, remember places, and recognize objects.

“In aged mice, we saw learning and memory significantly increased, returning animal cognition to its youthful prime,” Neely said. “What’s exciting is that this was achieved with a simple non-invasive nasal delivery system that builds on the same underlying mRNA-LNP technology platform many people became familiar with during the COVID-19 pandemic.”

For the Alzheimer’s experiment, the team used 5XFAD mice, a “humanized” model in which genetic mutations cause signs of the disease to appear rapidly. The researchers gave the mice nose drops twice a week starting at two months of age, when the first changes in the brain are usually detectable. At four months, when these mice typically begin to lose cognitive abilities, the treated animals showed no further decline.

The researchers also saw more new neurons forming in the hippocampus, a brain region critical for learning and memory. In the Alzheimer’s model, the drops preserved brain function without reducing amyloid plaques, the clumps of protein that are a hallmark of the disease.

“Current Alzheimer’s treatments largely focus on clearing these amyloid plaques,” Neely said. “However just under a third of Alzheimer’s patients have serious plaques but do not suffer from dementia, and these patients show naturally higher BDNF levels, suggesting if we raise BDNF, it’s possible to live with Alzheimer’s disease pathology.”

“Our approach seems to work not by clearing plaques but by supporting the health, survival and connectivity of neurons themselves. It raises the possibility these therapies could eventually work alongside each other.”

The researchers think the nasal delivery system could eventually carry medicines for stroke, traumatic brain injury, and rare genetic and developmental diseases. “This is a very exciting proof of concept for a method to deliver mRNA-encoded cargo to the nervous system directly through the nose,” Neely said.

The mice appeared to tolerate the drops well, with no major side effects detected during the study. “Before we can trial this therapy in patients, we need to perform a series of safety studies in animals,” Neely said. “It is a very promising pathway, but human noses are different from mouse noses, so we will need to test our drugs in humans to before we know whether it will work.

“We believe our new drug, if it works in humans, can promote general cognitive health as people age, should help treat a variety of neurodegenerative diseases, and may even increase cognitive abilities in healthy young people.”

The team plans to refine the delivery system and assess its long-term safety and effectiveness. “Based on previous clinical trials, we know the components used in this study to be safe in humans,” Neely said. “We hope we can move quickly through the requisite safety studies and trial this treatment in humans in the next two years.”

Reference: “Bdnf mRNA-LNP Drives Nasal Epithelial BDNF Production and Improves Cognition in Aged and Alzheimer’s Disease Mouse Models” by Maria Bergamasco, Hannah Scarborough, Anna Ponta, Teleri Clark, Scott B. Cohen, Lipin Loo, Kazuma Fujikake, Rebecca Carr, R.M. Damian Holsinger and G.Gregory. Neely, 18 November 2026, Advanced Science. DOI: 10.1002/advs.78225

#6435. Scientists Discover a Unique Gut Microbe Signature in People Who Live to 100

People who lived to 100 carried a distinctive chemical fingerprint in their guts, and boosting the bacterial enzyme linked to it helped older mice respond better to insulin.

A single dose of engineered gut bacteria made older mice more sensitive to insulin about five months later. The UC San Diego team also analyzed data from young adults, older adults, and centenarians to see how the same gut bacterial activity varies with age in people.

The study focused on bile acids, which the liver makes to help digest fats. Bile acids also carry signals that help regulate metabolism, inflammation, and the body’s internal clock. Gut bacteria make enzymes called bile salt hydrolases (BSH) that change the chemical makeup of bile acids and can alter the signals they send.

Older mice showed more microbial activity linked to BSH and more extensive changes to their bile acids than younger mice. The researchers then looked for a similar pattern in existing data from 48 young adults, 107 older adults, and 125 centenarians.

Centenarians had higher ratios of certain modified bile acids than either of the younger groups. Their gut microbiomes also contained more copies of a gene linked to BSH activity than those of older adults.

“Many studies of aging focus on what goes wrong as we get older, but our findings suggest that some changes in the gut microbiome may actually represent the body’s attempt to preserve metabolic health,” said senior author Amir Zarrinpar, MD, PhD, Stuart and Barbara L. Brody Endowed Chair in Circadian Biology and Medicine and professor of medicine at UC San Diego School of Medicine. “If we can identify those beneficial functions and safely strengthen them, we may eventually be able to develop new ways to promote healthier aging.”

To test whether boosting BSH activity could change metabolism, the team gave 82-week-old mice a strain of gut bacteria engineered to keep making the enzyme. The bacteria took hold after one treatment and continued producing BSH over time.

About 20 weeks later, the mice responded significantly better to insulin and were modestly better at clearing glucose from their blood than mice given a matched control bacterium. By week 32, the treated mice also showed changes consistent with lower body weight, less body fat, and more lean mass.

Other measurements suggested that the mice used more fat for energy and that their mitochondria worked better. The researchers also saw shifts in the activity of genes involved in inflammation and the body’s internal clock.

Centenarians and aged mice represent different stages of life, and the mouse experiment did not establish whether the treatment extends lifespan. Studies in people will need to determine whether higher BSH activity helps preserve health with age, reflects healthier aging, or both.

The researchers plan to test how different forms of the enzyme affect bile acid metabolism, inflammation, and energy use. They also want to see whether female mice respond similarly, given known differences in how males and females age.

“The goal isn’t simply to live longer—it’s to understand the biology that allows some people to remain resilient as they age,” said Zarrinpar. “The microbiome gives us an intriguing opportunity because, unlike many aspects of aging, it may be something we can modify. This study gives us a starting point for asking whether beneficial microbial functions can be amplified to help preserve metabolic health later in life.”

Reference: “Microbial bile acid deconjugation counters metabolic decline in aging” by Ana Carolina Dantas Machado, Wuling Zhong, Anand R. Saran, Baylee J. #6434. Slingshot Earth: NASA's Europa Clipper Will Gain Speed and Tests Its Instruments During Its Earth Flyby

NASA's Europa Clipper will soon bid farewell to Earth. On December 3rd, it will conduct its propellant-saving gravity assist maneuver and head for Jupiter. These types of maneuvers are a common part of missions beyond Mars.

Gravity maneuvers can be used to either accelerate or decelerate spacecraft, depending on their desired trajectories. When a mission requires acceleration to the outer Solar System, a spacecraft passes behind a planet's orbital path, and the planet's gravity pulls on it and accelerates it relative to the Sun. The maneuver also changes its trajectory. These maneuvers are the norm for missions beyond Mars.

The relative velocity is illustrative and does not represent Europa Clipper's velocity. Credit: Made with AI.

âWeâre coming down into the gravity well of Earth, following its curve, and shooting out again,â said Robert Pappalardo, Europa Clipperâs project scientist at NASAâs Jet Propulsion Laboratory. âThe spacecraft is able to get pulled by the gravity of the planet and continue on its way â now with a slightly changed trajectory and moving faster than it was before.â

When a mission needs to decelerate into the inner Solar System, the spacecraft passes in front of a planet's orbital path, and the planet's gravity decelerates it relative to the Sun. Bepi-Colombo, for example, relied on multiple gravity-braking maneuvers to slow down enough to orbit Mercury. The Europa Clipper performed one of these earlier in its mission, to set it up for the gravity-assist with Earth.

The relative velocity is illustrative and does not represent Europa Clipper's velocity. Credit: Made with AI.

The Europa Clipper is NASA's largest deep space mission, and this Earth flyby is critical to accelerating it toward Jupiter. So was its gravity braking maneuver at Mars in March, 2025, which slowed it down so it could perform this upcoming flyby of Earth.

The Clipper's closest approach to Earth will be within 3,140 to 3,450 kilometers on December 3rd, above West Africa, at at 3:14 p.m. EST. In Africa and southern Europe, it should be visible in backyard telescopes.

Even though about half of the Clipper's launch mass is propellant, it needs these flybys to complete its mission. The flybys get it to Jupiter, and the spacecraft is conserving its propellant for orbital insertion at Jupiter, the single largest burn of its mission. Jupiter's gravity well is powerful, and even with all of this propellant to place it in orbit, the Clipper will still perform a gravity breaking maneuver at Ganymede hours before insertion to save a little more propellant. It will enter its Jupiter orbit in April 2030.

The flyby of Earth serves another purpose, too: instrument calibration. All 11 of the Europa Clipper's science instruments will be active during the flyby. The mission has nine science teams organized around the 11 instruments, and each team will take the relevant data and compare it to known data about Earth. That will let them calibrate their instruments to a very fine degree.

âWeâre practicing the intricacies of the operation, but weâre also practicing how to work together to produce the best science,â said JPLâs Erin Leonard, Europa Clipper project staff scientist. âThe things we practice now will set us up for success at Europa.â

Since Earth's magnetosphere is so well-understood, this is an especially important opportunity for Clipper to calibrate one of its most important instruments, the Europa Clipper Magnetometer. The central goal of Clipper's mission is to determine if Europa truly does have an ocean under its icy shell, and the magnetometer will be able to do that after multiple flybys. It can also determine the ocean's depth, and even its salinity. It can also help measure the thickness of the icy shell.

This illustration shows what Europa's ocean could be like. Scientist know it has an icy shell, and they know it has a rock core and mantle. There are enticing hints that it has a subsurface ocean, but they aren't sure. Europa will find out. Image Credit: NASA/(Europa Lander Study 2016 Report)

Europa sits inside Jupiter's vast and powerful magnetic field which varies and oscillates as Jupiter revolves and Europa orbits. If Europa has a salty ocean, that will generate a separate magnetic field, because a salty ocean is conductive. The strength and orientation of these fields are always changing. There's also a large body of magnetospheric plasma that co-rotates with Jupiter at its magnetic equator, and its effects need to be accounted for, too. It's like a big, multi-faceted puzzle of magnetic fields that the Clipper's magnetometer is built to solve.

âThe magnetometer measures variations in the magnetic field as weâre orbiting Jupiter, but we need to pin these observations to something we know to understand the actual value that itâs measuring,â Pappalardo said. âThe flyby will enable us to calibrate the instrument absolutely, using its observations at Earth to refine other calibrations done before launch and in flight.â

Measuring Europa's magnetic field is also complicated because the Europa Clipper has its own unavoidable magnetic field. The spacecraft has more than 300 separate magnetic sources that its magnetometer must account for. Those range from magnets used in valves in its propellant system, to electrical current loops from its solar arrays. The magnetometer is mounted on a boom, called the Magboom, as far away from most of these sources as it can get, but it still needs to take them into consideration.

The Europa Clipper's magnetometer isn't its only important instrument. They're all important, or they wouldn't have survived the mission's rigorous design process. They'll all be active during the spacecraft's upcoming Earth flyby.

The E-THEMIS (Europa Clipper Thermal Emission Imaging System) instrument will scan Earth every eight hours as the spacecraft approaches. Its purpose is to find hotspots on Europa's surface where water from its subsurface ocean may be closest to the surface, or even escaped above the ice. Then other remote-sensing instruments will follow up those observations. The MISE (Mapping Imaging Spectrometer for Europa) can examine that water and map its composition.

The Europa-UVS (Europa-Ultraviolet Spectrograph) will also scan Earth during the flyby. It's job is to to study Europa's surface and its atmosphere. It will compare its Earth observations to similar observations from the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbit (LRO). When the Clipper is measuring Earth, the LRO will point at Earth and do the same with one of its instruments. Then the mission team can use both results to calibrate their instrument.

âItâs super-exciting when we actually do get to collect data thatâs really meaningful to the instruments, and get to share it with other people,â Leonard said. âThis is Earth, and everyone understands what that data means. Imagine what itâs going to be able to show you about Europa.â

The Europa Clipper is scheduled for a four-year mission at Jupiter. If there's no mission extension, then it will likely be crashed into Jupiter, Ganymede, or Callisto. NASA doesn't want to risk it crashing into Europa because of potential contamination. In 2022, Pappalardo suggested crashing it into Ganymede, because the ESA's Juice mission, which is also on its way to Jupiter, can observe that crash and use it to learn more about that moon's surface chemistry.

After this upcoming Earth flyby, the Europa Clipper will begin a long cruise phase. Not much happens during these cruise phases, which is good because it means nothing's gone wrong. Barring any significant problems, we may not hear much from the Europa Clipper until it reaches Jupiter in 2030.

Some time after that, we may finally get an answer to a long-burning question: Does Europa have a subsurface ocean with the right environment for life?

Astrophysicists have dared to ask a cosmological question never asked before: Do black holes "wear pants"? New research shows how fast-spinning black holes may split apart.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Black holes are known to collide and combine in monstrously violent merger events, but new research suggests these celestial stalwarts can also fragment into smaller bodies, like a cosmic pair of pants splitting down the middle.

In a paper published Oct. 22 in the journal Physical Review D, researchers used several mathematical modeling methods to propose a "pair-of-pants" topology for black holes. The hypothesis suggests that under extremely specific conditions, these dark behemoths could fragment into numerous less-massive black holes.

"Understanding precisely what is forbidden, what is merely unlikely, and what becomes possible once the assumptions are relaxed is the central goal of this work," the researchers wrote in the paper.

Black hole fragmentation could play into other cosmic mysteries. For example, it could help to explain black holes with masses that are too small to be formed through conventional astrophysical processes. These hypothesized black hole "morsels" would be so small that astronomers could see them evaporating before their eyes on observational timescales.

In the new paper, the researchers explored whether black holes' event horizons — the boundaries beyond which nothing, not even light, can escape — could split under various cosmological conditions. These situations included classical four-dimensional general relativity (Einstein's description of our large-scale universe as we currently understand it) as well as cosmologically esoteric frameworks such as higher-dimensional space-time and modified gravity scenarios.

But modeling black hole dynamics, especially the split of an event horizon, is messy work. So the researchers simplified it by comparing discrete slices of space-time, effectively condensing the fragmentation process into static snapshots from before and after the split.

In our classical cosmos, it seems mostly impossible for black holes to split, the researchers found, but they did identify a loophole that might allow it to happen.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The "pair-of-pants" topology for the fragmentation of a black hole.

The first impediment is entropy, the possible arrangements of an isolated system's energy, which cannot spontaneously decrease but only stay the same or increase. This has been theorized by Stephen Hawking and recently demonstrated through detections of ripples in space-time called gravitational waves, suggesting that a black hole's surface area cannot decrease.

For these reasons, splitting a static Schwarzschild black hole — the simplest type of black hole in our four-dimensional general relativity — would be strictly forbidden because it would violate the second law of thermodynamics.

The second impediment is kinematics, the motion of orbital dynamics, which precludes the possibility of a permanent split because the black hole fragments would recombine into a single body incredibly quickly.

But there is a loophole: A rapidly rotating black hole could literally spin itself apart.

"This is why, in four-dimensional general relativity, an isolated black hole in empty space could only split if it spins very close to the maximum rate the theory allows, what we call a near-extremal black hole," study co-author Manuel Del Piano, a theoretical physicist at the University of Southern Denmark, told Live Science via email. "Loosely speaking, the equator of the horizon is then dragged around at nearly the speed of light."

Through this theoretical process, the two resultant black hole fragments could be gravitationally slingshotted away from each other before they could recombine. So under conventional space-time conditions, it seems "black holes do not wear pants."

Then, the researchers mathematically modeled black hole fragmentation in versions of space-time with more than four dimensions.

In models of higher-dimension space-times, a black hole's rotational velocity is no longer limited because gravity weakens with increasing dimensionality. Therefore, any such ultrafast spinning black holes could theoretically fragment, the researchers explained in the paper.

A diagram from the new study illustrating the theoretical pants-splitting method.

In the "black string" model, a normally spherical black hole would become cylindrical or string-like, stretching across any extra dimensions. It could then pinch off to fragment into multiple smaller bodies, akin to "beads on a string."

Additionally, the researchers calculated that black hole fragmentation may be entropically favored in space-time models with modified gravity, which alter the gravitational interactions in extremely warped environments near the black hole.

"The fragments are tiny, though: in one of our benchmarks, a black hole of ten solar masses would favour fragments … a few times the mass of the Great Pyramid of Giza squeezed into a region smaller than a proton, and the heavier the parent, the smaller the fragments," Del Piano explained.

Fragmentation also may be more likely if there is a "bumpy horizon" around black holes, akin to a dense blanket or shroud of exotic matter that acts as a singular-but-gigantic quantum entity. The superfluid qualities of this matter could create strange vortices that eventually cause a black hole to fragment into multiple smaller bodies.

Scientists might see a black hole decrease in size, an actual fragmentation, or simply an indirect gravitational signature, depending on the dimensions and whether it intersects the viewer's "brane," or slice of dimensionality.

The researchers expect that smaller objects — like the hypothesized, miniature primordial back holes that may have formed shortly after the Big Bang — are more likely to split, compared with much more massive astrophysical black holes such as those at the centers of galaxies.

"Overall, we expect small black holes, such as primordial ones from the early universe, to be the most prone to splitting," Del Piano told Live Science.

Gamma-ray telescopes or gravitational wave observatories may one day offer evidence of a signal associated with the supposed split of a small black hole, but the specifics, including whether this actually occurs, are uncertain.

"One important caveat: our analysis shows when splitting is allowed by entropy and conservation laws, not that it actually happens," Del Piano noted. "As we put it in the paper, a shattered glass has more entropy than an intact one, yet glasses don't shatter on their own. Settling the question requires full dynamical simulations, which is the natural next step."

Cacciapaglia, G., Del Piano, M., Sannino, F., & Vellucci, V. (2026). When black holes admit pair-of-pants topologies. Physical Review. D/Physical Review. D., 114(8). https://doi.org/10.1103/cx69-t466

#6431. Scientists Develop a Powerful Two-in-One Treatment for Gum Disease

Gum disease can eat away at the bone that holds teeth in place, and a tiny cage made of DNA helped slow that damage in rats.

Researchers at Sichuan University built a DNA carrier that delivers two compounds together to treat periodontitis, a chronic form of gum disease and a leading cause of tooth loss in adults. The team, led by Geru Zhang, Yunfeng Lin, and Xiaoxiao Cai, published its findings in the International Journal of Oral Science.

Periodontitis starts when bacterial plaque builds up beneath the gums. The resulting immune response can gradually destroy the tissue and bone that anchor teeth. Deep cleaning and antibiotics can reduce the number of bacteria, but they may leave existing damage unrepaired and do not always stop the disease from progressing.

“We aimed to create a multifunctional DNA nanoplatform capable of delivering both curcumin and the antimicrobial peptide defensin directly to periodontal tissues, with the goal of overcoming the limitations of existing therapies,” Zhang said.

The team loaded both compounds into tiny, four-sided DNA structures called tetrahedral framework nucleic acids (tFNAs). The researchers tested the resulting complex, called Cur-de-tFNA, against bacteria linked to periodontitis and used a bacterial molecule to trigger inflammation in human periodontal ligament stem cells (PDLSCs) in the lab.

“The DNA carrier enhanced the stability and cellular uptake of curcumin while protecting defensin from degradation, allowing both therapeutic agents to function more effectively,” Lin said.

In lab tests, the combined treatment outperformed its individual components across several experiments. It acted against bacteria linked to gum disease, reduced oxidative stress, and dampened an inflammatory signaling pathway called TLR4/NF-κB. It also increased levels of proteins involved in bone formation.

In rats with periodontitis, the treatment reduced bone loss and inflammatory damage around the teeth. The researchers observed less activity from cells that break down bone, along with more collagen deposition and new bone formation. “As a result, the nanoplatform delivered stronger antimicrobial activity, better control of inflammation, and improved preservation of periodontal tissues in preclinical models,” Cai said.

The biodegradable DNA carrier was well tolerated in preclinical tests. Human trials are needed to determine whether the treatment is safe and can help preserve or rebuild the tissues that support teeth.

Reference: “DNA framework-based nanomedicine platform: a triple-function strategy for treating periodontitis via antibacterial, anti-inflammatory, and osteogenesis-promoting activities” by Geru Zhang, Weitong Cui, Haoyan Wu, Xiaowei Liu, Liwei Huang, Yunfeng Lin and Xiaoxiao Cai, 29 April 2026, International Journal of Oral Science. DOI: 10.1038/s41368-026-00439-2

#6429. Astronomers Discover a Hidden Binary in a Star System Used to Calibrate the JWST

When observatories like the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) conduct observation campaigns, they often start by observing star fields to calibrate their instruments. These stars must have precisely characterized spectra so that their radiant energy (or fluxes) can be measured accurately. However, some stars that appear as single objects have a binary companion that has not been resolved, altering their predicted stellar flux. In fact, a star that is used for JWST calibration (HD 158485), which was thought to be an A-type star, has been identified as a binary system.

The discovery was made by a team from the Xinjiang Astronomical Observatory of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS), who found the binary while reviewing long-term observations from NASA's Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS). Their study, published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, provides the first orbital solution and dynamical mass ratio for the system. HD 158485 is an example of a pulsating, variable, or Delta (Î´) Scuti star, which experiences brightness changes at a regular frequency (typically every 18 minutes to 8 hours)

From the TESS data, the team noticed that HD 158485 was pulsing in six distinct rhythms, otherwise known as Î´ Scuti pulsation modes. They further noticed that these pulses fell into two groups with opposing light-travel-time variations, meaning that the light from these pulses reached Earth at different times. This could only be explained by the presence of a binary companion. The team used the variation between the two signals to trace the star's orbital motion with HD 158485, which showed that they orbit each other every 382.8 days.

Pulsation timing results for HD 158485. The two groups of pulsation modes show opposite time delays, revealing the orbital motion of both stars. Credit: Chenglong, LV et al. (2026).

The data also allowed them to constrain the orbital parameters and the star's mass. According to their calculations, the companion has an eccentricity of 0.242, indicating a moderately elongated, closed elliptical orbit, and is about 80% as massive as its primary - making it a likely F-type (yellow-white) main-sequence star. Their findings are independently confirmed by an orbital model built from earlier TESS data, which accurately predicted the timing variations that were detected by a separate observation campaign.

The team further compared a two-star atmosphere model with a conventional single-star model using the system's mass ratio, which showed a flux difference of about 1.6% between one and five micrometers (Î¼m), and 2.5% between five and 28 Î¼m. These findings could have significant implications where JWST calibration is concerned. While they do not represent a measured error, they do show how mistaking a binary system for a single star can shift predicted fluxes, thus throwing off readings.

In essence, the team's results show that stellar pulsations can reveal binaries that conventional observations leave unresolved. It also underscores the need to account for hidden stellar companions when evaluating calibration standards for our instruments.

Further Reading: Chinese Academy of Sciences

#6428. I’ve Tested Vacuums for Years. These Are the 6 Best Cordless Stick Vacs Under $300, Ranked.

Clean hardwood, carpet, pet hair, and everything in between for less.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

The most powerful cordless stick vacuums will easily run you $500 or more, but in my experience, there are plenty of capable cleaners under $300. They may not rival the suction power, battery life, or features of their higher-priced counterparts, but many are perfectly capable of keeping up with typical household messes on hardwood, carpet, and every surface in between.

I’ve spent years testing vacuums for Popular Mechanics, and that experience informs a lot of my recommendations below. Some of these models have been through my own series of hands-on tests, while others made the cut based on my familiarity with their brands and product lines, along with research into their features and real-world performance. From budget-friendly everyday cleaners to options for pet owners, these are the best cordless vacuums that deliver the most for under $300.

The Shark PowerDetect is a feature-packed option for anyone who wants a cordless stick vacuum that does a lot of the thinking for them. The Detect mode automatically adjusts suction based on floor type and amount of debris, and a dual-roller floor head tackles tough messes on hardwood and carpet.

The hinged wand is great for cleaning under furniture and makes it a lot easier to reach hidden areas without having to bend down at all kinds of weird angles. It’s on the heavier side, and the long recharge time is a drawback, but strong pickup and smart features make it a good pick for whole-home cleaning.

Don’t let the price fool you: The Bissell PowerClean FurFinder is a strong and versatile cordless vacuum. It isn’t too heavy to carry between rooms, and the self-standing design means you don’t have to remount it or lay it flat any time you need to pause during your cleaning session.

It has a tangle-free brush roll that does a great job picking up pet hair (as well as your own stray strands around the house). I also like the LED headlights that show hidden dirt, dust, and debris on floors and furniture. The attachments are great for above-floor cleaning, too. Battery life drops considerably when you crank up the suction power, so it’s best for maintenance cleaning.

The LVAC-300 packs cleaning power and everyday convenience into a lightweight machine. It’s easy to maneuver, and it transitions between hard floors, rugs, and low- to medium-pile carpet without scattering debris all over the floor. The tangle-resistant brush roll is a major pro for homes with pets or long hair, and five-stage filtration and washable filters are valuable additions.

It converts to a handheld vacuum cleaner with attachments for upholstery, stairs, and car interiors, and it uses a pleated mechanical HEPA filter with a dense arrangement of fibers to capture even the tiniest dust particles. The smaller dustbin and shorter runtime on max power might negatively impact your overall experience using this vacuum, but still, it’s versatile enough to take care of a variety of common household messes.

The Tineco Pure One Station 5 is the sibling to the Station 5 Pro that I’ve tested and still use to this day. And luckily, this more affordable model doesn’t cut key features that I love, such as the self-emptying and self-cleaning bagless docking station and green laser light for dust detection.

This model also has HEPA filtration and smart features. Internal sensors detect dust and adjust suction accordingly, and the anti-tangle brush roll helps prevent hair buildup. You get a shorter runtime with this model than you do with the Pro (estimated 70 minutes compared to the Pro’s 100), but the automated cleaning capability is hard to beat.

The Dyson V8 is right at the edge of our $300 budget, but it’s a powerful option for homes with lots of carpeting or area rugs. I haven’t tried this specific model yet, but the motorbar floor cleaner is the same design that comes with other Dyson vacuums I’ve tried, such as the Dyson V15 Detect. It works well for hard floors, but I’ve found it particularly useful for dislodging embedded hair and debris from carpet fibers.

The V8 comes with three attachments and converts into a handheld vacuum if you need more portability. Runtime is on the lower end for Dyson, but if you’re looking for a premium design without the premium price tag, the V8 is it.

The Eureka ReactiSense 440 offers a number of features that make vacuuming less of a chore. It has dust detection sensors, automatic suction adjustment, floor head lights, and an anti-tangle brush roll with fins and a comb strip to prevent hair from getting wrapped around it.

I like that this model uses HEPA filtration to capture up to 99.7 percent of airborne particles and odors (which is great if you’re a pet owner). This model is lightweight and portable, converts to a handheld, and provides up to 60 minutes of runtime. Battery life will likely vary if you’re regularly cleaning at high power levels, but I’d reach for this vacuum for daily maintenance cleaning and quick pickups.

#6427. A Black Hole Smaller Than an Atom Could Trigger One of the Universe’s Most Violent Explosions

An ancient black hole no larger than an atom could consume a star from within and eventually trigger a spectacular explosion. New simulations by physicists at MIT and collaborating institutions suggest that these events could produce detectable bursts of radiation, offering a possible way to discover black holes formed shortly after the Big Bang.

The findings, published in The Astrophysical Journal, could also help scientists investigate dark matter, the invisible substance that makes up most of the universe’s matter.

Primordial black holes may have formed when exceptionally dense regions collapsed under gravity during the first fraction of a second after the Big Bang. The smallest would have evaporated through Hawking radiation, but heavier examples could survive today. Some might be as small as an atom yet contain the mass of an asteroid (or about a millionth of the mass of the Earth).

The researchers investigated what would happen if one of these black holes encountered a Sun-like star. Although a star’s gravity alone would not capture a passing black hole, interactions involving a companion star or planet could trap it. Repeated passages through the star would gradually reduce its orbital energy, allowing it to settle into the stellar core over thousands to millions of years.

“Then, this is where the action begins,” says lead author Ore Gottlieb, an assistant professor of physics at MIT.

The team’s three-dimensional simulations suggest that a captured black hole could grow by consuming stellar material. Within several million years, it might absorb approximately 1 percent of the star’s mass. If the star rotates fast enough, the remaining gas would form a spinning disk around the black hole.

“Inside the star, you have a black hole with a disk,” Gottlieb says. “The black hole is also spinning, and it’s twisting space and time.”

As material spirals inward, the black hole would twist magnetic fields in the surrounding disk, generating powerful jets capable of tearing through the star.

“Once the disk forms, this is essentially a death sentence for the star,” Gottlieb says.

“This twisted magnetic field will power very strong electromagnetic jets from the poles of the black hole,” Gottlieb explains. “And these jets will just explode the star, within a few dozen seconds. It’s very fast. Once you have a disk, you are done.”

The resulting explosion could produce a brilliant flash of blue and ultraviolet light, along with X-rays and gamma rays. As the event evolves, its emissions would shift across the electromagnetic spectrum.

“We would initially detect some X-rays and gamma rays, then over time optical and infrared emissions, and later on radio emissions,” Gottlieb says. “This is something we could potentially detect, if it’s not happening too far from us. It could be many galaxies away, not just in our backyard.”

Other cosmic explosions can produce similar signals, so astronomers would need additional evidence to identify a primordial black hole. One possible clue would be an explosion involving a star that would not normally be expected to explode.

“For instance, if the star is a certain mass that is not supposed to explode, it must be something that is happening inside that is a sort of parasite that is consuming the star from the inside,” Gottlieb says.

No primordial black hole has yet been confirmed through this mechanism, but the predicted signals could guide future observations.

“There is hope for us to probe primordial black holes through interactions with stars,” Gottlieb says. “We expect this to be visible, and it’s something we should look into.”

“The broader impact is that we can now place constraints on primordial black holes, and their contributions to dark matter, using observations.”

Reference: “The Life and Death of Stars that Capture Primordial Black Holes” by Ore Gottlieb, Matteo Cantiello, Cameron Norton, Ken Van Tilburg and Matthew Kleban, 19 November 2026, The Astrophysical Journal. DOI: 10.3847/1538-4357/aeb7e1

This work was supported, in part, by the U.S. Department of Energy Office of Science Advanced Scientific Computing Research Program, and by the National Science Foundation.

While scientists continue to work with theories, models and simulations, trying to find ways to prove dark matter, I’ve been performing and uploading online videos of cheaply and easily replicated experiments that demonstrate through gravity intensification through rotation/spin that dark matter is not needed to explain observations of stars revolving around their suns more rapidly than expected in the outer regions of spiral galaxies. Even my most recent ad-free video (https://odysee.com/@charlesgshaver:d/5Gravity:c) is more than a year old now. To try to preempt another comment that a published professional peer reviewed study is necessary for scientific acceptance of my lay findings, I’m resorting to paraphrasing an old adage: “A successful demonstration video is worth a thousand professional peer reviews.”

#6425. Should Space Data Centers Run on Solar Panels, Nuclear Reactors, or Both?

The last few days weâve been covering a series of papers by Dr. Slava Turyshev of NASAâs Jet Propulsion Laboratory about the constraints surrounding the use of orbital data centers in space. One that has come up repeatedly is weight, and the solar panels used to power these data centers contribute a significant portion of that weight. So why not go with an alternative power source? Nuclear energy in space applications is having a bit of a moment currently â maybe it could provide the power needed for the orbital data center revolution? According to another paper from Dr. Turyshev, released as a preprint on arXiv, it all depends on the mission requirements.

One major problem with using solar panels for orbital data centers is the Sun doesnât always shine in their orbit. During some seasons, each orbital pass will result in the satellite crossing over the Earthâs shadow for up to 21 minutes. And given that the orbits these data centers are on happen around 15 times each day, that means in a 24-hour day, the satellite spends around 5 hours and 13 minutes in the Earth's shadow.

To combat this problem, engineers turn to an obvious solution â batteries. But they are notorious for being heavy, and according to Dr. Turyshevâs calculations, providing enough storage capacity to combat a 21-minute stretch with no power, would require a 1 MW data center cluster to haul 6.46 metric tons of batteries into orbit. Combine that with the needed solar panels and radiators to get rid of waste heat as infrared light, and you end up with a total mass of 43 metric tons for a 1 MW cluster, even before counting any actual computing hardware.

Fraser talks about the potential of a nuclear reactor in space.

A fission reactor would eliminate the need for solar wings, as well as batteries. However, it doesnât really deal well with the other physical constraint on these systems â waste heat. While it eliminates the heat generated by the solar panels themselves, it introduces another engineering problem â getting rid of the heat at two different temperatures.

Running a nuclear fission reactor at 25% efficiency (which is pretty standard for thermal electrical conversion) would produce about 3 megawatts of conversion waste heat for every one megawatt of energy generated, meaning a one-megawatt computing cluster creates nearly four megawatts of ultra-hot waste heat from its power conversion machinery alone. This waste heat would be at around 700 Kelvin â more than double the maximum temperature that processors on the data centers need to be kept below in order not to fry themselves. While this higher-temperature heat can be radiated away with a relatively compact radiator, it would have to be separate from the thermal sinks cooling the processors below their 320 Kelvin ideal temperature. Ultimately, a nuclear-powered cluster would only need around 6% less low temperature radiator area than a fully solar-powered version.

Despite that, after adding all the mass of the reactor, radiation shielding, power converters, and all the other necessary equipment to run a nuclear reactor, fission originally looks like a winner. Compared to todayâs standard solar panels, a compact fission reactor is around ten metric tons lighter per megawatt. And since weight is money in space, that sounds like a win.

Fraser talks about the new nuclear reactor NASA will use for future Mars missions.

However, there are several caveats to that. First, lighter, next-generation solar arrays are coming along quickly, whose increased efficiency could eliminate nuclearâs advantage entirely. Or the engineers could boost the satelliteâs orbit up to 1,450 kilometers, where the Earthâs shadow problem completely goes away and the satellite can consistently bathe in sunlight â admittedly ignoring the potential space debris and trapped radiation problems this causes, as well as the need for higher power communications equipment.

Nuclear suffers from another disadvantage - radiation. Data centers in space already suffer from stray cosmic rays flipping bits unexpectedly. Putting one next to an active nuclear reactor subjects them to random gamma rays and neutrons as well. While this could be lessened a bit by putting the reactor on a long boom â physically separating it from the server racks and placing a dense âshadow shieldâ near the reactor to block radiation from reaching the computers, that would require extra weight in the form of cabling and the boom itself, eliminating more of nuclearâs original weight advantage.

Despite all these trade-offs, there does appear to be a situation where running a hybrid of both solar and nuclear is the best option. If a mission requires a data center to survive a 24-hour failure of its main power system while keeping 20% emergency power active for safe-mode operation, an 80/20 nuclear/solar split weighs in at around 36 metric tons, around a third of the weight of either as a standalone option due to the weight of batteries needed to meet those mission requirements. But to be clear, without that power maintenance constraint, either system in a standalone configuration wins out on weight.

Fraser talks aobut the advantages and disadvantages of orbital data centers.

Ultimately, Dr. Turyshev thinks the financial picture is dependent on the lifespan of the nuclear reactor. Another disadvantage of a nuclear-powered satellite is it canât just burn up in the atmosphere at the end of its life â it has to be boosted to a âgraveyardâ orbit at around 2,000 km, where a spent reactor would stay indefinitely. But, if a reactor lasts ten years, Dr. Turyshev calculates that it would save around $190 per kilowatt-year in launch costs, whereas if it lasts for only two years (as many experimental space-based reactors are designed to), then that flips to a $783 per kilowatt-year deficit.

What the paper doesnât tackle is the social aspect of whether the general public would support putting potentially tens of thousands of small nuclear reactors into orbit. Just this week, NASA and the U.S. Department of Energy locked in the mission architecture for a nuclear-powered reactor known as Space Reactor-1 Freedom to power the propulsion system of a future Mars mission, so thereâs at least some support for it (or at least the government thinks there is). But as more and more data centers are launched, how to power them with the best trade-off of weight vs cost vs safety vs capability will remain an ongoing debate.

S.G. Turyshev - Power-Architecture Crossovers in Orbital Computing: Thermal, Radiation, and Lifetime Constraints

UT - The Physics Wall Facing Orbital AI Data Centers

UT - Robots, Not Astronauts, Will Have to Fix Space Data Centers

UT - NASA Lays Out Ambitious Plans for Moon Base and Nuclear Mars Mission

Archaeologists discovered a stash of Celtic coins ahead of a construction project for an electrical substation in Hungary.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists in Hungary have discovered a stash of more than 200 Celtic silver coins that are over 2,000 years old. It's one of the largest hoards found there in decades.

Researchers unearthed the coins during excavations ahead of construction for an electrical substation in western Hungary between 2023 and 2025, according to a translated statement from the power company E.ON. The hoard dates to sometime between the late second century B.C. and the early first century B.C.

The coin cache weighs roughly 4.4 pounds (2 kilograms). In today's market, it's worth more than $2,000 as raw silver alone, but its rarity and historical value effectively make it priceless, the statement said.

The site was once part of a farm, and plowing there had unearthed several individual coins in recent decades, the statement said.

During the latest excavations, archaeologists initially found a few coins and then searched the area with metal detectors, which led them to the coin hoard. The treasure had been packed inside a small ceramic vessel and sat about 16 inches (40 centimeters) below ground.

"This is a rarity in Europe," Eszter Kreiter, an archaeologist at Hungary's National Archaeological Institute, said at a news conference, according to local news outlets. She added that the last similar find was made in Hungary in the late 1960s.

The hoard's silver coins are modeled on Greek tetradrachms — a very early type of large silver coin that was introduced in the late sixth century B.C.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The newfound Celtic tetradrachm copies are a type known as "Velem," which are named after Velem-Szent Vid, a fortified Celtic hilltop settlement, or oppidum. Similar coins have been found at that site, which is located about 10 miles (15 kilometers) to the west.

Each coin has a stylized head on one side that probably depicts the Greek god Apollo, and portrays a helmeted rider and horse on the other side.

Artifacts from more than 7,000 years of occupation have been found at the site, including a glass bead (bottom, center) thought to be about 2,500 years old.

The excavations have revealed evidence of more than 7,000 years of occupation at the site, officials wrote in the statement. The artifacts include a nearly 7,000-year-old polished stone chisel used for woodworking and a glass bead with a peacock's eye pattern that seems to have been part of jewelry from the sixth or seventh century B.C.

A Roman-era villa was built at the same site in later centuries, without disturbing the hoard of buried silver, Kreiter said at the news conference.

The site in Hungary's western Szombathely region was excavated between 2023 and 2025 ahead of the construction of an electricity substation.

The villa has long since been demolished, but the excavations enabled the archaeological team to reconstruct its floor plan, including its underfloor heating system, she said. They also found a Roman-era brick with a dog's paw print.

The artifacts from the site will become part of a museum exhibition.

According to Museum Wales, the Celts were loosely related Iron Age peoples descended from Proto-Indo-European speakers. Emerging in Central Europe, Celtic groups occupied much of Central and Western Europe from about the 10th to the first century B.C. The Celtic Gauls were finally defeated by the Romans, led by Julius Caesar at Alesia, now in eastern France, in 52 B.C. The Britons were also Celtic, though most people of Celtic descent would not have recognized that name.

Several modern ethnic groups, including the native Irish and the Bretons of coastal France, trace their descent to the Celts. Regions with strong Celtic origins are sometimes called the "Celtic fringe" of Western Europe.

Writing in the Journal of Roman Studies, the British coin expert Christopher Howgego, an honorary curator and professor emeritus of Greek and Roman numismatics at the University of Oxford, stated that Celtic tribes in the Carpathian Basin, now in Hungary and Romania, started minting their own silver coins after Celtic mercenaries had seen them when serving with Hellenistic armies in Greece and Macedonia.

Howgego has written that the Greek-inspired Celtic coins included adaptations of classical Greek portraits, as well as distinctive Celtic designs. These copycat tetradrachms held very high value for their makers, so they were rarely used for everyday purchases. Instead, they were often hoarded as wealth or buried as ritual offerings.

Tom writes mainly about science, space, archaeology, the Earth and the oceans. He has also written for the BBC, NBC News, National Geographic, Scientific American, Air & Space, and many others.
