#6421. The ESO is Deeply Concerned About Space Data Centers, and the Rest of Us Should Be Too

There's growing concern that AI is polluting our communal spaces. AI is replacing humans online, and we wonder if there's another human being behind what we're reading or viewing. We wonder where this will go, and how it will end.

There's also growing concern that AI, or at least its infrastructure, is taking over physical spaces. Data centers are proliferating, and citizens are concerned about their effects: power usage, water usage, noise, etc. The promise of a few jobs isn't placating concerns about what some say are resource-hogging data centers being forced on communities despite their opposition.

But now AI data centers are about to take their place in the sky, the last frontier of communal space. This is setting off alarm bells for astronomers, who are adamant that the growing cloud of satellites is taking a serious toll on their observations.

The FCC just approved SpaceX's application to launch a staggering one million new satellites in Low-Earth Orbit (LEO). Together, they will be the first orbital AI data center. The system is designed to avoid using energy and resources here on Earth. The satellites will operate in nearly constant sunlight for solar power, and will cool themselves by pumping liquid coolant through radiative panels. The individual satellites would stay in constant contact with each other with lasers.

With Musk/SpaceX's typical hubris, they're calling the system 'Starmind.'

But whatever they're calling it, not everyone is pleased that it's been approved, and many are questioning why the FCC, a purely American body, can be allowed to approve such a project.

There are really two parallel problems. One is the growing number of satellites overall, and the other concerns the proliferation of AI.

This artist's illustration shows the ESO's Extremely Large Telescope in the Atacama Desert in Chile. It's a 39 meter behemoth that will drive astronomical discoveries for decades. But a sky crowded with satellites will make its life difficult. Image Credit: ESO/L. CalÃ§ada

The European Southern Observatory (ESO) has made their thoughts known on the proliferation of satellites and how it affects astronomy. The ESO operates some of the most powerful existing and upcoming telescopes in the world in the Atacama Desert in Chile: The Very Large Telescope (VLT), the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), the ESO 3.6-metre Telescope, and the ESO's upcoming flagship telescope, the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT).

In a new statement, the ESO condemns the Starmind project as a serious detriment to astronomical observations. And, unlike some other opponents, they've analyzed the situation in detail.

âAs approved, this project would not only have profound consequences for astronomy, but also fundamentally alter the night sky for everyone on the planet. We demonstrated these impacts in an extensive technical analysis, and raised them in a response to the US FCC, as did other organisations worldwide. This approval highlights the urgent need for international mechanisms capable of assessing activities whose impacts extend far beyond national borders and affect a global common good,â said Andreas Kaufer, Director General at the European Southern Observatory (ESO).

Their technical analysis is peer-reviewed and was published in Astronomy and Astrophysics in March 2026.

"Large satellite constellations impact astronomy through both visible trails and the generation of diffuse and atmospherically scattered light. Quantification of this cumulative sky-background component is essential to assess the full ramifications of extant and proposed systems," the paper states.

These panels show the effect of one million satellites (V500km = 6), representing the SpaceX Orbital Data Center constellation in slight violation of the V > 7 recommendation. (a) shows the fraction of the Field of View lost for the LSST camera at the Vera Rubin Observatory. (b) shows example positions of individual satellites. The grey dots represent invisible satellites in the Earthâs shadow, whereas the coloured dots represent illuminated satellites. The 1867 orange dots correspond to satellites brighter than V = 7, and the 247 red dots to satellites brighter than V = 5. For comparison, about 3000â4000 stars are this bright. Image Credit: Hainaut 2026. A&A Volume 712, August 2026 A241

"This study evaluates the effect of proposed constellations â ranging from current deployments to mega-constellations and very bright reflector concepts â on direct trail losses, diffuse background, and scattered sky brightness."

Constellations with up to about 60,000 member satellites have a negligible, but not imperceptible, effect on observations. But above that number, things change for the worse. "Conversely, mega-constellations with 106 satellites render trails pervasive, thereby affecting the majority of long exposures," they write. Long exposures are critical in modern astronomy, so the astronomers are taking the issue seriously.

This figure illustrates the effect SpaceXâs one-million-satellite Orbital Data Center constellation on a 300-second exposure with the spectrograph at the Very Large Telescope. Even 1.3 h after the end of astronomical twilight, more than half the sky remains affected by satellite streaks, with an average of more than eight satellite trails per image at zenith. In some observations, more than 20 satellite trails will cross each image. The effect on a 15-second exposure with the 3Â° LSST camera at the Rubin observatory is similar. Image Credit: Hainaut 2026. A&A Volume 712, August 2026 A241

Long exposures are especially important when observing high-redshift objects or other faint objects. High-resolution spectroscopy and deep-time surveys also use long exposures. Astronomical telescopes can take short exposures and stack them to deal with some satellite light-streak pollution, but that has its limits.

"Bright satellites, such as spacecraft analogous to AST SpaceMobile, significantly impact saturating detectors even when their number is moderate. Extremely bright satellites pose a far more severe threat: a 5000-satellite Reflect Orbital-like constellation could elevate the scattered sky background by 20â30%, and a population of 50 000 could increase it by 200â300%," the ESO paper states.

The ESO's technical analysis said there are current proposals to launch 1.7 million new satellites into space, and many of them breach a critical threshold called V550km = 7. That figure indicates a satellite that can't be seen with the naked eye, so breaching that figure means it can be seen with the naked eye. That means that not only will we see them when we gaze upward, but astronomical telescope observations would be inundated with them. The ESO's analysis says dryly that they "would substantially degrade astronomical observations."

"Maintaining satellite brightness below V550km = 7 is important for all instruments but critical for safeguarding saturating instruments, such as the Rubin LSST camera, and for limiting sky-background pollution," the paper states.

Reflect Orbital has something other than AI or communications in mind. They intend to launch large reflecting satellites into orbit. Those satellites would reflect sunlight to customers on the ground. They could illuminate solar panel farms at night, or provide light to allow things like resource extraction to continue past nightfall. But things can always go wrong. Think of hackers or other malicious actors gaining control of an orbiting light source.

But the real problem astronomers face from Reflect Orbital is that their satellites would blow past the V550km = 7 threshold.

This figure shows scattered light as a fraction of the natural dark sky for 37 (a), 5000 (b), and 50 000 (c) extremely bright satellites (V500km = â4), representing the Reflect Orbital constellations envisaged for 2027, 2030, and 2035, respectively, as seen from outside their illuminating beam. Image Credit: Hainaut 2026. A&A Volume 712, August 2026 A241

Reflect Orbital's eventual 2035 constellation of 50,000 bright satellites would be catastrophic for the Vera Rubin and its LSST. "For the saturating LSST Camera, however, the effects of even a single satellite crossing its FoV will be devastating, compromising a very high fraction of the frame affected by that single trail. The 2030 constellation (5000 satellites) would ruin 3% (at zenith) to 12% (at 30Â° elevation) of the LSST FoV one hour after sunset. With the 2035 constellation (50 000 satellites), the losses would be catastrophic, about 30% at zenith to 100% at 30Â°: all LSST images would be entirely unusable," the ESO's paper states.

These panels show the fraction of exposures captured by the LSST that will be unusable because of Reflect Orbital's satellites. (a) is for 36 satellites in 2027, (b) is for 5,000 satellites in 2030, and (c) is for 50,000 satellites in 2035.

"Even under this constraint, the total satellite population should remain below â¼100 000 satellites to ensure that field-of-view losses do not exceed typical technical downtime," they state.

Companies like SpaceX aren't blind to the problem. They're trying to make their satellites less reflective. But their impact on astronomy is just one outcome of the ongoing crowding of LEO. What about the proliferation of space junk? There are efforts to develop ways of mitigating the space junk problem, but they're way behind the massive number of satellites being launched. SpaceX says they have a plan, and the FCC approves it, but the plan is really just disposal by atmospheric re-entry.

Most people aren't too concerned with astronomical observations, except when one makes the news headlines. But some are concerned about reflecting sunlight down onto Earth at night as a business model. For astronomers, it could be catastrophic.

Far more people are concerned with AI intruding where they don't think it belongs. Do we really need AI in space?

Some are saying that Starmind will never be built, that it's part of the SpaceX/Elon Musk hype machine. But those are just some of the opinions out there, and they don't touch on regular citizens' concerns about the encroachment of AI and its infrastrcture into their lives.

Besides, SpaceX isn't the only company contemplating a satellite AI data processing system. Blue Origin is also considering an orbital data center satellite system. It's called Project Sunrise and would have 51,000 satellites.

We've been warned about the growing number of satellites for years now. In a 2021 paper, researchers warned us about the danger associated with "the adoption of a consumer electronic model applied to space assets." Consumer electronics are creating mountains of electronic waste that we're struggling to manage. The proliferation of satellites is adding to our pollution problem.

In the 2021 paper, the authors point out that "satellite re-entries from the Starlink mega-constellation alone could deposit more aluminum into Earthâs upper atmosphere than what is done through meteoroids; they could thus become the dominant source of high-altitude alumina." High-altitude alumina is bad because it may trigger chemical reactions that destroy ozone. And the alumina isn't destroyed itself, so it could drive multiple cycles of ozone destruction.

This image is a 333 second-exposure from the Blanco 4-meter telescope at the Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory. It shows at least 19 streaks created by the second batch of Starlink satellites launched in November 2019. Image Credit: NSFâs National Optical-Infrared Astronomy Research Laboratory/CTIO/AURA/DELVE, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Crowding LEO with more satellites is fraught with problems. But our rapid and widespread adoption of AI in particular could be especially dangerous. AI data centers in space combine both problems into one. Implementing satellite AI systems may end up being a very bad decision, maybe humanity's last big, bad decision.

Who knows where this will go, and who knows if AI is going to destroy humanity. That type of thinking used to sound like an exaggerated science fiction nightmare, or an easily-dismissed, feverish thought experiment. But many AI experts say we're heading for trouble, we're moving too fast, and we're not building in safeguards. The people who build AI can't actually explain how it works. We all know about AI hallucinating and inventing facts, but AI has been caught scheming and deceiving, behaving one way outwardly while hiding its true intentions. That's truly alarming.

There's no denying that AI is a powerful tool. It's powering scientific discoveries and it's helping regular people every day. But that's just one side of it.

From a POTUSA who posted an AI video of himself wrestling a tigerâshortly after a real person was unfortunately killed by oneâto armies of bots spreading political misinformation designed to undermine a nation's sovereignty, to financial scammers with a global reach, AI's presence is proving to be toxic. It ranges from mildly problematic to outright hostile. Bad actors are rapidly adopting this new, powerful tool, and using it to harmful effect.

It's amost impossible to deny that we're on the cusp of something historic. Humanity always struggles with new powerful tools because wisdom lags behind intelligence. It always has and it always will; the only way to acquire wisdom is through experience. Do we have enough wisdom to make careful decisions regarding AI?

At different times in history, angry mobs of citizens have been the only thing standing in the way of terrible ideas and actions. To place AI in space, beyond the reach of the angry mob and its pitchforks, may end up being a terrible mistake.

#6420. Astronomers Discover the Sun Contains 55% More Silver Than Previously Thought

Some of the oldest rocks in the solar system hinted that astronomers were undercounting the Sun’s silver. A fresh look at sunlight suggests they were right.

Researchers at Uppsala University estimate that silver is 55 percent more abundant in the Sun than previous calculations indicated.

The revised estimate brings the Sun much closer to the silver abundance found in primitive meteorites. Both preserve material from the same cloud of gas and dust that gave rise to the solar system 4.6 billion years ago.

Silver atoms in the Sun’s atmosphere absorb light at specific wavelengths, leaving dark lines in the spectrum. The pattern identifies silver, but estimating how much is there requires a model that predicts how strongly those atoms absorb light.

The team modeled the motion of the Sun’s outer layers and used more detailed calculations of how silver atoms interact with light and other particles. The model accounts for how radiation changes the energy states of silver atoms, which affects the strength of the lines astronomers use to measure the element’s abundance.

“With our new model, we were able to interpret the spectral lines used to determine the solar silver abundance more accurately,” says Sema Caliskan, who conducted the research during her PhD studies at Uppsala University.

Hydrogen and helium make up nearly all of the Sun. Heavier elements such as carbon, iron, and silver account for just 1.5 percent of its mass. Many of these elements form inside stars or during stellar explosions, then become part of later generations of stars and planets. Measuring their abundance helps astronomers reconstruct how the Milky Way’s chemistry changed over time.

“The new knowledge about the Sun’s composition is important for the understanding of other stars, planets, and cosmic material, because the Sun is one of astronomy’s key reference points,” says Caliskan.

The team plans to apply the same method to other stars. “By studying the light of stars of different types and ages, we hope to understand where silver is formed in the universe, and how it has been distributed throughout the Milky Way over time,” says Caliskan.

Reference: “Ag I model atom and the 3D non-LTE solar silver abundance” by S. Caliskan, A. M. Amarsi, P. Jönsson, N. Grevesse and B. K. Sahoo, 17 July 2026, Astronomy & Astrophysics. DOI: 10.1051/0004-6361/202659578

This study was funded by the Swedish Research Counsil, KVA Kungliga vetenskapsakademien, and ANRF India.

#6419. A Train Carrying Deadly Materials Was on Fire for Nearly an Hour as It Barreled Toward a Small Town. Why Didn’t Anyone Stop It?

A small sensor failed to do its job—leading to one of the worst train wrecks in American history.

Editor’s note: In July 2024, after this story was published, the National Transportation Safety Board released its final analysis on the Norfolk Southern freight train derailment in East Palestine, Ohio. It also released a companion illustrated digest of the incident. The analysis determined that the train derailed after an overheated wheel bearing caused an axel to “burn off.” The punctured DOT-111 tank car leaked butyl acrylates, which are flammable and likely started the post-derailment fires. Further, the decision to intentionally “vent and burn” vinyl chloride tank cars was likely unnecessary and based on incomplete or misleading information, according to the report. The NTSB issued 34 new safety recommendations covering several needs, including defect detection systems, tank car standards, hazardous materials, and emergency response procedures.

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

On the frigid evening of Friday, February 3, 2023, at around 8:50 p.m., a Norfolk Southern freight train measuring more than a mile and three quarters long snaked its way through the town of East Palestine, Ohio. The train consisted of 149 cars, pulled by three locomotives—two at the front, one in the middle—and traveled just under 50 miles per hour. Of those 149 cars, 20 were tankers labeled with hazardous-materials placards. Several of the tankers contained liquefied vinyl chloride gas, the combustible and carcinogenic precursor material for PVC pipe; others contained ethylene glycol, a toxic ingredient in antifreeze. Driving the lead locomotive was Tony Faison, the train’s engineer; with him were the train’s conductor and a trainee.

Engineers chart their progress by designated mile markers along the track. About 20 minutes earlier, the train had crossed mile marker 69.0, just east of Salem, Ohio. While crossing that spot, an infrared sensor built into the track called a “hotbox detector” had reported elevated temperatures on one of the front axles of the 23rd railcar. The ambient temperature that night was 10 degrees Fahrenheit. The bearings on the axle had reached an abnormally hot temperature of 103. The car, a hopper designed to hold commodities like grain, wasn’t carrying hazardous materials, but the hotbox detector relayed an alert to Norfolk Southern’s Atlanta command center all the same. No further action was taken.

As the train left East Palestine, it approached Ohio’s border with Pennsylvania, passing within a few hundred feet of the State Line Tavern, a local watering hole. There, at 8:55 p.m., it crossed mile marker 49.8. As the twenty-third car crossed the next hotbox detector, the infrared sensors revealed that the temperature of the axle’s bearings had risen sharply, to over 250 degrees. Faison immediately received an audio message from the locomotive’s onboard computer to stop the train. He reacted quickly to apply the brakes, but it was too late. He didn’t know it, but for the previous 40 minutes, his train had been on fire.

The train took more than a thousand feet to come to a stop. As it did, the compromised axle gave way. The left-side journal box, which held the axle in place, broke off and landed on one side of the track; the wheelset, consisting of the axle with two steel wheels mounted at both ends, ended up on the other. The twenty-third car jumped the rail, and the cars behind it followed suit, creating a tremendous series of crashes that could be heard throughout town. Thirty-eight railcars piled up, including 11 of the hazmat tankers.

Faison leaped from the locomotive to inspect the damage. From his standpoint at the front of the train, he could see flames rising into the night. He immediately contacted 911. So did many of the town’s residents, reporting both the train crash and the fire. One thought a gas station had exploded.

In the next few hours, the toxic flames would force an evacuation of the town. The specter of chemical poisoning lingered over East Palestine for months. And even today, the question of how a system of detectors—expressly designed to prevent this kind of derailment—failed to notice a dangerously overheated train axle remains unanswered.

In the minutes after the derailment, first responders rushed to the blaze, but they were initially underequipped. Serving a town of fewer than five thousand people, the East Palestine fire department was a mostly volunteer force. The sole professional on staff was Chief Keith Drabick, who on that night was almost three hundred miles away, driving through Pennsylvania on vacation. Informed of the crash at 9 p.m., Drabick turned his car around and drove straight back to East Palestine, but he didn’t arrive until five hours later. For the first few minutes, volunteers had to fight the blaze alone. Meanwhile, following protocol, Faison cut the first two locomotives from the train and moved them a mile down the track. In the confusion that followed, some firefighters seemed unaware they were responding to a hazmat site and reported to residents that the burning train cars were carrying only malt liquor.

Some of the train cars were carrying malt liquor, but others contained stronger stuff. As the scope of the disaster slowly became clear, the volunteers were joined by professional firefighting crews from nearby counties, including a special hazmat squad. At 9:45 p.m., concerned about the risks of a vinyl chloride explosion as well as the toxic cocktail of flaming chemicals escaping into the night, officials began evacuating nearby homes. Meanwhile, some of the contents of the leaking tankers began seeping into nearby Sulphur Run, a stream that flowed directly from the crash site through the center of town.

Even before the official order, citizens had started to evacuate. East Palestine resident Jami Wallace had learned of the train wreck from her mother. Wallace, a human resources manager in her forties, had recently gotten engaged. She called her fiancé, who was with a friend at the State Line Tavern. Driving past the burning crash site, he raced home to collect Wallace and their three-year-old daughter. “Grabbed her a couple of changes of clothes and out the door we went,” she told me. “We didn’t even know where we were going. It was the middle of winter and the heater was broken in the car.”

After an hour and a half of firefighting, the Ohio State Police expanded the evacuation zone to one mile surrounding the derailment site. Around midnight, still fearing an explosion, the firefighters retreated. They then began to survey the crash site with aerial drones, in an attempt to determine which specific chemicals were leaking. The survey was challenging: The site was, well, a train wreck, and some of the plastic hazardous-materials placards had melted in the fire.

Eventually, responders determined that three hazmat cars had been physically breached. One contained ethylene glycol, the antifreeze ingredient, which can be lethal in concentrated doses. The other two contained acrylates, used as base ingredients in adhesives and paint. All three materials were burning off, releasing volatile organic compounds into the air. The fire was additionally fueled by nonhazardous but flammable railcar cargo, including several tankers loaded with petroleum lubricants. For days to come, an ominous toxic cloud hung suspended over the site. “You know how smoke, like, moves through the sky? Yeah, this wasn’t moving anywhere,” Wallace said. “It was almost like a green cloud that was, like, hovering.”

Initially, none of the vinyl chloride tankers were breached. (If they had been, a series of explosions might have occurred, and the cancer-causing chemical could have rained down on the town.) Still, five vinyl chloride tankers, containing more than 115,000 gallons of vinyl chloride in total, had piled up in the burn zone. Each tanker had an emergency pressure release valve designed to vent gas into the atmosphere. Over the next few days, as temperatures rose inside the tanks, these valves automatically opened and closed, periodically releasing excess vinyl chloride gas into the air—where it immediately caught fire. In one extraordinary display on the evening of Saturday, February 4, one of the tanker valves vented for 70 continuous minutes, creating a spectacular flamethrower.

With the crash site cordoned off and the tankers burping flames, officials deliberated on what to do. One worry was that the release valves on the tankers were starting to suffer thermal damage. Another was that the vinyl chloride inside the tanks might “polymerize,” forming into chains of PVC, which might cause the valves to stick, sealing the pressure in and causing the tankers to blow.

From the outside, the hazmat experts couldn’t be sure if polymerization was occurring. Eventually they settled on two options. One option was to deliberately puncture the tanks and conduct a controlled burn of the vinyl chloride gas. The other option was to wait it out and hope the tanks cooled down enough so they wouldn’t explode. Chief Drabick was presented with this devil’s bargain: Wait, and potentially watch the exploding tanks rain shrapnel and poisonous chemicals on his town, or release mass quantities of vinyl chloride—a known Group A carcinogen—into the atmosphere. “I was given 13 minutes to make a decision,” Drabick told investigators from the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB), the federal agency responsible for investigating the wreck.

After consulting with his chief officers, Drabick chose to vent and burn. Following an expanded evacuation order, specialists attached explosive charges to the exteriors of five damaged tanker cars. At 4:37 p.m. on February 6, the charges were detonated, sending twin columns of flaming vinyl chloride gas high into the air and obscuring the setting sun with thick, black smoke. The burn continued through the following day; it was not until February 8, five days after the axle on train car 23 had first started to burn, that the fire was fully put out.

East Palestine soon found itself host to another kind of toxic cocktail, one consisting of corporate communications specialists, blustering public officials, government bureaucrats, and enterprising class-action attorneys. Complementing this splendid company were the more respectable representatives of the NTSB. Leading the agency’s efforts was Ruben Payan, an NTSB veteran with a heavy build, a thick mustache, and a calm and measured voice. Under his patient command, the NTSB began a thorough investigation of the crash site and the events leading up to the derailment.

The agency published the first investigation update to its website in March 2023. And then on June 22, Payan presented his preliminary results at a public meeting in East Palestine. (It was the first onsite NTSB meeting in six years.) Using security camera footage collected from homes and businesses adjacent to the tracks, Payan was able to present a detailed videography of the train’s final minutes. Between the towns of Sebring and East Palestine, more than a dozen surveillance cameras had captured the train in motion; in ten of those camera feeds, the train was plainly on fire. In true-color camera feeds, the lower axle of the twenty-third car glowed a dull orange color; in infrared camera feeds, it blazed an intense white, throwing visible sparks.

The first two cameras to show the fire were in Salem, Ohio, some 26 miles west of East Palestine. The train passed the first camera at 8:11 p.m., 44 minutes before the derailment. That camera, which overlooked an alley of snow-covered cars, caught the train in the far background, its axle glowing orange. The camera was located six miles in front of the Salem hotbox detector—the one that had sent an alert to Atlanta but did not stop the train.

How had the Salem hotbox detector missed the fire? The cameras clearly showed flames and sparks along the length of the bottom of the twenty-third car, but when that same car crossed the hotbox detector 10 minutes later, infrared sensors registered the bearing temperatures at only 103 degrees. This wasn’t a case of a sputtering fire that started and stopped, either—the cameras along the route showed a steady blaze. The NTSB declined to comment for this story, citing the pending results of the final investigation. Norfolk Southern declined to comment as well.

I put the question to David Farwick, a veteran engineer who commanded trains in Ohio for Norfolk Southern for nearly 40 years. He told me that Norfolk Southern’s systems were well maintained and up to date. “Those hotbox detectors, they’re pretty sensitive,” he said. “It’s not like we were working with 1960s stuff. They were pretty good.” The detectors are positioned among the crossties on the track and use infrared sensors to scan the undercarriage of the train. More than 6,000 are deployed across North America. The sensors on the hotbox detectors line up directly with the roller bearings. Farwick seemed flabbergasted that a flaming train had crossed a detector and not tripped an immediate brake alert. “It blows my mind,” he said.

Regulators have also grown concerned in recent years about how long the trains are getting. Farwick told me trains are growing so long that engineers have trouble seeing the backs of them, even on a curve. I asked him whether the train crew would have known they were carrying hazardous materials. “Absolutely,” he said. Farwick explained that the conductor on each train carries a bound paper manifest of the train’s cargo known as a “consist.” In the event of a derailment or crash, a hard copy of this consist is to be immediately delivered to first responders. But Drabick, when questioned by NTSB investigators, said his firefighters never received the consist directly from the Norfolk Southern train crew: “I do not believe that we had any contact with those individuals,” he said. Drabick was only fully informed of the train’s hazardous contents when he arrived on site hours later.

The other looming question about the crash involves the degree of environmental poisoning East Palestine has suffered. In the months following the vent and burn of vinyl chloride gas, Environmental Protection Agency personnel repeatedly visited the town and surrounding areas to take soil samples. Per the EPA’s website, “the sample results indicate that impacts from the smoke and soot were minimal.” The EPA has also monitored the health of the town’s waterways. In the aftermath of the disaster, the agency recorded more than 40,000 dead fish and aquatic animals in the Sulphur Run creek adjacent to the derailment and burn site. While the agency claims that the creek “has not shown any contaminants at levels that exceed health standards since May 1,” it continues to maintain “Keep Out” signs posted around Sulphur Run.

East Palestine is immediately downstream of the crash site, and many local residents believe the creek has delivered poison into their homes. Two days after the derailment, Wallace returned to her evacuated residence to pick up some medication. “As soon as I pulled into my driveway, it hit me in the face—I started coughing ... until, like, I can’t breathe,” she said. “I look over because I know it’s the creek. I look over, and I see these chemicals free-floating down.”

Wallace told me water from the creek regularly seeps into the basement of her residence, and that she has since relocated. She has pushed for the EPA to start indoor monitoring in East Palestine homes; so far, the agency has declined. In any case, the damages Norfolk Southern owes the town are substantial. In June, Norfolk Southern announced that cleanup costs and injury compensation settlements related to East Palestine would cost the company nearly $1 billion, though it anticipated that much of that cost would be covered by insurance.

In a statement a couple of weeks after the crash, Jennifer Homendy, the chair of the NTSB, described the accident as “100 percent preventable,” but didn’t offer specifics. She was likely referring to the “hot axle” phenomenon. Train axles use ring-shaped bearings that keep the axle secure while permitting it and the wheels to rotate. A skateboard’s wheels rotate using lubricated ball bearings inside the wheels. Train cars instead use cylindrical roller bearings, which make contact with the axle, permitting easy rotation.

As of December 2023, the NTSB has not yet made a final determination, but multiple experts I talked with told me that they believed a failed roller bearing was the most likely cause of the East Palestine derailment. About two dozen trains derail this way in North America every year. Bearings can fail for any number of reasons, including insufficient lubrication, contamination, overloading, and, simply, age. Once a bearing fails, the axle begins to grind against the metal, and this friction causes a rapid rise in temperature; this was potentially the source of the fire. “Bearings do break down, but that’s the reason why you get these detectors, right?” Farwick said. “That’s exactly what these things are supposed to prevent.”

The roller bearings on train axles are sealed inside the wheel and can’t readily be accessed. A faulty one can easily escape visual detection. Hotbox detectors, by using infrared temperature sensors to monitor the bearings in motion, offer a second layer of protection. Generally speaking, they work. Since the early 1980s, train derailments in North America have fallen from more than 7,000 annually to just over 1,000, in part because of hotbox detectors.

The place to catch the failed roller bearing was not in East Palestine, but 20 miles west, in Salem, Ohio, where the train had crossed a detector 30 minutes before the derailment. That detector had recorded temperatures 93 degrees above the outside environment and sent a noncritical signal to Norfolk Southern central command in Atlanta. Whether dispatchers in Atlanta relayed this warning to the train crew remains unclear; the NTSB has yet to publish transcripts from the train’s black box recorder, and Norfolk Southern has refused to discuss the details of the accident.

Perhaps it is worth noting that in the days before the derailment, the East Palestine train had already been delayed twice by stops for unrelated mechanical issues.

In March, the NTSB opened a probe into Norfolk Southern’s safety culture. Regulators were concerned not only by the East Palestine derailment, but also two other Ohio derailments in the surrounding months, as well as separate incidents in which three railroad workers on Norfolk Southern lines were killed in a span of 16 months, starting in December of 2021. In a statement announcing the investigation, the NTSB urged Norfolk Southern “to take immediate action today to review and assess its safety practices.”

This October, Norfolk Southern unveiled a new layer of protection: giant metal sheds, festooned with cameras, that each train will pass through at various points on its journey. The shed is described as a “portal,” and its cameras take an average of 1,000 images per railcar, and send those images to an A.I. data center. Deep-learning algorithms are then employed to spot problems that track detectors and overworked railcar mechanics cannot.

Following the derailment, legislators introduced the bipartisan Railway Safety Act of 2023, which proposed decreasing the required distance between hotbox detectors to 15 miles, from an average of 25 miles today. The legislation is well intended, but it’s not clear if it would have prevented the East Palestine derailment: On that track, the hotbox detectors were an average of 16.7 miles apart. Closing the distance to 15 miles wouldn’t necessarily help.

The most striking revelation from the NTSB’s preliminary findings was the sheer number of camera feeds that had captured the train car on fire. It costs about $200,000 to install a hotbox detector, and critics have estimated the cost of compliance for the Railway Safety Act at up to $2 billion. Perhaps wireless video cameras could permit dispatchers and AI to regularly monitor the status of the cars, and would give engineers better visibility to the back of the trains.

Finally, there’s still the problem of the toxic derailment site. It remains a hazard zone, and the nearby State Line Tavern remains closed. Under the guidance of the EPA, much of the topsoil near ground zero was excavated. The soil was supposed to be shipped to a hazardous waste facility in Oklahoma, but that state’s governor, Kevin Stitt, blocked the plan in March. Similarly, the contaminated water from Sulphur Run was drained. The water was supposed to be sent to a treatment facility in Baltimore, but that fell through too.

For a while, the poisoned water and soil remained at the derailment site. “They have these big Shamu tanks,” Wallace said. “They each hold, like, 100 million gallons of water.” Wallace said a neighbor had flown a drone over the tanks, and seen the chemical sheen on top. Nearby, the toxic dirt was piled into giant mounds, and covered with tarps.

However, as of January 2026, the EPA reported that personnel had completed a “site-wide cleanup and restoration,” in which crews cleaned the remaining oily sheens from nearby waterways such as Leslie and Sulphur Runs, and removed more than 38 million gallons of wastewater. They also removed any remaining contaminated soil and debris for treatment or disposal, and completed the derailment site excavation. The EPA is now sampling groundwater, surface water, and drinking water quarterly and will continue monitoring the area. Comprehensive updates of the work are available at the EPA’s website.

#6417. All the Gaps We See in Protoplanetary Disks Aren't From Planets

When astronomers look out into the Milky Way at very young stars, they find rings in their protoplanetary disks. It's pretty clear that these rings are where planets are forming. They're carving gaps and rings in the protoplanetary disks, the reservoirs of material around stars that planets form from.

ALMA, the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, has captured images of many of these disks and rings. Those images are part of the effort to understand how planets form, one of the primary questions in contemporary astronomy. But it's not clear if every ring is because of a planet. Protoplanetary disks are complex, and there are many forces at work in them. Some rings could be planets, and some could be caused by other phenomena.

âThese new stars have bright rings and dark gaps patterned in concentric circles resembling the grooves of a vinyl record,â said Masayuki Yamaguchi, a post-Doctoral Fellow from Kyushu Universityâs Faculty of Science. âThese patterns arenât new; what was a mystery was how these grooves were carved. The most popular explanation is that young planets make these gaps as they orbit the star. However, when a disk has many rings, it becomes harder to explain since itâs hard to imagine that multiple planets have already formed.â

Yamaguchi is the lead author of new research in The Astrophysical Journal titled "A Hybrid Origin for the Multiple Ring-gap Structures in the Large Protoplanetary Disk V1094 Sco: A Low-mass Planet and Secular Gravitational Instability" Yamaguchi is a member of a team of Japanese astronomers who studied V1094 Scorpii, a young star about 500 light years away. V1094 Sco has a protoplanetary disk that extends out to 300 astronomical units, with multiple ring-gap pairs at great distances from the star.

This is ALMA's image of V1094 Sco reconstructed with PRIISM. The researchers detected rings and gaps in the disk and were able to determine which were from still-forming planets. Image Credit: By YMasayuki - Own work, CC BY 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/194635370

"High spatial resolution observations reveal that some protoplanetary disks host multiple ringâgap pairs at large stellocentric radii, yet their physical origin remains unsettled," the authors write. The researchers used ALMA images and observations with the Very Large Telescope's SPHERE (Spectro-Polarimetric High-contrast Exoplanet REsearch) instrument to analyze the V1094 Sco disk. "The continuum image shows four narrow dust ringâgap pairs extending to exceptionally large radii (r â¼ 380 au)," they write, and also "trace a spatially extended gas disk (r â¼ 760 au) in Keplerian rotation." Keplerian rotation means that objects further from the star orbit slower than those nearer the star.

Young stars with protoplanetary disks are T-Tauri stars, and among that group, V1094 Sco is known for having a giant disk with multiple rings, making it a rarity. It's the subject of a lot of research and observations. It was first recognized for its extended ring with multiple gaps and rings in a 2018 paper. That paper said, "In this work, the nature of V1094 Sco as a giant, multi-ringed protoplanetary disk is identified for the first time, based on data from the Lupus survey of protoplanetary disks." (The Lupus survey was an ALMA survey of disks in the Lupus star-forming complex.)

Ever since then, astronomers have been trying to understand V1094 and its unusual disk. There's not much doubt that still-forming planets are responsible for some of its features, but can they explain them all?

In an interesting twist, the researchers didn't use new ALMA observing time to study V1094 Sco. They relied on existing data and applied a new open-source super-resolution imaging technique called PRIISM (Python module for Radio Interferometry Imaging with Sparse Modeling.) It was built specifically to reconstruct sharper images with existing ALMA data, and replaces a previous technique called CLEAN. PRIISM proved its value in a 2025 study of 78 disks in the Ophiuchus star-forming region, where it found previously undetectable features in disks, only a few hundred thousand years after the stars formed.

This figure doesn't show V1094 Sco; instead it shows CrA IRS 2, a protostar about 430 light years away. It illustrates how much better PRIISM is at detecting disk structures in existing ALMA data than its predecessor, CLEAN. Image Credit: Ayumu Shoshi et al 2026 ApJ 998 214

PRIISM paid similar dividends in this work.

âWe observed that the disk extends approximately 380 astronomical units (AU)âabout 13 times the distance between the Sun and Neptuneâfrom the center. Within that, we found four narrow rings and gaps between 100â230 AU from the starâs center,â explained Yamaguchi. âWhen we compared the widths and depths of the gaps with the "one planet per gap" model, we could not explain the entire pattern. Instead, the origin appears to differ from place to place."

"The ensemble of gap widths and depths is inconsistent with a simple one-planet-per-gap interpretation," the authors write in their paper.

An exoplanet can explain the innermost gap, according to the results. "At r â 100 au, a double gap and its scattered-light counterpart are consistent with multigap excitation by a single low-mass companion of (55 Â± 35) Mâ," the authors explain.

But further from the disks, the rings were spaced more evenly. "At r â 170â230 au, the outer ring system shows regular spacing and no clear scattered-light counterpart," the authors write. "These outer rings are quantitatively compatible with secular gravitational instability." That means the outer rings aren't associated with exoplanets. Instead, they're dust clumping together under its own gravity, which requires low turbulence.

This is a near-infrared scattered-light image of the V1094 Sco disk obtained with VLT/SPHERE. It's overlain with the locations of dust continuum rings (solid lines) and gaps (dashed lines). The filled white circle indicates the SPHERE coronagraph. Image Credit: Masayuki Yamaguchi et al 2026 ApJ 1006 232

Secular gravitational instability intrinsically produces evenly spaced rings, while exoplanets don't.

"V1094 Sco therefore supports a hybrid pathway in which weak turbulence in an extended disk allows secular gravitational instability to assemble long-lived midplane dust concentrations that can cradle planet formation beyond â¼100 au, alongside planet-driven substructures at intermediate radii," the authors write.

These results don't mean that planets won't eventually form in these features that are at great distances from the star. It just means that there are no planets forming there right now. "In this framework, secular GI does not compete with planet formation; rather, it concentrates solids and establishes disk-wide conditions favorable for subsequent planet growth," the authors write in their conclusion.

ALMA doesn't image planets; that was never its job. But if exoplanets are in V1094 Sco's disk, other telescopes might find them.

âBecause ALMA is a radio telescope, we have not yet directly detected the planet that generates the gap closest to the star. Using other telescopes such as the Subaru Telescope will help us get a clearer picture of this hidden planet,â said Yamaguchi. âAs we analyze more disks, our understanding of the fundamental question of where and how planets form will deepen. Each new finding adds a thread to the tapestry of our knowledge of the universe.â

Evan Gough is a science-loving guy with no formal education who loves Earth, forests, hiking, and heavy music. He's guided by Carl Sagan's quote: "Understanding is a kind of ecstasy."

#6416. New Technology Could Help Astronauts Make Their Own Oxygen on the Moon

Astronauts on the Moon could one day breathe oxygen pulled from lunar soil using a technique borrowed from chipmaking.

Computer chip manufacturing and lunar exploration seem like completely different worlds. Yet our latest research suggests the two may be more closely connected than expected.

Using technology widely employed in semiconductor manufacturing, we have shown that it is possible to extract oxygen and products containing oxygen from material designed to mimic lunar soil.

This matters because oxygen is one of the most valuable resources for future space exploration. Astronauts need it to breathe, and it is also a major component of rocket propellant.

But transporting large quantities from Earth would be enormously expensive, so space agencies are investigating ways to obtain it directly on the Moon instead.

The challenge is that lunar oxygen does not exist as a readily available gas. Instead, it is chemically bound within minerals that make up the Moon’s surface layer. And although that layer contains a large amount of oxygen by weight, extracting it requires breaking strong chemical bonds within lunar minerals.

Many of the complex techniques that could potentially achieve this extraction would require large amounts of energy.

So our team decided to explore an alternative, lower-temperature approach inspired by a well-established industrial technology called “plasma-processing.”

Plasma is often called the fourth state of matter (after solid, liquid, and gas). It forms when sufficient energy is supplied to a gas, creating a mixture of charged particles, electrons, and highly reactive chemical species.

In semiconductor fabrication, plasma interacts with silicon dioxide in a process that underpins the production of billions of electronic devices every year.

We asked a simple question: if plasmas are highly effective at reacting with compounds containing oxygen in semiconductor processing, could a similar approach be applied to the oxygen-based compounds in lunar soil?

To investigate, we exposed artificial moon soil (known as lunar regolith simulants) to plasmas generated using gases that are commonly employed in semiconductor manufacturing.

The results were encouraging. During plasma treatment of the lunar regolith simulants, we detected oxygen and oxygen-containing gaseous products being released.

Further analyses confirmed that the plasma was chemically modifying oxygen-bearing minerals within the material, with some lunar minerals reacting more readily than others.

Understanding these underlying mechanisms is important for enhancing the efficiency of the process and identifying opportunities to improve future systems. But oxygen yields would need to increase substantially before any practical lunar system becomes possible.

One reason this approach is attractive is that it builds on decades of experience developed by the semiconductor industry. Space engineering often requires entirely new technologies, but there are advantages in adapting systems that already exist, are well-understood, and have been refined for years on Earth.

The semiconductor industry has spent decades studying how fluorine plasmas interact with materials containing oxygen. Rather than starting from scratch, future researchers can draw on that extensive knowledge base.

There are practical benefits too. Plasma processing is a dry process, avoiding some of the challenges associated with transporting and handling liquid reagents (chemicals added to the process to make a reaction occur) in space. The operating temperatures of plasma processing can also be significantly lower than those required by some conventional oxygen extraction methods.

The implications may extend beyond using oxygen for life support on lunar bases. Lunar soil contains useful elements, including silicon, aluminum, and iron. While our current work focused on oxygen-bearing reactions, future studies may explore whether plasma-based processes could contribute more broadly to the use of other lunar resources.

Much more research is needed to understand the chemistry, to improve yields, and to determine whether the process can be scaled economically.

But the plasma technology that enables the manufacture of billions of transistors may also help humanity tackle one of the biggest challenges of space exploration: learning how to live off the land on another world.

Reference: “Impact of oxygen extraction from lunar regolith simulant using fluorinated plasma processes” by Aneeta Jaggernauth, Sean Kelly, Brian K. Tanner, Robert O’Connor, Aidan Cowley and Rajani K. Vijayaraghavan, 2 September 2026, Scientific Reports. DOI: 10.1038/s41598-026-67891-2

#6414. Nuclear Pathfinder Mission To Ceres Would Usher In Era Of Interplanetary Transport

The Dwarf Planet Ceres has long captivated astrobiologists with the tantalizing possibility that it holds the kind of rich chemistry that could have led to ancient microbial life. NASA's Dawn mission which orbited this Main Belt asteroid in 2015 found that Ceres was rife with subsurface water ice, ammonia, nitrogen, and hydrogen.

But a new proposal by two aerospace veterans would capitalize on Ceres's rich chemistry to set up humanity's first interplanetary transport node. That is, a base to use for refueling and as a jumping off point for destinations in the outer solar system or even beyond. The mission would at the same time tackle Ceresâ astrobiological mysteries.

For sixty years every deep-space mission weâve flown has been a one-off: each carries all its own fuel from Earth, heads out, and leaves nothing behind, astrophysicist Pete Worden, co-author of the project proposal, Chairman of the Breakthrough Prize Foundation, and Laureate Professor at the University of Arizona in Tucson, told me via email. We propose replacing this plodding, inefficient approach with a scalable transportation network, and putting its hub at the dwarf planet Ceres, Worden told me.

In a 2026 paper submitted to the Journal of the British Interplanetary Society, Worden and aerospace engineer Fred Kennedy note that their proposed Project CERES (Ceres-Earth Resource Exchange System) has both a lander and an orbiter. Arriving a little over a year after a proposed January 2037 launch, the spacecraft would use nuclear thermal propulsion to fly directly to the dwarf planet.

Project CERESâ first flight would be a Pathfinder mission that surveys Ceres, lands, extracts water and returns samples within five years. The Pathfinder itself is a Dawn-class orbiter plus a lander, a sample capsule and a new engine.

Nuclear Thermal Propulsion (NTP) is the key.

It replaces the combustion chamber of an ordinary rocket with a small fission reactor, says Kennedy. Liquid hydrogen is pumped through the hot reactor core, heated to around 2,700 degrees Kelvin, and expanded through a conventional nozzle, he says.

Because the exhaust is pure hydrogen, it leaves the nozzle at about twice the speed of the best chemical exhaust.

Thus, a trip to Ceres takes a year rather than a decade.

Nuclear thermal rockets operate at two to three times the efficiency of chemical rockets and can make the trip from Earth in a little over a year, says Worden.

Credit: AI image provided by Kennedy/Worden.

Project CERES combines NTP with in-situ production of water, hydrogen, oxygen and ammonia, Worden and Kennedy note in their paper.

A transport node earns its keep by selling propellant to vehicles that pass through, says Worden. That requires something to sell, which at Ceres is water --- burned directly as steam in a nuclear engine, or split into hydrogen and oxygen, or combined with local nitrogen into ammonia, he says.

The nuclear thermal transport technology is mature and ready to deploy.

The reactor physics is sixty years old and was proven on the ground, Aerospace engineer Fred Kennedy, co-author of the project paper; CEO of Dark Fission and former head of the Pentagonâs Space Development Agency, told me via email. Between 1959 and 1972, NASAâs Rover and NERVA programs ran more than twenty reactors and engines at full power in Nevada: an hour at a time at full thrust, with dozens of restarts, he says.

Heat from radioactive decay early in Ceresâ history drove a global subsurface ocean that left behind the hydrated clays, carbonates and ammoniated minerals, before it froze into the ice-rich crust we see today.

The Pathfinder would spend four to five months in orbit mapping volatiles, sounding the depth of the ice table, and choosing a landing site against Dawn's base map, says Kennedy. It then deploys a five metric ton lander to an ice-rich high-latitude site, extracts water from the ground as a demonstration, loads samples, and returns them to the orbiting vehicle, he says.

The vehicle then spends roughly twenty months in an extended survey, before departing in June 2040. The Ceres samples itâs carrying land on Earth in May 2041. They would arrive in a protective capsule, not unlike the Earth return capsule used in NASAâs 2004 Stardust mission to Comet Wild 2.

Credit: AI image provided by Kennedy/Worden.

The Ceres return spacecraft brakes into a cislunar orbit where it becomes available for its next sortie.

A vehicle that refuels at Ceres launches 60 percent less mass per round trip, and on that savings alone the node pays for itself within the life of its first fleet, says Worden.

Ceres also has the added plus of being further out in the solar system. Thus, the next destination is cheaper to reach than from Earth or the Moon. With only a fraction of Earthâs gravity, launching a mission from Ceresâ surface requires much less initial thrust.

What does Ceres offer that our Moon doesnât?

Water, nitrogen and carbon, says Worden; the Moon has essentially none of the last two.

Dawn found water ice at about ten percent by weight within the top meter of Ceresâ regolith at mid-to-high latitudes.

Dawn also found ammoniated clay minerals across the surface, carbonates and organic compounds, and sodium carbonate brine deposits in Ceresâ Occator crater, says Worden.

These are the ingredients for propellant (water, hydrogen, ammonia) and for life support (water, oxygen, nitrogen).

What stays at Ceres is the infrastructure, built up in phases, says Worden. First, thereâs a surface extraction plant and an orbital tank farm, then electrolysis and hydrogen liquefaction with its own power plant, then fabrication, he says.

Ceres' crust is ice-rich; its surface minerals formed in liquid water; and the bright deposits in Occator crater are sodium carbonate salts left by brines that reached the surface within the last few million years, says Worden. The Dawn team interprets this as coming from a deep reservoir of briny liquid that persists beneath the frozen crust, he says.

Whether that water ever hosted anything more than chemistry is a question the Pathfinder's samples can answer, says Worden.

#6412. Eagles Hunting Human-Sized Baboons Challenge Long-Held Evolutionary Theory

Evidence of eagles hunting adult baboons suggests that aerial predators may have helped shape how early humans learned to communicate and protect one another.

In the middle of the Sahara, researchers have found evidence that eagles are killing primates as large as some of our early ancestors. One of the apparent victims, an adult male baboon, was estimated to have weighed more than 26 kilograms (57 pounds), challenging a long-held assumption about the dangers early humans faced.

Eagles have hunted primates for millions of years, yet no primate weighing more than 13 kilograms (29 pounds) had previously been confirmed to have been killed by a bird of prey. Scientists believed that humans and their ancestors had escaped this threat for roughly the past 2.5 million years because they were too heavy for even the giant eagles of the past to lift.

The discovery comes from the Ennedi Plateau in northern Chad, where an isolated population of baboons lives in the Sahara Desert. Researchers from the University of St Andrews traveled to the region with colleagues from Dartmouth College, the University of Konstanz, the Max Planck Institute of Animal Behavior, and African Parks.

Lead author Professor Catherine Hobaiter, from the School of Psychology and Neuroscience at the University of St Andrews, said, “This was such an extraordinary expedition, any primatologists dream! Some of the baboons there are so remote they rarely, if ever, see people, and so after a couple of days they ended up following us around—we were probably the most interesting thing they’d seen for a while!”

She added: “We saw the eagles while we were searching for the baboons, but we never imagined that they might be a threat to them. Then we found the first skull with a puncture mark, and then another, and another.”

In a new study published in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology, the researchers describe finding the remains of adult male baboons with telltale signs of eagle predation, including talon punctures in their skulls and distinctive scrapes and rake marks on their shoulder bones.

Senior author Professor Nathaniel Dominy from Dartmouth College said, “At first, the idea of eagles hunting adult male baboons seemed to exist on the thin edge of possibility, until it didn’t. Our skepticism slowly gave way to acceptance. The evidence was convincing.”

The behavior of the living baboons offered another clue.

Professor Hobaiter explained, “One of the most exciting observations was seeing the baboons respond when a pair of Verreaux’s eagles swept overhead—primates are very specific about only responding to eagles that are a genuine threat. We’d seen them very relaxed around other big birds of prey, but as soon as the Verreaux came into view they alarm called and dropped down to safety.”

For scientists studying human evolution, the possibility of attacks from above is particularly interesting. Primates defend themselves differently against eagles than they do against predators such as big cats and crocodiles. One strategy, known as mobbing, involves primates, particularly larger adult males, charging an attacker to drive it away. If our ancestors faced similar threats, eagles may have helped shape the evolution of communication and group cooperation.

Many primates living in areas where eagles hunt also travel in large groups alongside other primate species. For much of our evolutionary history, our ancestors shared their surroundings with other early human species and primates. Although these relationships are often viewed in terms of competition, protection from predators may have given them a reason to stay together.

Dr. Gisela Kopp, from the University of Konstanz and the Max Planck Institute of Animal Behavior, said, “Primatology often focuses on regions with a high diversity of primates, but shifting our attention to a place where no primatological data has ever been collected before, proved to be extremely rewarding.”

Dr. Jean Didier Akpona, from African Parks, said, “Having worked in this region for about three years, I had the opportunity to visit these gueltas (pockets of water that form within rock formations) and often observed Verreaux’s eagles. I had never imagined that these predators would target primates of this size until the research team stumbled upon evidence. This discovery leads us to explore further the mystery that surrounds the gueltas of the Sahara Desert.”

The researchers are eager to continue studying the isolated baboon population, whose unusual lifestyle is already challenging several assumptions about the species.

Professor Hobaiter added, “Baboons are some of the best studied monkeys in Africa, but our very first observations from Ennedi upended all sorts of notions about what these baboons should be doing—from their diet to their social lives, I can’t wait to see what new ‘rules’ they’ll break next!”

Reference: “Signs of Eagle Predation on a 22-kg Adult Primate” by Catherine Hobaiter, Tewogbade J. D. Akpona, Gisela H. Kopp and Nathaniel J. Dominy, 18 November 2026, American Journal of Biological Anthropology. DOI: 10.1002/ajpa.70377

This work was supported by the University of St Andrews (Global Partnerships Travel Grant), the Scottish Funding Council (International Science Partnership Fund), the Dartmouth College (Harris Distinguished Visiting Professorship program), the Marion and Jasper Whiting Foundation (Fellowship for Higher Education), the Rust Family Foundation; the Hector Stiftung II (Hector Pioneer Fellowship), and the Zukunftskolleg, University of Konstanz (ZENiT Fellowship, through the Federal Ministry of Education and Research (BMBF), and the Baden-Württemberg Ministry of Science as part of the Excellence Strategy of the German Federal and State Governments).

Editor's note: This article was updated on Tuesday (Nov. 24) to indicate that the full Beaver Moon rises tonight.

November’s full moon, known as the "Beaver Moon," will rise in the east at dusk tonight (Nov. 24), marking the first of three consecutive supermoons.

It will be the third and final full moon of fall in the Northern Hemisphere and the first in a series of unusually close full moons that includes December's spectacular Christmas supermoon — the closest full moon since 2018. These bright moons are just some of the many winter skywatching highlights headed our way in the coming months.

The Beaver Moon gets its name from the time of year when nocturnal beavers in North America traditionally build dams and prepare for winter under the full moon, according to TimeandDate. Other nicknames include the Frost Moon and Snow Moon, and the Anishinaabeg people in North America call it Baashkaakodin Giizis — the Freezing Moon — according to the Center for Native American Studies.

The moon will reach its full phase at 9:53 a.m. ET on Tuesday, when it will be below the horizon in North America. The best time to see the Beaver Moon is at moonrise that evening, as it rises in the east around the same time the sun sets in the west. That's when the moon will appear against a relatively bright twilight sky, making it easier to appreciate its size and color.

The moon will appear full on Monday and Wednesday as well, but Tuesday offers the best opportunity to see it rise during twilight.

The Beaver Moon will be the first of three consecutive supermoons, according to EarthSky. A supermoon occurs when a full moon coincides with the moon being relatively close to Earth in its elliptical orbit. The moon's distance from Earth changes throughout the month. On average, the moon is 238,900 miles (384,472 kilometers) from Earth. When a full moon occurs near perigee, or its closest point during its orbit, it appears slightly larger and brighter than usual. #6409. BepiColombo Captures Mercury Orbit After 8-Year Trip

The planet Mercury might be one of the least explored planetary bodies in the solar system, but its is arguably the most crucial in helping scientists better understand the formation and evolution of the inner solar system. Its position as the closest planet to the Sun makes it a prime target for how the rocky planets formed and evolved and what this could mean for finding life beyond Earth. However, just traveling to Mercury is a lengthy and time-consuming effort, often taking a spacecraft several years just to achieve orbit. More on that later.

Now, the lauded joint mission between the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) called BepiColombo might have just become the second mission to orbit Mercury. This is because mission leaders recently announced that BepiColombo successfully achieved Mercury orbit insertion (MOI) on November 21 at 18:27 UTC (1:27 pm EST/10:27 am PST). This historic achievement comes 8 years, 1 month, and 1 day since BepiColombo launched on October 20, 2018, and included one Earth flyby, two Venus flybys, and six mercury flybys to achieve orbit just a few days ago.

While MOI is essential for achieving Mercurian orbit, it is not the final orbit BepiColombo will achieve to conduct science operations, which are expected to commence in April 2027. Over the next several months, the team will fire the spacecraftâs thrusters several times to adjust its orbit to achieve a more permanent orbit. The first science operations phase is slated to run from April 2027 to April 2028 with a potential extended mission from April 2028 to December 2029. If the mission is extended until December 2029, the team will then assess the spacecraftâs remaining fuel and determine if continued science operations can be achieved or if it will crash into Mercuryâs surface.

âOur almost 600-strong science team will be delighted to see BepiColombo pass this key milestone and begin revealing more about Mercury, from its interior and surface to the space around it,â said Dr. Geraint Jones, who is the Lead Project Scientist for ESAâs BepiColombo and was previously was a Professor of Planetary Science and Head of the Planetary Science Group at University College London's Mullard Space Science Laboratory (UK).

As noted, BepiColombo just became the second mission to successfully orbit Mercury, with the first being NASAâs MESSENGER (MErcury Surface, Space ENvironment, GEochemistry, and Ranging) spacecraft, which orbited Mercury from March 2011 to April 2015 after initial estimates put the science phase of the mission lasting only one year. During this time, MESSENGER completed more than 4,100 orbits around the innermost planet to the Sun while obtaining almost 300,000 images of the entire Mercurian surface before its fuel was exhausted. Once this happened, the mission team intentionally crashed MESSENGER into the planetâs far side with the team confirming a loss of signal when the spacecraft was scheduled to emerge from the far side.

Unlike MESSENGER, BepiColombo consists of two orbiters, ESAâs Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and JAXAâs Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter ("Mio"), which are currently attached but are slated to separate in early December 2026. Once this happens, MPO will be tasked with studying Mercury surface features and composition while Mio will study Mercuryâs magnetic field and how it interacts with the solar wind.

As noted earlier, traveling to Mercury is a lengthy and time-consuming effort. This is because as an object travels closer to the Sun, our starâs immense gravity becomes greater, thus increasing the speed of the object. In the case of a spacecraft, this means it has to slow down enough to enter orbit around Mercury. However, this would require an insane amount of fuel, which adds weight to the spacecraft, and the financial and logistical costs spiral from there. This is why spacecraft like BepiColombo and MESSENGER conducted several planetary flybys to slow down, with MESSENGER performing three less mercury flybys compared to BepiColomboâs six Mercury flybys.

What new insights about Mercury will BepiColombo teach scientists in the coming years and decades? Only time will tell, and this is why we science!

#6408. Glaciers Are Melting at Alarmingly Different Rates and Climate Alone Can’t Explain Why

Where a glacier ends can influence how quickly it disappears, with implications for communities that depend on mountain meltwater or face the threat of flooding.

Between 2000 and 2020, the number of lakes in direct contact with glaciers worldwide grew by about 35 percent. Their expansion has consequences for the ice that remains. Lake water can melt glaciers from underneath, while chunks of ice can break away and fall into the water. Until recently, scientists had struggled to determine how much these processes contribute to glacier loss worldwide.

An international research team, including Tobias Bolch from the Institute of Geodesy at Graz University of Technology (TU Graz), used artificial intelligence to map glacial lakes from satellite images taken in 2000 and 2020. The researchers manually checked the results, distinguishing lakes that touched glaciers from those already separated from the ice. Their findings were published in Nature Climate Change.

Over the 20-year period, glaciers ending in lakes lost an average of 66 centimeters (26 inches) of water equivalent annually, meaning the lost ice would produce a layer of water that deep. By comparison, glaciers ending on land lost 40 centimeters (16 inches), and those ending in the sea lost 36 centimeters (14 inches).

“Our research has shown that contact with a lake further accelerates the loss of ice from a glacier,” says Tobias Bolch. “While the climate and the topography of the glacier are the most significant factors influencing glacial mass loss, lakes significantly exacerbate it.”

The number of lakes touching glaciers increased by more than 3,500, with particularly pronounced expansion in Alaska and the southern Andes. Their combined area grew by around 600 square kilometers (232 square miles). They also gained an estimated 66 cubic kilometers of water, enough to submerge the entire city of Vienna under approximately 160 meters (525 feet) of water

Using machine learning models, the researchers found that glacier characteristics such as elevation and slope accounted for 46 percent of the explained influence on ice gains and losses. Temperature, precipitation, and other climatic factors accounted for around 43 percent, while glacial lakes contributed approximately 11 percent.

“The findings from this study will help us to estimate future changes to the glaciers more accurately,” says Tobias Bolch. “This is particularly important for mountainous regions and their forelands, where meltwater is a significant source of water. Such findings are also relevant when assessing the risks posed by glacial lakes in the event of potential outbursts.”

Reference: “Climate and glacier geometry dominate global glacier–lake interactions” by Shaochun Zhao, Guoqing Zhang, Matthias Huss, Georg Veh, Jonathan L. Carrivick, Tobias Bolch, David R. Rounce, Qian Tang, Yifan Bu, Yan Song, Menger Peng, Xue Wang, Xinhai Zeng, Danni Huang, Mengjie Zhu, Tao Zhou and Jie Cheng, 20 November 2026, Nature Climate Change. DOI: 10.1038/s41558-026-02808-5

This work was supported by grants from the Basic Excellent Research Group for Tibetan Plateau Earth System, National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC ERGTPES project no. 42588201), the National Key Research and Development Project of China (2024YFF0809104), the National Natural Science Foundation of China (grant no. 42571153), the Second Tibetan Plateau Scientific Expedition and Research Program (STEP, 2024QZKK0301), the Department of Science and Technology of the Tibet Autonomous Region (XZ202502JD0025, XZ202403ZY0028) and the High-Level Talent Program of Xizang University (XZDXDR202501).

#6407. The Maya People Loved the Color Red. Scientists Say It May Have Helped Bring Them Down.

The reddish pigment cinnabar was so popular that it seeped into the water supply around Maya settlements, setting off a disastrous downstream effect.

The Maya people had a toxic relationship with the color red—quite literally, according to fresh research. The new analysis of the Yucatán Peninsula during the Maya era identified astronomically spiked levels of mercury, which might have contributed to the collapse of Maya culture.

“The mercury data was crazy,” Matt Waters, an environmental sciences professor and paleolimnologist at Auburn University, said in a university statement about the unexpected discovery on the peninsula. “Off the charts. These mercury levels aren’t normal.”

Matt Waters led a study published in Science Advances that explored sediment samples collected at two lakes—Lago Coba and Cenote Xcach—showing the intense spike in mercury (Hg) levels ranging from around 40 C.E. to 800 C.E.

“We show that Classic Period Hg concentrations in sediment cores from two lakes on the Yucatán Peninsula exceeded modern sediment Hg toxicity thresholds by orders of magnitude for centuries during ancient Maya occupation,” the authors wrote, adding that the heightened pollution coincides with aquatic food collapse, “confirming that Hg toxicity was an additional environmental stressor for Classic Maya populations.”

While Waters isn’t saying mercury caused the collapse of the Maya civilization, he also doesn’t want to ignore its impact. “It’s been confirmed that drought was an issue, deforestation was an issue, erosion was an issue, overpopulation was an issue, and feeding the population was probably an issue,” he said. “This study adds the impact of water quality. Let’s put that in the list. That’s what our study does. It establishes that list and moves it forward.”

The study actually began as part of a National Science Foundation project focused on harmful algal blooms, but a then-graduate student and study co-author, Savanna Wooten, suggested also testing for heavy metals. Sediment coring from the lake bottoms pulled up mud from thousands of years ago that contained the intense mercury spikes during the Classic Maya Period, which were then followed by an abrupt decline.

The powerfully high mercury concentration lasted for hundreds of years, and Waters believes the sudden change at the base level likely moved up the food web, impacting fish and other larger creatures. Not only would eating fish or drinking water have exposed humans to the toxic levels, but there may have even been fewer fish to catch. “They would have seen a strange color change in the water,” Waters told Live Science, “and a drop in its productivity, such as fish for protein.”

Waters linked to a study he’d worked on with a team from the University of Florida in the late 1990s that found a gap in ostracod shells during a specific period from Coba, correlating the missing shell timing to the rise in mercury. Further investigation into the cores found that declines in biological markers occurred throughout. “The algae was killed,” he said. “The cyanobacteria, they tanked. Purple sulfur bacteria, vanished. The biological community completely changed.”

The people “experienced this for decades and, in one case, for centuries.”

The source of that mercury was cinnabar, they believe, a vibrant red mineral made up of 86 percent mercury that Maya culture viewed as a sacred pigment. “This was not like mercury raining down from the sky,” Waters said. “This was not a regional thing. It was concentrated.”

Maya loved cinnabar, using the bright red in pottery, murals, temple walls, and burials. To keep up with demand, they heavily imported it, especially around Coba and Xcach. “It’s common knowledge that there was trade in obsidian, in jade, and beautiful stones, and weaponry,” Waters said. “I think this could start a conversation that cinnabar could have been a major trade commodity.”

It may also show a highly toxic love affair that contributed to Maya struggles.

Tim Newcomb is a journalist based in the Pacific Northwest. He covers stadiums, sneakers, gear, infrastructure, and more for a variety of publications, including Popular Mechanics. His favorite interviews have included sit-downs with Roger Federer in Switzerland, Kobe Bryant in Los Angeles, and Tinker Hatfield in Portland.
