Scientists are perplexed at discovering the world's deepest explosive volcanic eruption at Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A submersible mission to the deepest ocean trench on Earth has made a shocking discovery: the deepest pyroclastic volcanic flow ever found on the planet, in a place geologists didn't expect to see any volcanic activity.

This evidence of a violent undersea eruption was found 20,000 feet (6,000 meters) below the ocean surface on the walls of the Challenger Deep, the deepest point of the Mariana Trench and the deepest part of the ocean. It was a "complete surprise," said Robert Stern, a professor emeritus of geosciences at the University of Texas at Dallas and first author of a new study describing the discovery.

Typically, volcanic activity doesn't occur that close to an ocean trench, Stern told Live Science. And given the site's extreme depth, the lava that made the flow must have had some very strange chemistry. Normally, the intense pressure of seawater at these depths would prevent an explosive eruption, instead favoring a goopier, seeping type of flow. But the flows seen on the edge of the Challenger Deep were similar to the explosive, roiling gases that coated Pompeii in ash in A.D. 79.

"It's not something that as a geoscientist I would have said would be predicted," said Sune Nielsen, a geochemist at the University of Lorraine in France who was not involved in the study. "Very far from it."

A fish in the genus Pseudoliparis in an image taken during during a dive by the Jason/Medea ROV at 20,659 feet (6,297 m).

The Challenger Deep is in the remote western Pacific at the southern end of the Mariana Trench. There, the Pacific oceanic plate pushes under the Mariana oceanic plate in a process called subduction. At the trench where the two plates meet, the ocean floor plunges down 6.8 miles (10.9 kilometers). Mount Everest could fit in the chasm, with room to spare.

Geoscientists aren't sure why the trench is so dizzyingly deep, but they have turned up some clues. For instance, there is a tear in the Pacific Plate that allows one narrow strip of the plate to subduct particularly rapidly. The curvature of the plate is also very steep, perhaps because the rocks of the Mariana and Pacific plates aren't very strongly connected to each other, allowing the Pacific Plate to dive steeply and flex freely.

The new findings, reported Monday (Nov. 23) in the journal Frontiers in Earth Science, suggest that volcanism and magma also may play a role, Stern said. The researchers were exploring a segment of the Challenger Deep's forearc, a roughly 120-mile-wide (200 km) expanse that sits between the trench itself and the volcanic arc created by the subduction zone. These volcanic arcs are standard subduction zone features; for example, Mount St. Helens and Mount Rainier are part of the volcanic arc of the Cascadia subduction zone in the Pacific Northwest.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

But though there are some volcanoes north of Challenger Deep along the Mariana Trench, the Challenger Deep segment of the trench is odd in that there is not an organized volcanic arc there. Instead, there's an ocean ridge. Regardless, the space between this ridge and the trench was expected to be volcanically quiet because there is not usually enough heat in that region of a subduction zone to melt magma.

Nevertheless, the cameras on the deep-diving remotely operated vehicle Jason/Medea, which went to the site in 2014, caught strange, pancake-like rock features at three different spots in a 60-mile (100 km) stretch of the trench. Samples brought on board the ship revealed rock embedded with volcanic glass and a pyroclastic flow texture.

A sea cucumber in an image from the Jason/Medea dive at 12,726 feet (3879 m).

The researchers are currently getting the rock dated, but volcanic glass usually erodes quickly in the ocean, Stern said, so the presence of glass suggests the eruptions were fairly recent. "They're not yesterday," he said, "but I don't think they're a million years old."

The pressure of the water at the depths of the flows is equivalent to 592 atmospheres of Earth stacked on top of one another. Typically, that kind of pressure keeps a lid on the dissolved water and carbon dioxide in magma that expands rapidly to cause explosive eruptions. Thus, Stern said, the eruptions by the Challenger Deep may have been driven by a supercritical fluid ‪—‬ a weird state sort of in between a gas and a liquid.

"We just don’t know how those magmas will behave at those water depths," said Stephen Self, a volcanologist at the University of California, Berkeley, who was not involved in the study.

The mission's observations also suggest that the crust of this region is extending, or stretching, in two different ways. To the east, the stretch is caused by a mechanical pulling apart of the crust. To the west, volcanic eruptions are stretching the crust. It's a perplexing finding, Nielsen said, without a clear explanation.

Stern and his colleagues suspect that the two plates are starting a new subduction zone in this western part. That would be an exciting finding; subduction zones move around over tens of millions of years, and researchers don't know much about how new ones start. The geochemical studies of the rocks that Stern and his team pulled up could answer questions about where the lava that made the pyroclastic flows came from and why this bizarre region can generate magma where none should be.

"This region is really, really unusual for our planet, and there is quite a bit of, 'What, really? Wait, how is that? OK, yeah, I guess maybe.'" Nielsen said. "So obviously, I find it super interesting."

Stern, R. J., Pujana, I., Anderson, M. K., Chin, E., Dygert, N., Harigane, Y., Le Roux, V., Leybourne, M., Ohara, Y., Okumura, T., Segee-Wright, G., & Etheridge, E. (n.d.). ROVing in the deep: Tectonic and magmatic complexities of the challenger deep forearc segment, southern mariana convergent margin. Frontiers in Earth Science, 14, 1929806. https://doi.org/10.3389/feart.2026.1929806

Stephanie Pappas is a contributing writer for Live Science, covering topics ranging from geoscience to archaeology to the human brain and behavior. She was previously a senior writer for Live Science but is now a freelancer based in Denver, Colorado, and regularly contributes to Scientific American and The Monitor, the monthly magazine of the American Psychological Association. Stephanie received a bachelor's degree in psychology from the University of South Carolina and a graduate certificate in science communication from the University of California, Santa Cruz.

#6404. Crowded Proteins Can Change How Enzymes Work

Laboratory research suggests that nearby proteins can reshape enzymes, offering clues to how the physical environment inside our cells may help regulate the chemistry of life.

In laboratory droplets designed to mimic conditions inside cells, enzymes worked faster as the liquid became more crowded with proteins, up to a point. Active enzymes also helped nearby molecules move more freely through the liquid.

Many of the chemical reactions that keep cells alive occur in the cytoplasm, where proteins and other molecules can gather into compartments without an enclosing membrane. Researchers from the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST), in collaboration with the Max Planck Institute for Dynamics and Self-Organization (MPI-DS) and RIKEN, studied how enzymes interact with these crowded environments.

“What’s fascinating is that we can connect interactions between individual atoms to the movement of molecules across an entire droplet. Events at the smallest scales can shape, and be shaped by, the physical behavior of a much larger system,” says senior author Professor Paola Laurino, who leads the Protein Engineering and Evolution Unit at OIST.

The OIST researchers prepared tiny droplets containing different concentrations of a protein called bovine serum albumin (BSA). In separate experiments, they introduced two enzymes, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH), along with their substrates, the molecules upon which the enzymes act.

Enzyme activity increased as more BSA was added to the droplets. Only at very high protein concentrations did crowding begin to interfere with the reactions.

“This initial increase in enzymatic activity seemed counter-intuitive, as you’d typically expect any level of crowding to impair movement of the enzymes and substrates and increase the liquid’s viscosity, therefore slowing down the reaction from the start,” explains Laurino.

Laurino and her team also used fluorescent tracers to examine how enzyme activity affected the movement of molecules within the droplets. Both BSA proteins and fluorescent nanoparticles moved more freely in the presence of active enzymes. Droplets containing modified, inactive enzymes were more viscous, and molecules moved more slowly through them.

“Similarly, we found that higher concentrations of the enzymes or their substrates in the droplets also increased mobility,” says Professor Ramin Golestanian, director of the Department of Living Matter Physics at MPI-DS.

The researchers used fluorescent markers to track the movement of nanoparticles in the droplet. Credit: Dindo et al., 2026, 10.1038/s41467-026-77666-y.

Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations conducted by researchers at RIKEN suggested that crowding helped accelerate reactions by changing the shape of the enzymes. The simulations showed that the active site, the region where substrates bind and react, was open under dilute conditions and closed as the concentration of surrounding proteins increased.

“When closed, the energy barrier required was much lower, allowing the reaction to happen more readily,” explains Laurino. “To detect such a change in these simulations by MD was really surprising to us.”

Researchers at MPI-DS developed a theoretical model to explain the increased movement within the droplets. They proposed that enzyme activity creates differences in chemical concentrations throughout the liquid, generating tiny flows.

“These flows allow the molecules to move more freely and mix within the droplet, highlighting how enzyme activity can potentially lead to physical effects across larger scales,” says Golestanian.

Laurino plans to investigate whether these interactions also occur in complexes where several enzymes operate in close proximity. Her team will also conduct experiments in living bacterial cells to determine whether the findings hold under more complex biological conditions.

Reference: “Enzymes can activate and mobilize dense biomolecular condensates across scales” by Mirco Dindo, Jakob Metson, Weitong Ren, Michalis Chatzittofi, Kiyoshi Yagi, Alessandro Bevilacqua, Erika Fukuhara, Yuji Sugita, Ramin Golestanian and Paola Laurino, 30 October 2026, Nature Communications. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-77666-y

Funding: Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology Graduate University, Japan Society for the Promotion of Science, Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology Japan, RIKEN

#6403. The Government Tested How Dangerous AI Could Get—Then Four ChatBots Helped Plan a Terrorist Attack

The Government Accountability Office secretly tested ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Grok and found that all four would help make plans when prompted.

The dawn of artificial intelligence brings with it both rewards and risks. With the ability to sift through unfathomably large data sets, AI could help detect cancers in their infancy, unlock some of the most enduring mysteries of mathematics, and even help contain the beating nuclear heart of future fusion reactors.

Unfortunately, the risks of this technology are far from minuscule, including its impact on human education, the environment, and potentially the survival of the human race (an all-too-plausible scenario put forward by AI tech CEOs). Even the everyday LLMs that now litter our digital lives—Claude, Gemini, ChatGPT, and Grok—can aid and abet some of the most dangerous actors on the planet.

At least, that’s the latest conclusion by the Government Accountability Office (GAO), a nonpartisan watchdog housed in the legislative branch of the U.S. government. Typically, GAO turns its investigative gaze on efforts to limit fraud and wasteful spending in the government itself, but in a new tactic at the urging of U.S. Senator Maggie Hassan (D-NH), the office instead performed real-world tests on the platform to see if these four popular AI models would aid in planning a terrorist attack.

“A terrorist can log onto an AI platform and in less than 12 hours walk away with a concrete playbook for how to carry out a deadly attack,” Hassan, incoming Chair of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, said in a press statement. “Today’s new report makes it clear that the AI public safety threat is no longer theoretical.”

GAO conducted this test in the spring this year, and earlier this week reported some disturbing results. Two of the platforms, according to an official GAO release, provided guidance on building and detonating an improvised explosion device, or IED, and two other AI models showing differing methods for targeting the electrical grid. Within 12 hours, all four models also gamed through potential locations and methods for carrying out such an attack.

Although these violent lines of questioning triggered each platform’s safeguards, GAO got around them using common safeguard-bypassing techniques. Additionally, they confirmed the validity of the information provided with experts. The results of this investigation were published in a 61-page report that will be central to future senate hearings on AI safety.

“We set out to do two different types of evil,” GAO director Kevin Walsh said in an interview posted on YouTube. “The first type is we wanted to create a bomb. And we didn’t just want to know how to create a bomb, we wanted it to help pick out a target, a location, and a time, and to give us instructions all the way…Evil scenario two, we wanted to do a bunch of economic damage, and in both cases that ended up being targeting the electrical grid.”

In one case, Walsh reports that one AI model would refuse to answer questions or divert the user to more safe behaviors but said that “it wasn’t always successful.” Walsh says that companies theoretically call law enforcement when suspicious activity is detected, but whether that occurs and at what frequency is uncertain.

“As AI capabilities evolve, AI providers will continue to refine their safeguards,” the report concludes. “However, in its current state, this technology can potentially be dangerous and its misuse represents a growing risk to national and economic security.”

The GAO officially released these terrorist-abetting findings on November 18, 2026, the same day Anthropic, creators of Claude, went public on the stock exchange. Despite the company’s own admission of AI being an existential threat to humanity, its IPO at one point reached a meteoric a $2 trillion valuation before dipping back down to a (measly) $1.6 trillion.

Darren lives in Portland, has a cat, and writes/edits about sci-fi and how our world works. You can find his previous stuff at Gizmodo and Paste if you look hard enough.

#6402. Physicists Crack a 44-Year-Old Nuclear Fusion Mystery

Scientists have found a way to predict the heating requirements of future fusion machines, offering valuable insight into one of the biggest challenges of harnessing the energy that powers the Sun.

In 1982, scientists studying nuclear fusion discovered something unexpected. Once the heating power inside an experimental fusion machine reached a certain level, the fuel suddenly became much better at retaining heat. This discovery offered a way to overcome one of the biggest challenges in fusion research. More than four decades later, predicting how much power is needed to trigger this change remains a difficult problem.

Nuclear fusion releases energy when light atomic nuclei combine, the same process that powers the Sun. Recreating this process on Earth requires heating a gas to extreme temperatures, turning it into plasma, a state of matter made up of electrically charged particles.

Machines called tokamaks use powerful magnetic fields to confine this plasma inside a doughnut-shaped chamber. However, keeping the plasma in place does not necessarily keep it hot. Turbulent motion within the plasma can carry heat away, making it difficult to maintain the conditions needed for fusion.

The phenomenon discovered in 1982 occurs when heating power crosses a critical threshold, causing turbulence near the outer edge of the plasma to drop sharply. Scientists call this the transition from low confinement (L-mode) to high confinement (H-mode), a state in which the plasma retains energy much more efficiently.

Achieving H-mode is essential for future fusion reactors. The difficulty is that the amount of heating power required depends on several factors, including how densely packed the plasma particles are and the direction of the magnetic field. Existing theories have struggled to explain both effects together.

In a study published in Physical Review Letters, researchers led by Brenno De Lucca, a doctoral assistant at EPFL’s Swiss Plasma Center (SPC), developed a theory that explains these effects within a single physical framework.

Using computer simulations, the researchers recreated the behavior of plasma inside a tokamak as heating power increased. They identified the physical processes responsible for the transition, developed a mathematical model to describe them, and compared its predictions with experimental measurements from existing tokamaks.

Their results showed that turbulence generates flows within the plasma that move at different speeds across its outer region. As neighboring layers move past one another at different speeds, they help disrupt the turbulent motion that created them in the first place. This reduces heat loss, allowing the plasma to retain more energy.

The researchers also found that the direction of the magnetic field, the movement of the plasma, and collisions between particles work together to make H-mode easier to reach in one magnetic field configuration than in the other.

Plasma density presents another complication. Increasing the density can reduce the amount of heating power needed in one range and increase it in another. The researchers derived equations describing these changes and other operating conditions, explaining why there is a particular density at which the heating requirement is lowest.

The model could help researchers determine whether future fusion machines will have sufficient heating power to achieve H-mode. For ITER, the world’s largest international fusion project, currently under construction in France, the researchers predicted a minimum requirement of 43 megawatts, comfortably below its planned heating capacity of 73 megawatts.

The outlook is tighter for SPARC, a compact tokamak that uses powerful magnetic fields and is being developed by the U.S. company Commonwealth Fusion Systems. Its predicted minimum heating requirement is 26 megawatts, slightly above its planned capacity of 25 megawatts, leaving considerably less room for uncertainty.

Reference: “Theory for the Power Threshold of the L−H Transition in Tokamaks” by B. De Lucca, P. Ricci, B. Labit, D. Mancini, L. N. Stenger and Z. Tecchiolli, 13 November 2026, Physical Review Letters. DOI: 10.1103/rw25-wy15

Funding: EUROfusion Consortium, European Union Euratom Research and Training Programme (Grant Agreement No. 101052200), Swiss State Secretariat for Education, Research and Innovation (SERI), Swiss National Science Foundation (SNSF), and Swiss National Supercomputing Center (CSCS)

#6401. This Company Wants to Make Fuel From Carbon Dioxide—Using the Power of a Nuclear Reactor

AIRCO hopes to make a carbon-neutral fuel from captured CO2 and hydrogen. Some sustainability experts are skeptical.

The fossil fuel industry is the largest contributor to climate change, and it’s not even close. According to the United Nations, the industry is responsible for 68 percent of all greenhouse gas emissions and an incredible 90 percent of all carbon dioxide emissions. Stick a stake in the vampiric heart of fossil fuels, and beating back the worst effects of global warming becomes suddenly much more possible. But as the recent climate summit at Antalya, Türkiye, this month displayed, the industry shows no interest in giving up its polluting ways, leading some countries to say the world is now “held hostage by the oil mafia.”

Despite this unwillingness to change, some companies are trying to find ways to make some good out of a bad situation. One of those companies AIRCO (originally named Air Company), based out of New Britain, Pennsylvania, did just that by developing a technology that creates jet fuel of a thin “air”—well, kind of.

Instead of making fuel at a massive refinery and transporting it long distances, the system is designed to produce fully formulated synthetic jet or diesel fuel closer to where it will be used,” Nick Steinke, the company’s director of programs, government and defense, said in a recent interview with Waste360. “It takes captured CO₂ and hydrogen and integrates the conversion process into a modular, containerized system.”

Instead of relying on centralized fuel producers, the idea is that synthetic fuels could be created on-site where they’ll be used directly, circumventing the climate impacts of transporting the fuel entirely. Also the ingredients AIRCO uses also aims to come from green sources by leveraging carbon capture technologies for the required CO2 and using electrolysis to supply hydrogen from water.

Chemical & Engineering News reported earlier this year the company hopes to supply the U.S. military with a complete reactor system by 2027 that will be powered on a government site using a small nuclear reactor (SMR), and supply a sufficient flow of energy required for both carbon capture and electrolysis to provide the volumes of ingredients needed to make these mobile, fuel-creating systems viable. It’s a task that at least one expert says sounds easier said than done.

“The technology seems like it holds a lot of promise, especially on the fuel-conversion side, but the part that I have a lot of questions about is, where are you getting the carbon from?” Sarah Gleeson, a materials scientist at Project Drawdown, told WHYY, a local radio station. “Because if they’re saying that there’s some kind of direct air capture functionality in this really mobile device, I would be skeptical at the capacity and efficiency of it.”

Carbon capture is central to the company’s promise of its technology’s carbon-neutral nature with the company’s CEO telling WHYY that “using more CO2 in our production process to make the fuel than we are putting out in the entire process.” Carbon capture, as a broad technology category, still remains unproved even as some climate models rely on its implementation (and the fact that the oil industry likes the technology is concerning to say the least).

If humanity hopes to secure a healthy planet for future generations, ending its reliance on fossil fuels is priority number one. But step one in the process is first limiting—and eventually eliminating— new fuel from being extracted from the ground in the first place while the advancements in green chemistry try to put to work the carbon dioxide that’s already here.

#6400. Scientists Watch Electrons Make an Impossible-Looking Quantum Leap

Experiments with graphene have revealed how remarkably effectively light can control electrons, offering a possible route toward a new generation of high-speed electronics.

Imagine riding an elevator whose floor indicator climbs from 1 to 2 to 3 before suddenly jumping to 20. You arrive at the twentieth floor without ever passing through the floors in between. In the quantum world, electrons can make a comparable leap in energy, and physicists have now found a way to watch it happen in slow motion.

Researchers from the University of Regensburg, Philipps-Universität Marburg, and Forschungszentrum Jülich combined laser technology with electron microscopy to capture this unusual behavior in graphene, a material made of atomically thin layers of carbon. Their findings, published in Nature, could help lay the groundwork for future high-speed electronics that use light to control the movement of electrons.

In semiconductors and related materials, electrons can occupy only certain ranges of energy, known as energy bands. Separating these bands are gaps containing energies that electrons are not allowed to occupy. Electrons normally remain within their respective bands, though under certain conditions, they can jump from one band to another without occupying the forbidden energies in between. Physicists call this process a Landau-Zener-Majorana transition.

The researchers used the electric field of an intense light pulse to accelerate electrons in graphene, observing how they switched between energy bands as they moved. Under these conditions, the probability of electrons crossing the gap through a quantum process known as tunneling reached as high as 100 percent.

Even when energy states are well separated, electrons can have a high probability of making the jump. What matters is how quickly they approach the energy gap. This makes the process fundamentally different from conventional quantum tunneling, in which a particle passes through an energy barrier in space.

Capturing these fleeting transitions required the researchers to observe large numbers of electrons simultaneously.

“If you want to know who has won a race, you have watch all participants,” explains Vincent Eggers, first author of the study. “Likewise, we must observe as many electrons as possible at one time to catch those that undergo a quantum mechanical transition while moving.”

To do this, the team used an instrument called a photoemission momentum microscope. Rather than producing magnified pictures of objects, the microscope measures the energies and states of motion of electrons, creating a map of how they are distributed. The challenge was combining these measurements with powerful, rapidly oscillating light fields that could drive electrons in a controlled manner.

“Our team worked on this experiment for many years. Now, we can track electrons moving across the entire energy landscape of a solid in real time,” says Rupert Huber.

The experiment also depended on exceptionally pure graphene samples specially produced at Forschungszentrum Jülich.

Ulrich Höfer, Huber’s research partner and one of the pioneers of ultrafast electron spectroscopy, recalls, “Being able to observe such a fundamental quantum mechanical process during our first measurement campaign was a very special moment for us—it was also made possible by the samples we used.”

“These precision experiments require material that is nearly perfect at the atomic level. This ensures that impurities do not obscure the delicate quantum dynamics of the electrons. Another important factor for the study was the use of “rotated” graphene, a specialty from Jülich, which allows the quantum dynamics to emerge particularly clearly,” emphasizes Stefan Tautz from Forschungszentrum Jülich.

Beyond capturing quantum transitions, the new technique allows researchers to investigate what prevents electrons from moving in a controlled way. The graphene experiments already revealed how interactions with the crystal lattice, the repeating arrangement of atoms within the material, disrupt the initially orderly motion of electrons.

Understanding these disturbances could become increasingly important as researchers explore technologies that use the extremely rapid oscillations of light to control electrons directly, rather than relying solely on electrical voltages.

“Our experiment opens a panoramic window into the quantum world. Now, we can follow in real time how electrons move through the energy landscape of a material. And this is just the beginning. Our method can be applied to many other quantum materials, opening up completely new possibilities for controlling their electronic properties selectively with light,” says Giacomo Inzani from the University of Regensburg.

Reference: “Subcycle videography of Landau–Zener–Majorana transitions in graphene” by V. Eggers, G. Inzani, M. Meierhofer, L. Münster, J. Helml, R. Wallauer, S. Zajusch, S. Ito, L. Machtl, H. Yin, C. This silver pepper shaker reveals the Romans' love of the spice and the lengths they would go to procure it.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The pepper shaker was discovered as part of an ancient Roman hoard.

Where it is from: Hoxne, Suffolk, England

In 1992, a farmer in the village of Hoxne in southeastern England was searching for a lost hammer with a metal detector when he stumbled upon a massive hoard of more than 15,000 ancient Roman coins, jewelry and tableware. Among the artifacts in the Hoxne hoard was a silver spice container in the shape of an imperial lady.

The artifact, named the Empress, is one of four pepper pots ("piperatoria" in Latin) discovered in the Hoxne hoard, according to the British Museum. The silver container stands about 4 inches (10 centimeters) tall and is decorated with gold around the woman's eyes, mouth, hair and accessories, including a scroll in her left hand. The woman's elaborate hairstyle helps date the creation of the pepper pot to the fourth century, but experts think the hoard may have been buried in the early fifth century, when Roman rule in Britain was ending.

At the bottom of the pot, which rests on a four-legged base, there is a disc that can be set at three positions: wide open, closed and partly open. The pot would have been filled in the open position with cracked pepper and then used in the partly open position for sprinkling the spice over food.

The ancient Romans were huge fans of pepper, Neil MacGregor, former director of the British Museum, wrote in "A History of the World in 100 Objects" (Penguin Books, 2010). Pepper didn't grow in the Roman Empire, so merchants procured it from India. This made it an expensive spice, and filling up the pepper pot would have been costly.

A wealthy Romano-British family likely used the pepper pot as elaborate tableware, MacGregor wrote. It is unclear whom the Empress was meant to depict, but researchers don't think it features a member of the Roman imperial family. However, the fact that she holds a scroll could indicate that she was both wealthy and well educated.

The ancient family who lived near Hoxne seems to have left its wealth behind during the breakdown of Roman rule in Britain, since the pepper pot was found in a chest that contained dozens of pieces of silverware, 29 pieces of gold jewelry, and more than 15,000 coins.

"This was the mobile wealth of a rich Roman family — precisely the type of person who is in danger when the state fails," MacGregor wrote.

#6396. Caltech Scientists Make Billions of Atoms Flash in Perfect Quantum Harmony

Caltech scientists aimed a laser at a crystal and watched billions of atoms fall into step, firing bursts of microwaves and infrared light in perfect sync.

In early 2024, researchers in Andrei Faraon’s Caltech lab discovered that a laser could make billions of atoms inside a crystal emit regularly spaced pulses of light. A tiny superconducting circuit trapped the microwaves the atoms emitted, creating a shared field that brought the atoms into sync.

“Remarkably, the atoms were flashing in two very different kinds of light at once, microwaves and infrared light, in perfect step with each other. That had not been observed before,” says Andrei Faraon (BS ’04), Caltech’s William L. Valentine Professor of Applied Physics and Electrical Engineering and the Fletcher Jones Foundation Director of the Kavli Nanoscience Institute.

Faraon’s team and Stanford University researchers led by Joonhee Choi traced the rhythm to a quantum phenomenon called superradiance. They used it to create a frequency comb, a light source with evenly spaced frequencies that serve as the ticks on a ruler. Frequency combs help atomic clocks keep precise time, let scientists measure distances and track ultrafast events, and identify chemicals by the light they absorb. The new comb generates both microwave and optical signals, a combination that could help connect quantum devices.

The team embedded billions of ytterbium ions, or charged atoms, in a yttrium orthovanadate crystal beneath a thin layer of superconducting material that trapped microwaves. A laser energized the ions, and the microwave field they generated enabled them to influence one another and synchronize. At first, they emitted microwaves steadily. Once the laser power crossed a threshold, the steady emission gave way to regularly spaced pulses.

Scientists have known about superradiance for more than 50 years. In this process, a shared electromagnetic field synchronizes atoms so they emit light together. Earlier experiments had produced a single flash or a steady beam. In the crystal, the ions settled into a rhythm and flashed repeatedly.

“Imagine a crowd suddenly starting to clap in perfect rhythm without anyone leading them. That’s essentially what these atoms are doing when they produce repeated flashes of light, and it’s remarkable that they can organize themselves this way,” says Choi, a Stanford assistant professor and former Caltech postdoctoral scholar.

In a conventional laser, light bouncing between mirrors prompts excited atoms to release energy in step with the passing light. The spacing between the mirrors helps set the frequency, so even a tiny shift can change it. With superradiance, the atoms themselves can set the emission frequency.

“Other mode-locked frequency combs depend on bouncing light off mirrors in a cavity, and those cavity lengths can fluctuate due to things like temperature,” says Tian Xie (PhD ’25), lead author of the Nature paper. “Because superradiance comes from atom–atom interference, it’s absolutely frequency-stable, and therefore it can, in principle, be a much better platform than previous frequency combs.” Xie completed the work as a graduate student in Faraon’s lab and is now a postdoctoral researcher at Stanford.

The team wants to use the laser to control how the ions pulse, “so that the atoms become a kind of programmable light source,” Faraon says. “Being able to tune each emission strength, pulse separation, and emission format would be very useful to suit each specific application,” he says.

Superconducting quantum computers use microwave signals, which easily lose their quantum information outside the ultracold conditions near absolute zero (about minus 460 degrees Fahrenheit). Infrared light can carry information over long distances through fiber optic cables. For a superconducting circuit to use that connection, its microwave signals would need to be converted into optical signals.

Ytterbium ions can interact with both. Each ion has three energy levels relevant to the experiment. The smaller gap between a pair of levels matches the energy of a microwave photon, while a larger gap matches the energy of an infrared photon.

“Whenever these ions generate a microwave field, there is a process that naturally generates a corresponding optical field at the same time,” Xie says. “That’s why in the experiment, you send a laser light to pump the atoms, and you see two emissions coming out at very different frequencies.” The paired emissions suggest the ions could one day link superconducting circuits to optical fibers.

Reference: “Observation of tunable superradiant frequency combs” by Tian Xie, Rikuto Fukumori, Wai-Keong Mok, Jiahui Li, Joonhee Choi and Andrei Faraon, 18 November 2026, Nature. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11289-7

The work was primarily funded by the Office of Naval Research with additional support from the Institute of Quantum Information and Matter (IQIM), the US Department of Energy, the Co-design Center for Quantum Advantage, and the Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation Experimental Physics Investigators. Individual researchers were supported by the Air Force Office of Scientific Research, the Terman Faculty Fellowship at Stanford University, the Quad Fellowship, and the Eddleman Fellowship.

Tune up your smart house, your home theater, and your body with deals as much as 50% on the best tech this Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

When I say “Black Friday deal,” what kind of object pops into your head? Be honest. It’s a TV, isn’t it? Even before so much of Black Friday was conducted online and before Cyber Monday was invented in 2005, people would line up to stampede for the best deals on the latest televisions. There are plenty of TV deals this Black Friday and Cyber Monday. We even highlight one of our favorites. But there’s so much more than just TVs on sale this season when it comes to tech. Here are a few of our very favorites.

Warm up, work out, cool down. You know the routine. Why shouldn’t you have the same options when you’re using your massage gun to ease away muscle soreness and alleviate pain? The RENPHO Active Thermacool 2 doesn’t just pulsate at up to 3200 RPM. It has four heat/cold settings from 46 to 113 degrees so that you can ice away muscle pain and heat away muscle tightness.

Of all the times over the past decade in which I’ve recommended SimpliSafe to friends and family, no one has ever come to me later and regretted it. Setup is simple for even the most DIY-allergic folks. There’s no professional installation needed, no waiting around between the hours of nine and five for a crew, and no contracts to lock you into using it. Most SimpliSafe components come with double-sided tape, which I can confirm doesn’t peel away your paint when you remove it from your walls.

SimpliSafe offers a few kits to get you started, from five pieces to 12, but the SimpliSafe 8-Piece Wireless Home Security System is the best pick for most homes. It’s the one that I used to set up in my two-bedroom apartment. Adding additional pieces, from motion sensors to indoor cameras to entry sensors and more, is simple. You just buy them individually and follow the easy-to-use instructions through the SimpliSafe app.

Ever since TCL landed on the US market in the last decade, it’s consistently offered among the best value in TVs. I’ve owned a few and used many. For the money, they offer high-end performance for a low-mid-range price. The TCL QM8L 65” 4K TV is even cheaper right now at $998. That’s even $500 less than the regularly “on sale” price of this past summer. And this isn’t an outdated TV that TCL is trying to unload before the holidays. The QM8L in a 2026 model. Along with 4K resolution on its SQD-Mini LED QLED display, it supports Dolby Vision IQ, Dolby Atmos, HDR10+, and IMAX Enhanced formats, and can achieve a 144Hz refresh rate.

Hey Alexa, tell me which Echo device I should get for the kitchen if I like asking you for help with recipes or for the nightstand if I want more detail when I ask you for the weather? The Echo Show 8 is the 8”-display version of Amazon’s smart home hub, which ties together all your Alexa-compatible smart devices, from Fire TVs to other Echo Dot speakers, and even non-Amazon-brand components that support Alexa, such as Sonos surround sound systems and Philips Hue smart bulbs. You also have the choice of the Echo Show 5, Echo Show 11, Echo Show 15 and Echo Show 21 if you’d prefer a smaller or larger (or much larger) display.

There aren’t many solid state drives (SSDs) on sale these days, not since AI data centers have been snapping up so much storage that it’s causing shortages for consumers and driving up the price of storage for the limited stock that remains. That’s why it’s remarkable to see the SanDisk Extreme 1 TB Portable External SSD for $199 ($101 off). You should be backing up your precious files and photos to an external drive in case Apple iCloud, Dropbox, or Microsoft OneDrive have a catastrophe or you accidentally delete your files. I’ve used this SanDisk, and it’s both quiet and fast (much more so than any hard drive I’ve used) and durable, with IP65-rated water and dust resistance and an ability to survive being dropped from three meters (about 9.8 feet).

Vitamix is legendary among blenders. Clinging stubbornly to its 1980 aesthetics, every model Vitamix makes signals that it means business. The Vitamix Propel Series 510 comes with a 48 fluid ounce jar, two-horsepower motor, and a self-cleaning mode, because cleaning out a blender is the worst part of using it.

#6393. The 9 Robot Toys for Kids That Make STEM Learning Fun

Get them working on those science and engineering chops out of the classroom.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

STEM-based schoolwork is a key part of your kid’s curriculum, but encouraging genuine enthusiasm for science, technology, engineering, and math that extends beyond the classroom requires more than a good teacher. For the right kid at the right age, a robotics kit may be a perfect fit. It can give a budding inventor the chance to learn about science in a practical way, on their own terms, and allows them to get creative. It also shows that science can be fun, and more than just a subject at school.

A good robotics kit balances out learning and problem solving with play. Not all of them do that effectively, though: Choosing the right one for the child in your life may not be so straightforward—particularly if you’re unfamiliar with the basics that robotics kits teach. To help you find a STEM gift this holiday season that's both fun and educational, we’ve compiled a lineup of editor-approved robotics kits. Whether you're getting ahead of shopping season or looking for a great last-minute holiday gift, these toys are both fun and give your child's mind a chance to grow.

During our research, we drew from our collective experience covering STEM toys and equipment for kids, including topics like the best microscopes and the best graphing calculators. We also read through studies on the importance of STEM education.

To make our selections, we looked for kits from reputable companies within the robotics space, such as Learning Resources and Wonder Workshop. We also took a look at toys and items that parents on the staff have bought for their own kids, making special note of any that ended up as household favorites.

While evaluating each kit, we gauged value for the price (especially because some kits cost upwards of $100), the STEM topics it covers, as well as how intuitive and (just as importantly) fun it is to use, according to parents’ reviews. Furthermore, we considered a wide variety of toys to account for different kids’ interests, ages, and skill levels.

If you’re on the search for a robot kit with a variety of play options that isn't too expensive, this is it. The solar robot toy from Sillbird includes the pieces necessary to build 12 different robot designs, so your kid will never run out of new ways to play.

The robotics kit offers two levels of difficulty, with half of the builds being simpler to assemble while the other half are more complex. So, once your kid masters the easier builds, they can move on to more challenging designs, all without ever needing a new toy.

A unique feature of this robot in particular is its power source. Instead of burning through heaps of batteries like other robot toys, it relies exclusively on an integrated solar panel that sits on the robot’s head. Whenever it slows down, simply place it in some sunshine and wait for it to recharge.

You can always count on Lego to be fun and engaging, but this kit throws in some coding and robotics to the classic building experience. This 1,177-piece set includes three Lego Star Wars droids—R2-D2, a Gonk Droid, and a Mouse Droid. Each of the droids looks like a standard Lego creation, but is designed to hold color and distance sensors, as well as an interactive motor.

Once they're built, kids can use the free Lego Boost smartphone app to program their droids and give them 40 different coding missions. Lego Boost is available on iOS, Android, Kindle, and Windows 10 devices.

With additional pieces included in the kit, kids can build and attach tools and weapons directly onto the droid for extra fun as they play.

This 77-piece activity set is reasonably priced and is perfect for beginners to coding and robotics. Botley the Coding Robot comes to life with an easy-to-use remote, so there are no apps to download (and no screen time involved). All coding is done directly on the remote control and Botley can be programmed to follow up to 120 steps in a row.

The kit includes coding activity sheets to help beginners learn the basics and get the most out of their robot. The kit also comes with several fun accessories, including black line pieces that Botley can follow on its own like a track, as well as several cubes and rods you can use to build obstacle courses.

For parents who want to introduce young kids to coding or build confidence in their new skills, Wonder Workshop’s Dash is a smart choice for young enthusiasts. Where many kits require extensive building before they’re up and running, Dash comes fully assembled and ready for about five hours of playtime before it needs a charge.

Each Dash is programmed to respond to external stimuli, so it can recognize and respond to dancing, singing, and the sound of your voice.

This coding toy is compatible with Lego, allowing kids to use it as a base for making their own Lego creations. There are also five free apps to download that give kids fun coding project ideas, from beginner concepts to more advanced ones as they gradually get the hang of programming.

Makeblock’s mBot is an excellent toy for young programmers looking to challenge their knowledge and electronics skills in practical application. The small robot takes about 15 minutes to build using an easy-to-follow guide and step-by-step instructions in 3D.

Kids learn to code in Scratch, a graphic programming language, with free included software. There’s also an app with game-based tasks to challenge kids and help them advance their skills.

The robot itself also has several features that expand its range of capabilities, such as the line follower sensor, the infrared sensor for the remote control, and the Bluetooth chip for controlling the bot from your phone. The toy is compatible with Lego bricks and has four expansion ports where you can add additional parts later on.

There’s a lot to like about this very cute little robot ball. It’s reasonably priced for what it offers, has a super-cool LED matrix that shows off characters and vector graphics, and boasts a top speed of 4.5 mph. The Sphero also has built-in sensors that detect light, cardinal directions, gyroscopic direction, and speed.

What makes this robot special is how it allows users to grow along with it. Once basic skills are mastered, young coders can move on to learning JavaScript, Scratch, and Swift.

Another plus is this robot toy’s durability. It’s waterproof and scratch-proof, so young explorers can take it outside through ponds and over rocks.

Robotics toys are, at their core, building toys. This kit from KiwiCo comes with internal motor pieces, external body parts, and blank robot skins so kids can design their own robot.

The finished product uses springs and a spinning mechanism to help the robot jump forward and rotate its arms. The key reason we like this kit so much is how well it focuses on hands-on application.

Unlike other options that are based in coding and higher-level thinking, this helps kids work with their hands and see how each individual piece interacts with the other.

Coding and basic electrical engineering are the focuses of this rover from Snap Circuits. Kids are challenged to build a full circuit board piece by piece, with over 30 parts to snap together, and then attach the board to the wheeled base.

Once the rover is built, kids code commands and directions for their “missions,” including patterns of flashing lights and sounds to get into the action.

One of the great things about this robot toy is that it takes kids from beginner to intermediate as their skills improve. After kids get a grasp of how to code through the app, they can create more advanced commands on their own using Blockly.

The robot also functions as a fun remote-control car that kids can drive in real time through the app.

This kit encourages kids to build and rebuild the robots, cars, and creatures of their dreams. It’s perfect for the budding inventor who likes to tinker with things around the house. There’s even a game element—10 playing cards that challenge kids to build various creations on the spot.

Protective goggles and a screwdriver accompany the included wooden pieces, electric motors and batteries, and hardware and tools. All the wooden pieces fit together easily and are designed with multiple purposes in mind.

While there is no coding element to the toy, its main focus is on helping kids build creative solutions to prompts and bolster their engineering and problem-solving skills.

Studies show that in addition to STEM literacy, robotics can help develop core skills like hands-on creativity, problem solving, communication, and teamwork. So teaching robotics isn’t just about setting up your kid to have a career as a computer programmer or engineer—it equips them with tech know-how and critical thinking they’ll need for virtually any type of education or work.

Choose toys that allow your kid to use their imagination and play out multiple different situations, both real and made up. Furthermore, make sure even if you want the toy to help them learn STEM skills, it still fits their interests and passions. A toy that gets played with often will help them learn a lot more than a more educational one that collects dust.

While you may think robotics clubs are only for middle and high schoolers, research has shown that children are also able to master basic robotics and programming skills when they’re introduced in pre-K to second grade.

Many of these kits are appropriate for children as young as 3 years old, while some are more advanced with an age suggestion of 8 and up. Before you buy, check the recommended age range listed by the company or on the box to make sure you’re choosing a robotics kit that challenges your kid while still being accessible to them.

You don’t have to shell out hundreds of dollars right away on a robot, especially if your kids are still learning what they like. There are plenty of robotics kits that run under $50 if you aren’t sure your kids are going to enjoy this kind of play and learning. Pricier options over $100 offer more complexity and can often grow with the kids, since they’re customizable to continue challenging them as they get older and gain experience.

#6392. Solo meerkats can find their way back home

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Meerkats live, forage and raise their young in large groups. But they’ve still got solo skills

To test meerkats’ solo navigating skills, researchers outfitted the animals with GPS trackers, separated them from their packs, and followed their journeys back home.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

It was a hot, dry day in the Kalahari Desert, and Mathilde Martin was running after a meerkat.

The animal wore a GPS tracker around its neck and bolted between shelters, like an action hero running for cover, says Martin, a biologist at the University of Zurich. She and her colleagues had captured the meerkat earlier that morning, driven it 1.5 kilometers from its pack and then released it into the desert. They were trying to find out how well individual meerkats could find their way back home.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The answer was quite well, the researchers reported November 19 in the Journal of Experimental Biology. The results suggest that meerkats can navigate expertly on their own, perhaps relying on mental maps charted early in life. “They all seem to be very, very good,” Martin says. It’s a surprise finding for a species known for its group cooperation.

Meerkats (Suricata suricatta), which live in southern Africa, form tight-knit family groups of up to 50 members. These social animals cooperate in many aspects of life, including by babysitting each other’s pups and watching for predators while traveling along foraging paths. Martin and her colleagues thought meerkats might also rely on one another for navigating. Some pack members, perhaps those who’ve had more opportunity to explore solo, might have spatial knowledge of their territory and lead the rest, she says. But that’s not what the team discovered.

In separate catch and release experiments with 20 individual meerkats, 18 made a beeline back home, back to their group or back to the site where they were captured. (The other two may have been too stressed to get moving, Martin says.)

Neither age nor individual experience, which researchers had been tracking, seemed to factor into the meerkats’ homing skills. Nearly all of them knew where to go, Martin says. She thinks these crackerjack navigators relied on visual cues to orient themselves. They’d pop up on their hind legs and scan the landscape before scampering off in a direct line to their target.

It’s likely that scent played a role, too, though distant scent marks may have faded by the time the meerkats were released. The researchers dropped the animals off in territory they hadn’t visited for at least 30 days. “Otherwise,” she says, “it would have been a bit too easy for them to find their way back,” she says.

#6391. Quitting statins after age 70 initially appeared to be safe, yet heart attacks, strokes, and deaths increased after four years off those meds

A trial of adults aged 70 and older without cardiovascular disease found that stopping preventive statins may carry greater long-term risks.

When adults aged 70 and older stopped taking statins for preventing a first heart attack or stroke, they did not see a significant jump in heart attacks, strokes, or deaths two years later.

A research team followed participants for a median of 103 weeks, and up to four years for some.

During that time, 12.7 percent of the group that stopped taking statins suffered a heart attack, a stroke, or death. That compares with 9.2 percent of the group that continued taking them.

The results were presented on Nov. 7, 2026, at the American Heart Association (AHA) Scientific Sessions in Chicago and published the same day.

Named STREAM, the trial enrolled 1,880 adults aged 70 or older with no known cardiovascular disease. The name stands for statin discontinuation as prevention among the elderly and multimorbid.

Every participant was taking a statin to lower cholesterol as primary prevention. That term means the drug is meant to head off a first such event, not a second one.

Each also had at least two chronic conditions, such as a past cancer or lung disease. The average age was 77, and 47 percent of the group were women.

Of those enrolled, 938 were randomly assigned to stop the drug and 942 to carry on.

STREAM ran from November 2021 to April 2026 at 24 clinical centers in Switzerland, France and the Netherlands. Hospitals in Bern, Lausanne, Geneva, Zurich and Basel were among the Swiss sites.

The main outcome combined three events: a nonfatal heart attack, a nonfatal ischemic stroke, or death from any cause.

During the first two years, 100 people in the group that stopped and 77 in the group that continued had one of them. That works out to 10.7 percent against 8.2 percent.

STREAM was built as a noninferiority trial, a design that asks whether stopping is not meaningfully worse than continuing. The two-year difference stayed within the limit set in advance.

Outcomes were judged by reviewers who did not know which group a patient belonged to, according to the University of Bern, which led the project.

Patients and their doctors knew the assignment, because STREAM was run open-label.

Its rationale was that the value of these drugs is uncertain after age 70 in people with no heart disease. Side effects and risky combinations of drugs are also common in that age group.

Across the full follow-up, 119 events occurred among those who had stopped, against 87 among those who had continued. The counts come from the AHA’s late-breaking science report.

The design centered on the two-year comparison.

Nicolas Rodondi led the work. He is professor of primary care and internal medicine and director of the Institute of Primary Health Care at the University of Bern.

He estimated that over two years, one additional major cardiovascular event or death would occur for every 40 people who stopped their statin.

The association’s report notes that the estimate requires further investigation.

A second set of measures looked at how people felt. Pain, quality of life, fall risk and muscle weakness showed no difference between the two groups.

Sarcopenia, the loss of muscle mass and strength that comes with age, was also no more common in one group than the other. Reports of muscle pain were no different either.

Roughly 14 percent of participants crossed over along the way. Some who had stopped restarted, and some who had continued quit.

Extra analyses that took those switches into account did not change the result.

“Our findings provide information for shared decision-making about cautious statin discontinuation when statins are used for primary prevention only,” Rodondi said.

The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) advises a statin for some adults aged 40 to 75. They must have at least one risk factor and a 10-year cardiovascular risk of 10 percent or more.

When that risk falls between 7.5 percent and 10 percent, it tells clinicians to offer the drug selectively, because the likely benefit is smaller.

For adults 76 and older, the task force concluded that the evidence is insufficient to weigh the benefits and harms of starting one. The recommendation dates from August 2022 and replaced a 2016 version.

Its advice turns on a patient’s overall risk, not on LDL cholesterol alone, and it addresses starting a statin. STREAM tested the opposite question: what happens when older adults already on a statin stop.

“Although deprescribing inappropriate drugs in older adults appears to be safe, the results of our trial suggest that additional randomized trials of discontinuation are needed for specific drugs,” Rodondi said.

The study was published in the journal The New England Journal of Medicine.

Archaeological discoveries can offer remarkable insights into the lives, cultures and beliefs of ancient peoples. From richly furnished royal tombs to caches of silver coins, some of the most significant finds have revealed how people lived, traded, fought, governed and died thousands of years ago.

Other discoveries stand out for their extraordinary preservation or historical significance. For example, the most expensive shipwreck on record — the 300-year-old Spanish galleon San José that's worth an estimated $17 billion — was found off the coast of Colombia in 2015 and continues to inform archaeologists and challenge governments that can't agree about its modern ownership. Meanwhile, ancient texts can provide invaluable clues about long-lost languages and civilizations. The Rosetta stone opened up the world of ancient Egypt to scholars, but researchers are still trying to decipher the mysterious Indus Valley script, one of the world's earliest urban civilizations.

Each type of discovery offers a new window to the ancient world. But which of these archaeological treasures would you most want to uncover? Vote in the poll below and let us know your thoughts in the comments.

#6389. Astronauts could turn everyday trash and moon dust into something surprisingly useful

Researchers have combined paper fibers and simulated lunar dust to develop lightweight insulation that could be manufactured on the moon.

Trash on the International Space Station is bagged by astronauts and loaded onto a cargo ship.

The ship then either returns it to Earth or burns up in the atmosphere. On the moon, part of that waste might be put to use as insulation.

Paper fibers have now been ground together with imitation moon dust by a team of chemists.

The mixture was dried into an aerogel, an ultralight solid made mostly of empty space. Very little heat passes through such a material.

According to the results, some insulation for a lunar base could be made on site. Two ingredients would be needed, and both should be plentiful there: waste paper and the ground outside.

The recipe was developed by Alexander Wei, a chemistry professor at Purdue University, and graduate researcher Jacob Staker. Their colleagues included researchers at NASA’s Glenn Research Center in Cleveland.

Wei said a lunar settlement will generate waste rich in cellulose, the plant fiber found in paper and cardboard packaging.

“And I can guarantee that astronauts on the moon will never run out of moon dust,” Wei added.

For now, the aerogels exist only as samples made on Earth. A manufactured stand-in was used for lunar soil, and the paper was clean laboratory filter paper.

The final drying step relied on a method the team considers less practical on the moon than freeze-drying.

Between 60% and 70% of wastepaper by weight is cellulose. When cellulose is torn into much finer threads, it can strengthen a material in ways the original fibers cannot.

A stand-in for lunar soil, or regolith, has already been mixed with recycled plastic by other engineers. Wei’s team paired the dust with paper instead and used it as a grinding aid.

Filter paper was first shredded in a food blender. The team then loaded it into a mill together with water, ceramic cylinders, and a powder called Lunar Highlands Simulant.

This powder is made from Earth rock to match soil from the moon’s highlands.

For two hours, the jars were spun at an acceleration about 60 times that of Earth’s gravity.

The team expects a mill of this kind to work in the moon’s weak gravity.

The paper fibers were thinned by the ceramic cylinders alone. Once dust was added, they became much thinner still.

The most common fiber width fell to about 4 millionths of an inch (0.1 micrometers).

Fibers milled with dust were eight times thinner than those milled without it. They were also at least 30 times thinner than the original paper fibers.

The milled mixture was frozen in small molds, and its water was replaced with alcohol.

The team then removed the alcohol with pressurized carbon dioxide, which is a standard way of drying aerogels.

“Imagine an aerogel as a high-tech thermos for a lunar base,” Staker said. “Most of it consists of empty space that insulates the interior, helping it maintain the temperature of what’s inside.”

Empty space accounted for 79.3% to 98.6% of the volume in these samples.

In total, 18 batches were made, and the recipe was varied between them. Cellulose made up 1% to 9% of the wet mixture by weight. Dust made up 25% to 75% of the finished aerogel.

Insulation is rated by its thermal conductivity, which describes how easily heat passes through a material. A lower value is better.

The batches scored between 30 and 45 milliwatts per meter-kelvin when measured in air.

An earlier attempt had produced a freeze-dried aerogel of imitation regolith and natural polymers. Its lowest reported figure was 70 in the same units.

The best new batches therefore had less than half the thermal conductivity of the earlier material.

The best insulation came from the batches with the least cellulose. Among the 18, the lightest batch was made from a mixture with 1% cellulose. Its conductivity of 30.9 was the lowest in that group.

When exposed to the moon’s near-vacuum environment, the pores would contain virtually no gas.

The team expects the aerogels to insulate better under those conditions. Several times less heat is conducted by other aerospace aerogels in a near-vacuum than in air.

Temperatures on the lunar surface can reach 266°F (130°C). That heat is a problem for many of the organic materials used in aerogels.

A sample heated in nitrogen did not start to break down until about 653°F (345°C).

Insulation and stiffness responded to the recipe in opposite ways. Heat was generally blocked best by the low-cellulose batches.

However, those batches were also soft, and they shrank the most during drying.

A batch made with 1% cellulose came out 52% narrower than its mold. Only 3.2% shrinkage was seen in a batch made with 9% cellulose.

The stiffest batch was also made with 9% cellulose. Under compression, it was nearly 300 times stiffer than the softest batch.

“Rather than trying to make the world’s best aerogel, we’re looking for the sweet spot where we can get the properties we need with the limited resources we have available,” Wei said.

To look for that balance, the team fitted a statistical model to the 18 batches. Three recipes suggested by the model were then made and tested.

Dust would be far more plentiful on the moon than waste paper. For that reason, one recipe was required to be at least 60% dust by weight.

A figure of 61.2% was suggested by the model. The resulting aerogel had a conductivity of 30.5, which was the lowest in the study.

The same aerogel shrank by about half. It also did not meet the standards for the strength test.

A second recipe was balanced across six measured properties. It insulated nearly as well, at 30.8, and shrank by 18.5%. This aerogel was stiff enough to be tested, but only 25% of it was dust.

The aerogels have not yet been made the way a lunar crew would make them. The team wrote that freeze-drying would be far more practical on the moon than the carbon dioxide method.

According to Wei, the lunar surface offers a natural vacuum and subfreezing temperatures at night. Wei said the water removed from the aerogel could also be recovered and reused.

However, this kind of material can be damaged by freezing. Growing ice crystals pack the fibers and dust together.

That packing is known to lower the quality of cellulose aerogels. To slow the growth of the crystals, the team proposed adding simple alcohols or sugars.

Only one kind of imitation dust was used, and the paper was not real trash. Every heat-flow measurement was taken at 73°F (23°C) in air.

For the weakest recipes, additives known to strengthen cellulose aerogels should be tested, the team suggested.

Freeze-drying is now being studied by the team for its next batches. Those tests should show whether a freeze-dried aerogel can insulate as well as the samples made so far.

The full study was published in the journal ACS Sustainable Chemistry & Engineering.

#6387. A fast-growing heart is good for the Grinch. People are another story

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Unlike in the Dr. Seuss tale, a swollen heart can be an alarming sign of stress or disease

The Grinch’s change of heart turned him from grumpy to radiating joy. Is such a transformation possible in real life?

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

In the classic Dr. Seuss tale, How the Grinch Stole Christmas, the Grinch starts out with a heart “two sizes too small.” He’s a mean one, disguising himself as Santa Claus and stealing all the Whos’ toys, food and decorations. Poised to throw it all off a mountain, the grumpy loner has a change of heart as joyous song rises from Whoville.

“They say that the Grinch’s small heart grew three sizes that day,” giving him “the strength of 10 Grinches plus two,” says the narrator of the 1966 movie version. With a beatific smile, he pulls the stolen goods back from the brink and returns everything.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Would a too-small heart make you grumpy like the Grinch? And what would happen if your heart went from too small to really big in an instant? The answer depends on what causes the heart to shrink or swell, experts say. And whether or not you are a snake.

Heart size is generally pegged to body size, says Michelle Kittleson, a cardiologist at Cedars Sinai Smidt Heart Institute in Los Angeles. Bigger people tend to have bigger hearts. But some people, she says, have hearts that are naturally bigger or smaller than average for their bodies. It’s not clear why. However, she says, “there are negative consequences of having a too-small heart.”

In one 2025 study, researchers looked at medical records from more than 360,000 people in Australia. Those with smaller-than-average hearts had a higher risk of dying within five years than people with average or larger hearts, the team reported in JACC: Advances.

Smaller hearts may not pump blood as well as larger ones, making it harder for people to exercise. And if the Grinch didn’t exercise enough, maybe “then that made him really tired, and that made him grumpy,” Kittleson says. “Or maybe he did the research, and he found out that his life expectancy was shortened because of it, and that made him even grumpier.”

But would rapidly increasing his heart’s size be good for the Grinch?

As the Grinch slides downhill toward Whoville, pulled by a sled piled high with presents he’d stolen and now was returning, he physically undergoes a change. What started as a heart two sizes too small swelled three sizes, both curing his grumpiness and giving him super strength. Or so the classic tale goes. A person going through such a dramatic change may not fare as well.

There are many ways a heart can grow, says Leslie Leinwand, a molecular biologist and geneticist at the University of Colorado Boulder. With vigorous exercise, “your heart gets bigger in good ways,” Leinwand says. That can be true for athletes who do lots of cardio, such as swimmers and marathon runners.

“Their heart gets bigger and thicker,” Kittleson says. “But it’s a good thing in them because it helps them pump more blood per minute than someone with a normal-size heart.” Pregnancy also makes the whole organ expand to boost blood to the developing fetus. If people stop exercising, or give birth, their hearts will shrink back to normal size within months.

Some diseases, though, can enlarge hearts in deadly ways. “If you’ve got untreated high blood pressure,” Leinwand says, “you can get a huge heart, and it’s not good for you.”

Stress, bad heart valves and some genetic diseases can also result in bigger, but weaker, hearts. In those cases, the heart muscle grows in order to pump more blood. At the same time, the inside of the left ventricle — the heart chamber that pumps oxygenated blood to the body — can shrink. That makes it harder for the heart to push blood out. This kind of growth takes time, Kittleson says.

There is one rare condition in which the heart can inflate suddenly. Called takotsubo or stress cardiomyopathy — or in some cases, broken-heart syndrome — it is brought on by extreme stress. That can include positive things like winning the lottery or entering a surprise party or negative stress such as break-up or losing a job.

A surge of epinephrine, or adrenaline, from stress can make the left ventricle bulge into the shape of a pot used to catch octopuses. (Takotsubo is Japanese for “octopus pot.”) That causes immediate heart failure as the heart chamber gets too big to pump blood.

So instead of becoming super strong, the Grinch “would have keeled over and collapsed,” Kittleson says. (People can survive with prompt medical care and their hearts can return to normal size in a few months.)

Given the Grinch survived his rapid growth, there’s another possible scenario: Maybe his heart is more like a snake’s.

Pythons’ hearts can balloon by up to 25 percent in a day after the snakes eat a large meal — sometimes as big as an adult deer. And the bigger a python’s meal, the more its heart grows. Larger hearts pump blood with more force, Leinwand and her colleagues reported in 2024 in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The researchers don’t know if this makes the snakes stronger overall.

Once a meal is digested, the heart shrinks again. Snakes can go through many shrink-and-grow cycles with no ill effect. Leinwand hopes that studying these snakes will lead to treatments that make human hearts healthier.

But becoming kinder, like the Grinch? Maybe not.

Notes Leinwand, “our snakes, when they eat a lot, they get rather aggressive.”

After eight years slingshotting around the inner solar system, the joint European-Japanese spacecraft BepiColombo has finally entered into orbit around Mercury — becoming only the second mission ever to orbit the closest planet to the sun.

Mission scientists confirmed on Saturday (Nov. 21) that the spacecraft reached Mercury's orbit and is transmitting data back to the ground team.

However, the orbital insertion didn't go entirely as planned, European Space Agency (ESA) representatives said in a statement on Monday. Due to a software glitch, the spacecraft didn't fire its thrusters for the full 37 minutes required to slow its approach to Mercury.

ESA has investigates the issue and confirmed the spacecraft's new trajectory; meanwhile, BepiColombo remains "safe," the statement noted. The spacecraft should be ready to begin a year of intensive science observations of Mercury starting a few months from now.

An illustration of BepiColombo approaching Mercury for orbital insertion.

Built jointly by ESA and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA), BepiColombo is actually two separate probes, which are currently stacked one atop the other in orbit. The ESA-built orbiter, named the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO), and the JAXA-built orbiter, the Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (Mio), carry separate science instruments, and they will soon diverge into separate orbital paths around the mysterious inner planet, operating as two probes gathering different streams of data.

A selfie of BepiColombo during a flyby of Mercury's north pole in 2025.

The pair of probes launched together aboard an Ariane 5 rocket in October 2018, and spent the following eight years on an interplanetary journey that took them past Earth, the moon and Venus. It even passed by Mercury itself six times. (During one of these flybys, in January 2025, Bepi snapped an incredible closeup photo of Mercury's north pole.)

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

This complicated cosmic choreography was necessary to prevent BepiColombo from picking up too much speed and overshooting Mercury's orbit, according to ESA. Mercury sits about 36 million miles (58 million kilometers) from our star, or roughly one third of the distance between Earth and the sun. That makes it very difficult for a spacecraft to reach Mercury without being captured by the sun's considerable gravitational pull and dragged off course.

Only one other spacecraft — NASA's MESSENGER probe — has succeeded in entering Mercury orbit before, circling the planet from 2011 to 2015 after its own seven-year journey through space.

BepiColombo will spend the next few months getting both probes in position to start mapping Mercury in the greatest detail ever.

MPO and Mio are expected to separate in early December, with Mio entering a highly elliptical orbit around Mercury's poles. MPO will then take a few more months to fine-tune its trajectory, reaching a lower and more circular polar orbit in March 2027, according to ESA. Its science operations are expected to begin in April.

The sibling probes will each orbit Mercury several times a day, with MPO completing an orbit every 2 hours or so. Observing the mysterious inner planet from several different vantage points, the probes will make the most comprehensive map of Mercury ever. The mission's suite of science instruments will study the planet across the electromagnetic spectrum, taking observations in X-rays, gamma-rays and ultraviolet light, as well as collecting detailed measurements of the planet's magnetic field.

With this information, scientists hope to unravel many mysteries of the least-explored planet in the solar system. The new data should enable scientists to tackle myriad long-standing questions: What is Mercury's interior made of, and where does its magnetic field come from? How was the planet formed, and to what extent is it still tectonically active today? By making precise measurements of the spacecraft's orbit and position, a radio experiment will also provide a new test of Einstein's theory of general relativity.

Stay tuned for more updates from ESA about humanity's first visit to Mercury in more than a decade.

Brandon is the space / physics editor at Live Science. He holds a bachelor's degree in creative writing from the University of Arizona, with minors in journalism and media arts. His interests include black holes, asteroids and comets, and the search for extraterrestrial life.
