#6373. Power shutoffs meant to prevent wildfires may carry unexpected health risks

Planned power shutoffs in California were linked to more respiratory-related hospital visits, particularly when wildfire smoke was also present.

When the wind picks up on a hot, dry day in fire country, the power company may switch off the electricity on purpose. A line with no current in it can’t start a fire when it drops into dry brush.

A planned shutoff has a cost of its own, though. In California, on days when a large shutoff reached a neighborhood, people there were more likely to turn up at an emergency room with a breathing problem.

The rise was largest among people with chronic lung disease, and wildfire smoke in the air at the same time made it larger still.

Lauren Blair Wilner, an epidemiologist at the University of Washington, led the analysis with colleagues at Scripps Institution of Oceanography and Columbia University.

Utilities call these planned outages public safety power shutoffs, or PSPS, and no study before this one had measured what they do to hospital traffic.

In an interview with Earth.com, Wilner pointed to the days when the two overlapped.

“Surprisingly, the effects of a PSPS event and wildfire smoke co-occurring were not simply additive – we found evidence that their effects on health were multiplicative,” she said.

Three major California utilities serve 88% of the state’s electric customers. They have run these power shutoffs since 2012 and report each one to the California Public Utilities Commission.

The research group PSE Healthy Energy compiled those reports.

Wilner’s team matched the reports for 2013 through 2019, by zip code, against every emergency room visit and unplanned hospital admission by adults across 1,504 California zip codes.

Those records came from the California Department of Health Care Access and Information and included more than 6.6 million visits for breathing problems.

Each visit day was compared with the other days of the same weekday that month, so every patient served as their own comparison.

A large shutoff meant more than 593 customers in a zip code without power.

On those days, the odds of an emergency room visit or admission for a breathing problem were about 6% higher. Smaller power shutoffs made no measurable difference.

Shutoffs and smoke arrive together more often than not. Of the 11,293 zip-code days with a shutoff, 7,656 also had wildfire smoke in the air.

Asked by Earth.com what else the study showed, Wilner came back to those overlapping days. “Co-occurrence is what we really need to think about here,” she said.

Because days with both outnumbered days with a shutoff alone, she added, shutoffs should be studied together with the fires they are meant to prevent.

Picture a day with a large shutoff and 10 micrograms of smoke particles in each cubic meter of air. The odds of a breathing-related visit that day were 16% higher than on a day with neither.

The shutoff alone added about 6% and that much smoke alone about 1%, so the pair did more than add up.

The pattern was strongest among people with COPD, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, a long-term illness that narrows the airways and makes breathing hard work.

On days with a large shutoff, the odds of a COPD visit were 29% higher. With smoke on top, they were 37% higher.

Many people with COPD rely on an oxygen concentrator, a machine that pulls oxygen out of room air.

It runs on electricity, and its battery typically lasts three to four hours. A typical shutoff in this study lasted 86 hours, more than three days.

Wilner said planners should take simultaneous outages into account as they prepare for wildfires and expand healthcare capacity.

“It is essential to put measures in place to ensure that people relying on electricity dependent medical equipment have access to power and can readily access healthcare, if needed,” she said.

Visits for heart problems didn’t rise during shutoffs, with or without smoke, and neither did visits for mental health crises.

Earlier studies of blackouts in New York State and Florida largely agree, suggesting that outages may be more strongly associated with respiratory problems than heart problems.

How long a shutoff lasted also mattered less than how many people it reached.

When the team counted total hours without power over the previous week instead, they found no link between duration alone and hospital visits.

Each additional 1,000 customers without power, on the other hand, was linked to about 2% higher odds of a breathing-related visit. For COPD visits, the figure was 6%.

Utilities report outages by circuit, so the team can’t say who inside a zip code lost power.

The researchers assumed customers were spread evenly along each circuit, which means some people counted as exposed weren’t.

Nor can the records show whether a patient was home during a shutoff. People may travel to a place that still has power, and breathe more smoke on the way.

Only adults 20 and older who reached a hospital are counted, so anyone who got sick at home and stayed there is missing.

The study covered 2013 to 2019, when planned power shutoffs were less common than they are today.

Since 2022, utilities in Washington, Oregon, Idaho, and Hawaii have used shutoffs too. California requires utilities to warn customers first and to open centers where people can charge devices.

Wilner’s team didn’t test whether those centers keep anyone out of the emergency room.

Wilner’s team is turning to what happens after a wildfire or other disaster, when outages and evacuations overlap.

“There are not complete datasets on historical evacuations and power outages after disasters, making it impossible to study the ways in which these things play out and affect health after an event,” she told Earth.com.

Those records, she said, would show what affected communities need and how to reach them.

For now, seven years of California records offer valuable insight into the potential health consequences of planned power shutoffs.

The full study was published in the journal PLOS Medicine.

Archaeologists have found the remains of a 2,900-year-old sanctuary on an island mountaintop, where ancient Greeks may have worshipped the goddess Artemis.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The discovery of a 2,900-year-old mountaintop sanctuary on a Mediterranean island shows the ancient Greek veneration for high mountains and their link to the Greek gods, archaeologists say.

The sanctuary was found during new excavations on Euboea, a very large island only about 30 miles (50 kilometers) northeast of Athens. The sanctuary did not include any buildings, such as a temple. Archaeologists think it was used for offerings and feasting by worshippers for hundreds of years, from about the ninth century B.C. until the first or second century A.D., during Imperial Roman times.

"We know that in the ancient Greek world, religious life was not limited to large temples and urban sanctuaries," excavation leader Chloé Chezeaux, an archaeologist at the Swiss School of Archeology in Greece, told Live Science in an email. "There were also many places of worship in the countryside and in the mountains."

Chezeaux led the excavations this year near the summit of Elatias, one of the highest peaks of Mount Olympus on Euboea. It is not, however, the mainland Mount Olympus traditionally regarded as the abode of the Greek gods.

Chezeaux said that her team first spotted signs of the sanctuary during an archaeological survey in 2025. In excavations throughout Greece, "mountaintop sanctuaries are not uncommon," she said. "The problem is that these sanctuaries often left very little archaeological evidence, sometimes with no visible structures at all, which makes them particularly difficult to identify."

Archaeologists found the sanctuary during a survey in 2025 and first excavated it in 2026.

The sanctuary on the Euboean Olympus, however, has yielded "an exceptional concentration of pottery," she said. The earliest is from at least the ninth century B.C., during the early Greek Geometric period — named after the distinctive patterns on ceramics of the time.

"This means that people were coming to this summit over several centuries, perhaps even for more than a thousand years," Chezeaux said.

The sanctuary was used in ancient times mainly by people from the nearby city of Eretria, where the Swiss School of Archaeology is now based.

"Reaching the summit is quite a physical challenge even today," Chezeaux said. "The final part of our ascent involves walking about 3 kilometres [1.8 miles], with an elevation gain of 650 metres [2,130 feet]"

Researchers now reach the summit from the nearest mountain pass in about an hour, but "it's difficult to estimate how long the journey would have taken in antiquity," she said. "Travel conditions were different, we don't know which routes people followed, and … not everyone visiting the sanctuary necessarily came from the city of Eretria."

The effort required to get to the mountaintop is part of the mystery.

"People were willing to devote considerable time and energy to reaching these places, and in our case they seem to have done so over many generations," Chezeaux said. This raised questions of what the mountain meant to worshippers, and why this particular summit remained important for so long, she said.

The immortal Greek gods of ancient myths were said to watch the affairs of mortal humans from their home on the summit of a different Mount Olympus, in a mountain range between the northern Greek regions of Thessaly and Macedonia. The highest mountain in Greece, it stands at over 9,500 feet (2,900 m) high, while the Euboean Olympus is almost 3,800 feet (1,100 m) high, and the Elatias peak on it is about 100 feet (30 m) lower than its highest peak.

The Mount Olympus in northern Greece is the highest of several mountains with that name.

The tradition of the northern Olympus on mainland Greece dates from the poems of Homer and Hesiod, which were written in about the eighth century B.C. But the name Olympus was already widespread for high mountains, and modern Greece has several mountains bearing this name.

Chezeaux said religious ceremonies were often held at the sanctuary high on the Euboean Olympus, as well as at other sites on the island.

"In antiquity, Eretria had a very rich religious life, with sanctuaries both within the city and throughout its territory," Chezeaux said. "Mount Olympus dominates much of the surrounding region, and its prominent position probably played a role in the choice of this location."

High mountains held particular significance for the ancient Greeks, and the journey to reach the sanctuary may have been part of the religious experience, she noted.

The excavation team has yet to find an altar at the sanctuary. While the chief Greek god Zeus is traditionally associated with mountaintops, an inscription at an ancient site in Eretria mentions "Artemis Olympia" — an epithet that suggests the wild nature goddess Artemis was worshipped at the mountaintop sanctuary.

The remains of offerings found in crevices at the site include bones from sheep and goats.

"Several of them show signs of burning, sometimes at very high temperatures," Chezeaux said. "These finds naturally suggest practices involving animal sacrifice and ritual meals, which played an important role in ancient Greek religion."

Tom Metcalfe is a freelance journalist and regular Live Science contributor who is based in London in the United Kingdom. Tom writes mainly about science, space, archaeology, the Earth and the oceans. He has also written for the BBC, NBC News, National Geographic, Scientific American, Air & Space, and many others.

#6371. Some of the most effective treatments for back pain are also the most affordable

A review involving nearly 15,000 people suggests that several drug-free treatments for lower back pain can improve health outcomes and reduce overall costs.

Treatments such as yoga, acupuncture, and cognitive therapy might seem like added expenses for people with lower back pain.

However, a new review suggests that these approaches can improve health outcomes while reducing overall costs.

Researchers reached that conclusion after reviewing 20 papers covering 24 studies and 14,884 people.

Eight treatments that use no drugs and no surgery were both more effective and less costly than usual care in at least one way of counting the costs.

The authors wrote that these treatments are still far from routine in most countries.

Manuela Ferreira, a professor at the George Institute for Global Health in Sydney, was the senior author. Her team included researchers at the University of Sydney and the University of Warwick in England.

“Low back pain is the world’s leading cause of disability, but many effective treatments can also save healthcare dollars,” Ferreira said.

“Our review found that approaches such as exercise, yoga, acupuncture and psychological support can help people recover while providing good value for money.”

Pain in the lower back is the leading cause of disability worldwide, and treating it costs a lot. In Australia, back problems accounted for about 2.2% of all health spending in the 2020 to 2021 financial year.

The team searched ten research databases for studies that compared what a treatment cost with what it achieved. They kept only treatments backed by at least one of three major guidelines.

Those come from the World Health Organization, the United Kingdom’s National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, known as NICE, and the North American Spine Society.

Benefit was measured in a unit that combines how long a person lives with how well they live during that time. Health economists call it a quality-adjusted life year.

The team converted every cost to 2024 British pounds and used the same cutoff NICE uses. A treatment counted as worth paying for if each extra year of healthy life cost less than £20,000.

Twenty papers published between 2005 and 2026 met those criteria.

They covered 24 studies, 55 comparisons with usual care, and 14,884 people in nine high-income countries, most often the United Kingdom.

Usual care in these trials meant ordinary first-contact care: a doctor’s advice, a booklet, some medication, and sometimes a referral to a physical therapist.

Six single treatments came out both more effective and less costly than that.

They were yoga, acupuncture, cognitive therapy, support for people managing their own pain, education aimed at reducing fear of the pain, and mindfulness-based stress reduction.

Two combinations did the same: workplace advice paired with a gradual return to activity, and a program of diet and physical activity.

In an interview with Earth.com, Ferreira was asked what someone with back pain should ask a doctor first. She suggested two questions.

“Is there anything more serious causing my back pain? If not, which is the case for most people, can you teach me or refer me to someone who can teach me how to manage my own symptoms?” she said.

In health economics, a treatment that is both more effective and less costly is described as dominant.

In the whole review, only one comparison went the other way, and that was a British massage program.

Massage cost about £324 more per person than usual care in 2024 money, and it gained no extra healthy time at all.

Whether a treatment saves money depends on whose bills get counted.

The review sorted every result three ways: the health system’s costs, an insurer’s or employer’s costs, and society’s costs, which add in lost wages and missed work.

A British yoga trial shows why that matters. In it, 313 people with chronic or recurring back pain were offered 12 weekly group classes.

Counting only health care, the classes added about £715 per person, and each extra year of healthy life cost about £19,300, just under the £20,000 bar.

Counting lost workdays too, the yoga group cost society about £293 less per person than the usual-care group. And the yoga group still gained more healthy time.

The biggest saving in the review came from a Dutch program for workers on sick leave with chronic back pain.

It paired workplace advice with a gradual return to activity, and it cut society’s costs by about £7,315 per person compared with usual care. An Australian cognitive therapy program cut them by about £2,671.

Savings like those count only when lost work is part of the sum.

A treatment did not have to save money to be considered cost-effective.

Counting the health system’s costs, 14 of 18 comparisons passed, including exercise alone, spinal manipulation, and exercise paired with cognitive therapy.

Counting society’s costs, 15 of 19 passed, and counting an insurer’s or employer’s, 11 of 14 did. Passing was the rule, but confidence in each pass varied.

Where a study reported how likely its treatment was to be good value, the figure ran from 50% to 99.6%.

One of the clearest savings came from an enhanced course of acupuncture in the United States, with extra sessions added to a standard 12-week course. It cut health care costs by about £396 per person.

Acupuncture and massage were tested in many of the studies, and their results were inconsistent.

The authors wrote that this points to context, who is paying, and how the treatment is delivered. A Belgian modeling study found osteopathy was dominant from a payer’s perspective.

The three modeling studies in the review met far fewer items on their quality checklist than the trials met on theirs, though. The weakest of them met two of 57 items.

A review in 2011 of 26 studies reached a similar verdict on some of these treatments, including exercise, acupuncture, and cognitive behavioral therapy.

Nine new economic evaluations have come out since the most recent review of the topic, in 2019.

The authors wrote that theirs is the first to cover every treatment the current guidelines recommend, measured against usual care.

Ferreira’s team wrote that yoga, acupuncture, cognitive behavioral therapy, and treatments aimed at reducing fear and stress still aren’t routinely offered or paid for in most countries.

Working out why, the team wrote, should be the next focus.

Asked what surprised her most, Ferreira said it was that these treatments are not always available to patients.

“I was pleased to see so many options can benefit both patients and society,” Ferreira noted.

“The good news for people with back pain is that some of the most effective treatments are also among the most cost-effective.”

“Investing in evidence-based care such as exercise, physical therapies and psychological support could help more people get better while reducing pressure on health systems.”

Every one of the 24 studies came from a high-income country, so the authors wrote that their findings are unlikely to carry over to lower-income settings.

Ferreira said testing them in poorer countries would take new trials and studies with local patients, clinicians, and policymakers.

Those would check that the treatments are safe, suited to local conditions, and acceptable.

Costs are tied to the health system that recorded them, and the studies measured them too differently to pool into one estimate.

Some people were left out by design. Studies of sciatica, where the pain runs down the leg, weren’t included, and neither were people who had back surgery in the past year.

Out-of-pocket costs, community services, and lost work were reported less often than the treatment’s price.

The larger gap is in what the review had nothing to compare. Not one of the studies that met its criteria tested a drug, an injection, or an operation for chronic pain in the back. Those treatments are paid for all over the world.

“We have not found studies on guideline endorsed pharmacological or surgical interventions for low back pain and therefore highlight the urgent need for those as well,” Ferreira told Earth.com.

The authors wrote that future studies should count lost work and community costs too.

The full study was published in the journal PLOS Medicine.

#6370. The 7 Best Garage Heaters for Your Workshop

These editor-approved electric and gas models turn chilly spaces warm fast—so you can pull off your gloves and get your projects done.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Garages and unfinished basements are often poorly insulated, making them prone to extreme cold in fall and winter. A garage heater can turn this typically frigid space into a warm, practical area for woodworking projects, vehicle maintenance, and more. If you plan to spend time in your garage this winter tackling projects at your workbench, raising the ambient air temperature is a must.

Garage heaters come in various styles, though the most popular models are electric and propane. Electric heaters are convenient and easy to install if a power outlet is nearby. Propane heaters are more portable and can cover more surface area. Natural gas garage heaters are also powerful options for larger garages and can offer long-term heating solutions.

Heaters can benefit not only comfort but also safety. Cold temps can cause condensation to collect on tools and stored items, which may lead to rust and other damage. Wintry environments can also cause car engines and batteries to wear out faster. A well-heated garage protects your investments and provides a warmer, safer place to work.

If you're ready to prep for winter weather, read on for our in-depth reviews of the best garage heaters, followed by the most important things to know before buying.

Although we haven’t tested the models below ourselves, we applied our experience testing space heaters and patio heaters to supplement our search for the best garage heaters. We spent a lot of time vetting features and specs, checking manufacturer websites, gauging prices, and consulting user reviews before deciding which ones made the cut. We spoke with mechanical and electrical engineering experts to understand what makes a great garage heater, and we considered heat types (electric, propane, or kerosene), as well as whether the heaters are permanent or portable.

This 240-volt compact garage heater is the best all-around choice for most spaces, with 7,500 watts of heating power and the option to mount it on the wall or ceiling.

According to the manufacturer, it warms a typical garage or unheated building to between 50 and 85 degrees Fahrenheit and should be installed with a foot of clearance from combustible surfaces.

The garage heater’s adjustable louvers let you direct air where you need it most, and a remote-controlled thermostat is built into the front of the heater. A wall-mounted thermostat is available for the unit as well, but it’s sold separately.

Thanks to its Wi-Fi capability, you can operate this heater from virtually anywhere to ensure your garage is warm when you get home, or to heat the space before you spend time at your workbench. You can turn the unit on and off and set recurring schedules through the app.

The garage heater is rated to warm a 1,000-square-foot area, with an adjustable output of up to 20,000 BTUs. It can be mounted to the wall or ceiling, and its large digital temperature display is easy to read, even from across the room.

But for the price, it’s disappointing that the garage heater doesn’t include wiring.

For a powerful 5,600-watt portable garage heater, we recommend this NewAir model. It’s designed to warm spaces up to 600 square feet, and it includes a 6-foot cord that neatly coils on top of the unit, with brackets to hold it down.

The fan has two settings: automatic (which turns on when the heating element activates) and continuous. You can switch between the two manually.

Use continuous mode to keep air moving in spaces with high ceilings or when you’re operating an air-cleaning appliance, like a bench-top air filter, as it helps push dusty air through to speed up the process.

Designed for outdoor areas like patios, this Briza heater still works well in a garage thanks to its dust-resistant properties. It comes with an adjustable tripod that you can set between 44 and 84 inches tall. Selecting between its three heat settings—900, 1,200, or 1,500 watts—is easy with the unit’s remote control.

The heater has a built-in safety sensor that automatically shuts the appliance off if it tips over. A timer provides additional safety (and energy savings) by automatically shutting the heater off after 1 to 9 hours of operation.

For a compact, affordable garage heater ideal for targeted heating, this propane-fueled unit from Mr. Heater is a great choice. It delivers 4,000 to 9,000 BTUs from a single 1-pound liquid propane canister and can heat up to 250 square feet. It works great on the floor by your workbench or desk.

The heater can run for up to three hours on high, or you can upgrade to a 20-pound tank with a separately sold adapter. The heater’s size and weight make it easy to reposition, and it’s easy to bring with you to a shed, campsite, or other workspace.

This heavy-duty, 240-volt garage heater is ideal for climates with major temperature swings, featuring a two-stage high-and-low heating system.

Its lower heat output suits mildly cool days, while the higher stage can warm garages in single-digit temperatures. It also has a fan mode ideal for increasing airflow in a potentially stuffy garage, plus an energy-saving setting that defaults to the lowest wattage to maintain the desired temperature.

A universal bracket is included for easy mounting to a ceiling or wall, and this heater has a remote-controlled thermostat. The only drawback is that it doesn’t offer much coverage for the price.

If you have an uninsulated wood garage or another minimally insulated space, this large, ceiling-mounted garage heater is worth a look.

It runs on natural gas (a propane conversion kit is included) and, with a built-in electric fan, can warm areas up to 2,000 square feet thanks to its impressive 80,000-BTU output. It also has a powered exhaust that allows for vertical or horizontal venting.

Note that the Big Maxx does not come ready to install; you’ll have to purchase a thermostat, gas hose, fittings, and regulator separately. For most people, it’s best to have a licensed heating-cooling contractor install this garage heater.

There’s a lot to consider when using a heater to keep your garage safe and comfortable. So we picked the brain of Pat Porzio, a mechanical engineer and multi-licensed tradesman (electrical, plumbing, HVAC). He’s also the HVAC manager for Russo Brothers in East Hanover, New Jersey. We also spoke with David Shapiro, an electrician, author, and expert on old house wiring who contributes to electrical product and installation standards.

Both agree on one thing: Your overarching concern in heating a garage is safety. The first words out of both their mouths were identical: “Pull a permit.” That is, if you plan to use a permanently installed electric or gas-fired garage heater, you need to file a building permit for the work—whether you do the work yourself or hire a contractor. Permitted installations are inspected by the town or other authority with jurisdiction over this work where you live, which increases the likelihood of a safe installation.

Aside from pulling a building permit for the electrical work, Shapiro steers homeowners away from any heater without a UL (or other safety-related U.S. testing agency) listing.

Using a 120-volt space heater is simpler; same goes for small propane-fired and kerosene heaters. You don’t need a building permit to use one of these in a garage. Still, there are safe and unsafe ways to use these heaters. For more on that topic, check out our garage heater safety tips below.

As we mentioned earlier, there are a couple of different types of garage heaters. Electric heaters are easier to install, don't require a vent, and are generally safer. But depending on your local electricity rates, they can be more expensive to run. Gas heaters use natural gas or propane, and they can be a more cost-effective option for heating larger garages. They require ventilation, which can be a pain if you don't already have the right setup.

Infrared heaters heat objects rather than the air, so they can be a good companion for localized projects at your workbench. Forced-air heaters use a fan to distribute heat quickly and work well for large spaces, but they require good insulation to run efficiently and may kick up dust around your workshop.

For most garages, an electric heater is often the most viable option because it's easy to install, safe, and effective. But if you have a larger or poorly insulated garage, a gas heater might be the way to go.

“A bigger heater is not necessarily better,” Porzio says. “An oversized heater will short cycle. That is, it will turn on and off too frequently. It satisfies heating demand very quickly and abruptly turns off. A heater that is too small will do just the opposite. It will run and run and never fulfill the heating demand, eventually wearing itself out.”

Before contractors install a boiler or furnace, they perform a series of calculations, called a Manual J, to determine the correct size. While homeowners can get a rough estimate by multiplying the area's square footage by 50 to get the required BTUs, Porzio recommends using simplified Manual J forms online or a sizing tool like those on King-Electric.com and Newair.com.

For reference, a two-car garage will need a heater ranging from 30,000-50,000 BTUs to reach a consistent, comfortable temperature.

Whether you attempt the electrical work or hire it out, Shapiro has two more recommendations. First, don’t install the heater so that a power cord leading to a machine or tool could be draped directly in front of it. The heat can damage the cord.

Second, consider installing a CO alarm in the garage. A CO alarm can make the garage a safer place to work, especially if you’re heating it with gas, and it can also protect the occupants of the house.

#6369. One of Russia’s most active volcanoes rises above a sea of clouds

A striking Landsat 9 image reveals the snow-covered summit and active lava dome of Shivelyuch volcano on Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula.

Today’s Image of the Day features one of Russia’s most active volcanoes rising above a blanket of clouds on the Kamchatka Peninsula.

Snow covers the upper slopes of Shivelyuch, while a dark formation near the summit offers a glimpse of the volcanic activity taking place within the mountain.

The image was captured on November 8, 2026, by the Operational Land Imager aboard Landsat 9. Although clouds concealed much of the surrounding landscape, the volcano’s summit remained visible from space.

The contrast between the snowy mountainside and the exposed volcanic rock offers a striking portrait of a landscape that is continually being rebuilt from within.

Shivelyuch, also known as Shiveluch, is among the largest and most active volcanoes on the Kamchatka Peninsula in Russia’s Far East.

The mountain has a complex geological history. Its older structure, known as Stary Shiveluch, dates back roughly 65,000 years.

A younger volcanic complex, Molodoy Shiveluch, subsequently developed within the remains of the older mountain.

The Smithsonian Institution’s Global Volcanism Program has documented at least 60 major eruptions at Shivelyuch during the Holocene, the geological epoch that began approximately 11,700 years ago.

Successive eruptions and collapses have left extensive deposits of volcanic material across the surrounding terrain. These deposits preserve a record of the mountain’s turbulent past.

One of the most intriguing features of Shivelyuch is its enormous caldera, a depression measuring approximately 5.6 miles (nine kilometers) across.

Within this depression, a lava dome has developed as magma reaches the surface. The dome stands out against the snow in the satellite image.

Unlike the fluid lava commonly associated with Hawaiian volcanoes, the thick lava that builds volcanic domes does not travel easily across the landscape.

Instead, it accumulates around the opening from which it emerges.

As more material reaches the surface, the dome can expand, develop fractures, and become increasingly unstable.

Sections of these domes sometimes collapse. Such events can unleash pyroclastic flows – rapidly moving mixtures of scorching gas, ash, and fragmented rock that sweep down a volcano’s slopes.

The process can dramatically alter the appearance of a mountain, sometimes within minutes.

Kamchatka’s extraordinary volcanic landscape owes its existence to the movement of enormous sections of Earth’s outer shell.

The peninsula sits along the Pacific Ring of Fire, a vast region of geological activity surrounding much of the Pacific Ocean.

Here, the Pacific tectonic plate descends beneath another plate in a process called subduction.

Water released from the descending plate promotes melting in the overlying mantle, generating magma that can eventually rise toward the surface.

Over millions of years, this process has created a remarkable concentration of volcanoes, along with hot springs, geysers, and other geothermal features.

Kamchatka provides scientists with an opportunity to observe some of the fundamental processes responsible for reshaping Earth’s surface.

The effects of volcanic activity at Shivelyuch can extend well beyond the peninsula.

Although volcanic ash resembles ordinary dust, it consists of tiny fragments of rock, minerals, and volcanic glass.

These abrasive particles can damage aircraft engines and other critical equipment.

High-altitude winds can carry ash clouds across international borders and oceans. In July 2026, ash from Shivelyuch reached Alaskan airspace after traveling across the Bering Sea, disrupting air travel.

Even between major explosions, previously deposited ash can become airborne again when strong winds sweep across the landscape.

This means that an ash plume does not necessarily indicate that a new explosive eruption has occurred.

Volcanic activity at Shivelyuch had persisted for several months when Landsat 9 acquired this image.

Monitoring a remote volcano surrounded by unpredictable weather presents considerable challenges.

Satellites offer scientists an invaluable perspective on places where direct observations are difficult.

In addition to capturing changes in the appearance of volcanic landscapes, instruments aboard some satellites can detect infrared radiation associated with unusually hot surfaces.

These measurements help researchers identify areas of elevated temperature that may be associated with freshly exposed lava or other volcanic activity.

By comparing observations collected over extended periods, scientists can also track the growth and destruction of lava domes, map volcanic deposits, and document changes to the surrounding environment.

Weather clouds can interfere with many of these observations, making clear views of active volcanic features particularly valuable.

Seen from hundreds of miles above Earth, Shivelyuch appears almost serene. Its snow-covered slopes emerge from the clouds, revealing a rugged summit seemingly isolated from the world below.

Yet the mountain’s appearance belies the geological activity taking place beneath its surface.

The dark lava dome visible in today’s image represents the latest chapter in a history of destruction and renewal spanning thousands of years.

Long after the surrounding clouds have dispersed, the forces responsible for building Shivelyuch will continue to transform the mountain.

Image Credit: NASA Earth Observatory /Lauren Dauphin, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey

#6368. The libido drug women want is testosterone

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The FDA has yet to approve a testosterone product for female libido. That hasn’t stopped demand

One urologist says she has seen testosterone therapy for female libido "change people’s lives." But the data — and regulators — still need to catch up.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

These days, Jessica Yih spends a lot of time talking to women about testosterone. Interest is “coming from all directions,” says the University of California, Irvine Health urologist. A major source: women who hope testosterone can boost the female libido. Only about a decade ago, women looking for libido treatments had few medical options — even though women of all ages struggle with low sexual desire.

Some non-hormonal treatments are now available, but the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has yet to approve a female testosterone product, despite years of research suggesting it can boost sexual function and desire among postmenopausal women. Female testosterone products are approved in countries including the United Kingdom and Australia.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Not many studies have looked at testosterone’s effects on libido in premenopausal women, but preliminary data in that area are also promising, according to a 2026 research review in The Journal of Sexual Medicine that Yih coauthored. “I have seen it change people’s lives,” Yih says. The hormone seems to make the female brain more receptive to sexual stimuli; it also promotes physical effects that enhance sexual pleasure, such as increased blood flow to the genitals. Right now, American women interested in these potential benefits have to look for them off-label. But that may change. In September, the FDA held a public meeting on testosterone use among menopausal women, “with the goal of informing future research and potential drug development in this area,” says Kaveeta Vasisht, the FDA’s associate commissioner for women’s health.

The hormone has a rocky regulatory past. In 2004, an FDA advisory panel unanimously voted against approving a testosterone patch for women, citing a lack of safety data. There are still outstanding questions on that front, Yih says—like how, if at all, long-term use affects risk of conditions such as breast cancer and heart disease. Then, in 2011, a pair of Phase III trials found that testosterone therapy didn’t significantly outperform a placebo — a benchmark the FDA looks for when deciding whether to approve a new drug. That’s not to say testosterone didn’t work, says Tami Rowen, an ob-gyn at UC San Francisco. Rather, it seemed that hype about the hormone was so strong that study participants went in with sky-high expectations, leading even the placebo group to report benefits. The treatment was a “victim of its own success,” Rowen says.

Interest hasn’t let up, though. By one estimate, the U.S. female prescription rate for all uses rose from 0.4 out of every 1,000 women in 2018, to 1.8 out of every 1,000 women in 2026. That’s an increase of nearly 400 percent. With so much buzz, the potential placebo effect remains “the biggest problem with testosterone right now,” Rowen says.

Another outstanding question, Yih says, is whether using testosterone long-term increases the risk of breast cancer and heart disease.

Women seeking a libido boost do have non-hormonal options. In 2015, the FDA approved Addyi, the first treatment for low libido in premenopausal women. The drug seemingly raises levels of neurotransmitters that promote sexual desire while tamping down those that block it. A competitor, Vyleesi, hit shelves in 2019. Then, last year, regulators expanded Addyi’s use to postmenopausal women younger than 65. An international group of experts, including Rowen, issued recommendations for treating low female libido in 2025 in Sexual Medicine Reviews. Psychological therapies and Addyi are backed by the strongest evidence, the group found.

Rowen currently has her eye on in-development products including Lybrido. The drug, which is slated to enter a Phase III clinical trial in Europe, aims to rev sex drive in the brain and enhance physical arousal. The demand for new treatments is there, Rowen says. “Women deserve better than placebo.”

#6367. Narwhals may have a hidden vulnerability as the Arctic warms

Narwhals and seals rely on the same Arctic fish, but warming waters could leave narwhals with fewer options.

A narwhal and a seal do not appear to have much in common. The narwhal is a whale with a long spiral tusk. It can also dive much deeper than most seals.

In one Arctic fjord, however, the summer diets of these animals share a great deal.

Four marine mammals share those waters each summer. A new study found that narwhals, ringed seals and harp seals all lean heavily on one small fish, polar cod.

Of the group, narwhals had the narrowest diet. That could leave them with the least room to adjust if warming changes the fjord’s prey.

Monica Ogawa led the research. She’s a specially appointed assistant professor at Japan’s National Institute of Polar Research. She is also affiliated with the Arctic Research Center at Hokkaido University.

“Our findings provide further insights into potential changes in the Arctic marine ecosystem associated with climate change,” Ogawa said.

The fjord is called Inglefield Bredning, or Kangerlussuaq in Greenlandic. It lies in northwest Greenland. About 700 Inuit live in three settlements along its shores: Qaanaaq, Qeqertat and Siorapaluk.

Hunting marine mammals is how people there make a living. These animals are hard to watch while they feed underwater. So the team checked what they had already eaten.

Stomachs were collected over three summers, from 2022 to 2024. They came from animals taken in regular subsistence hunts, within existing rules and quotas. Local hunters and biologists did the collecting.

In all, 126 stomachs were gathered. Ringed seals supplied 54, harp seals 17, bearded seals 23 and narwhals 32. Each stomach’s contents were washed through a series of sieves, and every item was identified.

How big were the fish? To find out, the team measured tiny ear stones found inside fish heads.

“The collection of a large number of stomach samples would not have been possible without the cooperation of local Inuit hunters,” Ogawa said.

“Continued sample collection through collaboration with hunters will play an important role in the long-term monitoring of Arctic marine ecosystems.”

In total, 62 types of prey were identified in the stomachs. These included 27 species of fish and 19 species of shrimp. Clams and snails were also recorded, along with squid and tiny drifting animals.

Polar cod was found more often than any other prey. It was the main food of ringed seals, harp seals and narwhals.

Polar cod was present in 77.5% of ringed seal stomachs that contained food. By estimated weight it made up 82.1% of their diet.

The narwhal results were similar. Polar cod and one closely related fish accounted for 93% of the prey weight in narwhals. Squid or related animals were present in 88.9% of narwhal stomachs with food.

The diets were then compared between species. A meaningful overlap was found between ringed seals and harp seals. Harp seals and narwhals overlapped to a similar degree.

“The dietary niches of all species, excluding bearded seals, substantially overlapped, suggesting a high potential for interspecific competition,” Ogawa said.

The polar cod eaten by narwhals averaged about 4.7 inches (119 mm). Seals ate larger polar cod that averaged 6.4 to 7 inches (163 to 179 mm).

Narwhals also ate much more of a second fish. It is known as Arctic cod and is sometimes called ice cod. This fish is most often found between about 660 and 2,600 feet (200 and 800 meters) deep.

Narwhals can dive deeper than 2,600 feet. In this fjord they have repeatedly collided with research equipment moored at about 1,300 feet (400 meters).

This behavior suggests that narwhals may feed close to the seafloor. The authors propose that narwhals may use their diving ability to reach fish in deep water. In this way they could avoid competing with seals for the larger polar cod.

The diets of individual narwhals were also much more alike than those of individual seals. Narwhals were the only species in which this similarity was large enough to be considered ecologically meaningful.

Narwhals had already been ranked by earlier studies among the Arctic mammals most at risk from warming. Their limited range of prey is one reason for this.

Greater variation was found among seals, even within a single species. Seal pups ate smaller cod than older seals. Young ringed seals ate more tiny drifting animals and moved toward polar cod as they grew older.

The widest diet was recorded in bearded seals. A total of 52 types of prey were found in their stomachs. No meaningful overlap was found between their diet and those of the other three species.

Sculpins were the main prey of bearded seals. These are spiny fish that live on the seabed. Clams and snails were present in 70.6% of bearded seal stomachs with food. They were not found in any of the other species.

Most of the bearded seals were taken in shallow water where the seafloor can be reached easily. The shrimp they ate also lived on the bottom. In contrast, narwhals ate shrimp that live in open water in deeper areas.

Bearded seals are considered by the authors to be the most resilient of the four species. “Overall, dietary specialization and age structure emerge as key determinants of ecological resilience in marine mammals,” Ogawa said.

Something else turned up in the stomachs. It hints that the fjord itself may be changing.

Earlier studies were done here from 1938 to 1941 and again in 1998. Back then, the tiny drifting animal seals ate most was a cold-water crustacean called an amphipod.

The cold-water amphipod species recorded in earlier studies tends to avoid water warmer than about 36°F (2°C).

This time, krill were the most common drifting animal in ringed seal stomachs. Krill had never been recorded before in marine mammal stomachs from Inglefield Bredning.

The krill species found here can handle warmer conditions. They’re spreading north as Arctic seas heat up.

Redfish turned up too, in bearded seals. This fish comes from more southern waters and is moving north. It hadn’t been recorded as prey in this area before.

No such change was seen in narwhals or harp seals, compared with older studies. That difference may reflect how flexible each species’ diet is, the authors suggest.

A stomach shows only an animal’s last few meals. It can’t tell us how a narwhal eats across a whole year.

The fjord’s cast also changes with the seasons. Narwhals and harp seals leave in winter. Once sea ice returns, walruses arrive. So the study is really a summer snapshot from one fjord.

Harp seals may become important in this story. At present they visit the fjord only during summer. Warming is expected to push them farther north and keep them there for longer periods.

According to the authors, competition for the same cod could then develop among the three species.

How many cod live in the fjord, and where do they gather? The team doesn’t know yet. That information could help determine whether seals and narwhals actually compete for food.

Stomachs can’t show how deep each animal hunted, either. The authors called for tags that record each animal’s dives. A survey of the fish themselves is needed too.

“Building on the findings of this study, we hope to better understand how Arctic marine ecosystems will change in the future and how these changes may affect marine mammals and the local communities that depend on them,” Ogawa said.

Future studies could test whether narwhals would switch prey if polar cod and Arctic cod decline. That decline is expected as Atlantic fish move north.

The full study was published in the journal Marine Ecology Progress Series.

Quantinuum's Helios processor achieved a record-low failure rate of just 0.0005%, suggesting fault-tolerant quantum systems may need far fewer qubits than previously thought.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists at Quantinuum say they've set a new record in quantum error correction that brings large-scale, fault-tolerant systems one step closer.

The team claims their 98-qubit quantum system, Helios, demonstrated a failure rate of just 0.0005% in tests of its quantum memory, which is equivalent to an estimated five uncorrectable errors per million rounds of error checking.

This rate bests the previous benchmark set by Google's 105-qubit Willow quantum chip, which demonstrated an estimated 772 uncorrectable errors per million rounds in comparable tests, for an error rate of 0.0772%.

The result brings quantum computing closer to the "megaquop regime," where systems can run over a million operations without encountering an error, the researchers said. They detailed their findings in a study uploaded Oct. 16 to the arXiv preprint server.

In a statement, Robin Blume-Kohout, co-director of Sandia National Laboratories' Quantum Performance Lab, called the achievement "a significant milestone that quantum computing researchers have been working toward for many years."

"A scaled-up version of this system could reach the reliability required for useful fault-tolerant computation at a feasible size — less than a million physical qubits — which improves the outlook for practical quantum computing," added Blume-Kohout, who was not involved in the research.

Preserving the fragile information stored in qubits is one of quantum computing's greatest challenges and presents a major barrier to making systems practical.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Qubits, the most basic units of quantum information, are extremely sensitive to interference. Their delicate quantum states can be easily disturbed by heat, vibrations and other forms of environmental "noise," and if this happens in the middle of a calculation, the result becomes far less reliable — if it survives at all.

Quantum error correction has become a focal point for researchers for this exact reason. It introduces redundancy to quantum systems to ensure that small, potentially manageable errors don't wipe out entire calculations.

This involves spreading quantum information across multiple physical qubits to form a "logical" qubit. If a single qubit loses its quantum state due to interference, the redundancy provided by the logical qubit helps to keep the information it collectively stores intact.

The challenge is packing enough qubits into computers to ensure redundancy for longer, more complex calculations. This presents something of a catch-22: Adding more qubits provides more redundancy, allowing for larger quantum systems, but it also increases the opportunity for errors.

Unlike Google's Willow processor, which is based on superconducting circuits, Helios uses electrically charged barium ions that can be dynamically rearranged.

By shuttling ions around the processor, scientists can unite different pairs of qubits, allowing them to exchange information directly. That way, it doesn't have to pass through multiple qubits — a process that can introduce additional errors.

The team also developed a technique called "leakage repumping," which uses precise, split-second laser pulses to bring qubits that have slipped out of their information-storing quantum state back into a usable state.

To test how effectively Helios could correct errors as more physical qubits were added, the researchers used a type of error-correcting code known as a color code. They tested three progressively larger versions ‪—‬ known as code distances 3, 5 and 7 ​​—‬ which could correct one, two and three physical-qubit errors, respectively.

They found that Helios became substantially more reliable as they added more physical qubits. Each increase in code distance reduced the likelihood of an uncorrectable error by roughly 12 times. At the highest level tested (distance 7), Helios achieved a record failure rate of approximately one uncorrectable error per 200,000 rounds.

In the study, which has not been peer-reviewed yet, the scientists suggested that future quantum computers using the same technology as Helios could achieve extremely low error rates without needing an impractically high number of physical qubits.

According to estimates from Quantinuum representatives, a future trapped-ion system could support 100 logical qubits using approximately 30,000 physical qubits, compared with around 900,000 for a competing superconducting system.

"There is still substantial engineering ahead to scale to much larger systems and integrate all the elements of fault-tolerant computation, but this work demonstrates that our underlying hardware and error-correction approach can deliver the exponential improvement in reliability that large-scale quantum computers will depend upon," Dave Hayes, director of computational design and theory at Quantinuum, told Live Science in an email.

The researchers said they plan to apply their latest findings to Quantinuum's upcoming quantum

#6365. Surrounded by female cows, a bull named Achille chose to form a close bond with a male donkey named Patroclo that lasted for weeks, leaving scientists baffled

Achille the bull and Patroclo, a male donkey, mated and groomed each other for weeks in an Ethiopian pasture, forming a very unusual and mutual bond.

On a beautiful plateau in Ethiopia, a bull named Achille spent his days in a pasture full of female cows and other bulls. Yet over two weeks in March, researchers watched him ignore the females, and his own species, to mount a male donkey named Patroclo.

This happened not once, not twice, but at least 51 times.

Male cattle sometimes mount each other when no female cows are around, but Achille had plenty of them right beside him, and Patroclo never tried to get away.

The researchers concluded that the pair shared a selective, mutual bond, and that the mounting was part of it.

Elisabetta Palagi, an associate professor of biology at the University of Pisa in Italy, and her colleagues described the pair in a two-page report.

Martina Francesconi and André da Cruz, both PhD students at Pisa, are the lead authors. Da Cruz is also affiliated with CRIA, an anthropology research center in Lisbon.

Their report focuses on this one bull and one donkey, who they watched and studied very closely for eight days.

In an interview with Earth.com, Palagi said the team discovered the pair unexpectedly. They were in Ethiopia studying geladas, a kind of monkey, for a University of Pisa project called BRIDGES.

“It is a lovely reminder that careful field observation can reveal questions we had never thought to ask,” she said.

The pasture is in Debre Libanos, in Ethiopia’s Oromia region. Achille and Patroclo belonged to different owners. They met only during the day, when cattle and donkeys shared the pasture in mixed herds.

At night, Achille was housed with another adult bull, a cow, and a calf. Patroclo was housed with two other male donkeys.

Both animals had other possible partners in the same pasture. On any given day, there were three to six bulls and three to seven cows. There were also three male donkeys and two to seven female donkeys.

When the bull and the donkey kept interacting, Palagi said, the team began documenting the pair systematically.

The researchers recorded how Achille and Patroclo behaved toward each other and toward the rest of the herd. They kept recording even when nothing sexual was happening.

In all, the team saw the two together on four days and apart on four more.

Thirty-four of the 51 mounts included penetration. The researchers saw no avoidance and no aggression between the two animals.

Asked what surprised her most, Palagi named two things. One was how selective the two animals were about each other. The other was how actively Patroclo took part.

“What initially looked like an unusual encounter turned out to be a persistent pattern of preferential interaction,” Palagi told Earth.com.

Patroclo often presented his hindquarters to Achille and nipped him. Twice, another bull tried to come near Patroclo. Patroclo chased and bit him.

The two animals also licked, rubbed, and nuzzled each other. The team looked closely at the six seconds or so around each mount.

In about a quarter of the mounts, that friendly contact happened just before. In nearly three-quarters, it happened just after.

Contact before a mount isn’t a surprise, the authors wrote, because it may make mounting easier. Contact afterward is harder to explain. It appears to keep the social interaction going after sex is over.

Palagi said Achille and Patroclo had friendly contact with each other more often than with other animals, and it lasted longer.

The two also stayed close. When both were in the pasture, they spent more time near each other than apart.

Achille approached and mounted another male donkey only twice. That donkey avoided him and flattened its ears, a threatening expression.

When Achille tried to mount the other donkey, Patroclo moved toward Achille. Achille immediately stopped and directed his friendly behavior at Patroclo instead.

The researchers also analyzed Patroclo’s facial expressions using a coding system developed for horses. They compared four situations: Achille mounting him, Achille making friendly contact, Achille standing close by, and Patroclo alone.

Across all four, Patroclo’s face showed no detectable difference. To the team, that suggests Patroclo didn’t see Achille as a threat.

Achille courted cows the way bulls usually do, but he never tried to mount one. The other bulls nearby may have discouraged him, the researchers wrote.

After similar courtship with Patroclo, Achille did mount him.

The one time another bull tried to mount Achille, Achille rejected him. Among the rest of the herd, the team recorded no mounting between cattle and donkeys during the study.

Same-sex sexual behavior is widespread in animals. It has been documented in several species of the horse family.

But the team couldn’t find a published report of such behavior in donkeys. They also found no report of a lasting sexual relationship between domestic hoofed animals of two different species.

Classic explanations for same-sex sexual behavior include one animal forcing another, mistaken identity, and a shortage of opposite-sex partners.

The authors wrote that none of these seems to fully explain Achille and Patroclo. Their relationship was selective and mutual.

A bond like this must also come at a cost. The two spent time and energy on each other that could have gone into producing offspring. To the authors, the strength of the bond seems to outweigh that cost.

“Their relationship reminds us that sexual behavior can be part of a social bond beyond reproduction, and that these bonds can cross species boundaries,” Palagi said.

Nobody knows yet what the bond does for either animal. The behavior may benefit one or both of them directly. Or it may be a result of the way cattle and donkeys form social bonds.

Palagi said the team can’t tell whether sex helped keep the bond going or came out of an attachment the two animals already had.

Domestication may have played a part in the behavior too. The authors wrote that it changes animals’ social settings and their chances to interact with other species.

The next step, Palagi said, is to find out how often relationships like this one occur and to follow them over time.

She suggested comparing friendly behavior and signs of tension before and after sex. That could help test whether sex is linked to keeping a relationship going or to easing tension.

The team would also need to observe different pairs in different social settings to tell those two possibilities apart, she said.

The full study was published in the journal Current Biology.

#6363. The 6 Best Wood Stoves for Warmth, Ambiance, and More

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

These simple appliances can generate an impressive amount of heat safely, and without increasing your energy bill.

The crackle of a fire on a cold winter night can add charm to any home. However, fireplaces aren’t particularly efficient heat sources, especially in chilly temperatures. And electric fireplaces, space heaters, and other supplementary heat sources can leave you in the dark (and out in the cold) during a power outage.

Instead, consider adding a wood stove—an appliance that provides a country aesthetic and serves as a primary or secondary heat source. Modern wood stoves can be safe, affordable, and efficient if you clean and maintain them regularly.

More than 2 million of the roughly 12.5 million wood stoves in the U.S. are older, uncertified models that put out far more particulate pollution than newer ones, according to the EPA, and some states prohibit or restrict these wood-burning devices. All of the wood stoves recommended here are EPA-certified, and they still crank out enough BTUs to make your home or cabin cozy.

Before you buy, think carefully about where you’ll install your stove. You’ll need proper clearance from combustible materials in walls and floors, and the stove’s weight has to work for your house.

The Expert (Alex Rennie): I'm a freelance writer who specializes in the Home Improvement, DIY, and Tool space. As a former residential and commercial carpenter, I use my hands-on experience to write practical buying guides, how-to articles, and product reviews. Based in Los Angeles, I spend my free time exploring the beaches and mountains with my fiancé and our dog Louie.

To choose my wood stove recommendations, I selected non-catalytic models that are affordable while still meeting EPA emissions standards. Among the wood stoves that made the cut, you’ll find a wide variety to meet your space limitations and style preferences while maintaining efficient BTU output.

One of the best things about having a huge fire in the middle of your home is that it lets you make the most of those rustic vibes. Many of the stoves I picked have a cooktop (very convenient) or a large window, so you can put your feet up and enjoy watching the flames. I also relied on prior research conducted by writer Alex Rennie, who also contributed to this article.

This pedestal stove from Ashley Hearth hits the sweet spot between size, heat output, and price. Its 2,500-square-foot heating range fits the average home with room to spare, and the brick-lined, 2.7-cubic-foot firebox accepts logs up to 21 inches long. That means fewer trips to the woodpile on cold nights.

One of the best features is the cast iron door with air-washed ceramic glass, which helps keep soot off the window so you can enjoy the view of the fire. A non-catalytic secondary burn extracts more heat from every load and keeps emissions within EPA standards. It’s mobile-home approved when paired with the optional fresh air kit. The stove runs fine without electricity, but an optional blower will help push warm air into the rest of your house.

If you don’t need to heat your entire home, this compact Ashley Hearth model delivers plenty of warmth for the money. Its 68,000 BTU output covers up to 1,200 square feet. That makes it a smart fit for a cabin or an open living area, or as a supplemental heat source that takes some pressure off your furnace.

It shares many features with our Best Overall pick, including a firebrick-lined firebox and a non-catalytic secondary burn that keeps emissions within EPA standards. It also has a heavy cast iron door with air-washed ceramic glass. It ships with both legs and a pedestal, so you can choose the look that suits your space. At 258 pounds, it’s relatively easy to move into place, and it’s mobile-home approved with the optional fresh air kit. The trade-off is a smaller 1.3-cubic-foot firebox, so you’ll load logs more often than with a larger stove.

If watching the fire matters more to you than heating every corner of the house, this Superior stove is built around the view. A large rectangular ceramic-glass door gives you a wide view of the flames, and the built-in air-wash system sweeps air across the glass to keep soot off.

The high-density firebrick holds heat longer for a more efficient burn. It puts out just 2.1 grams of particulate per hour, well under EPA limits. It fits logs up to 18 inches long, and one control handles the airflow. A black pedestal base comes standard, and an optional variable-speed blower can push warm air into nearby rooms.

The trade-off is a heating range of up to 1,400 square feet, so it’s best suited to a living room, a cabin, or a smaller home.

The WoodPro 300 is the largest model in the WoodPro line, built for anyone heating a large open floor plan, a farmhouse, or a drafty workshop. Its 2.26-cubic-foot firebox takes 18-inch logs and can burn for up to 12 hours on a single load, so you won’t have to refill it every couple of hours.

The stove is made of heavy-gauge steel with a cast-iron door. The Smart Air Control uses two levers, so the lighting procedure is simple: get the fire going, set the air, and leave it alone. It meets EPA 2020 standards at 1.6 grams of smoke per hour with 74.2 percent efficiency, and it’s approved for mobile homes with the outside air kit. Its peak output of 61,700 BTU is modest for a stove rated for 3,000 square feet, so treat that number as a best case in a well-insulated home, not something to count on in a cold climate.

This rustic model from Ashley Hearth—under the US Stove Company umbrella—the US1269E, is a natural fit for log cabin homes that want a rugged addition to their living space, or for anyone looking to add woodsy charm to their home.

My favorite feature is the oversized safety handle, which is comfortable to grab when opening or closing the door and stays cool to the touch, even when the stove is in operation.

Tested and certified to U.L.1482 by Warnock Hersey International, this stove’s 900-square-foot heating range isn’t the largest of my selections, but it's still impressive for its size. The integrated cooking surface on top is also a valuable feature.

If you’re looking for a pint-sized stove for a small space, including a mobile home, US Stove's Tiny Wood Stove may provide the perfect fit. The slim profile doesn’t mean it’s short on efficiency or on meeting emissions standards, and it still qualifies for the 30-percent Biomass federal tax credit.

A compact design, however, comes with a few caveats, including a rather small log size and a relatively low BTU output. Still, the US Stove Tiny Stove is a great trade-off for a single-room cabin or a more compact space in your home.

Wood stoves come in all shapes, sizes, and designs. Choose one that suits your space in terms of style and efficiency. Here’s how to decide what you need in a wood stove and what you don't.

There are two types of modern wood stoves: catalytic and non-catalytic. Both reduce air pollution by reburning exhaust to limit emissions, but catalytic stoves use a different process that is slightly more efficient at this second burn. Non-catalytic stoves are popular because they’re less expensive and slightly more efficient at producing heat.

Because the cost of a wood stove with a catalytic converter is currently prohibitive for the average homeowner, the wood stove models we’ve recommended below are all non-catalytic.

More Hot Stuff: Smokeless Fire Pits • Fire Pit Tables • Portable Fire Pits • Heated Blankets

The size of your wood stove matters not just for the space it can heat, but also for safety. Before you install a wood stove, check your state requirements for clearance. Federal guidelines stipulate that the stove should be installed at least 3 feet from any combustibles in the wall, ceiling, or floors.

If you have children, also consider how much clearance you might need around the stove for a child safety gate and where you plan to stack and store firewood.

British Thermal Units (BTUs) might sound fancy, but it's just a measurement of how much heat is being generated. This differs from the heating area of a wood stove because it refers to the energy the stove produces in an hour. A rule of thumb: You need 20 BTUs for every foot of space you want to heat. Use this online BTU calculator to dial in exactly how many thermal units your home needs.

Decide whether you’re using your wood stove as a main heating source or for supplemental heat in the winter. In general, a small wood stove can heat about 500 square feet, while a medium wood stove warms up to 1,000 square feet. A large model will heat a room of 1,500 square feet or more.

More isn’t always better. To keep costs in check and your wood stove efficient, consider if you really need to heat every space in your home or just the living areas your family frequents.

Modern wood stoves are lighter than ever, but many large models can still tip the scales at several hundred pounds. Depending on the stove's weight, you may not be able to install it in a mobile home or in certain structurally vulnerable spots in your house. Instead, look for a wood stove approved for mobile homes by the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD).

If your goal is an outdoor wood stove portable enough for camping or backpacking, choose a lightweight model with components that collapse into a compact package.

The size of the logs and the kind of wood you put into your wood stove is about more than convenience or cost. It can also affect burn time and efficiency, which is especially important if you’re using your wood stove as a main heating source.

Generally, most wood stoves fit logs about 16 inches long and 3 inches in diameter. As you can imagine, wood stoves designed for smaller logs may leave you rolling up your sleeves and grabbing the axe more often than you might like.

Since 2020, nearly all new wood stoves sold in the United States must be certified by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to meet its 2020 emissions standards, which limit fine particle pollution to 2.0 grams per hour (2.5 g/h when tested with cordwood). All of the wood stoves we’ve recommended below meet this standard, and you can look up any model in the EPA’s database of certified wood-burning heaters.

A wood stove’s effectiveness in converting wood into heat is expressed as a percentage of combustion efficiency. Efficiency matters because it directly translates into how much wood you’ll burn to keep your home warm. Most modern EPA-certified stoves fall between 70 and 80 percent efficiency, and every few points add up over a full heating season in fewer logs split, stacked, and hauled inside.

From insulating the chimney to adhering to proper stovepipe clearance, to wall shields and floor pads, there’s quite a bit to do when you install a wood stove, and much of it is mandated by building codes and state or federal laws. To protect your safety, it's critical that you don't miss a step, which is why I recommend leaving the installation of the wood stove to a professional.

Clean your wood stove (and chimney) thoroughly and often to avoid creosote buildup, a highly flammable byproduct of burning wood.

While cleaning your chimney, tidying up your wood stove is pretty straightforward. When the stove is cool, lay down a cloth or newspaper, then empty the ashtray and any ashes from the firebox into an ash bucket. Then wait at least 24 to 48 hours before you dump the ash bucket so any slightly warm embers don’t catch fire.

You can wipe down the interior with a soft, wet cloth and use a chimney brush to scrub out the stovepipe and loosen any residue. If the exterior has rust, you can use a wire brush or sandpaper to remove it.

Yes, you can leave a wood stove unattended for a few hours or overnight, but with some caveats. You should tamp down or mostly close some vents to ensure the fire stays under control. Also, shut and lock the door, and clear any objects from around the stove.

Just be aware that if you plan to leave the fire unattended and it goes out overnight, you’ll have to restart it, which is harder than simply feeding a live fire.

Most new wood stoves you can buy in the U.S. will be EPA-certified, but you should still check the packaging to verify.

EPA certification means the wood stove has been independently tested to meet a particulate emissions limit of no more than 4.5 grams per hour. If you have an old model that is not EPA-certified, check whether your state has a program that provides tax deductions for replacing your wood stove.

#6362. Smartwatch screens are too small to pinch and zoom, so engineers turned the forearm into a touchpad

A radar wristband turns the forearm into a smartwatch touchpad that reads two-finger gestures and press force, beating a touchscreen in tests.

On a phone, pinching to zoom or scrolling with two fingers is second nature. On a watch face the size of a postage stamp, there is no room for it.

Engineers have now moved those gestures off the screen and onto the skin of the forearm, turning it into a touchpad for the smartwatch.

A small radar on a wristband points at the skin next to the watch. Fingers pressing there leave tiny dents, and the radar reads where the fingers are, how many there are, and whether a press is gentle or firm.

In tests with 20 volunteers, the system recognized gestures about 93 percent of the time after a calibration of under four minutes. In a head-to-head task, people missed their targets less often on their own arm than on a watch touchscreen.

The work comes from Chenhan Xu, an assistant professor of computer science at North Carolina State University, and doctoral student Yuliang Fu, with Rakshita Ranganath and Huining Li. They call the system EpiPad.

“Smartwatch screens are too small for the touch interactions people use every day on phones and laptops, such as two-finger scrolling, pinch-to-zoom, or pressing harder to trigger a different command,” Xu said.

“Our goal was to develop a small, wearable technology that would provide that level of interactive control for users.”

On a watch touchscreen, a fingertip covers a small target it is trying to tap. The authors wrote that a typical on-screen keyboard on a commercial smartwatch gives each key about 0.12 inches (3 millimeters) of width.

Earlier attempts to use the forearm skin as a touchpad mostly tracked a single finger, or relied on landmarks such as knuckles, which limited taps to a few fixed spots.

Rotating, zooming, and other two-finger moves were out of reach.

The back of the forearm offered room to work with. The system turns a strip of forearm skin about 6 inches by 1.6 inches (15 by 4 centimeters) into a touchpad input area. The padding of muscle under that skin makes a hard press comfortable.

The sensor is a millimeter-wave radar chip with one transmitting antenna and three receiving ones. It sends out a pulse every thousandth of a second and times the reflections.

Because the radar faces across the skin from the side, a press straight down barely changes the distance it measures.

So the team mounted the chip about 0.55 inches (14 millimeters) above the skin, roughly the thickness of a chunky smartwatch case, and angled it slightly downward.

“With the EpiPad, a compact millimeter-wave radar worn on a wristband reads the tiny dents fingertips make as they press the skin, so the system tracks multiple fingers and how hard each one presses,” said Fu, the paper’s first author.

The system distinguishes two levels of pressure, gentle and hard. The hard press is where the signal gets tricky, because a finger arriving on the skin shifts the radar reading in the same way the dent does.

The team found the pressure signature in the moment the finger holds still after landing.

The 20 volunteers, 14 men and six women, were all young adults. Each spent about an hour and a half tapping, pressing, sliding, rotating, and zooming on a numbered grid stuck to the left forearm.

People press differently and have different skin. A model that was trained on everyone except one volunteer, was then tested on that volunteer. It recognized gestures only about half the time.

Each new user therefore performs a short set of standard taps and gestures first, a calibration that takes just under four minutes. Afterward, the system identified the gesture 92.8 percent of the time and told a gentle press from a hard one 90.2 percent of the time.

The system also placed a fingertip to within about 0.4 inches (10 millimeters). In other words, the calibration brought a new user almost up to the accuracy the system reached on people it had trained on.

Ten of the volunteers came back twice more over three months and put the wristband on again. The original calibration still held, at about 91 percent for gestures.

Twelve participants then raced a cursor between targets on a smartwatch display, using their forearm skin as a touchpad. The standard pointing test required them to select each target with a hard two-finger press. The smallest targets were 0.05 inches (1.28 millimeters) across, narrower than a key on a watch keyboard.

The same people did the task on a touchscreen and with a tilt cursor steered by angling the wrist. On the touchscreen they missed 21.7 percent of targets.

With EpiPad they missed 6.5 percent, and they moved between targets faster than with either other method.

“EpiPad outperformed the other two tasks with regard to both error rate and efficiency,” Fu said.

The system responded in about 90 milliseconds, within the range of commercial devices. Reading pressure took longer, about half a second. The authors found that most hard presses lasted at least that long anyway.

In a test on two people, a tight sleeve barely mattered. A loose jacket dropped gesture recognition to 72 percent and pressure detection to 63 percent, because the fabric moves on its own and reflects the radar.

Models calibrated for the index and middle fingers also stumbled when people switched to thumb and index, until they recalibrated for the new pair. Five volunteers who walked slowly while using it kept accuracy near 90 percent.

The prototype is a wristband with a circuit board sticking out, and it still needs a laptop to process the signal.

The authors wrote that custom hardware with more transmitters could let the radar sit lower, to fit thinner watches. Longer studies in daily life, they wrote, would be needed to judge how people take to it.

Xu said the parts cost less than $10 and could go into smart glasses and other screenless wearables, using “the wearer’s own skin as a full touch surface.”

The paper was presented at the UbiComp/ISWC conference in Shanghai in October. The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the ACM on Interactive, Mobile, Wearable and Ubiquitous Technologies.
