#6361. This year’s El Niño is unlike any other on record

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

El Niño’s hallmark tongue of warm water extends thousands of kilometers from South America's Pacific coast. This map from November 14 shows the tongue’s average surface temperature was at least 3 degrees Celsius (dark red) above normal.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

It was an unprecedented year for El Niño, the weather-changing ocean pattern defined by warmer-than-normal surface waters in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific. By October 18, the ocean area that researchers use to monitor El Niño’s severity climbed to an average temperature of over 30° Celsius (86° Fahrenheit) for the first time in history. From there, it kept on rising.

In September, the region’s daily average sea surface temperature reached the most extreme level ever recorded: more than 3.03 degrees Celsius above the 30-year average (dashed line). The World Meteorological Organization predicts that sea surface temperatures may peak at 3.7 degrees above that average by January. The two previous strongest El Niños on record emerged in 1997 and 2015.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

All that hot water has fueled the most active Pacific hurricane season on record. By mid-October, 331 units of cyclone energy had accumulated, beating out 2018’s record of 318 units. It has also unleashed heat into the atmosphere, affecting distant circulation patterns and leading to an extraordinarily quiet Atlantic hurricane season.

2026’s El Niño will be felt well beyond the New Year. Precipitation and drought impacts are expected across the world through spring 2027. And the global heating effect could compound with human-caused climate warming to make 2027 the hottest year ever recorded.

The heat that El Niño unleashes into the atmosphere shifts storm tracks and weather patterns globally. Here are some of the most significant observed and anticipated effects.

#6359. The rocks beneath forests may hold a hidden key to carbon storage

New research reveals how the weathering of limestone may help forest soils accumulate and preserve carbon from microbial remains.

Dead leaves are the obvious source of the carbon in soil. About half of soil organic carbon, though, comes from the remains of dead microbes.

What soil bacteria and fungi leave behind when they die outlasts the plant matter it was built from.

A team in China has now tied that microbial carbon to the rock underneath. Forest soils over limestone and dolomite, rocks that dissolve in rainwater, hold more of it than soils over other rock.

At the sites where the rock was dissolving fastest, there was more of it still.

Peilei Hu led the work at the Institute of Subtropical Agriculture, part of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, with Wei Zhang and Kelin Wang as senior authors.

Co-authors came from CREAF in Barcelona and Aarhus University in Denmark.

The team worked at three scales. There was a reanalysis of forest soils worldwide, a survey of 60 plots in southwest China, and a run of jars on a laboratory bench.

Plants pull carbon out of the air, and some of it reaches the soil as litter and root material.

Microbes eat it, grow, divide and die, and what is left of their bodies is called necromass.

That necromass can last a long time, especially once it sticks to mineral surfaces where other microbes can’t easily reach it.

So two steps decide how much piles up. First, plant carbon has to be turned into microbial bodies.

Then those microbial remains have to resist decomposition.

Soil chemistry governs both steps, and the rock below sets much of the chemistry.

Carbonate rocks underlie more than 15% of the continental land surface and dissolve at least ten times faster than many silicate-bearing rocks.

As they go, they release calcium and raise soil pH.

Studies of carbonate weathering have mostly asked how much carbon dioxide the dissolving rock itself consumes. That left the organic side of the ledger open.

The team started with an existing global database and kept 466 forest topsoil records.

Each one measured total soil organic carbon and amino sugars, the fragments of microbial cell walls that stand in for necromass.

A karst aquifer map sorted the records into 69 over carbonate rock and 397 over other kinds.

Per unit of soil, karst sites held 43.4% more amino sugars than the rest, and 57.6% more organic carbon overall.

As a share of the carbon present, though, microbial remains were no higher over carbonate rock than anywhere else. Globally, both pools simply ran bigger together.

The field survey in southwest China came out differently.

The work ran across six regions: Nanchuan, Suiyang, Dushan, Huanjiang, Wuming and Longzhou. In each one, the team paired a forest on carbonate rock with a forest on clastic rock and sampled five plots of each.

The karst forests carry less wood and fewer tree species than their neighbors, on soil that is shallow and patchy. Total soil carbon came out about the same between the pairs.

But the proportion of carbon derived from microbial remains was 19.3% higher in karst soils, and 57.8% more of their amino sugars were bound to mineral surfaces.

To put a number on the weathering itself, the team buried limestone tablets in the karst plots and left them there for a year.

One lay on the soil surface, one sat 4 inches (10 centimeters) down, and one was wedged at the boundary between soil and bedrock. Weighing what each tablet had lost gave a rate.

Those rates were the strongest predictor of microbial carbon in the karst soils, ahead of the microbes’ own numbers and diversity.

Of the combined weight the model gave its predictors, weathering rate accounted for 46.5%, and the abundance of genes for breaking down tough plant compounds another 31.9%.

Lignin, the stiff compound that makes wood woody, was scarcer in karst soils and more chemically chewed up. Over non-karst rock, the same analysis turned up climate and plant community instead of weathering.

Field patterns cannot settle which way the arrow points. Microbes help dissolve rock as surely as dissolving rock changes microbes, and the authors say as much.

The laboratory part was built to answer that. The team stirred 4 grams of either limestone powder or quartz sand into 40 grams of karst soil, 54 jars in all.

Each jar was then fed plain water, glucose or glycine, an amino acid.

The glucose and the glycine were built with carbon-13, a heavier form of carbon that can be traced wherever it goes. The jars then sat at 77°F (25°C) for 64 days.

Limestone raised the pH and the calcium available in the soil, as expected. It also shifted which enzymes the microbes made.

They put less into splitting simple sugars and more into attacking tougher material, though that second shift was only marginal.

The labeled carbon is the result that matters.

With limestone in the jar, more of it ended up in microbial remains rather than breathed out as carbon dioxide. The gain was 22% for glucose and 71% for glycine.

For the second step, keeping the necromass, the team separated the calcium in the field soils into four forms and asked which tracked the mineral-bound amino sugars.

Two did: a loosely held, readily exchangeable form, and a form tied up with carbonate minerals themselves.

Calcium can bridge organic matter to mineral surfaces, and carbonate surfaces can take up and bury the remains directly.

Neither bond is permanent on its own, the authors note, but together they put microbial carbon somewhere microbes have trouble getting at it.

That connects the two halves. The same dissolving rock that helps turn plant carbon into microbial bodies also supplies the calcium that keeps those bodies in place.

The global half of the study is forest topsoil only, down to 8 inches (20 centimeters), and 69 karst records against 397 others.

Whether the pattern holds in grassland, farmland or deeper soil is untested. The regional work did not measure leaf litter directly, so plant inputs enter it only through proxies.

And the jar experiment cannot say which part of weathering did the work. Limestone changes pH, calcium and probably nitrogen and phosphorus all at once.

Telling those apart, the authors wrote, needs “longer-term factorial experiments.”

Crushed rock spread on farmland is already being tested as a way to pull carbon dioxide from the air, and limestone is one of the rocks on the table.

This study does not measure how much carbon that would store, or for how long. What it offers is a mechanism to test.

The rock may add carbon to the soil through the microbes living in it, and not only through the chemistry of its own dissolving.

The full study was published in the journal National Science Review.

On Wednesday (Nov. 25), the distant ice giant Uranus will be at its best and brightest. Here's when, where and how to look for the seventh planet.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

One of the hardest planets to see in the solar system — the distant ice giant Uranus — reaches its annual opposition on Wednesday (Nov. 25), just a day after the Beaver Supermoon. It's the best time to see the seventh planet from the sun, but you'll need to use stargazing binoculars or a good backyard telescope to find it.

Uranus is faint, slow-moving and rarely a target for casual stargazers. However, on Nov. 25, and, for a few weeks on either side, it will be at its closest point to Earth this year and will appear at its brightest, making it possible to spot.

Opposition occurs when Earth passes between Uranus and the sun; Uranus will be "opposite" the sun, hence, "opposition." The moment of opposition will happen at 6 p.m. ET on Nov. 25, according to EarthSky. Consequently, Uranus will rise in the east around sunset, reach its highest point in the sky around midnight and set in the west around sunrise.

You can find it in the constellation Taurus, close to the Pleiades open star cluster, also known as the Seven Sisters and M45. Uranus will be a few degrees southeast of the cluster, appearing as a faint point of light, about two-fifths of the distance between the Pleiades and Aldebaran, the brightest star in Taurus.

At magnitude +5.6, Uranus is technically visible to the naked eye under very dark skies. However, binoculars or a telescope will make it much easier to find.

Uranus as seen by NASA's Hubble Space Telescope.

At opposition, Uranus will be 18.4 astronomical units (AU) from Earth — about 1.7 billion miles (2.7 billion kilometers) away. Through a telescope, it will appear as a tiny blue-green disk. Its color comes from methane in its atmosphere, which absorbs red wavelengths of sunlight.

Named after Ouranos, the ancient Greek god of the sky and the heavens, according to the Planetary Society , Uranus is one of the least understood planets in the solar system. A day on Uranus lasts for about 17 hours, and the planet rotates sideways, according to NASA. It takes 84 Earth years to orbit the sun.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Uranus also has 13 faint rings and at least 29 known moons, the most recent of which was found in 2025 by the James Webb Space Telescope. It was named Uranus XXVIII and orbits between the moons Ophelia and Bianca. Many of Uranus' moons are named after characters from the works of William Shakespeare and Alexander Pope.

The distant planet has been visited only once, by NASA's Voyager 2 spacecraft on Jan. 24, 1986. However, contrary to what the probe found, scientists now think the planet emits its own internal heat. That could increase pressure on NASA to prepare a Uranus Orbiter and Probe (UOP), a mission concept the National Academy of Sciences recommended in 2022 as a high-priority planetary science mission for the next decade.

Uranus will next come to opposition on Nov. 30, 2027.

#6356. How do tumors talk to nerves? This scientist is finding out

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Sebnem Ece Eksi wants to see how nerves change as cancer progresses. She hopes those changes could offer clues for detecting tumors earlier.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Sebnem Ece Eksi did a double take. Proteins typically studied in the brain were turning up in prostate cancer cells from high-risk patients. These proteins, called neuronal adhesion molecules, play a key role in the circuitry associated with memory.

The finding, made during her Ph.D. days at the University of Illinois Chicago, raised so many questions to which Eksi is still seeking answers. Now at the Oregon Health & Science University in Portland, Eksi has made it her lab’s goal to find out how nervous systems communicate with cancer. What were once two separate fields might be connected more closely than previously thought.

“What we’re learning is that tumors are actively communicating with the nervous system,” Eksi says. “In a way, it makes sense to me that a growing tumor in our bodies, in an organ, would be immediately sensed and detected by the nervous system.”

Eksi now plans to test an AI image-based recognition algorithm to identify nerve fibers in human patients. This is exciting, she says, because these nerves aren’t normally visible in patient tumors. But through biopsies, she hopes to map out and observe how the nervous system — which impacts sleep, cognition and pain — changes as cancer progresses. The implications are significant, she says. Could experts use the nervous system to detect cancer early? Can they improve patients’ quality of life?

“This field of cancer neuroscience can change all different stages of cancer diagnosis and treatments,” Eksi says. “It’s growing so quickly, the field itself.”

#6355. The Sky Today on Thursday, November 26: Thanksgiving turkey in the sky

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

Celebrate Thanksgiving with a celestial turkey: The famous Orion Nebula (M42) is also playfully known as the Turkey Nebula because it looks to some like a turkey, particularly in deep astrophotos. But whether you’re a photographer or not, this bright deep-sky treat is easy to enjoy tonight while dinner digests.

By about 9 P.M. local time, Orion the Hunter has risen above the eastern horizon, his recognizable three-star belt standing in a vertical line. The lowest star in that line is Alnitak (Zeta [ζ] Orionis), and the Orion Nebula lies just 3.7° south-southwest of this star, to its lower right on the sky this evening. You might be able to spot its glow without optical aid, although the bright Moon nearby may make that difficult. Binoculars or any telescope will easily show it.

At 4th magnitude and spanning some 85’ by 60’, the Orion Nebula is a huge and bright star-forming region that sits roughly 1,350 light-years from Earth. In the brightest portion of the nebula lies a small grouping of young stars called the Trapezium Cluster. Take your time with this gorgeous sight, scanning around the region to pick out detail in the nebulosity. And if you are an astrophotographer, consider turning the view into a Thanksgiving memory to share for years to come.

#6354. Every fall and winter evening, tens of thousands of American crows fly to the same spot to sleep, and scientists can only guess why they do it

American crows gather in huge winter roosts, possibly for protection, warmth, access to food and opportunities to share information.

On fall and winter evenings, American crows leave their daytime haunts and fly to shared sleeping sites called roosts.

Some roosts hold fewer than 100 crows. Others hold hundreds of thousands, or even more than a million. Roosts that number in the tens of thousands are common.

Dr. Kevin J. McGowan of the Cornell Lab of Ornithology addressed the question in a guide last updated in 2010. Why crows do it is “largely a matter of conjecture,” he wrote, listing four hypotheses.

American crows often live in family groups made up of a breeding pair and offspring from the previous two years. The whole family helps raise the young.

Their diet runs from grains, seeds, fruits and insects to small animals, carrion and garbage. They are also known for solving problems and finding unusual food sources.

Partners in Flight estimates the species’ global breeding population at 28 million. Numbers declined slightly between 1966 and 2019, according to the North American Breeding Bird Survey.

During the nesting season, most breeding crows sleep on their own territories. Afterward they join the roosts.

“It appears that all crows will join winter roosts, even territorial breeding crows,” he wrote.

Non-breeding crows may stay on the home territory, wander between foraging flocks or leave the area for months.

Roost numbers peak in winter and fall away near the start of the breeding season, usually in March.

An hour or two before full darkness, crows collect in an area away from the final roost. There they spend their time calling, chasing and fighting.

Groups from several of these congregation areas may merge at one staging area. At dark, the main body moves to the roost itself.

That final site can be a single dense woodlot or a spread of many suitable trees.

A 1972 report put one roost at Fort Cobb, Oklahoma, at more than two million crows.

The first hypothesis is about the site. Crows may gather because one spot offers good shelter, protection from predators or suitable trees.

The guide compares that kind of roost to a crowded hotel, where the guests share a building but do not really interact.

The second idea is safety in numbers. Large owls are the predators crows fear most, and a crow in a group may be safer than one alone.

“Owls probably are regular attendants at crow roosts,” he added.

Crows also work together to harass or drive off predators, a behavior called mobbing.

Under the third hypothesis, the roost works as an information center. A hungry crow could watch for well-fed arrivals in the evening.

It could then trace their flight paths back, or follow them at dawn, to a rich food source.

The fourth is called patch-sitting. Roosts may form close to food that is reliable and impossible to defend.

Landfills, commercial composting facilities and certain farm fields all qualify. Sleeping nearby gives the crows breakfast before they disperse.

A 1997 study in The Auk, led by Donald F. Caccamise, followed color-marked and radio-tagged crows.

By day, most stayed faithful to their group territory all year. They frequently left it to forage up to 2.5 miles (4 kilometers) away.

At night they roosted either at home or at a large roost about 11 miles (18 kilometers) away, next to a landfill. They slept on their territories 87 percent of the time in spring and 42 percent in winter.

Each crow reached the communal roost on its own, not with its group.

Group cohesion was high on territories. The team tied keeping a territory to holding a breeding site.

The team linked communal roosting to likely foraging benefits. Those count most in winter, when food on a territory is scarcest.

Crows have gathered in large fall and winter roosts “for as long as there have been crows,” according to McGowan. By 2010, the roost at Auburn, New York, was downtown.

A large roost was recorded near that town in 1911-12. In the winter of 1932-33, about 25,000 crows slept 3 miles (4.8 kilometers) south of it.

Hunting is one possible reason. The Migratory Bird Treaty Act was extended to crows in 1972, and firing a gun inside city limits is prohibited.

Cities are also often 5 to 10 degrees Fahrenheit (about 3 to 6 degrees Celsius) warmer than the surrounding countryside. Great horned owls should be scarcer in urban areas.

Streetlights and parking lot lights may help crows spot a threat such as an owl and find a new perch at night. Large old trees in parks and cemeteries may be especially attractive for roosting.

The information was obtained from the Cornell Lab of Ornithology’s crow FAQ.

#6353. The 8 Best Smokers to Cook Low and Slow

From wood pellets to charcoal, these cookers use a little heat and a lot of time to make incredible barbecue.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

The best smokers help you achieve the sweet and savory flavor combinations that make smoked meat so tasty. Whether pulled pork, brisket, ribs, or chicken is on the menu, this type of specialized home grill brings a new dimension to your backyard barbecues all year long.

There isn’t just one type of smoker. Purists prefer the iconic offset or “barrel” smoker, which reflects an array of regional barbecue traditions found in Texas, Memphis, Kansas City, and the Carolinas. In the last decade or so, increased interest in the art of barbecue has led to an expanded range of more beginner-friendly alternatives, including hardwood charcoal smokers and low-maintenance wood pellet smokers.

Some models have made the cooking process even easier with WiFi-enabled smart features for monitoring and adjusting internal temperature via an app on your phone. That way, you don’t have to stand by for hours as you cook.

If you’re in the market for a new smoker, we have one for every setup and skill level. Continue reading for our choices of the best smokers and tips on what to consider before you buy.

We’ve tested dozens of grills and smokers of all different shapes and sizes over the years. Tony Carrick, coauthor of this article, currently uses a Masterbuilt charcoal-fed gravity smoker and a Weber Smokey Joe at home. David Dritsas is a reviews editor at Popular Mechanics and is an amateur cook who has tested a variety of grills. Both drew on their combined experience with smokers, along with external research, to inform our recommendations.

We supplemented our own experience and criteria for smokers with extensive research into the various types that are available. We compared specifications of dozens of smokers and consulted user reviews to find trends or qualities that stand out (both positively and negatively) and might impact your ultimate choice. Our final recommendations span a range of designs and price points, and each offers solid performance, durable build quality, and great value.

One of the first things you notice about the Pit Boss Navigator 1600M is how well-constructed it is. The metal frame is sturdy, the hardware is strong, and the main section is well-insulated, including a heavy hood that is lined all the way around the edges by a fireproof, padded seal that keeps the heat in. (The Navigator performed very well in that regard.)

It has a large hopper that holds up to 30 pounds of pellets, and the controls are easy to understand. There’s WiFi on board, and we experienced a one-time issue where the app disconnected and would not reconnect, but it otherwise worked well, and navigation was intuitive. The Navigator also has two wired thermometer probes, for which you can set temperature alerts, so you know when your meats are ready.

For our main cooking test, we smoked a flat iron steak, as well as a mix of garlic-marinated zucchini, onions, and red peppers (that was enclosed in aluminum foil, open at the top). We were impressed with how quickly the grill heated up and how efficiently it maintained the temperature (even as we grilled in cold weather).

The only feature we did not find exceptional was the flame broil setting, which allows you to expose food to the flames of the burner cup directly. While it technically works, the cooking area of this feature is only roughly 3 inches in diameter, so it’s not very effective for large pieces of meat or more than one burger. But that complaint is a minor one.

You don’t have to spend a lot of money to get proficient at smoking food, and Oklahoma Joe’s Laredo Deluxe proves that point. It’s a very basic charcoal barrel-shaped model that requires you to stay near and mind the coals to maintain the temperature, but it offers a few nice extra features to help you do it.

The biggest is the three-position charcoal tray. Set it high to sear meat while grilling or set it low to help keep temperatures down around 250 degrees Fahrenheit when smoking low and slow. Of course, airflow is integral to smoking, and there are three control options here, including a side vent, a chimney, and a large front door that you can also open to gain access to the coals for adjustment without having to remove the cooking grates. We used it several times to spread out the charcoal when things were getting a bit too hot.

There’s also a built-in thermometer that’s easy to read, even from a short distance, two side tables, and a lower shelf. All said and done, even if you don’t use it as a smoker, we think this makes for a fantastic charcoal grill with plenty of cooking area (940 square inches) to make a ton of burgers for your next barbecue party.

The Laredo Deluxe is not as solidly constructed as some of the other selections on our list, but that’s to be expected for a grill that’s usually on sale for under $300. We smoked a delicious brisket with ease during our tests, and we’d happily do so again.

Full Oklahoma Joe’s Laredo Deluxe Grill and Smoker Review

Masterbuilt’s Gravity Series 800 gives you unique flavor from hardwood charcoal smoke in your barbecue without dealing with all the fuss of micromanaging your smoker. It pairs a large gravity-fed hopper for hardwood charcoal with a digital thermostat that controls the internal temperature. The hopper keeps your cooking fire fed, while an internal fan system regulates temperature to maintain consistency. Just load it up, light it, and let it cook for hours with minimal maintenance.

As with our top pick, the Gravity Series 800 features wireless-enabled smart controls, which allow you to monitor the temperature from your phone. It also includes a digital meat probe.

With 800 square inches of cooking surface, you’re getting a lot of space here. There’s plenty of room for ribs, whole chickens, and pork butts. But at nearly five feet wide, the Masterbuilt 800 is a big boy—possibly too big for some decks and patios. That said, it also functions as a standard charcoal grill and a flat-top griddle, so you could ditch your standard grill to make space for it.

This Woodridge Pro is a midrange model in Traeger’s line of pellet smokers, featuring some of the technology found in its higher-end models but at a lower price. When we unboxed the grill, we were impressed by how easy it was to put together, despite the large number of loose parts. Traeger’s assembly guide was one of the best we’ve seen, with clear directions and marked boxes with icons that corresponded to the instructions.

Some construction elements, such as light plastic wheels and thin grill grates, seemed lacking, and there’s no seal around the interior of the hood (which helps with heat retention). Once together, however, this grill is sturdy and not at all difficult to move around. We really appreciate that the top of the pellet hopper serves as an extra shelf, which is handy and something you don’t always get with other grills. There’s also a special pellet sensor that lets you know if pellets are running low.

The Woodridge Pro is extremely straightforward to operate. The rather retro display with large block numbers is readable from a distance, and basic temperature control is quick to adjust and set with a large push-button dial. You can also set a timer, check probe temperature, and with the press of a button, add extra smoky flavor for slow cooks under 225 degrees Fahrenheit. One thing we really liked was a motion graphic that shows whether the grill is heating up or lowering the temperature. During our tests, it was helpful to have that feature as a reminder as we multitasked. Wireless control is available with WiFi and Bluetooth, and the app, named WiFire, is easy to use.

The food we made turned out delicious, whether slow-cooked for a deeper smoky flavor or grilled at a higher temperature for just a hint. We used both the included wired probe to monitor temperature, as well as a Meater thermometer, and found some slight discrepancies between the grill’s temperature setting and the ambient temperature on the Meater. We found ourselves pushing the temperature up a few degrees to get it where we wanted it to be. This didn’t mar the experience too greatly, however. The Woodridge Pro is a reliable pellet grill that’s fun to use and a worthy addition to any back patio.

In many ways, the 18-Inch Smokey Mountain from Weber is a standard water smoker (a 14-inch model is also available). Like similar models, it has a bottom rack and retaining ring for the charcoal, a large bowl for water, and two racks for smoking food. But it stands out because it’s made from heavier porcelain-enameled steel, which helps retain heat and maintain a consistent temperature, as well as a heat shield on the bottom to protect your deck or lawn. It also comes with a cover.

When we first fired it up to season the smoker, we took the opportunity to get familiar with how to use the three air vents around the bottom, as well as the top vent, to help hold a desired temperature. To help you gauge this, there’s a thermometer in the lid that shows a highlighted smoking zone from 200 to 275 degrees Fahrenheit, and we found it was relatively easy to keep it in that range.

We put this to the real-world test when smoking some beef jerky. To do this, we wanted to keep the temperature on the lower side at around 200 degrees Fahrenheit. This proved a little challenging; the temperature kept creeping up, so we watched it closely and adjusted the vents as needed. In the end, the jerky smoked a bit faster than we intended. In hindsight, we used a little too much charcoal, which generated more heat than we needed. While this was our mistake, it shows just how well this smoker can retain heat.

When smoking a smaller-sized brisket, we more successfully managed the temperature and were able to hold close to 225 degrees Fahrenheit for the 5 hours it took to smoke it. One thing we really appreciated during longer smoking sessions was the large door, which made it easy to add fuel and wood chips. The Smokey Mountain is a basic smoker that will require a little experience to use effectively, but will ultimately be worth the time and produce great results. — tested by Bradley Ford

Though they are frowned upon by traditionalists, electric smokers like this one from East Oak are the quickest way for new barbecuers to enter the world of smoking. Its digital controls make it easy to maintain specific temperatures, and the combination of a side wood chip loader and glass door means you can check on your cook without opening the door, which could impact your cooking temperature.

The 725-square-inch cooking surface gives you plenty of room to experiment with various types of food in a single session, but the smoker itself is quite slim, measuring nearly 19 inches wide and 18 inches deep, so it won’t take up a lot of space on your deck or patio. Bottom line: This is a straightforward and, above all, convenient way to try smoking barbecue at home.

If a grill could be a pop-culture icon, the Big Green Egg is it. The brand has a whole group of fans—known as Eggheads—who gather at grilling events called EGGfests held all across the country. And it’s not just home enthusiasts. According to the company, nearly 1,800 restaurants use this extremely popular kamado grill. Its excellent heat retention and temperature range, enabled by its shape and porcelain-coated ceramic enclosures, make them an instant upgrade over your average gas or charcoal grill.

That thick ceramic body is also very effective at retaining heat, making it very effective for cooking low and slow. Just add some smoking wood, and you can smoke a brisket overnight. This grill can get as hot as 750 degrees Fahrenheit when you’re grilling, but smokers will want to maintain a stable 225 to 300 degrees using the air vents at the top and the bottom of the egg. And it’s large enough to feed a crowd—we’re talking about smoking a 20-pound turkey for Thanksgiving.

This small electric smoker from GE lets you take your smoking indoors. It uses two heat sources—one to cook food and the other to burn pellets—along with a filtration device to prevent the smoke from filling your kitchen. Its modest 293 square inches of cooking surface is enough to smoke three half racks of ribs or a small pork butt.

There’s a bevy of controls for setting smoke levels and adjusting temperatures. There are also preset food settings, including brisket, ribs, pork butt, and chicken wings. Built-in probes and WiFi connectivity let you monitor meat temperatures remotely, and this smoker is compatible with voice controls via Amazon Alexa and Google Home.

Traditional offset or “barrel” smokers feature two parts: A large main cooking chamber for your food and a smaller cook box for the fuel. The wood or charcoal burns, heating the main chamber and filling it with smoke, which slowly cooks the meat with indirect heat and infuses it with smoky flavor. Offset smokers, like the Royal Gourmet model we recommend as our Best Value pick, are beloved by barbecue aficionados, but are also the most challenging to use. Learning how to control the temperature in an offset smoker takes practice.

Vertical or “cabinet” smokers have a tall, closet-like design with a single door on the front and three to five racks for food inside. The heat source sits in the base, allowing the heat and smoke to waft upward and fill the space. Going high instead of wide makes a vertical smoker more compact, so it’s a good option if you don’t have much room on your patio. That said, the narrow profile may limit your ability to cook large pieces of meat, such as a full rack of ribs.

Like vertical smokers, the pill-shaped bullet smoker has a fuel area at the bottom with the main cooking chamber above. Vents on the bottom and top of the smoker allow you to control the temperature inside the chamber, and a water pan sits just below the cook area to keep food moist. Bullet smokers are compact, however, and some models are stacked so tightly that you may have trouble accessing the food on the middle racks mid-cook.

Most pellet smokers, including the Traeger Ironwood 885, look more like a grill than a smoker, with a wide cook box and a clamshell lid that opens up to reveal a broad cooking surface. To generate smoke and heat, an electric auger feeds small hardwood pellets from a hopper on the back or side into a fire inside the cook box. The auger automatically adds fuel to the fire based on the temperature you dial in on the smoker’s digital thermostat, so you don’t need to babysit the smoker to maintain the proper temperature. However, they require a power source and tend to be the most expensive.

Kamado grills, like the famous Big Green Egg, are hybrid grill-smokers. These large, acorn-shaped ceramic cook boxes can maintain low temperatures for many hours or build up scorching heat with temperatures that eclipse 800 degrees. It’s an incredibly versatile option, which has made it a gateway device for new barbecuers.

Smokers can use a variety of fuel types, including hardwood, charcoal, gas, electricity, or wood pellets. Hardwood and charcoal are the fuels of choice for smoking purists. This combination creates a lot of smoke, maximizing that flavor. Maintaining a consistent low temperature takes time to learn, though, and it makes more of a mess with leftover ash.

Electric and gas smokers are convenient because they require little to no maintenance, but they don’t inherently produce smoke. Instead, they rely on wood chip trays that aren’t as effective as wood, charcoal, or pellets at instilling flavor into food. However, they still can produce decent results.

Pellet smokers use compressed wood pellets that generate real smoke for instilling flavor into food, while minimizing maintenance with automatic temperature regulation. Pellet grills offer excellent heat retention and temperature control, but don’t need as much constant attention as charcoal or wood grills.

Smoking meat can take eight hours or more, depending on the cut, so you’ll probably want to cook as much as you can in one session. It’s important to look for a smoker with an efficient interior design that has space for everything you want to cook. The average cooking surface size for a smoker is around 550 square inches, which is enough to fit five full racks of ribs, four whole chickens, or five pork butts. That said, I’ve seen cooking surfaces range in size from 250 square inches to more than 800.

Some modern smokers can connect to your smartphone via Wi-Fi or Bluetooth, allowing you to track their internal temperature, change temperature settings, and monitor meat probes remotely through an app. They can also send you alerts if the smoker’s internal temperature rises or falls, the food reaches a target temperature, or if it’s low on fuel, allowing you to keep tabs on your smoker without having to hover over it.

What’s the best temperature for smoking meat?

With a smoker, you want to keep the temperature low and cook for a long time. Depending on what you’re cooking, I’d recommend maintaining your heat between 190 and 225 degrees. In that range, you will cook your meat slowly enough to make it incredibly tender and infuse it with smoky flavor.

It depends on what you’re cooking. Smoking a rack of ribs typically takes between four and five hours, but a pork butt may need 8 to 10 hours. Brisket is well-known for needing an especially long smoke—around 12 to 18 hours.

Technically, yes. You can add a smoker box to a gas grill, which holds wood chips to generate smoke. So long as you keep the top of the grill closed, that’s a smoker. Make sure to set up the grill so that the food is not sitting directly above the heat source, and set the burners so that the grill only heats to a maximum of 225 degrees with the lid closed.

That said, it’s far from ideal. It’s more difficult to maintain the consistently low temperatures needed for smoking with a gas grill than it is with a dedicated smoker. On top of that, flames from a gas grill will not impart the same distinctive taste as a proper smoker burning charcoal or hardwood. (Purists don’t even like gas as a fuel for dedicated smokers.)

#6352. Physicists break through a major speed barrier in quantum computing

Physicists achieved exceptionally fast and accurate quantum operations by correcting an overlooked source of error in superconducting qubits.

Inside a quantum computer, speed and accuracy are supposed to pull against each other.

Flip a quantum bit faster and you have to hit it harder, and a hard hit tends to knock it into states it was never meant to occupy.

A team in Germany has now flipped a qubit in 6.8 nanoseconds and got it right more than 99.98% of the time.

Such operations usually take several tens of nanoseconds, and light travels only about 6.5 feet (2 meters) in 6.8 of them.

The gain came from an error that earlier correction methods had overlooked, and it was measured on a single isolated qubit, so larger processors are still untested.

A qubit holds its fragile quantum state for only a limited time.

Every basic operation, or gate, has to fit inside that window, and complex algorithms and error correction need a great many of them.

So the shorter each gate, the more useful work a quantum computer can do before its qubits forget.

The catch is physics. A gate on a superconducting qubit is a pulse of microwaves, and a shorter pulse has to be stronger to do the same job.

Physicists at Forschungszentrum Jülich, working with colleagues at RWTH Aachen University and the University of Cologne, set out to find how far that could be pushed.

Yuan Gao and Rami Barends ran the experiments at the Institute for Functional Quantum Systems, and Felix Motzoi’s group at the Institute for Quantum Control supplied the theory.

The type of superconducting qubit used in this study isn’t a true two-state system. It has a ladder of energy levels, and a computer uses only the bottom two.

Think of an elevator meant to run between the ground floor and the first floor. Push it too hard and it overshoots.

Engineers have known since 2009 that a strong pulse can carry a qubit one level too far.

The standard fix, a pulse-shaping method called DRAG, was built to stop that. Motzoi was a co-author of the 2009 paper that introduced it.

What the new work showed is that a strong, fast pulse can also lift the qubit two levels at once.

Those double jumps come from absorbing two packets of microwave energy together, and at very short gate times they turned out to be the main source of error.

They’re also hard to undo, the authors wrote, because a qubit stuck on a high level can stay there through many steps and corrupt error correction.

The team’s solution, called R2D, applies the DRAG correction twice to suppress the microwave frequencies that cause the qubit to jump two energy levels at once.

The researchers adjusted just three parameters, testing the qubit repeatedly to find the optimal settings.

The team also needed a new way to measure the result, because leakage this small is hard to see.

So they built a sequence that repeats a gate hundreds of times with a twist of phase between repeats, which makes the stray population pile up instead of washing out.

With it, they could measure leakage down to about one part in a million, where the standard method starts to blur.

The new sequence gave a clear leakage signal within 400 operations, where the standard method needed 800 gates for a weaker one.

Compared with the standard DRAG correction on its own, the new pulse shape cut leakage by more than a factor of 20 at the same gate length.

The researchers ran the test on a single transmon qubit, built at Jülich’s Helmholtz Nano Facility and run at 5.323 gigahertz.

They tried pulses from 6.6 to 9 nanoseconds long, with 1 nanosecond of padding after each to absorb distortion.

Shorter pulses made the math unstable, and longer ones overflowed the memory of the control electronics.

At 6.8 nanoseconds, the two basic gates, a full flip of the qubit and a half flip, came out with accuracies of 99.981% and 99.989%.

The chance of the qubit escaping to a higher level stayed below 0.002% per gate. So the researchers achieved exceptionally high accuracy even at this short gate time.

Pushed to 6.6 nanoseconds, leakage to the third level took over, which the team’s simulation had predicted.

For the full flip, control error also grew as pulses got shorter, which the team attributed to distortion of the microwave pulse on its way in.

Most of the remaining error came from decoherence, the qubit losing its state on its own, at about one part in 10,000 per gate.

The authors called the pulse strength, measured against the spacing of the qubit’s levels, a record for single-qubit gates on superconducting hardware.

Everything here happened on one qubit sitting by itself. Whether the pulse shape works as well inside a larger processor, and during gates that act on two qubits at once, hasn’t been tested.

The authors wrote that the same approach should carry over to two-qubit gates and to other kinds of qubits.

The next step is the hardware. With longer-lived qubits and a tighter handle on pulse distortion, the team wrote, the method could reach gates that are right 99.999% of the time.

That is one more nine than this experiment managed.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Communications.

#6351. Nov. 26, 2018: Mars InSight lander touches down

InSight, short for Interior Exploration using Seismic Investigations, Geodesy, and Heat Transport, landed on Mars Nov. 26, 2018, tasked with a simple yet challenging mission: unlock the mysteries of Mars’ interior. Top priorities included uncovering Mars’ internal structure by measuring the thickness of the crust, obtaining the size and density of the core, and sussing out the structure and composition of Mars’ mantle.

In addition to bountiful seismic data, which included more than 1,300 marsquakes, InSight recorded about a year’s worth of weather data at the lander’s location with unprecedented accuracy, according to Bruce Banerdt, the mission’s principal investigator and principal research scientist. The InSight lander also took the first magnetic field measurements on the surface of Mars and measured several properties of the soil around it.

Not everything was a rousing success, however. Most famously, the mission’s “mole” subsurface probe only penetrated about 16 inches (40 centimeters) deep, despite being designed to burrow to a depth of at least 3 feet (10 meters). It turned out that the soil beneath InSight’s struts was unlike any previously encountered on the surface; it simply didn’t cooperate with the instrument’s design. But even that cloud has a silver lining, as it provided scientists with important details about the terrain upon which InSight landed.

InSight’s successful initial two-year mission was extended to run at least through the end of December 2022. But the stationary lander relied on power generated from its two large solar panels, which steadily gathered dust. That dust reduced the panels’ efficiency over time, forcing mission planners to make tough choices regarding power allotment. In May of 2022, engineers placed the craft’s robotic arm into a final resting pose and turned off all its instruments, save one: InSight’s seismometer continued to operate on what little power was available, running about half the time, according to Banerdt. InSight last contacted Earth Dec. 15, 2022, after which two attempts were made to raise the lander. Both failed, and a few days later, NASA officially brought the mission to a close.

Alison Klesman is senior editor of Astronomy magazine. She holds a Ph.D. in astronomy and has studied a variety of topics, from minor planets to supermassive black holes.

#6350. How do scientists learn from failure? This researcher has clues

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Cornell computational social scientist Yian Yin turns the tools of science on science itself. He’s studying how AI-assisted submissions are changing what gets through peer review.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Yian Yin seeks to understand the dynamics of science itself. The computational social scientist is particularly interested in how innovations happen and how they may be accelerated.

“I want to understand what the secret sources or recipes of success are,” says Yin, of Cornell University.

He applied machine learning techniques to accepted and rejected research proposals to understand how scientists learn from failures. What he found was that scientists fail, and they fail often. Some switched gears after some rejections, but others who continued their research and incorporated feedback found success at a faster rate. Those who changed ideas or scrapped original proposals did not leverage a lot from their experience.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“A group that’s not only failing better and better,” Yin says, “is also failing faster and increasingly faster towards their eventual success.”

More recently, Yin has been investigating how generative AI is changing scientific publishing. Journals are receiving more AI-assisted submissions than ever before, which is leading the peer-review process to falter. More seemingly well-written papers that lack substance are getting through, he found. Coming up with large-scale solutions requires looking at the issue in a measurable way, Yin says.

“Considering both the technological and social side of scientific ecosystems would be something that’s really beneficial for the ongoing public debate and discussion about how we accelerate science in the age of artificial intelligence,” Yin says.

#6349. AI chatbots may be recommending medications for the wrong reasons

Researchers found that leading AI chatbots disproportionately recommend brand-name medications, potentially driving up prescription drug costs.

Ask a chatbot which version of a blood pressure pill to take, and you might expect it to weigh the options the way a pharmacist would. Instead, five leading AI models kept naming the same product.

It was usually a brand-name drug with a big online footprint, and usually not the one doctors prescribe most.

Following those recommendations would raise U.S. drug purchase costs by tens of millions of dollars a year, the researchers estimated.

Daiju Ueda of Osaka Metropolitan University led the study with colleagues at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center.

His team tested the models on made-up patients, not real prescriptions, so the cost figure is a projection rather than a bill anyone has paid.

The team wrote 177,120 short patient scenarios. Each named a common disease and the active ingredient a doctor planned to prescribe, such as amlodipine for high blood pressure.

Each also described the patient by age, sex, race or ethnicity, LGBTQ+ identity and income, with any of those details sometimes left out.

The scenarios covered 123 disease and drug pairs, each run through 1,440 patient profiles.

Five AI models answered every scenario: GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 3.1 Flash, Llama 4 and MedGemma.

Each was asked to list up to three FDA-approved products by name, in order of preference. Four physicians then checked more than 883,000 answers against the FDA’s drug registries.

On average, 5.5 approved products existed for each ingredient. Yet across the disease and drug pairs, the most favored product accounted for an average of 97.5% of first-choice picks.

The alternatives, in other words, almost never came up first.

Pooling the five models together, one product drew more than 90% of first choices in 96 of the 123 pairs. The models also agreed with one another, almost all of the time, on which product that was.

The team then compared those picks with what Americans are actually dispensed, using the Medical Expenditure Panel Survey, a national survey of prescription use, for 2019 through 2023.

The most commonly prescribed product matched a model’s first choice in only 29.7% of cases, and landed anywhere in its top three in 58.8%.

Weighted by how many prescriptions each drug accounts for, the first-choice match fell to 17%. So, the models’ preferred product was usually not the version most commonly prescribed.

Prices came from the federal National Average Drug Acquisition Cost database, which tracks what retail pharmacies pay.

Complete pricing existed for 51 of the ingredients, and for 38 of those the models’ preferred products cost more than the ones in real use.

More often than not, then, the models leaned toward the pricier option.

The team then asked what would happen if doctors prescribed exactly as the models recommended, across those 51 ingredients, at current prescription volumes.

“We found that annual acquisition costs would increase by approximately US$55.6 million,” Ueda said. “This represents a 1,019% increase in the cost of purchasing these prescriptions.”

The $55.6 million covers only the 51 ingredients with full price data. It also assumes a pharmacy fills exactly what the model names, with no generic substitution at the counter.

What made a product the favorite? Being the original brand-name version mattered most. An originator product had about 20 times the odds of being recommended over a generic with the same ingredient.

“The recommendations were mostly for brand-name drugs, those highly visible in Google searches, and treatments with dedicated Wikipedia pages,” Ueda said.

A product with its own Wikipedia page had three times the odds of being named, and more Google search results raised the odds too. Products approved more recently, and products that doctors prescribe more often in practice, were recommended less. Heavier advertising spending by the manufacturer slightly lowered the odds.

Not every answer was a product a pharmacist could fill. Between 12.4% and 14.7% of each model’s recommendations failed a regulatory check. In nearly all of those cases, the model had named a product that was once FDA-approved but is no longer sold. GPT-5.4 had the lowest rate and Claude Sonnet 4.6 the highest.

The patient’s description changed those odds. Scenarios describing a Black patient had 1.64 times the odds of drawing a regulatory miss, compared with scenarios that left race unstated. For an Asian patient the figure was 1.16 times.

The authors wrote that such outputs were a minority and do not necessarily mean a clinically wrong choice. But any evaluation of these tools, they added, should report its results by patient group.

When the team rewrote the prompt to ask for the lowest-cost or generic option, the chatbots did shift.

The top pick changed in 63% of comparisons under the lowest-cost prompt and 78% under the generic prompt, and when it changed, it usually moved to a generic.

But the answers stayed just as concentrated, with a single product still taking 93% to 98% of first choices under each new prompt.

The scenarios were synthetic, and the authors wrote that they shouldn’t be read as a measure of how people actually prescribe.

The researchers also stopped at the recommendation and left out rare diseases and complicated cases.

The study didn’t follow what a doctor, an insurer or a pharmacist would do next. Whether a chatbot’s pick changes what a patient finally receives is the open question.

The authors wrote that the next studies need realistic clinical scenarios, tests of whether lower-cost prompts actually work, and a look at how doctors use these AI assistants.

“Combining AI systems with trusted drug information sources and human oversight may help support more appropriate medication choices,” Ueda said.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Health.

#6348. The 8 Best Portable Refrigerators If You’re Tired of Buying Bags of Ice

This convenient appliance works better than your average cooler and offers versatile power options. Here are the ones we recommend.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Even the best coolers we’ve tested from names like Yeti, Coleman, and RTIC with superior insulation eventually get too warm for ice to stay frozen. That’s where portable refrigerators shine, offering cooling capability that you just can’t get from a regular cooler. They’re great for long camping trips where you need to keep meat and other food at safe temperatures and come in plenty of sizes to suit hardcore camper rigs and RVs or fit in a standard sedan.

Portable refrigerators—often called car refrigerators—plug into your car’s 12-volt outlet, an AC outlet, or a portable power station. They’re pricier and heavier than the standard cooler, but they're more efficient at cooling. And you get to skip the expense and hassle of dealing with bags of ice. They can also be helpful around the house if your fridge breaks or there’s a power outage.

We used our expertise on coolers, power stations, and camping gear to find the best portable refrigerators. We checked camping and overlanding gear reviews and forums to find models that hold up on long treks in remote areas and are viable alternatives for people who don't want to deal with bags of ice for a cooler.

We chose options in different capacities and across a range of prices and prioritized models that offer convenient features like USB chargers, wheels, and LED lights. If you want some extra cooling power on-the-go, consider one of the portable refrigerators for your next trek.

This portable fridge from Bodega has great build quality, convenient features for easy portability, and cools down fast. The compressor can cool the interior down to 32 degrees Fahrenheit in about 30 minutes.

It has two separate compartments to keep things organized. They can’t be individually controlled but the smaller section typically gets cooler than the larger side. It also has a user-friendly app for setting the temperature and a USB port to charge other devices. Some customers report minor differences between the temperature they see on the app versus the actual internal temperature, but say it’s only off by a couple degrees.

The portable refrigerator has sturdy handles and a built-in LED light so you can quickly find what you need in the dark. Standout features include wheels and a drain plug—two things that are standard on most larger coolers but something a lot of portable fridges lack. The lid can be opened from either side or popped off entirely for fast loading.

This portable refrigerator is a great value for efficient cooling, a low power draw, and large capacity. The 59-quart space is split into two zones for easy organizing and the unit comes with a removable wire basket.

Its tall, slender shape fits easily behind a row of seats in the car. The handles are also removable to make for easy stowing. The app lets you set and monitor temps, though you can’t do much else. Some users report the app is user-friendly but wish it had more features.

The Alpicool is a budget portable refrigerator that cools down fast to roughly zero degrees Fahrenheit and operates quietly in comparison to most other models.

It has an automatic shutoff to ensure it doesn’t drain your car or portable battery and eco mode that pulls less energy. An external LCD display and control panel shows you the interior temperature. This budget option also has an LED light inside and a drain plug.

Setup is rather easy but the included manual doesn’t show you how to convert from Celsius to Fahrenheit. The brand’s website has a detailed owner’s manual that's more helpful.

Thinking of Igloo might still conjure the image of the old-school Playmate cooler you had as a kid. But the ICF electric cooler is anything but that. The portable refrigerator has a sturdy plastic build that can handle the bumps and bruises that come with transporting it to sporting events, grocery stores, and campgrounds.

Its spacious interior works as one large storage space or, with the help of the included removable divider, two separate areas. This helps separate dry items like canned drinks from wet items like fruit and sandwiches. The ICF is also remarkably simple. All the controls are built right onto the body, so all you have to do is turn it on and set the temperature.

Like other portable refrigerators, the ICF has a three-stage battery protection system to prevent it from draining your car battery.

The Bouge comes in a compact package that can serve as a personal cooler for a remote overnight, or extra storage on long treks. It has a single compartment that works as a fridge or freezer.

Set the temperature from the external control panel and monitor through the LCD thermometer. There’s no app to keep tabs on the temperature while driving but customers report it stays consistent even in hotter ambient temps. Recessed handles add to its space-saving design.

Some reviews mention the external thermometer can be off as much as seven degrees—a bit higher than most other models.

The Travoca Rigel eCooler has a number of small, but notable, features that intrigued us right away. For one, it’s somewhat modular. You can unscrew the wood paneling on the front and replace it with attachments such as a small shelf for placing drinks or snacks.

The lid is fully detachable and reversible, so you can pop the whole thing off and get a full look at everything inside. Beyond this, dual-zone cooling is powerful. Each section can work as either a fridge or freezer.

And if you don’t need separate sections, the internal divider comes out, converting the entire interior to one large space at the same temperature. Travoca also sells internal baskets separately for easier organization.

Dometic is the best-known brand of portable refrigerators, with a reputation for turning out models that are durable and reliable With that comes the higher price tag, but overlanders and outdoor enthusiasts are still fans—I see this one touted most in forums as the main fridge people use while traveling on long remote treks.

It’s on the heavier side at 60 pounds when empty, but its compressor is more powerful than other models on this list—and it operates quietly.

The portable refrigerator has a sleek display and an intuitive app to set and keep tabs on the interior temperature, plus a USB port for charging for mobile devices.

With a wheeled base and telescopic handles, this portable fridge from BougeRV is a well-built mix between portability and size. The interior comes with two separate sections. You can tune each to different temperatures, allowing you to have both a functional fridge and freezer at the same time.

One of the more user-friendly features the CRD2 has is an opening for a standalone battery. While sold separately, the battery allows the cooler to operate without any large power source, like a wall outlet or car, nearby. With the attached battery, the portable fridge can run for up to 20 hours with no other power source, making it an ideal way to escape to the beach or sleep overnight in the woods away from your car and still wake up to fresh produce and unspoiled milk.

Portable refrigerators run on a compressor just like your kitchen fridge and freezer and keep food fresher a lot longer than a cooler and ice. Most reach an average minimum temperature of -4 to -7 degrees Fahrenheit to freeze and refrigerate food, though some are refrigerators only, reaching a minimum temperature of 32 degrees Fahrenheit.

Although portable refrigerators don't rely solely on insulation for cooling power, they're still well insulated enough to take some of the load off the compressor when it comes to temperature regulation.

Don’t confuse portable refrigerators with electric coolers, as that’s another product category entirely. Electric coolers rely on thermoelectric cooling, which isn’t as efficient because it's impacted by ambient temperatures. As such, they can only cool to about 40 degrees Fahrenheit. Unlike portable refrigerators, electric coolers don’t have a compressor and don’t have the power to achieve freezing temperatures.

Portable refrigerators typically draw an average of about 45 watts of power, which is less than a standard mini fridge. This won’t blow out any car fuses or drain a car battery unless the unit is kept on for days without the car running. We chose portable refrigerators that have features like eco modes and automatic shutoff so there are precautions in place to prevent it from draining a car or portable battery.

While portable refrigerators offer more storage than coolers because they don’t need ice, their built-in compressor makes them relatively heavy at about 30 pounds or more. Still, some are more portable than others thanks to built-in handles and wheels. They don’t have shoulder straps and aren’t meant to be carried over a far distance. Also, most don't have drain plugs like standard coolers because condensation is minimal and can easily be wiped out with a small towel.

#6347. The closest exoplanets may host magnetic fields

In all the universe, Earth is the only planet known to have life. A big part of the reason life is possible here is our planet’s magnetic field. It acts like a shield, deflecting harmful energy from our Sun as well as cosmic rays from deep space that could otherwise erode Earth’s atmosphere and irradiate the surface, a death sentence for evolving life-forms.

But Earth is far from the only planet we know of. As of this writing, there are more than 6,300 confirmed exoplanets on the roster, with more added by the day. Scientists have discovered stars with as many planets as our own Sun hosts. In other systems, planets as big as Jupiter whip around their sun in only a few days’ time. Astronomers have even discovered planets that orbit multiple stars at once, and they recently caught a glimpse of a possible atmosphere around a rocky, Earth-sized world in its star’s habitable zone. But until 2026, they had no compelling evidence that any terrestrial exoplanets had magnetic fields of their own.

Because of their protective role, magnetic fields have major implications in the search for life beyond Earth. Astronomers have long suspected that part of the reason Mars now appears dead is that its magnetic field fizzled out billions of years ago. This let the solar wind strip the water and other volatile compounds from its atmosphere, leaving it cold and barren.

Beyond the solar system, in 2019 researchers reported “indirect detections of exoplanetary magnetic fields” in four hot Jupiters. Then, a 2021 study found a strong signature of a magnetic field around HAT-P-11 b, a Neptune-like planet. Two years later, a pair of studies detected possible signs of a magnetic field around YZ Ceti b — this time, a rocky, Earth-like planet roughly the same size as, and only a bit less massive than our own. But this find has not yet been confirmed.

In July 2026, a study published in Astronomy & Astrophysics found possible evidence of magnetic fields around two rocky exoplanets. Not just any exoplanets, either — Proxima Centauri b and d, the closest confirmed planets beyond our solar system, orbiting the red dwarf Proxima Centauri 4.2 light-years away.

Proxima b, roughly Earth’s mass and size, orbits every 11.1 days. Proxima d, likely a quarter to a third of our planet’s mass and 70% its size, orbits closer in with a period of 5.1 days. Because Proxima Centauri is smaller and less massive than our Sun, Proxima b is inside the habitable zone, where temperatures allow liquid surface water. A third planet, Proxima c, was tentatively detected in 2019 but is still unconfirmed. Astronomers don’t yet know if any of these worlds host atmospheres.

The new study, led by María Rosa Zapatero Osorio of the Centro de Astrobiología in Madrid, Spain, used 117 separate observations made with the Echelle SPectrograph for Rocky Exoplanets and Stable Spectroscopic Observations (ESPRESSO) instrument on the Very Large Telescope atop Cerro Paranal in Chile. The research followed up on previous studies conducted with ESPRESSO in 2020 and 2022, which focused on confirming the presence of planets around Proxima Centauri. Zapatero Osorio and her collaborators used the data to identify a peculiar correlation between the timing of flares emitted from Proxima Centauri and the orbital periods of its planets.

“We detected low-energy flares occurring with a characteristic period of about 5.1 days,” Zapatero Osorio says. “This is very close to Proxima d’s orbital period.” But flares did not occur during every orbit of Proxima d, so the team ran statistical analyses to determine whether the flares were preferentially occurring at particular phases of the planet’s orbit. They found strong statistical evidence “that the occurrence of the flares is not randomly distributed over the planet’s orbital period,” Zapatero Osorio says. “Instead, a significant number of flares tend to occur at particular times in Proxima d’s orbit.” This is a possible indication that Proxima d could be interacting magnetically with its parent star, which would be likely to happen if the planet has a strong magnetic field of its own.

Using a model adapted from the physics of solar flares, Zapatero Osorio’s team calculated that Proxima d could have a magnetic field anywhere from 8 to 230 gauss in strength, with the best median estimate limited to around 16 gauss. This is about 27 times more powerful than Earth’s magnetic field (0.6 gauss), which protects life on Earth from the worst of the Sun’s energy.

Their model assumes that the star and planet are magnetically connected, Zapatero Osorio says. Each sustains its own magnetic field, and these fields are interconnected. As a result of this connection, stress builds up on the stellar surface. From time to time, this stress is released in the form of low-energy flares, whose period is closely tied to the planet’s orbital period.

Although there was not as strong a correlation between Proxima b’s orbital period and the stellar flares, the team did find that Proxima b could also be interacting with the star, albeit in a lesser capacity. This suggests that although the finding is less sure, Proxima b may also sustain a magnetic field.

There are alternative explanations for the findings. One possibility is that there could be intrinsic, long-lived active regions on Proxima Centauri itself that account for the peculiar timing of the flares. Another explanation is that gravitational interactions between the planets and Proxima Centauri could induce disturbances on the star without requiring a strong planetary magnetosphere, although the team suggests this is less likely. It’s also possible that when Proxima’s stellar wind reaches the planets, it interacts with them in a way that mimics the effects of a planetary magnetic field without requiring one.

Like most red dwarfs, Proxima is a highly active star, regularly belching out intense flares that would be hazardous to any fledgling life-forms on the worlds in close orbit. Because Proxima is so close to Earth and has at least one rocky planet in its habitable zone, it makes a perfect testbed for studying how stellar flares could affect habitability around red dwarfs — the most common stars in the universe.

Astronomers looking for habitable worlds around these stars must contend with the likelihood that any planets would be effectively sterilized by the intense radiation in the flares constantly washing over them. Now, though, there is a glimmer of hope. If Proxima b and d do have magnetic fields, as this research suggests, they could act much like Earth’s own protective magnetic shield, deflecting enough harmful stellar radiation that life might just be able to take hold.

“Earth’s magnetic field plays an important role in protecting life and supporting human progress,” says Zapatero Osorio. “It shields our planet from the solar wind and energetic particles, and it has also played an important role in navigation.”

Unfortunately, Proxima d is so close to its host star that it is likely too hot to sustain life as we know it. Proxima b, however, lies within the habitable zone. “Based on the results of our study, both Proxima d and b may have magnetospheres capable of providing some protection against their host star’s activity,” Zapatero Osorio says.

The importance of this find goes deeper than simply a pair of neighboring planets. In the last few years, evidence has emerged that gas giant exoplanets similar to Jupiter and Saturn host magnetic fields. These are the easiest types of planets to detect and study, but while magnetic fields around such worlds are certainly fascinating, the implications for planetary habitability are limited.

But as the number of known planets continues to swell, so, too, does our sample of Earth-like worlds. And if the two closest rocky planets beyond our solar system do indeed have magnetic fields, then perhaps these features are common. If true, it increases the chances that rocky worlds across the galaxy could be habitable — at least, for life-forms as we understand them. And the more planets capable of hosting life, the more likely it is that we might someday discover we are not alone.

Nick Oakes is a science writer for NASA’s Heliophysics Education Activation Team at Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland.
