Live Science spoke with Nobel laureate Francis Halzen on how he got into physics "by accident" and built a neutrino detector that changed it forever.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When Francis Halzen first proposed burying a $271 million telescope deep beneath the South Pole, he expected to be laughed off stage. Four decades later, it won him a Nobel Prize.

Consisting of thousands of light sensors strung like rosary beads inside a cubic kilometer (0.2 cubic miles) of pristine ice, his detector, aptly named IceCube, is not an obvious way to study the universe. But Halzen, a theoretical physicist at the University of Madison-Wisconsin, isn't looking for something obvious.

His quarries are neutrinos, near-massless, chargeless, shapeshifters that are the most abundant material particles in existence. They form from nuclear processes and high-energy collisions, swarming out of our sun and whizzing from the outskirts of black holes. Yet though neutrinos stream through stars, planets, and us every second in their trillions, you still have a 75% chance of living your entire life without a single one striking an atom in your body.

On the rare occasions neutrinos do interact with atoms, they create charged particles that zip through water or ice faster than light does, casting a faint blue cone — the optical equivalent of a sonic boom.

Since 2011, IceCube has been retracing this blue light to study neutrinos produced by the most violent astrophysical events, probing energies far beyond those of Earth-based laboratories to find cracks in the laws of physics.

In the wake of his Nobel win, Live Science sat down with Halzen to discuss neutrinos, IceCube's journey from fanciful proposal to historic success, and the future of mapping the cosmos using the trails of ghosts. Here's what he had to say.

Ben Turner: What first got you into physics?

Francis Halzen: I got into physics kind of by accident. When I came out of high school, I didn't know what to do. I was interested in languages, I was interested in science. I'm a bad example of an inspirational career.

Francis Halzen is a Belgian-American particle physicist at the University of Wisconsin-Madinson who won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics for his contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory. Halzen first proposed the telescope's prototype, called AMANDA, in 1988.

I did mathematics because in the Belgian system it was very much in the old French style — in fact, it was created by Napoleon — and hadn't changed when I was in high school. And so, if you were a good student, mathematics was the thing to do, right? So I did mathematics for two years, and then I did physics in parallel, and then switched to physics. When I switched, I got a professor who became my supervisor and he gave me the paper of George Zweig [who co-proposed quarks alongside Murray Gell-Mann] on quarks, which was a fundamental discovery.

George Zweig was actually an experimentalist, and he made these calculations using little figures. I recognized, as I had done mathematics, that this was group theory; and I said "I can do this better." I actually wrote several papers on the subject; and so suddenly I was a theoretical particle physicist. And that's what I still am. My heart never left particle physics.

BT: And then quarks eventually became neutrinos for you. Why neutrinos?

FH: I actually didn't study neutrinos until I really got involved in starting this experiment. Half of my career, which was passed by the time I started AMANDA [IceCube's prototype] and IceCube, I really had very little overlap with neutrino physics.

I became interested in neutrinos again [while] solving a theoretical problem. In fact, the idea of detecting neutrinos with ice originated with [Gurgen] Askaryan, an Armenian physicist, in 1963.

You cannot see neutrinos. They have no charge. They have basically no mass. So the way to detect neutrinos is when they interact with the nucleus. We are moving now in a sea of neutrinos, but neutrinos don't interact with atoms, so we don't know it. But if they accidentally hit the nucleus of an atom, then they make a nuclear reaction, and that emits charged particles. It's like a spark, and you can detect a spark with antennas.

So Askaryan's idea was to put radio antennas in ice. We are doing exactly that. But instead of looking at the radio emission, we look at the light that's emitted, which is just blue light. We use that blue light to reconstruct the neutrino and all its properties, including its direction — [that's] why it is a telescope, right?

Building on Askaryan's idea, The Askaryan Radio Array (ARA) complements IceCube by searching for high-energy neutrinos with radio antennas buried 200 meters (670 feet) below Antarctica's ice.

I was worrying about that experiment because they had not been able to calculate the power of the spark, so they didn't know if this worked or not. Then someone told me at some point that the Russians — I guess it was still the Soviet Union — are actually doing this at a station in Antarctica by pointing [radio] dishes into the ice. I said: "This is crazy."

But I had ice all over my brain, right? When I saw in the late 80s how difficult it was to do these experiments in deep ocean water it was normal to have the idea to do it in ice. And, to our credit, we understood that it actually may be simpler.

BT: Why is being able to calculate the power of the spark so important?

FH: [It's about] how much light is made, and how far it travels through your detector. If you don't make enough light, and it's immediately absorbed, then you have no experiment.

The reason we are talking to each other [today] is because we had this incredible luck that blue light travels 100 meters [328 feet] and more through this ancient ice without being absorbed. So it's relatively easy to instrument an ice block of a kilometer cubed with light sensors.

BT: When you first proposed melting 61 two-kilometre [1.2-mile] holes in the coldest place on Earth, you said you expected to be laughed off stage. Then when you weren't, you said you continued to worry about it. What were you worrying about?

FH: Well, the worry was that I was totally out of my league. I didn't understand glaciology, I am not an experimentalist, so I didn't really grasp the technological challenges of doing this. The experiments in water were not doing very well: There was the leading experiment off the coast of Hawaii [the Deep Underwater Muon And Neutrino Detector, or DUMAND, project] and it happened that the man leading this experiment, John Learned, was a good friend of mine, and I eventually contacted him.

And the glaciology, of course. Nobody knew what the optical properties were of ice at a depth of one kilometer [0.6 miles] or more under the South Pole. There were [ice] cores that had been taken, but cores are small — the size of a teacup — so you cannot tell how far the light travels [through the ice]. So people thought it was a cute idea that would never work.

If I had known more about glaciology, about hot water drilling, and about the technical challenges, I would never have started this experiment. It's the advantage of being ignorant. It's why young people make great discoveries, and when you're 82 years old you don't make this progress — you know too much.

An artist's illustration showing what the interior of IceCube would look like without the ice.

BT: You speak about AMANDA and IceCube with a lot of ambivalence. You said you "got dragged into it by accident" and "tried to get out of it many times."

FH: Oh yes, absolutely. You know, theorists write two types of papers: [the first are] papers where they think they contribute to the progress of science — they usually don't. But the other type of paper is just to show you're smart. And this was definitely in the second category. And then two people from Berkeley [Doug Lowder and Andrew Westphal] actually started the experiment.

BT: Well, you won a Nobel Prize for it. If you wanted to look smart, you succeeded.

FH: Yeah, without a lot of luck, I wouldn't be sitting here.

They're this almost non-existent piece of reality.

BT: But surely it wasn't just showing off? Despite all of the uncertainties and worries, there must have been something about neutrinos — these barely detectable, misbehaving particles — that's so important it made you stick around. What's the draw to learn about them?

FH: Neutrinos are something really special, right? When you look at the Standard Model of matter [which describes all the known particles and forces], it has quarks, leptons, and neutrinos.

But neutrinos are special in the sense that they're supposed to have no mass. They're just like photons: they travel at the speed of light, so you can do astronomy with them. But then they have the advantage that they go through planets; they go through the Earth; they reach you from the beginning of time; they reach you from the edge of the universe. They're this almost non-existent piece of reality.

So they always had a special fascination. We knew they existed since 1930; because without neutrinos you cannot change a proton into a neutron. They were ghosts — that's where the name "ghost particle" comes from. They were part of physics, and particle physics, and nuclear physics, but they had never been seen.

It's only in 1956 that [Frederick] Reines and [Clyde] Cowen finally discovered the neutrino by putting a detector close to a nuclear reactor, where there are lots of them. If they don't interact, then you compensate by going to a place where there are lots of them, and a nuclear reactor was an opportunity.

It's a fascinating particle. Of course now it fascinates us because they do have mass, which is not allowed by the structure of the Standard Model, and so they carry some information on new physics — the new physics we are looking for with the Large Hadron Collider in Geneva. They are the particles that have carried the message of that new physics most directly, and that's our domain.

We should have all the advantages. Sadly, they just behave like the Standard Model in everything we have done over the first 15 years of this experiment.

Construction workers inside one of the two colossal caverns created for the particle detector modules of Fermilab's Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE). By probing the properties of neutrinos, physicists are hoping to assess key theories, including neutrinos' hypothesized role in tipping the universe into containing more matter than antimatter.

BT: Famously, in 1993 to '94, microscopic air bubbles trapped in Antarctica's ice scattered neutrinos' blue light like frosted glass, nearly killing the project. You saved it by drilling to where the ice sheet's weight crushed those bubbles out of existence, up to 2.5 kilometers [1.6 miles] beneath the surface and one kilometer deeper than you originally planned. How hard was that?

FH: Well, the drilling almost killed the project twice.

It's actually an interesting story, because we now detect a neutrino every minute as we are speaking, but they are produced in the atmosphere. They [atmospheric neutrinos] are our background — interesting background, but a background.

As energetic particles called cosmic rays strike Earth's upper atmosphere, they create showers of smaller particles, including neutrinos, that can be detected on the surface. IceCube's scientists filter out lower-energy atmospheric neutrinos (alongside those produced by the sun) to find only those made in astrophysical cataclysms.

After we had solved all these problems and could detect neutrinos, the only threshold to cross was to produce a drill that could build IceCube. That involves melting ice over two and a half kilometers over an area the size of a basketball. The technique existed in glaciers, but [produced] a shallow hole about the size of a bottle of wine.

So we went to companies specialized in building hoses, and we needed a hose that was 2.5 kilometers long. The first company we went to told us: "Look, you hang a hose the size of a tea cup over two and a half kilometers of hot water and what do you think will happen?" It will collapse. Even the theorists could understand that it would collapse.

And that was the end of the project. For weeks I thought it was finished. I told one of our engineers, a brilliant guy who contributed much more than what I'm going to tell you, and he didn't give up. He found a company in Padua, Italy, near Venice and they said: "We can build anything." And they did.

Then, when we started drilling, it was still a problem. We drilled one hole over a whole [South Pole] season. We had brilliant engineers working on this totally new piece of equipment — you have no idea how complex this is — and they learned from the mistakes of the first year and the second year it worked. They deployed 86 strings without ever failing, which is amazing actually. It's like when you launch 86 satellites, you're probably going to fail some. That's what we thought. But they never did.

A view down along one of IceCube's 86 detector strings, dangling in holes drilled up to 2.5 kilometers into the ice.

BT: The detector went online in 2011, then that year and the next came "Bert" and "Ernie" — the first ever detections of astrophysical neutrinos from beyond our solar system. After all that effort, all those near misses, and every doubt you ever had, what did it feel like when they arrived?

FH: We were not sure we believed it. It was clear then that this was a major discovery — if it was true. It took us six months or more to have the courage to write the paper.

I remember seeing the first events on my screen in October of 2012, and they looked like they couldn't have come from the atmosphere — such high energy! We discovered the first two serendipitously in the first two years of data. Then, after we went to look for more knowing what these events look like, we had 28. So we had the courage to publish.

But then, three weeks later, we were declared the physics breakthrough of the year. I must say I was not happy about that. I had to give a press conference, and I was all the time thinking: "If this is not true, how am I going to walk this back?"

It took me quite a while to convince myself that this wasn't just something that looked like cosmic neutrinos. But this is such an unusual corner of science, you don't know whether you are fooled by some other phenomena you haven't thought of.

FH: Well now we are seeing sources of neutrinos. You see 100 neutrinos come from an active galaxy, and you point [a different telescope] back at it with 0.04 degree resolution. There's no doubt now. But being convinced was a continuous process; at least in my case. My colleagues always refer to me as a total optimist, but it took me some time. I was not my usual self on this.

But now there's no doubt. The statistics of observing cosmic neutrinos is totally impossible [to deny] with the precision we have now. But we're talking about 14 years of data. It's really incredible how quickly we've progressed.

A crane deploys the Baikal-GVD neutrino telescope from the ice cover of Lake Baikal, Siberia.

And you realize that, officially, none of the things we see have been confirmed by someone else. There are two experiments, [Baikal-G in Lake Baikal and [KM3NeT] in the Mediterranean Sea, but they're under construction. And they both have produced some kind of evidence, but a real confirmation of seeing the same thing we see has still not happened. So the Nobel Prize [Committee] had more courage than me.

I had forgotten that it was Nobel season.

BT: You were in a hotel room in Italy when the call came from Stockholm. What went through your mind in the first quiet moments after hanging up?

FH: Well, after hanging up, I was sent a Zoom link, and they asked me questions, which I answered. But I didn't know that I was actually giving a press conference. I still haven't looked back at that press conference.

But that's how crazy it was, because I had forgotten that it was Nobel season. The call came by total surprise. Well, it wasn't a total surprise because there's a game of predicting the Nobel Prizes. And I had been there [in the running to win] for several years.

So I cannot say that I was unaware of this. But this was a difficult season for me, right? People literally would send me condolence messages every year for not winning. And they meant it — they're my friends — but it makes you feel strange. You feel you've disappointed your collaborators.

So that's the first thing I thought: "Okay, the problem is solved now. Everybody can get credit for this experiment." And deservedly. Because IceCube was becoming mostly me, and data and science. The fact of its history and the contributions people made was being forgotten very fast. The great thing about this Nobel Prize is that it's for a difficult problem that was solved by so many brilliant people over almost four decades.

BT: Aside from winning the Nobel, what's been the highlight of working on IceCube?

FH: The highlight for me was to show that the technique works. Seeing these neutrinos go through the Earth, and then through the detector, was incredibly exciting because there was no doubt you were looking at a stream of particles going through your detector initiated by neutrinos that came through the Earth. There was no doubt. What you see is what you get.

We had this attitude that if you build something this big you're going to do interesting science. This is so different from anything that has been built before. I don't want to insult astronomers, but our joke was: "We are all particle physicists, guys. God forbid we have to do astronomy." But that's what we are doing.

I must say, it's very, very exciting to learn astronomy when you're 82 years old.

BT: IceCube–Gen2 is targeted to come online by 2033 and will be eight times larger than the original detector. What do you want for its future?

FH: Whenever I give a talk, I have a list of conclusions, and my first is always that neutrino astronomy exists, and that's our contribution. Doing neutrino astronomy will require more instruments, bigger instruments. In astronomy there's not just one telescope, right? To do real astronomy we'll need more instruments covering the sky completely, and we'll need more neutrinos with better angular resolution.

The nice thing is that will happen: There are ambitious projects in China now, and [the upgrade of] our own project too. How can you pass it up? Because now the technology is much better: we understand the ice perfectly; we can design this detector, optimize it, and gain an order of magnitude [improvement] for the same cost as the original.

China's Jiangmen Underground Neutrino Observatory (JUNO) detector while it was under construction in 2024. The detector, which is designed to probe neutrinos from space and from Earth, came online in August 2026.

BT: You famously don't like to make predictions, even one year ahead, about what we might learn about neutrinos. So I'm going to try to be sly with this final question: What do you hope the future has in store for neutrino astronomy?

FH: I hope for a galactic supernova [within the Milky Way]. I don't know if you know the history, but in 1987 there was a supernova in a [nearby] satellite galaxy, but it [meant physicists] detected 20 neutrinos. And what we learned from these neutrinos is incredible — literally thousands of papers have been written about those 20 neutrinos, and they're all interesting.

Neutrinos are supposed to have no mass and be just like photons. The best limit we could set on the [tiny and still unexplained] mass of the neutrino came from that supernova. So we made very fundamental measurements that we hadn't been able to make with [laboratory] neutrino beams. And then the whole story that a star really collapses into a neutron star. All that suddenly became reality. I was not, and am still not, an astronomer, but from the point of view of stellar physics this was a major event.

Now, instead of three experiments, we have multiple neutrino detectors of all kinds. Some will detect thousands of neutrinos; we'll detect a million neutrinos. We can't actually reconstruct them, but we can make a very detailed movie telling you everything that went on in a supernova while the star collapsed and then exploded. The science we will do from a few seconds of data will be incredible.

I can tell you it hasn't happened since the mid-1990s because we have been looking for it continuously with AMANDA and Ice-Cube. There are supposed to be like two per century. We are due.

Editor's note: This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Ben Turner is the features editor at Live Science. He covers physics and astronomy, among other topics such as tech and climate change. He graduated from University College London with a degree in particle physics before training as a journalist. When he's not writing, Ben enjoys reading literature, playing the guitar and losing at chess.

#6345. Scientists just documented Bolivia’s first Amazon river dolphins, though local fishers knew about them all along

Scientists just confirmed Bolivia’s first Amazon river dolphins after three sightings along the Acre River at Cobija, even though local fishers knew about them all along.

On the Acre River, in the Bolivian Amazon, fishers have been seeing pink dolphins for years. Until recently, scientists had no confirmed record of even one sighting.

The first confirmed record came in April 2025, when two pink river dolphins appeared in the river at the city of Cobija and a biologist photographed one of them.

In a new study, researchers describe that sighting and two later ones as the first documented evidence in Bolivia of the Amazon river dolphin, often called the pink river dolphin.

The finding extends the species’ known range into a river where scientists have been suggesting since the 1970s that it might live.

The biologist was Ximena Morales Mamani, the study’s lead author. She is with the Shimanú Amazon Conservation Program in Cobija.

Her co-authors are from Shimanú, the Universidad Mayor de San Andrés in La Paz, the group Juventud Proactiva de la Amazonia, and the Wildlife Conservation Society.

So far, the team has photographs, video, and fishers’ accounts but no genetic tests. That means scientists still have to confirm which species these dolphins are.

The April sighting came during the City Nature Challenge, a yearly event held in the last week of that month.

People in cities around the world photograph and record the wildlife near them. They upload the results to iNaturalist, a citizen science website.

The 2025 event was the tenth, and the first that Cobija joined. On April 27, two dolphins were seen in the city’s Junín neighborhood.

Morales Mamani photographed one of them while it was near the riverbank.

In an interview with Earth.com, the biologist said she trained in Cobija and has lived and worked there for many years. Adding to what is known about the region’s wildlife, she said, “is especially meaningful to me.”

The Shimanú program is a group of young volunteers from different professional backgrounds, led by biologists, she added.

Fishers recorded the next two sightings. On November 28, 2025, a local television channel broadcast video that fishers had filmed near Puerto Alto.

On May 3, 2026, fishers posted images on social media of two dolphins near the Frontera neighborhood.

Together, the three records show that dolphins were in the Acre River during two rainy seasons in a row.

Until now, Bolivia’s known river dolphin was the Bolivian river dolphin, which is found in the Mamoré and Iténez river basins. Many specialists count it as a separate species.

Rapids and waterfalls on the upper Madeira River, in Brazil, separate that dolphin from Amazon river dolphins. The barrier has limited breeding between the two.

The Acre River doesn’t have a barrier like that. It flows into the Purús River, which flows into the main channel of the Amazon.

Because of that open route, scientists suggested as early as 1973 that Amazon river dolphins might be in the Acre.

Robert Wallace, a senior conservation scientist at the Wildlife Conservation Society and a co-author of the new study, raised the same possibility in 2010.

Local residents reported dolphins in the river from time to time, but none of those reports came with evidence that scientists could check.

The open route is also the team’s reason for calling these animals Amazon river dolphins. The authors wrote that the species should be confirmed with genetic tests or a study of the animals’ anatomy.

The record adds to what is known about Bolivia’s mammals, Morales Mamani told Earth.com, and shows “there is still much to discover in Pando,” the department that includes Cobija.

In May and June 2026, the team surveyed 34 fishers who work along the Acre River in three areas of Cobija. The survey was designed to record their local knowledge of dolphins and other river animals.

Some of the fishers had worked on the river for a few months, and others for more than 30 years.

Only five of the 34 said they had never seen a river dolphin. Twenty of the fishers, or 58.8%, had seen dolphins between one and five times.

The fishers’ answers agreed with the photographs and video. Dolphins may be in the river more often than three records suggest, the authors wrote.

Asked how many dolphins they saw at a time, 44.1% of the fishers said two, which was the most common answer. Another 20.6% said one.

The team noted when a sighting took place only if a fisher mentioned the timing unprompted.

“What surprised us most was learning that fishers had been observing these dolphins repeatedly for many years. One account even describes a first sighting more than 30 years ago,” Morales Mamani said.

About two-thirds of the fishers, 64.7%, said they see dolphins more often in the rainy season, which runs from October to May. All three recorded sightings fell in those months.

In the middle section of the Acre, the water level rises and falls by 39 to 49 feet (12 to 15 meters) with the seasons. That’s about the height of a four-story building.

The authors wrote that Amazon river dolphins may regularly use parts of the Acre, especially in the rainy season. The dolphins can get there because the Acre connects to the wider Amazon basin.

The river also ran unusually high in both rainy seasons covered by the records, which may partly explain why no records existed before, they added.

Several fishers also told the team they had begun seeing dolphins more often after floods that affected Cobija and other border communities, Morales Mamani said.

She called the fishers’ account “an interesting observation for future research” and said there’s no scientific evidence yet that the floods and the sightings are related.

All of South America’s river dolphin species are threatened, the authors wrote. To keep dolphins in the Acre, they called for protecting riverside forests, maintaining water quality, and keeping the river connected to the rest of the basin.

Forest loss in the Amazon and changes in river levels caused by climate change may alter river habitats, they added.

The Acre River forms part of the border between Bolivia and Brazil. Morales Mamani said a first step would be cooperation agreements between the two countries to conserve the species.

“It is also essential to involve local communities,” she said.

Fishers told her team they wanted to help protect the dolphins and the river. The fishers proposed one idea themselves: planting trees along the riverbanks.

Wallace wrote in an email to Earth.com that the Acre River needs conserving anyway, for what it provides to those same fishers and to Cobija, the capital of Pando.

“The Amazon river dolphins are a nice symbol and potential important catalyst for those conservation efforts,” he added.

The study can’t say how many dolphins use the Acre, where they travel, or how closely they are related to dolphins elsewhere in the Amazon.

The records also say little about the dry season, from June to September.

The authors called for surveys in those months to learn whether dolphins stay in the area all year, keep to particular habitats, or move as the water level changes.

No new sightings have been documented since the study was written, Morales Mamani said.

Her team wants to set up monitoring to record future sightings. The team will need resources to keep that work going over the long term, she said.

The fishers have said they’re willing to help with that monitoring.

The full study was published in the journal Neotropical Hydrobiology and Aquatic Conservation.

#6344. The 7 Best Smokeless Fire Pits We Tested (and Yes, They Produced Hardly Any Smoke)

From set-it-and-forget-it backyard centerpieces to grab-and-go options for weekend camping trips, we tried well-regarded options from Solo Stove, Breeo, Blue Sky, and more.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Engineered to contain flames and burn fuel more completely, smokeless fire pits deliver ambient warmth with a lot less smoke in your eyes than a traditional campfire. They achieve this through two points of combustion: The first happens at the bottom, where airflow feeds burning wood; the second occurs at the top, where the fire’s smoke and gas output are burned off. And while no smokeless fire pit is 100 percent smokeless, if you use best practices (like burning dry wood) they come pretty darn close.

We tested smokeless fire pits in our New York and Pennsylvania backyards, building fires rather than judging them on specs alone. Along with smoke output, we considered size, which affects wood capacity and where the heat actually lands, as well as how easy each pit was to empty of ash and store once done, among other factors. We also used them repeatedly over time to see how their finishes held up, because a brand-new pit can look very different after several fires.

Solo Stove is the brand most people associate with smokeless fire pits (though Breeo was the first game in town). The latest joiner in Solo Stove’s lineup is the Summit, an upgraded take on the ever-popular Bonfire. Its 23-pound weight makes it just as easy to lift and store off-season, and there’s even less setup required. All-in-all, it’s the best smokeless fire pit for most people who want to enjoy a backyard fire pit that can be stored off-season.

Because the Summit is four to five inches shorter than the Bonfire, it does a better job of keeping your feet warm, one of the major gripes our Test Editor Brad Ford had of the earlier model. He says that while it holds less firewood, it undoubtedly produces a higher flame that extends well above the rim.

Another improvement he points out is the Summit’s integrated stand, which he says is sturdier and allows for better airflow than that of the Bonfire’s detached stand. There’s also a deeper ash pan, which is particularly helpful because the Summit burns through wood fast and needs frequent reloading. In terms of price, the 19.5-inch Summit is $100 more than a Bonfire of the same size, an extra cost that’s well worth the investment.

Full Solo Stove Summit Smokeless Fire Pit Review

After trying out the Breeo X Series 24 for several months, test editor Brad Ford loved it. According to Ford, “One of the coolest details of the X Series 24 is its Corten finish. (It is also available in a stainless-steel finish.) Corten is a structural steel alloy you often see used for bridges or power line towers. It’s designed to oxidize, or rust, creating a natural finish that protects the steel rather than continuing to degrade it. This eliminates the frustration I’ve had with some stainless-steel fire pits that discolor after a couple uses.”

Beyond this, Ford also liked, “that Breeo intended for their smokeless fire pits to be used for cooking from the get-go, which means they’ve got accessories for the X 24 that work very well. And most of their cooking accessories are compatible with all their fire pits. Top this all off with the fact that the X 24 is made right in Lancaster PA, USA, unlike most other popular brands.”

The Breeo X 24 weighs more than twice as much as the other models we’ve tested, so it’s not exactly portable—but it is long-lasting.

As the largest pick of the lot, the X Series was easy to load with wood and start a fire. We fit 18- to 20-inch logs into it, laying them across the raised X in the bottom of the pit. This patented design keeps the logs high, allowing air to flow in and feed the fire from the bottom.

Cleanup required scooping ash out, as the unit is too heavy to dump out easily—Breeo sells a shovel designed to ease this process. The brand also offers several accessories for cooking over the fire, which make the X Series as much a grill as it is a fire pit.

This hefty, all-black fire pit is a great-value addition to an outdoor setup. Its wide diameter gives you plenty of room to build a substantial fire, and the shape and airflow make for a good, largely smokeless burn. It takes both wood and pellets right out of the box, no adapter or switch-up required. And the lift-out ash catch has two handles, making it one of the easiest models to empty. (You still have to reach into the drum to lift it out, though, so wear gloves.)

The black coating is practical, too: Unlike stainless steel, it doesn’t show every fire mark. Once in place, it blends nicely with patio furniture, particularly setups with black metal legs. While it does scratch more easily than others we tested, you can touch it up with high-heat spray paint, just like you would a grill.

Some things to bear in mind: At 35 pounds, it’s heavier than many of the models we tested, so you’re unlikely to move it around much once it’s situated. The price doesn’t include a cover, which you’ll definitely want if it’s going to live outside for the season.

Because the ash catch sits inside the main body, with no separate base beneath it, we’d also place this one on a fireproof mat to be extra safe. And this may be petty, but the branding is the most prominent of any pit we tested: you’ll be looking at the words “Blue Sky” on the base every time you sit down.

If you want to bring the campfire with you wherever you go, the Packfire portable fire pit is an ideal choice. It packs down into a backpack, so you can carry it on your shoulders and set it up wherever your adventures take you. In fact, its innovative design won it a spot in our 2026 Home Awards.

The fire pit is composed of three sections: the base, which serves as a stand and ash pan; the body, which, when fully set up, surrounds the base; and the ring, which holds the body in place. Cleanup is easy: Simply lift the ring and body off the base, pour the ashes out, and break everything back down for travel.

It’s worth noting that even though it’s built for travel, the fire pit is still a bit cumbersome to carry around. While our Director of Product Content, Will Egensteiner was testing the Packfire, he said its 27.5 weight was a factor. “As I heaved it onto my back to put it away, I almost tipped over. And I’m not a small guy.”

The substance of this fire pit starts with the box: One of the largest and heaviest we had to maneuver into location for testing (only the Breeo was heavier), moving it really requires two people or a dolly. Some of that initial box weight comes from the generous bag of wood pellets packed inside, but the pit itself, at 45 pounds with nothing in it, is hardly lightweight.

Assembly is a little less impressive. Attaching the legs required a drill, as, while an Allen key and screws were included, some of the holes weren’t perfectly aligned, making the process more fiddly than it should have been. It does, however, come with spare screws.

Once assembled, though, this thing is a very good-looking workhorse. The large bag of wood pellets kept going for about 35 minutes before burning down to embers; produced virtually no smoke; and the heat output was surprisingly high.

Simply by flipping the inside container, you can also fire up 14-inch logs inside. The exterior frame stayed remarkably cool and, given it’s black, didn’t discolor the way the stainless steel ones did. While the inside picked up some black streaks from the flames, they looked more like evidence of a real fire than damage, which we actually liked.

The ash disposal is a true highlight. You don’t have to lift, twist, or tip the pit to empty it: An ash pan slides out from the side, shovel-style, so you can dump the refuse without moving the fire pit at all. It also comes with a perfectly fitted cover, which is particularly useful given how difficult this one would be to haul away when not in use.

This seriously smart, compact fire pit is made for small spaces and taking on the road. It’s lightweight, straightforward to assemble, and comes with six pieces: a pit and ash can that sit on top of one another; two pieces that twist together to form a fire poker (a little tight to sync up, but ultimately quite a useful piece); and a spark screen with a screw-in knob to lift it (also a very nice extra).

Truly, the whole kit is quite remarkable, given the price. The ash catch is also cleverly designed to fit inside the fire pit for storage, so there’s nothing extra to haul around when not in use. The black finish looks sharp and has the added benefit of hiding burn marks better than lighter finishes. (The downside is, it scratches easily.)

The whole thing packs into a carrying bag with a shoulder strap and drawstring closure. It’s also lighter than any other model we tested, making it an excellent choice for beach parties, camping trips, or anywhere you need to carry your fire pit more than a few feet.

There is one important caveat: Because the pit is so compact, you’ll mostly be limited to twigs, which burn quickly. Use wood pellets instead, for a longer, more consistent fire. The carrying bag also feels flimsy, like it could break down quickly with repeat use, but, for the price, that may not matter.

This one looks like a saucer and comes with just three pieces: a main body that locks securely into the ash holder base and a wind guard that twists onto the rim. It’s also one of the roomier pits we tested, with a wider, more-open design that accommodates both more and larger pieces of wood than many others. The manufacturer says it handles logs up to one pound. We’d have preferred a measurement in inches, but went with 16 inches, which it handled better than the Tiki. You can also add a griddle attachment to turn it into a cooker.

This one really does produce a roaring fire that can warm four people comfortably. The wide, funnel-like shape seems to encourage a bigger, more expansive flame; sitting around it felt more like a bonfire than simply burning wood in a container. After 25 minutes, we still had a substantial fire going. Its lower stature kept our feet warm too.

The biggest downside is ash removal. The pan in the base is relatively shallow, and the wide fire pit is awkward to twist and lift off for cleaning. You’ll want long arms—or a second person—to do it comfortably. The stainless-steel finish also turned a light bronze after just one use. A cover costs extra.

Before lighting a single fire, we evaluated the things that can make or break a smokeless fire pit before you ever use them. We assessed the packaging and how well each pit was protected in transit, weighed every model, and evaluated assembly. We read the instructions, noting whether they were clear, complete, and actually useful.

We considered whether it could be disassembled for storage, and what came in the box versus what required an additional purchase. While We had plenty of outdoor space to work with, safety always came first: we set every pit on heavy-duty pavers and kept a fire extinguisher close at hand.

Then we lit them up. We used comparable loads of seasoned firewood to assess how easily each pit started, how much smoke it produced, how evenly it burned, and how much heat it put out. We paid attention to flame height and consistency, too, and whether the fire actually warmed people sitting around it—not just looked good from a distance. We measured logs to see exactly what each pit could accommodate and tested wood pellets where models supported them.

Finally, we evaluated the less glamorous but equally important details: how easy each pit was to tend, how much ash accumulated, how easily that ash could be removed, and what it took to clean and put each model away. And because a fire pit can be beautiful at 7 p.m. and a pain in the ass at 10 p.m., we tested for both.

Whether you want a smokeless fire pit to heat your outdoor space or be more of an ambient seasonal moment is an important consideration. For long nights by the fire with family and friends, you’ll likely want to invest in a larger model that measures 24 inches in diameter. In testing, models that size and up exuded warmth for several feet, and could easily warm four to six people.

They could also handle 14- to 16-inch-long logs. The trade-off: Models this size are a lot heavier and harder to move. If you’re looking for more of a warming accent, narrower fire pits work wonders. You can also maximize some models’ output by adding a heat deflector that sits above the flames and pushes heat out laterally, instead of letting it escape upward.

Ideally, the smokeless fire pit should work right out of the box, with limited-to-no setup, besides setting the pit on a base. It should also break down easily. If you’ll be storing it between fires or seasons, a model that’s easy to disassemble, carry, and put away is key.

The shallower and wider the smokeless fire pit, the easier it is to make a fire from scratch. You simply have more base room to work with to set up your paper, kindling, and wood, and less depth to maneuver to light your fire once ready. No matter your choice, you’ll definitely want a lighter with a long metal wand and a safety catch. None of the models we tested included one.

Burning pellets instead of wood was the closest we got to a truly smokeless fire during our testing. Made of compressed wood waste like sawdust, chips, and shavings, pellets are easy to light, always bone dry, and produce a hotter, more consistent flame than logs. There are trade-offs, though: They lack the classic crackle and pop of a wood-burning fire and that wonderful smell.

Bags of the stuff also typically cost more than a handful of logs at the hardware store, yet burn about the same length of time. But, if you’re allergic to smoke, don’t want your sweaters to smell of it, have wet wood drying out, or want a reliable and even fire every single time, pellets are an excellent way to go. Some fire pits work with them right out of the box; others need an adapter.

Every smokeless pit burns wood. Many smokeless fire pits can also use wood pellets right out of the box. Some, like Solo Stove, need an adapter, so the tiny pellets don’t drop right through the pit’s air holes into the ashcan below. Some portable options may only be wide or deep enough to handle twigs (pellets may be a better option for those).

Pro tip: Wet or green wood will always be slow to burn and emit a lot of smoke; use a moisture meter to suss out whether your logs are dry enough to light up before putting a match to them.

If you plan to use your fire pit regularly, easy ash removal should be a deciding factor. The last thing you want to have to do is pick up and tip a heavy steel drum over a trashcan in order to empty it of ash. Instead, look for a removable ash pan or tray that allows you to lift the ash out cleanly once the pit has fully cooled (usually 12 to 24 hours after a fire has ended). Otherwise, you’ll need a shovel to scoop out the ash.

If you don’t have space to leave your fire pit outside all year, think about who will move it and how often. Even a small pit designed for camping trips can weigh as much as 20 pounds. Fortunately, these options usually come with a carrying bag, so you can sling them over your shoulder. Meanwhile, larger models can top 45 pounds (the 24-inch Breeo weighs just over 60 pounds), which matters when you have to move it under cover or into the garage at the end of the season. Units that come apart make this easier; having a dolly or hand truck on hand helps, too.

Material affects how long your new pit will look the way it does on arrival. While stainless steel looks shiny and modern from the start, heat from the flames will discolor it, and potentially quite quickly, as some testing showed. (You can restore its original shine with a stainless-steel cleaner such as Bar Keepers Friend, but that’s extra work.) Corten-steel usually costs more but forms a protective rust-colored patina that looks attractively weathered over time. Painted or powder-coated steel usually costs less, but can scratch and chip with repeat use.

Whatever finish you choose, keeping your smokeless fire pit empty of ash and covered when it’s not in use will help extend its life. Rainwater sitting in a fire pit full of ash can create a corrosive, alkaline slurry that accelerates rust and can damage the metal. Some models come with a cover as part of their bundle; others charge extra for it. Our reviews note whether a cover is included in every pick.

Smokeless fire pits can be a lot more than a place to warm your hands on chilly nights. In some cases, you can turn them into an outdoor kitchen. Brands like Breeo, Solo Stove, and Cuisinart have grill grates, griddles, pizza ovens, or roasting sticks that let you cook over an open fire. Other add-ons also make a difference, like a cover, if you plan to leave it outside when not in use; a spark screen, particularly if you have toddlers and pets around (though, warning: they can also get hot to the touch); and fire pokers or ashtray lifters, so you don’t get your hands dirty. Definitely check the accessory lineup before you buy your pit; they’re often model-specific. A pair of fire-resistant gloves is always a good investment.

While product photos often depict smokeless fire pits sitting on wood decks or backyards, it’s worth noting that their bases can get hot enough to scorch or discolor lawns, wood decks, composite, and asphalt. Ideally, yours should sit on brick, concrete, stone, or sand. But in the absence of that, a dedicated base (sometimes included, other times sold separately) helps raise the unit off the ground. For an even safer setup, consider adding a fireproof mat underneath. You should also keep a bucket of water or a fire extinguisher nearby and check for local burn bans before lighting. For more on fire pit safety, check out our story.

Arabella Bowen is a seasoned product tester who specializes in travel, design, tech, home improvement, and outdoor essentials. She’s reviewed everything from roller bags and cameras to hiking equipment and home decor for outlets such as The Montreal Gazette, Fodor's, AFAR, and US Park Pass. Arabella can often be found immersed in DIY projects at her mid-century modern house in upstate New York—a hands-on pursuit that inspires many trips to Lowe’s.

#6343. The Sky This Week from November 27 to December 4: Brilliant Venus

Friday, November 27As fall deepens and winter approaches, the wintertime star patterns are reappearing in our evening sky. One is a large asterism called the Winter Hexagon, now fully above the horizon by about 10 P.M. local time. You should be able to spot this shape even with the Moon nearby, as each point in the Winter Hexagon is a bright, well-known star.

Look east late tonight to locate the waning gibbous Moon near the border of Gemini and Cancer. This will help you find the first point in the Hexagon, the pair of stars Castor and Pollux, the heads of Gemini the Twins, glowing just above the Moon at this time. From there, look upward for another bright star in neighboring Auriga — this is Capella, the next point in the Hexagon. From Capella, look left and down just a little to find the V-shaped face of Taurus the Bull, where the bright star Aldebaran shines, marking the next point. Then it’s down to Orion’s bright knee, Rigel, before you drop down and a little left, close to the horizon, to land on Sirius, the brightest star in the sky and the nose of Canis Major. The Hexagon closes out with the luminary of the Little Dog, Procyon.

Sunrise: 6:59 A.M. Sunset: 4:36 P.M. Moonrise: 7:53 P.M. Moonset: 10:26 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (82%) *Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

Saturday, November 28Saturn remains a bright naked-eye object all evening, setting around 2 A.M. local time. Around 8 P.M., you’ll find it high in the south, to the left of the Circlet of Pisces and above the body of Cetus the Whale.

Tonight and for the next few nights, Saturn’s strange, two-faced moon Iapetus is skimming north of the planet, making it easier to find. Now glowing at 11th magnitude, it is heading west toward a late December western elongation, when it will shine about a magnitude brighter but sit far from Saturn. Once you’ve got Saturn in your scope, look about 2’ northeast to land on Iapetus. Over the next few nights, it will move westward, reaching inferior conjunction and standing due north of the ringed world by the 30th.

If you can catch 11th-magnitude Iapetus, you’ll also see four brighter moons: 10th-magnitude Dione, Rhea, and Tethys closer to Saturn; and mid-8th-magnitude Titan, about 3’ to Saturn’s west. The latter is the planet’s largest and brightest moon, easy to spot in any size scope and often even binoculars. If you keep returning each night to track Iapetus, also keep an eye on Titan, which is moving eastward toward the planet and will pass south of Saturn on December 2. Dione, Rhea, and Tethys have smaller orbits and shorter periods, so they move visibly over the course of several hours, frequently swapping places and passing in front of or behind Saturn. For example, Dione disappears behind Saturn’s southwestern limb in an occultation around 12:20 A.M. EST on the 29th (still late on the 28th in time zones farther west).

Sunrise: 7:00 A.M. Sunset: 4:36 P.M. Moonrise: 9:10 P.M. Moonset: 11:09 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (73%)

Sunday, November 29Have you ever seen your shadow by planetlight? Venus reaches greatest brilliancy at 2 P.M. EST, now shining at magnitude –4.9. Rising nearly three and a half hours before the Sun, Venus will be so bright that it could potentially cast a shadow if you’re in a location with particularly dark skies (Bortle 1 or 2).

Even without perfect viewing conditions, this morning star can’t be missed. By an hour before sunrise, Venus is roughly 25° high in the southeast, blazing just to the lower left of Spica, the brightest star in Virgo. Far to Venus’ lower left, closer to the ground, Mercury stands nearly 5° above the horizon, shining at magnitude –0.7.

Compare the two planets through a telescope. Venus is a 27%-lit crescent, but its disk stretches 40” across. Mercury, by comparison, is much smaller, just 6” across, but its phase is 82%. Now through the first week of December is the best time to catch the solar system’s smallest planet, as it remains bright but appears to sink toward the horizon day by day. By the 5th, Mercury will be less than 2° high an hour before sunrise, making viewing challenging both because of potential obstacles on the horizon as well as the more turbulent layer of air near the ground.

Venus, meanwhile, stays at roughly the same altitude an hour before sunrise all month, its phase growing to nearly 50% lit by the end of the year. Earth’s sister planet will remain prominent in the morning sky through the first half of next year.

Sunrise: 7:01 A.M. Sunset: 4:36 P.M. Moonrise: 10:25 P.M. Moonset: 11:43 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (62%)

Monday, November 30Venus remains a brilliant and unmissable morning star, but it’s not the only object worth paying attention to before dawn. Leo is hosting a celestial get-together this morning as the Moon joins two planets and the star that sits at the heart of the Lion, just beneath the Sickle asterism.

The waning gibbous Moon is the brightest object here; next brightest is Jupiter, located to the Moon’s upper right and glowing at magnitude –2.2. The gas giant stands nearly side by side with Mars (to Jupiter’s left); the Red Planet is fainter but still a respectable magnitude 0.4. Both planets are slowly growing in brightness and size as they approach opposition early next year. Through a telescope, Jupiter stretches 39” across, offering excellent views of its alternating light and dark cloud bands, and Mars is now 8” wide.

Shining between Mars and the Moon is 1st-magnitude Regulus, often drawn as both the heart of Leo and the base of the Sickle asterism’s handle. The curving backward question mark of stars that forms the Sickle’s blade and the Lion’s head in profile lies above the grouping in the sky before dawn.

Sliding along the ecliptic, the Moon passes 1.2° south of Jupiter at 4 A.M. EST, then 1.1° south of Regulus at 10 A.M. EST and 3° south of Mars at 3 P.M. EST.

Sunrise: 7:02 A.M. Sunset: 4:35 P.M. Moonrise: 11:36 P.M. Moonset: 12:11 P.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (51%)

Tuesday, December 1Last Quarter Moon occurs at 1:09 A.M. EST. A few hours later, asteroid 2 Pallas reaches a stationary point at 7 A.M. EST. Located in Cetus, it is visible all evening, setting around 1 A.M. local time. It stands highest around 8 P.M., when it’s roughly 30° above the southern horizon, about 4.2° southeast of 2nd-magnitude Diphda (Beta [β] Ceti).

Glowing at magnitude 9.0, Pallas is easy to find with a small scope. It sits near a neat triangle of 5th- to 6th-magnitude stars, which lie about 1.5° southwest of the asteroid and act as a great reference point to find it tonight. Pallas is 1° east of the easternmost star. Previously, Pallas was closing on that star, moving westward. But after tonight, it will turn and move slowly eastward again, pulling away from the little triangle night by night.

Drop about 5° south of this region for an added treat: 8th-magnitude globular cluster NGC 288, just over the celestial border in Sculptor. Spanning about 13’, this ancient ball of stars lies nearly 49,000 light-years away. It’s also near another deep-sky target, the 7th-magnitude galaxy NGC 253. Often called the Silver Coin or Sculptor Galaxy, this stunning edge-on spiral lies about 1.7° northwest of NGC 288 and can be viewed together with the cluster in wide-field instruments such as binoculars or finder scopes.

Sunrise: 7:03 A.M. Sunset: 4:35 P.M. Moonrise: — Moonset: 12:35 P.M. Moon Phase: Waning crescent (40%)

Wednesday, December 2It’s now asteroid 4 Vesta’s turn to reach a stationary point at 11 A.M. EST as it, too, swims through the domain of Cetus the Whale. Visible in the evening sky, Vesta sits more than 40° above the southern horizon around 7 P.M. local time. Previously moving retrograde, or westward, it will now begin moving prograde, or eastward, against the background stars.

This month Vesta is located roughly halfway between bright Saturn to its northwest and magnitude 3.6 Theta (θ) Ceti to its southeast. Saturn is impossible to miss, as it’s the brightest object in this region of the sky. To locate 7th-magnitude Vesta, find Saturn early in the evening and slide about 8.1° east-southeast to land on the main-belt world. There aren’t a lot of background stars in the immediate vicinity, so try to match your view to the star chart above to locate the asteroid in your eyepiece. Because it’s moving slowly, you’ll need to come back every night or two to check out the view and note the light that’s shifted position — that’s Vesta.

Sunrise: 7:04 A.M. Sunset: 4:35 P.M. Moonrise: 12:43 A.M. Moonset: 12:58 P.M. Moon Phase: Waning crescent (30%)

Thursday, December 3Look north a few hours after sunset to find the W-shaped star pattern of Cassiopeia on her head, looking more like the letter M as this circumpolar constellation swings above the North Celestial Pole. Just 1.9° northwest of Navi (Gamma [γ] Cassiopeiae), the midpoint of the M (or W), is a lovely open cluster cataloged as NGC 225 and known as the Sailboat Cluster.

Longtime Astronomy contributor Rod Pommier gave the cluster its nickname because he saw an arc of stars within the cluster that looked to him like the sail of a boat catching the wind, connected to a straight line of stars forming the mast and another eight stars outlining the vessel itself. The stars of the cluster are roughly 2,100 light-years distant, and this grouping was discovered by Caroline Herschel in 1783.

For added visual interest, the cluster is set against a complex of dark nebulae made of dust, which block the starlight behind them.

Sunrise: 7:05 A.M. Sunset: 4:35 P.M. Moonrise: 1:49 A.M. Moonset: 1:20 P.M. Moon Phase: Waning crescent (21%)

Friday, December 4The waning Moon puts even faint deep-sky objects within reach on these early December evenings. Tonight, let’s look toward a distant elliptical galaxy nestled in the far southeastern corner of Lacerta the Lizard. Cataloged as NGC 7426, this 13th-magnitude stellar smudge sits close to a lovely pair of contrasting stars, making finding it a rewarding sight for all: While you do need a larger scope to track down the galaxy, the stars are visible even through smaller instruments, offering something for everyone.

Around 7 P.M. tonight, our target is still more than 35° high in the west. The zig-zagging figure of Lacerta sits just above cross-shaped Cygnus as the Summer Triangle sinks toward the western horizon. To Lacerta’s left (southeast) is Pegasus, and we’ll use 3rd-magnitude Matar (Eta [η] Pegasi) as our jumping-off point. From here, slide about 5° north-northeast to find a pair of stars, 6th and 8th magnitude, roughly 1’ apart. The brighter star glows blue-white, while its dimmer neighbor shines orangey-gold. NGC 7426 lies roughly 4’ east-northeast of this pair, appearing as a faint, grayish-white smudge. It measures roughly 2’ by 1.5’, its compact size helping to keep its faint light confined to a relatively small area.

Sunrise: 7:06 A.M. Sunset: 4:34 P.M. Moonrise: 2:54 A.M. Moonset: 1:44 P.M. Moon Phase: Waning crescent (14%)

Alison Klesman is senior editor of Astronomy magazine. She holds a Ph.D. in astronomy and has studied a variety of topics, from minor planets to supermassive black holes.

#6342. NASA’s Curiosity rover, expected to last 23 months, has now climbed 1 kilometer up a Martian mountain 15 years after launch

Curiosity rover has now spent more than 5,000 sols on Mars, gained 0.62 miles of elevation on Mount Sharp and drilled its 49th hole into Martian rock.

On November 26, 2011, NASA launched the Curiosity rover toward Mars. When it left Earth, it was the largest and most capable rover ever sent to the planet, according to NASA.

The car-size robot landed in Gale Crater on August 6, 2012. Its job was to find out whether Mars was ever able to support microbial life.

NASA described that first phase as a “23-month primary mission.” Fifteen years after launch, Curiosity is still working, and it is now one kilometer (.62 miles) up the side of a Martian mountain.

Curiosity did not need all 23 months. NASA said in 2013 that evidence of a past environment well suited to support microbial life came “within the first eight months” of the primary mission, from the first rock sample ever drilled on Mars.

“We now know Mars offered favorable conditions for microbial life billions of years ago,” the mission’s project scientist, John Grotzinger, said at the time.

On June 24, 2014, the rover completed its first Martian year, which lasts 687 Earth days. By then it had driven almost 8 kilometers (about 5 miles), according to a NASA video from the team, and was heading for the base of a mountain.

That mountain is Mount Sharp, a peak about 3 miles (5 kilometers) tall in the middle of Gale Crater. Curiosity has been climbing it since 2014.

On August 26, 2026, the rover “marked an elevation gain of 1 kilometer in its journey from Gale Crater on Mars up the slope of Mount Sharp,” NASA said.

That is one kilometer of height above the crater floor, not distance driven. NASA called the milestone the high point of the mission so far.

William Farrand, a senior research scientist at the Space Science Institute who was on the science team for the earlier Spirit and Opportunity rovers, put the climb in perspective on NASA’s Curiosity blog.

When the Spirit rover reached the top of Husband Hill in August 2005, it had climbed 106 meters (about 348 feet) above its landing site. Curiosity has passed 1,000 meters (about 0.62 miles).

Three days later, on August 29, Curiosity marked 5,000 Martian days, or sols, on Mars. Because a day on Mars lasts 24.6 hours, that is more than 5,137 Earth days, the blog noted.

The rover keeps photographing the mountain as it goes. Earth.com has reported on Curiosity’s photos of Martian cliffs with a layer in the wrong color.

The rover is still collecting samples. After drilling in late October, the team wrote on the mission blog: “We successfully drilled our 49th drill hole, called ‘Nazca.'”

The team chose that rock because it was full of small disc-shaped forms that they interpret as possible crystals. If they are crystals, the team wrote, they could be “very interesting indicators of the environmental conditions.”

In mid-November, the team said it was time to “hit the Martian road again and resume our climb up Mount Sharp.”

The rocks in its path are covered in small polygons with raised ridges, a texture that can form when water is lost from minerals, among other causes, according to the blog.

“After over 5,000 sols of exploring with Curiosity I’ve learned Mars is full of surprises,” said Abigail Fraeman, the mission’s deputy project scientist, in the post.

Curiosity has company on Mars. NASA’s younger rover, Perseverance, has now driven farther than any vehicle on another world.

The information was obtained from NASA’s Curiosity mission page, the news releases NASA Curiosity Rover Approaches First Anniversary on Mars (2013) and Curiosity Reaches 1-Kilometer Elevation Gain (2026), and the Curiosity team’s mission blog.

#6341. What helps land recover after fire? This ecologist looks to the past

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Jennifer Grenz, an ecologist and member of the Lytton First Nation, asks how changes in the way people care for the land may have left it more vulnerable to wildfire.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

In an increasingly fire-prone western North America, Jennifer Grenz, an ecologist and member of the Lytton First Nation, looks at fire with a holistic eye. She considers her work with landscapes recovering from catastrophic wildfire to be “deliberately unfocused,” spanning soil microbial ecology, restoration ecology, invasion biology and historical biology.

Grenz analyzes historical ecological records, like how Indigenous people have shaped and cared for ecosystems over time, to paint a comprehensive picture. “I’m interested in how those histories leave ecological legacies and hints of the stewardship of the past,” says Grenz, who leads the Indigenous Ecology Lab at the University of British Columbia in Canada. “What changed on the land that made it more vulnerable?”

Grenz spends time with many kinds of specialists, such as archaeologists, anthropologists and Indigenous elders who provide oral histories.

Moving forward, her lab will examine ecology below ground, including soil, microbial communities and root networks. The goal is to understand the role of underground ecology in critical topics like carbon sequestration, climate change, biodiversity and sustainable management.

“My motivation is in our interior Salish Territories in the southern interior of British Columbia, where my ancestors rest and where my people are,” Grenz says. “The responsibility I feel to them and to our Tmícw, which means our lands, [is] to not take us back to the past, but to show that we have the deep knowledge to help us move forward.”

#6340. Nitrogen boost

The Pacman Nebula (NGC 281) is an emission nebula about 9,600 light-years away in Cassiopeia, lit by the star cluster IC 1590 at its center. Dark dust lanes cut across its glowing gas, shown here primarily in Hubble-palette colors — with a subtle enhancement.

To enrich the color palette, the imager also added data that reflects singly ionized nitrogen (NII) emission at 658.3 nanometers. This emission line lies just redward of Hα (656.3 nm). Although the imager did not have a dedicated NII filter, he created a proxy by taking an image with a 7-nm Hα filter — which includes NII emission — and subtracting an image taken with a narrower 3-nm Hα filter. The light left behind traces NII, though it can still contain some Hα.

A 15th-century shipwreck is yielding clues to the medieval tragedy that destroyed Griffin, King Hans's "floating castle."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists have recovered high-quality chain mail armor from the 15th-century wreck of Gribshunden or Griffin, a royal warship that doubled as a "floating castle" for King Hans of Denmark. The ship exploded and sank in 1495, but maritime archaeologists have just begun exploring the area beneath the forecastle, an elevated combat platform at the front of the ship, where they discovered the armor and a unique munitions chest.

The chain mail was, "rather surprisingly, completely exposed," Rolf Warming, an archaeologist at Stockholm University and lead investigator of the Griffin project in collaboration with Södertörn University, told Live Science in an email. "It was only by chance that we came across it, and it shows just how much is still on the wreck site."

The mail armor was made of copper alloy and was found in a part of the ship that may have been used as a storage area for military gear, according to a Nov. 24 statement. "Historical sources indicate that German mercenaries, or Landsknechts, were aboard Griffin when it sank in 1495," Rodrigo Pacheco-Ruiz, an archaeologist at the University of Southampton in the U.K. who is the co-investigator on the project, said in the statement. The mercenaries may have stored their armor in the area, "although we've yet to establish a precise function for the space," Pacheco-Ruiz said.

The 15th-century warship was rediscovered in the Baltic Sea off the south coast of Sweden in the 1970s but formally identified by archaeologists as Griffin in 2013.

An X-ray image of the chain mail recovered from the Griffin.

Griffin was the flagship of the naval fleet of King Hans of Denmark and Norway. In 1495, Hans was sailing to Kalmar in Sweden to negotiate a political alliance and force Sweden back into a union with Denmark and Norway. He had brought with him around 150 German mercenary soldiers. "It was important to demonstrate military prowess, and the German and Swiss mercenaries were the finest you could get at that time," Warming told Live Science.

During a stop at the port of Ronneby in what is now Sweden, Griffin caught fire, perhaps after being struck by lightning, and sank. Eyewitnesses who escaped reported that many men died in the tragic event. King Hans, however, was onshore when the warship sank.

The warship has been well-preserved over the centuries thanks to the low salinity of the Baltic waters and the lack of shipworms, marine mollusks also known as the "termites of the sea" because of the damage they do to wood.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The chain mail recovered in October is of exceptionally high quality, Warming said in the statement, but it was not necessarily the armor of an elite knight. "This kind of armour could remain in use for extended periods, often undergoing repairs or being reused, so these fragments may represent older military equipment that was still active," he said.

Archaeologists discovered an unusual munitions chest and chain mail in the medieval shipwreck.

But the researchers discovered more than just the chain mail.

"This year's campaign was an unusually exciting investigation!" Warming told Live Science. The team found a unique munitions chest called a "zeuglade" in German. "We have taken different samples to try to determine the contents of the chest and perhaps find traces of gunpowder," Warming said. The chest may have belonged to the German mercenaries who were aboard.

"It was in the process of documenting the chest that I unexpectedly discovered exposed mail-armour fragments in the vicinity of the chest, along other items that could indicate more chests," Warming added. "This leads us to believe this may have been a stowage area, located just beneath the forecastle."

Warming said that the research team is currently using chemical analysis to investigate the origins of the armor and the chest to learn more about medieval military matters.

"It is probable that the mail armour belongs to the mercenaries, but it could also belong to someone else," Warming said. "The chest might also belong to them, but we don't know yet. It is actually a really fascinating research question of ours that could illuminate supply chains and the military logistics. Did the mercenary forces bring their own ammunition and tool kit aboard, or was this supplied by the royal fleet?"

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.
