A woman's heart issues seemed to be tied to her rapid gulping of ice-cold drinks.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The patient: A 46-year-old woman in California

The symptoms: After an uneventful 10-hour work shift, the woman was walking to her car and drinking an ice-cold beverage when a sudden, burning pain struck the middle of her chest. The pain spread to both of her forearms and lasted about 20 minutes.

About 10 minutes after this pain began, she started sweating and felt nauseated and lightheaded, as though she might pass out.

What happened next: The pain continued as the woman began driving home, so she changed course and instead drove to the nearest emergency department.

An electrocardiogram (EKG), which records the heart's electrical activity, showed subtle abnormalities. A blood test for troponin, a protein released into the bloodstream when heart muscle is damaged, was normal. However, a second troponin test taken before she left the hospital came back elevated after she had been discharged. Doctors called her about the new results and advised her to drive to the nearest emergency department.

There, a third blood test showed that her troponin level had risen even further, and doctors diagnosed a heart attack. An angiogram — a scan that shows the structure of blood vessels — revealed a small tear in a branch of her right coronary artery, which supplies blood to the heart.

About 30 hours after she was discharged, the woman developed similar chest pain after taking several gulps of ice-cold green tea and subsequently jogging up a flight of stairs. The pain began when she reached the top of the stairs and was accompanied by the same lightheaded feeling she had experienced before.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

She called 911 and was again brought to an emergency department, and although an initial EKG showed no clear signs of a heart attack, subsequent recordings revealed heart-activity changes consistent with one. A second angiogram revealed a new tear in the left circumflex artery, a branch of the left coronary artery.

The woman developed tears in both her right and left coronary arteries, which supply the heart with oxygen-rich blood.

The diagnosis: Doctors diagnosed the woman with spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD), a condition in which a tear develops in the wall of a coronary artery. In SCAD, blood collects within the artery wall, and this compresses the channel that blood normally flows through to reach the heart. As in the patient's case, this compression can sometimes trigger heart attacks by drastically restricting the heart's blood supply.

Doctors also found fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD) in a blood vessel in the woman's pelvis. FMD changes the structure of artery walls, making them too weak or too stiff, and it's known to occur in some people with SCAD. It may have made her arteries more prone to tearing, the doctors wrote in a report of the case.

The treatment: During her first emergency department visit, doctors gave the woman aspirin, fluids, medicine for nausea and an antacid. Her chest pain eventually went away. At the second visit, doctors gave her the blood thinner heparin to reduce blood clotting and the beta-blocker metoprolol to slow her heart rate. She was discharged the following morning with prescriptions for cholesterol- and blood-pressure-lowering drugs.

After the second episode, doctors gave her opioid painkillers and medicine for nausea to take as needed, along with aspirin and a cholesterol-lowering drug. The cholesterol-lowering drug was soon stopped because she did not have high cholesterol. Doctors eventually stopped the blood-pressure medication, too, after a follow-up heart ultrasound showed that the affected part of her heart was moving normally again.

She continued taking nebivolol, a different beta-blocker that slows the heart rate and can reduce stress on the organ, for years after these two episodes. And for several months after the second episode, the woman avoided cold drinks on her own initiative. She gradually reintroduced them, taking small sips rather than gulping. Ten years later, she remained free of symptoms, the report noted.

What makes this case unique: Years later, the woman learned that cold drinks had been linked to atrial fibrillation (AFib), an irregular heart rhythm. She told her healthcare team that she suspected cold drinks might have triggered SCAD in her case, too.

Separately, a 2017 case report described another woman who developed chest pain and a heart attack after drinking cold water. Doctors subsequently found that she had SCAD and FMD. However, that report did not investigate cold water as a possible trigger of the patient's symptoms.

The authors of the current report proposed that rapidly swallowing a cold drink may trigger a brief rise in blood pressure, known as a pressor response. This is associated with increased activation of the body's fight-or-flight system, which can then release stress hormones. These changes may make the heart contract more forcefully and cause the coronary arteries to narrow temporarily, thereby increasing the forces acting on their walls. In someone whose arteries are susceptible to tears, that added stress could contribute to rips in the tissue and the accumulation of blood within the artery wall.

However, the report authors stressed that they cannot establish that cold drinks caused the woman's dissections in this instance. They hope their findings will encourage doctors to ask patients with SCAD about potential triggers, but they said further research is needed to determine whether rapidly drinking cold beverages can really trigger the condition.

For more intriguing medical cases, check out our Diagnostic Dilemma archives.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Heringer, G. V., Smith, C. M., Takeuchi, K., Goh, C. H., & Vinson, D. R. (2026). Association of ice-cold drink ingestion with spontaneous coronary artery dissection: a case report. BMC Cardiovascular Disorders. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12872-026-06669-w

#6327. ‘Political malpractice’: Calls grow to delay Senate GOP leadership elections

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., walks through the Ohio Clock Corridor this summer. Now he’s pushing to delay leadership elections for his conference, urging a discussion of last week’s larger than expected losses. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

After last week’s midterm elections saw them lose at least seven Senate seats and the majority, some Republicans are pushing for a reckoning, saying the conference should stop and think about its future.

“After the stunning defeat [we] just can’t continue on business as usual. That kind of defeat demands change,” Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., said on Monday evening.

Asked if he himself would want to run for Senate minority leader, the Wisconsin Republican responded with a question of his own: “That’s part of our problem. Who’d want the job? Would you want it?”

Though no hopeful had emerged as of Monday afternoon — at least publicly — to challenge current Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., for the top GOP post, the frustration was palpable as Republican senators returned to D.C. and grappled with the election results. Calls grew throughout the day to delay the conference’s leadership elections planned for Tuesday morning.

“Well, I mean, I’m open to hearing what the arguments are for that,” Thune told reporters Monday when asked about the possibility of postponing the leadership votes. “I don’t know if that solves anything, but like I said, it’s going to be a decision that’s ultimately made by Republican senators. We’ll hear them out.”

Johnson told reporters on Monday that if the election is held, he would “leave the room” and walk out. Either way, he seemed certain to at least get a “fulsome” discussion of the topic, as he requested in a letter he sent to Republican Conference Chair Tom Cotton, R-Ark. Four other Republican senators signed on to the letter, hitting the threshold to call a conference meeting under internal GOP rules.

Also signed by Sens. Mike Lee of Utah, Ted Budd of North Carolina, Rick Scott of Florida, and John Kennedy of Louisiana, the letter obtained by CQ Roll Call cites last week’s “stunning defeat” and reads in part: “Holding leadership elections without engaging in a robust discussion and evaluation of how those running for leadership intend to lead would be political malpractice.”

Kennedy said Monday evening that he was asking to postpone the leadership elections because “we need time to talk to each other.”

“We’re like a shop owner who’s losing his customers. It’s not the customer’s job to fix that. It’s the shop owner’s job, and I’m not looking for blame-shifting. I’m looking for self-examination,” he said, adding that he wouldn’t consider running for minority leader himself.

In the letter, the group asked that at the time the leadership elections were set to begin, 9 a.m. on Tuesday, they instead “have a fulsome conference discussion and delay holding leadership elections until we all have a chance to hear from leadership candidates as to what type of collaborative conference governing model we should adopt and what our strategy will be to counter the emboldened Democrats.”

Thune echoed that wording Monday as he spoke to reporters, saying, “I do think that we need to have a very fulsome, robust conversation about where we go from here, and then we’ll see what the consensus of the conference is.”

But Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., who serves as chair of the Senate Republican Policy Committee, said she has seen such requests launched in the past and didn’t think it would do much to affect the ultimate outcome. “I think Sen. Thune will be reelected,” she said.

And several Senate GOP aides said that they suspected a “robust” conversation wouldn’t do much to delay the plans and that leadership elections were still expected to take place Tuesday. They noted similar efforts from some of those same senators in previous years to sow discord in the ranks.

That includes Scott, who unsuccessfully challenged Thune in 2024 and then-GOP leader Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., in 2022. But Scott told Fox News over the weekend, “I don’t want to run again. I’ve run twice.”

Republicans “failed. We had a horrible night,” Scott said. “Instead of having an [leadership] election, the first thing you do is you say, ‘OK, what are we going to change? We have to change something.’”

Lee floated the idea of waiting until after the uncalled Senate races in Mississippi and Alaska are officially resolved.

An online pressure campaign was building in some of the same MAGA corners of the internet that have pushed to pass a sweeping voter ID bill, known as the SAVE America Act, that has stalled in the Senate. On Monday morning, influencer Scott Presler in an X post urged constituents to call their senators while praising the lawmakers who have already pushed for the leadership elections to be postponed. “Where is everyone else?” he wrote.

Sens. Jim Banks of Indiana and Dave McCormick of Pennsylvania also called for a delay, though they did not appear on Johnson’s letter.

“A week ago, we had the worst election results in decades,” McCormick said in a post on X, calling Tuesday “too soon” to vote for leaders. “I know it’s been practice to go straight to leadership elections in recent years, but we should not rush it.”

Banks similarly said Tuesday was “too soon,” posting on social media, “Our conference needs to sit down and have a frank conversation about where we fell short, what we stand for, and what we’re going to do for the working families who sent us here.”

One senator speaking out in Thune’s defense was Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, who competed with Thune for the top spot in 2024 but on Monday said the leader isn’t to blame for the midterm results.

“I think the president needs to look in the mirror and look at the flawed candidates that he endorsed, and the kind of environment that we’re in,” said Cornyn, who is still smarting from losing his primary to a challenger backed by President Donald Trump.

Cornyn’s loss means he has no say in the coming conference leadership elections. But he said, “I think Thune’s a good man, and did as well as he could against a president and an environment that was pretty hostile.”

#6326. Motion under the ocean explains the depth of the world’s deepest spot

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A tight bend in the subducting Pacific plate may help explain Challenger Deep

The ROV Jason/Medea (Jason shown here during a 2021 dive at the East Pacific Rise) can descend up to 6,500 meters below the ocean surface. In a new study, it helped researchers discover volcanic deposits in the Mariana Trench.

D. Fornari, WHOI-SSSG, MISO Facility, NDSF Jason Team, NSF

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Challenger Deep is the deepest valley in the deepest trench in the ocean, plunging to roughly 11,000 meters below sea level.

Now, scientists have a new clue about how it got to be so … well, deep.

Challenger Deep is found within the Mariana Trench, a crescent-shaped gouge in the seafloor east of the Philippines in the Pacific Ocean. The trench is the scene of a slo-mo tectonic collision called a subduction zone: The Pacific plate is diving beneath the Mariana plate, bending downward as it sinks into the mantle, forming a steep trench on the ocean floor.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

All subduction zones are deep, but “it’s interesting why this is the deepest spot in the Earth’s ocean,” says geoscientist Robert Stern, an emeritus professor at the University of Texas at Dallas and a visiting researcher at the University of California, Los Angeles.

He and colleagues employed a remotely operated robot called ROV Jason/Medea to descend to more than 6,000 meters and explore the Mariana Trench seafloor around the edges of Challenger Deep. The rocks turned out to contain pyroclastic deposits, evidence of an erstwhile explosive volcanic eruption. Those deposits included platelike blocks that could indicate eruption pulses, and lobe-shaped rocks where the volcanic flows ended and quickly cooled.

These are the deepest pyroclastic deposits found on Earth, the scientists report November 23 in Frontiers in Earth Science.

How explosive an eruption is at Earth’s surface depends on the chemical makeup of the magma. When the molten rock contains a high proportion of volatile gases, including water vapor, those gases suddenly expand when the magma reaches the surface, producing a violent explosion.

Such explosive volcanism shouldn’t be possible in the deep sea; the pressure is too high for any escaping gases to expand, Stern says. Along with that mystery, the volcanic deposits were found unusually close to the trench, compared with what would be expected for a subduction zone.

Stern and his colleagues developed a hypothesis that incorporates these disparate pieces of evidence: The extreme depth of Challenger Deep, they say, may be at least partially due to an especially sharp bend in the Pacific Plate as it sinks into the mantle.

That tighter bend would explain why volcanism is happening closer to the subduction zone than usual. The classic subduction zone scenario is that the sinking plate heats up and melts partially as it descends; the magma rises through the overhanging plate and erupts, forming volcanic island arcs several hundred kilometers from the collision zone. Here, the volcanic deposits were just a hundred kilometers or so from the trench — which makes sense if the plate is dipping more steeply.

As for the pyroclastics, “we can’t answer if the eruptions were really explosive,” Stern says. But at those pressures, any gases such as water vapor contained in the magma wouldn’t be able to explosively expand as they would at the surface.

Instead, the pyroclastic rocks might have formed through a new version of deep-sea eruption, one in which water emerging from the magma is initially in a supercritical fluid state. That would minimize any explosive expansion during the eruption and could also produce fragmented, dense deposits like those seen by Jason/Medea.

The discovery of deep-sea pyroclastics is “surprising and unprecedented,” says William Chadwick, a geologist at Oregon State University in Newport. Challenger Deep may be the only place on Earth “with the ingredients to produce explosive volcanism in the super-deep ocean,” he says. “Imagining this happening is … pretty mind-boggling.”

A lot more work remains to be done to evaluate all of these new ideas, Stern says. “But a lot of things are now coming together.”

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

R. J. Stern et al. ROVing in the deep: tectonic and magmatic complexities of the Challenger Deep forearc segment, Southern Mariana convergent margin. Frontiers in Earth Science. 2026. doi: 10.3389/feart.2026.1929806

Carolyn Gramling is the earth & climate writer. She has bachelor’s degrees in geology and European history and a Ph.D. in marine geochemistry from MIT and the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution.

#6325. The 7 Best Portable Jump Starters to Bring Your Vehicle Back to Life

The days of needing jumper cables and another motorist to revive your vehicle are over.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

If you’ve got a dead car battery, you’ll want the option to revive it without waiting for help. According to AAA’s most recent report, of the 27 million calls received across the country for roadside assistance, 7 million of those vehicles had battery trouble. The causes may include anything from neglecting to turn off your car’s ignition or headlights, residing in an extremely cold climate, or even a slowly deteriorating alternator.

A portable jump starter, which is a compact and powerful battery consisting of lightweight lithium-ion, is a handy device that’s faster, safer, and more convenient than jumper cables because you don’t need to find another car with a willing driver.

Like all batteries, lithium-ion cells have different power ratings and can become depleted from repeated use or by sitting idle over time. That’s why before purchasing a portable jump starter, consider these two specs: peak amperage (amps) which conveys how much power a device can deliver, and capacity (rated in milliampere-hours, mAh), indicating how long a device can hold a charge when stored and still have enough power to provide a jump. It’s also important to monitor the charge level on your portable jump starter from time to time. I do this regularly while waiting to fill my gas tank.

There are other convenience features these devices offer, like USB ports to recharge portable electronics and lights for illumination when it’s dark. Many portable jump starters have what’s called a boost button, which I recommend having, as it supplies extra momentary power for severely drained batteries. After several rounds of testing, research, and evaluation, these are the top portable jump starters to buy now.

I’ve owned close to a dozen vehicles during my 30-year-plus career writing about cars and have had plenty of dead batteries. I keep jumper cables in each of my three current vehicles, and now I also have a portable jump starter on board along with a portable tire inflator, dash cam, and Cobra RAD 700i radar detector, which I move between vehicles depending on which I decide to drive.

In short, each device in this roundup can quickly start a vehicle with a depleted battery. While testing each product, I also evaluated its peak instantaneous power measured in amps, power capacity measured in milliampere-hours, the quantity and variety of output ports to charge portable electronics, and extras such as lights and a boost button.

My recommendations are based on a product’s price, capability, and capacity to fit a wide array of vehicles and budgets. I took into account my own experiences with portable jump starters, each brand’s reputation, and for further background, I spoke with fellow car enthusiasts and auto journalists to get their impressions.

With 6,000-amp peak current to jump-start a vehicle with up to a 12.0-liter diesel engine coupled with 27,000 mAh of power capacity, the Gooloo GT6000 is the most powerful device in our guide. The GT6000 offers up to 24 months of standby time—and with that, you get incredible peace of mind. This device can sit unused for long stretches and still be counted on to crank your car when needed. If its battery is depleted, the GT6000 is ready to jump-start a vehicle after just 7 minutes of recharging and is fully recharged in 1.4 hours via its 100-watt USB-C in/out port.

This device also stands out for its generous quantity and variety of charging ports. In addition to a 100-watt USB-C in/out port, it also has a 12-volt/cigarette-lighter cord to recharge its battery in a pinch. A 15 volt/10-amp DC port can be used to power assorted car accessories like portable air pumps and power inverters. There are two USB-A power ports, one rated at 5-volts/2.4-amps and another rated for 5/9/12-volts

The GT6000 is one of only two devices here with an LCD screen, which makes checking battery level, charging output, temperature, and jump-start status quick and easy. There are 10 safety features, in addition to a built-in LED flashlight with three lighting modes (flashlight, strobe, and SOS) that provides illumination when using the device in low-light situations—important so other motorists can see you if you’re stuck on the side of the road.

While the GT6000 admittedly provides more power than most motorists will likely need, and it’s one of the heaviest of our picks, it is without question the best overall jump starter for maximum instantaneous power, long standby time, quick recharging, and plenty of output ports.

The AstroAI S8 isn’t the most powerful jump-starter recommended but it’s one of the lowest-priced and is user friendly and small enough to fit in your car’s glove box or map pocket. Although it taps out on vehicles with anything larger than a 6.0-liter gas or 3.0-liter diesel engine, it’s fine for most vehicles. I’ve kept this in one of my vehicles for months and used it several times to provide jump-starts to others without an issue.

Protection against reverse polarity, overcurrent, overvoltage, overload, overcharge, over discharge, and short circuiting are built in. The AstroAI S8 has two 5-volt/2.4-amp USB-A output ports to charge portable devices and an LED flashlight with normal, strobe, and SOS modes. It is supplied with a USB A to USB C charging cable to recharge the device.

The interface is one of the most barebones of all the units tested—just a power button and four blue LEDs to indicate power level. It does have a boost button but is the only unit of our selections without a shut-off switch; instead it automatically powers off after 30 seconds.Full AstroAI S8 Portable Jump Starter Review

This is the smallest device I tested (only slightly larger than most smartphones) and the lightest at 1.2 pounds. With 2,000 amps of peak power, the Gooloo GP2000 can jump-start vehicles with up to 8.0-liter gas or 6.0-liter diesel engines and its 12,000 mAh of capacity is impressive for its size and price.

It has 10 safety protection features including short circuit and reverse polarity, and a 400-lumen LED flashlight with normal, strobe, and SOS modes to provide light in dark environments and during emergency roadside stops. It comes with two USB-A outputs—one 5/9/12-volt and one 5-volt/2.4-amp—for charging portable devices, a USB-C charging cable, and a storage case instead of a bag like many portable jump starters at this price.

Like the AstroAI S8, it has only an on-off button. It’s easy to use and has a boost button. I recommend this option for anyone looking for a small, inexpensive, and hassle-free portable jump starter.

With an IP65 water-resistance rating and rubberized casing, the Noco Boost Plus is the portable jump starter I turn to during the rainy season in Oregon—which means anytime other than summer. I go for this one because it has spark-proof and reverse polarity protection for safe use in wet or dry conditions.

Its 1,000-amp peak power rating can start vehicles with up to 6.0-liter gas and 3.0-liter diesel engines. However, its 2,150 mAh capacity is the lowest of any product here, so it may not hold a charge as long as jump starters with a higher capacity. While this is adequate, I don’t recommend a mAh rating any lower.

The Noco GB40’s 100-lumen flashlight is dimmer than that of some of the other units in this roundup but it has the most modes, six total, which include 100-, 50-, and 10 percent; blink, SOS, and strobe. It also comes with a 1-foot USB-C charging cable, but it has only one 5-volt/2.1-amp USB-A output port for charging your portable electronics.

If you own a large vehicle, the Noco Boost X GBX155 cranks out 4,250 amps to boost batteries instantaneously for vehicles with up to 10.0-liter gas and 8.0-liter diesel engines, and has an impressive 26,750 mAh capacity, just shy of the Gooloo GT6000’s 27,000-mAh spec. A 60-watt USB-C input/output allows recharging from 0-to-100 percent capacity in 2.7 hours to ensure it’s ready to jump-start a vehicle after charging only 5 minutes (slightly faster than the Gooloo GT6000’s 7 minutes.)

I found the Noco Boost X GBX155 more complicated to operate than the other portable jump starters I tested. For example, it doesn’t have a boost button like other units but rather a manual override feature that’s used to jump start severely depleted batteries if the device detects the battery is below 3 volts. Aactivating the feature requires holding the Manual Override button for 3 seconds, which can send the GBX155’s maximum output of 4,250 amps to jump start a vehicle. This Manual Override shuts off the Noco’s automatic spark-proof and reverse-polarity protection so users need to be extra careful to attach the jumper cables correctly (red to positive, black to negative) to avoid damaging the car’s electrical system, and not touch the clamps together, which can create dangerous sparking.

The Noco is heavy, too, at 5.8 pounds. In addition to its 60-watt USB-C input/output, it has only one 5-volt/2.1-amp USB-A port whereas other lower-priced devices have at least two. But you won’t be working in the dark if you are trying to start your battery at night. This device has a 500-lumen LED flashlight that’s the brightest of the portable jump starters in our roundup. Another perk: it’s got an IP65 waterproof rating (with its input/output ports covered) that only the Gooloo GT6000 and Noco GB40 also have.

For motorheads with multiple vehicles and a garage or shop to keep them, the Clore Automotive Jump-N-Carry JNC660 is a worthy device to have on hand. Its 120-volt male receptacle connects to an extension cord so that it can be powered by a regular wall outlet and is always charged and ready.

This device uses a lead-acid battery instead of a lithium-ion one. This makes the battery replaceable, so this device is not ultimately disposable like portable jump starters with a lithium-ion battery. At 18 pounds, it’s by far the heaviest here, but also has the longest (46 inches) and thickest (2-gauge) jumper cables.

With 1,700 peak amps, it’s not the most powerful portable jump starter included but makes up for that with a 22,000 mAh rating which means its internal battery holds a charge longer. A built-in digital voltmeter shows the battery’s state of charge before and after a jump start and it has a DC outlet to power 12-volt accessories such as a tire inflator or power inverter. A notable drawback: It doesn’t have USB output ports.

For years, I relied on a Battery Tender trickle charger to supply a slow, steady current to keep the battery in my classic Chevy Impala SS charged. If you also have a vehicle that sits idle for months on end, check out the Battery Tender Charge N Start 4120. It does double duty as a trickle charger and a jump starter. However, combining two devices in one comes with compromises such as not having output ports to charge portable devices, or a boost button.

With 1,200 amps of instantaneous current, this device can jump start cars with up to 6.0-liter gas or 4.0-liter diesel engines and proficiently cranked the engine on several large and small vehicles during my testing. Its basic push-button interface makes the Charge N Start a breeze to operate. Safety features include spark-proof connection, reverse-polarity protection, and more.

This portable jump starter sends a small amount of current to traditional lead-acid as well as lithium batteries at 4 amps, and an onboard microprocessor maintains the optimal voltage to keep a battery at 100-percent capacity without overcharging during long-term storage. It also includes temperature compensation to handle a range of climates.

Something you may need to think about is its size. Its larger than other trickle chargers I’ve used, which affects placement. Ideally, a trickle charger should be located close to the battery under a car’s hood. The Charge N Start may be too large to tuck away under the closed hood of certain vehicles, but a supplied 6-foot extension cable that attaches to low-profile battery-charging clamps allows locating the device away from the engine on, say, a shelf next to a wall outlet.

The Noco AX65 is another portable jump starter we’ve tested and recommend, but we moved it out of our guide because it’s not singularly a portable jump starter like the others. This is a combo device with a portable air compressor so you can start dead batteries and inflate flat tires. What I like is that the unit doesn’t skimp on either function. The jump starter has an impressive 16,000 mAh capacity and delivers 2,000 amps of peak power while the tire inflator pumps out 67 liters per minute of airflow, which converts to 2.3 cubic feet per minute (cfm)—well above average for the portable tire inflators I’ve tested.

The portable jump starter can crank a dead battery on vehicles with gas engines as large as 8.0 liters and diesel engines up to 6.0 liters. It can be used for SUVs, boats, and snowmobiles. The not-so-good news: It’s short on output ports compared to the other portable jump starters here, and heavy at more than 9 pounds.

Portable jump starters are essentially heavy-duty batteries that come with jumper cables, controls, and accessories like lights, charging ports, and air pumps. Here’s what to look for when shopping for a portable jump starter that fits your vehicle, needs, and budget.

The two most important specs to look for when comparing portable jump starters are peak amperes (amps) and milliampere-hours (mAh). Peak amps indicate the maximum short-term current a device can deliver, while mAh measures how much electrical charge a battery can store.

Bigger is better for both specs, although mAh isn’t always as prominent or even stated with portable jump starters compared to peak amps. About 400 to 600 peak amps is sufficient to jump-start vehicles like cars and crossovers, although large SUVs, trucks, RVs, and commercial vehicles may require up to 1,500 or 2,000 amps. Some portable jump starters come with a boost button that provides roughly 10 additional amps and is helpful when reviving a very dead battery that needs an extra jolt of juice. At least 10,000 mAh of capacity means the battery in a portable jump starter will hold enough charge for 3 to 6 months to deliver 5 to 10 jump-starts.

Portable jump starters are a much safer alternative to using jumper cables to revive a dead battery because connecting jumper cables to a battery’s terminals can cause sparks that can sometimes ignite gas produced by the battery and cause an explosion. Also, if you connect the cables incorrectly, called reverse polarity, it can severely damage a car’s electrical system. Unlike jumper cables, portable jump starters have built-in protection against issues like sparking and reverse polarity in addition to other safety features and are much less risky and easier to use.

Most portable jump starters also come in handy for recharging phones, tablets, and other portable devices. USB output ports are the most common, but a few devices also provide a 12-volt outlet. While USB ports typically charge at 2.5 to 5 volts, a 12-volt outlet can not only charge a device faster but can also be used to power devices such as portable air pumps and coolers.

If you need to jump-start a vehicle at night, you’ll be thankful your portable jump starter has an LED flashlight. Typically a portable jump starter’s lighting feature also provides strobe or SOS patterns to warn other motorists on the road of your presence.

Look for a portable jump starter with a boost button to give an extra jolt of juice to a very depleted battery when the device’s standard output can’t crank the engine. This surge of power gives you about 15 to 30 seconds to start the car once the boost button is pressed.

A portable jump starter rated for 400 to 600 amps is sufficient to jump-start most passenger vehicles such as cars, crossovers, and smaller SUVs. But for larger SUVs, trucks, RVs, and commercial vehicles you want to look for a device with at least 1,500 to 2,000 amps. Weather also affects a car battery and engine, so if you live in a very cold climate more power may be needed to jump-start a low or dead battery.

Yes and no since it depends on the wide range of passenger vehicles available. A portable jump starter with a lower amp rating can jump-start smaller vehicles such as most cars, crossovers, and small SUVs. But a large SUV or truck with a large engine will require a portable jump starter with a higher amp rating.

Peak power rating (measured in amps) to ensure a portable jump starter has enough juice to crank your vehicle and capacity (measured in milliamp hours) that indicates how long it can potentially hold a charge are the most two important. Other features to look for include the number and types of output charging ports, whether it has a 12-volt output and charging input, a boost button, and a flashlight.

Definitely. Make sure to first read the owner’s manual to understand how your portable jump starter works before connecting it to a car’s battery. When using it, take off any jewelry and wear safety glasses and gloves anytime you work on a vehicle and especially around a battery. Most portable jump starters come with built-in safety features that will issue a warning if they are connected incorrectly. But it’s up to you to double-check that the jump starter’s red/positive and black/negative clamps are connected to the (typically) red positive and black negative terminals of the car battery.

Yes, a portable jump starter is a much safer alternative to using traditional jumper cables to start a vehicle with a dead battery. Connecting jumper cables to a battery’s terminals can cause sparks that have the potential to ignite gas produced by a battery which in some instances can lead to an explosion. And if you connect the cables incorrectly (in reverse polarity) it can severely damage a car’s electrical system. Unlike jumper cables, most portable jump starters come with built-in protection against issues like sparking and reverse polarity and are much less risky and easier to use. Plus, with a portable jump starter you don’t have to find another car—and a driver—like you do with jump cables. That said, I carry a set of jumper cables as a backup.

#6324. New Congress will still be filled with losers

The Capitol Dome is illuminated before dawn on Oct. 13. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

OPINION — Once again, the next Congress is going to be filled with losers.

This is not a personal judgment about their character or personality, but a simple recognition that many members have lost races before getting elected. And the incoming class is no different.

I’ve written many versions of this column for more than a decade, and yet the lesson always seems to get lost, no pun intended. Parties routinely attack candidates who enter a race with losses on their record. And, of course, it happened this cycle as well.

“We beat him once. We’ll beat him again,” National Republican Senatorial Committee Chairman Tim Scott declared when Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown announced his challenge to appointed GOP Sen. Jon Husted in the summer of 2025.

“Ohioans gladly sent him packing last year, and they’ll not hesitate to toss him aside again,” said a Republican strategist.

Brown lost reelection to Republican Bernie Moreno in 2024 but came back to defeat Husted for the state’s other Senate seat. And Brown is far from the only candidate to avenge a loss with an electoral victory last week.

The fact of the matter is that losing a race doesn’t have to be the end of a political career. Losses can lay the foundation for future success by building name ID or a fundraising network. Or sometimes it takes a change in the political environment or change in circumstances, such as running for an open seat instead of challenging an incumbent.

In addition to Brown, there are more than a dozen losers coming into the next Congress:

In some instances, though, the losses are piling up.

Republican Rep. John James of Michigan now has three statewide losses on his record. He lost Senate contests in 2018 (taking 46 percent of the vote) and 2020 (48 percent) and came up short in his bid for governor this year (44 percent).

Republican former Sen. John E. Sununu of New Hampshire, who lost reelection in 2008 to Democrat Jeanne Shaheen, fell in his comeback attempt for the open seat last week.

But they could take heart from another repeat loser. Charlie Crist, a former Florida governor and congressman, has had a handful of high-profile losses over the years, including for Senate and two gubernatorial comeback bids. He was just elected mayor of St. Petersburg.

So even though I know it’s a futile request, let’s have a bipartisan agreement not to attack candidates for past losses, because losing doesn’t mean they can’t later pull off a win.

One tooth from a cave in southern China may upend how we think about early human origins in Asia.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In a cave in southern China, archaeologists have discovered an unusual 100,000-year-old tooth that may add a brand-new branch to the human family tree. A genetic analysis of the enamel revealed that the tooth is distinct from all other examples discovered in the area and may have come from an individual who belonged to a previously unknown ancient human lineage.

In a study published Wednesday (Nov. 25) in the journal Nature, researchers described four isolated teeth recovered from two cave sites in southern China that date to around 100,000 years ago, when our extinct cousins the Denisovans roamed Asia. Teeth from one cave site are similar to Denisovans', but a tooth from the second site has a unique shape and genetic variants in the tooth enamel, suggesting it is from an "unresolved archaic Homo" group, the researchers wrote.

The teeth were recovered from archaeological cave sites named Longchuandong and Chuanshandong in the Guangxi region. Based on uranium-series dating, the two teeth from Longchuandong — a molar and a bicuspid (the teeth between the canines and molars) — date to about 104,500 to 42,600 years ago, while the two teeth from Chuanshandong — which are both bicuspids — are at least 100,800 years old.

To try to figure out which ancient human group these teeth belonged to, the researchers studied the shape and characteristics of the teeth and extracted proteins from the tooth enamel. The heritable traits of the two Longchuandong teeth lined up well with Denisovan teeth that had previously been identified, revealing that a Denisovan-related group was living in southern China in the Late Pleistocene (129,000 to 11,700 years ago), according to the study. But the Chuanshandong teeth — which the team thinks may be from the same individual — were very different.

The shape of the Chuanshandong bicuspids "did not align well with any established East Asian Homo member," the researchers wrote. For example, the Chuanshandong teeth had a complex tooth root system typically seen in Homo erectus, but they also had traits more aligned with Homo sapiens, including a more symmetrically shaped tooth crown.

The root system of the Chuanshandong tooth was complex and similar to what experts see in Homo erectus.

The researchers extracted proteins from the Longchuandong teeth and one of the Chuanshandong bicuspids and discovered they were all from chromosomally male individuals. But while the Longchuandong proteins matched those from Denisovan remains that were unearthed elsewhere in China, several of the Chuanshandong protein variants have only been identified in H. erectus and Homo antecessor, an ancient human distantly related to Neanderthals and modern humans.

The protein analysis "showed that Chuanshandong formed a sister group to the common ancestors of Neanderthals, Denisovans and H. sapiens," the researchers wrote in the study. This means that "at least two non-sapiens Homo populations may have existed in southern China's subtropics during the Middle and Late Pleistocene," they wrote.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Given the small number of 100,000-year-old fossils from China that have been analyzed to date, it is unclear what the morphology and genetics of the Chuanshandong teeth mean for our understanding of human evolution, researchers say.

Denisovans were first identified in 2010, when DNA analysis of a tiny pinkie finger bone found in a Siberian cave revealed that the group was distinct from Neanderthals and modern humans. Since then, paleoanthropologists have discovered fossils all across Asia from our extinct cousins and learned that Denisovans, Neanderthals and modern humans all interbred when they had the chance. But Denisovans' and Neanderthals' genetics are known from full genomes — the complete set of their genetic material — while due to preservation issues, most of the fossils from China have only produced proteomes, a more limited set of genetic data that provides information on the body's proteins.

The Chuanshandong proteome included an ancestral genetic variant linking them to H. erectus and H. antecessor, two groups that lived before H. sapiens arrived on the scene. The presence of these variants suggests that the Chuanshandong teeth were from someone who belonged to a primitive Homo lineage, the researchers wrote. Their unique ancient proteins could also be explained by interbreeding with H. erectus.

It's not clear whether they are our cousins.

It's too early, though, to call this a new human group, study co-author Qiaomei Fu, director of the Ancient DNA Laboratory at the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology, part of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, told Live Science in an email.

"We could call it the Chuanshandong group temporarily, but we need more fossil and molecular evidence to determine its affinity with other archaic Homo," Fu said. "It's not clear whether they are our cousins."

The Guangxi region of China is known for its caves, many of which have Pleistocene mammal fossils.

The new Chuanshandong proteome is extremely interesting, said John Hawks, an anthropologist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who was not involved in the study. But "the paper characterizes this as an 'unknown Homo'. I wouldn't put it that way. The question is which group has variation of the proteome," he told Live Science in an email.

Hawks noted that it is currently unclear whether H. erectus or Denisovans had the specific variant identified in the Chuanshandong tooth, as paleoproteomic analysis is still a relatively new technique. If the genetic variant existed in H. erectus, then the Chuanshandong teeth, which are more similar to H. erectus in shape than they are to Neanderthals, may actually be from an H. erectus individual rather than a brand-new human group. But the comparison is further complicated by the fact that no one has yet found other Denisovan bicuspids — the type of tooth found in the Chuanshandong cave.

"I have a feeling that a comprehensive analysis with all the teeth together would be stronger than these separate papers" that Fu's research team has published recently, Hawks said. "I think there is more to learn from compiling more complete analyses."

The researchers noted in the study that excavations have been ongoing in Guangxi caves for a decade, revealing a rich variety of Pleistocene mammal fossils, including ancient human relatives. This may mean that the pace of discoveries about our species' past will soon accelerate.

"We have some new findings from this region, and we are conducting analyses on them," Fu said.

Xing, S., Rao, H., Xie, G., Bai, F., Ge, J., Bennett, E.A., Wu, Z., Shao, Q., Li, X., Viola, B., Sun, Q., Zhou, K., Li, Z., Jiangzuo, Q., Zhao, Y., Liu, F., Liu, Y., Feng, X., Lin, Q., Fu, Q. (2026). Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. #6320. The Best Galapagos Cruises in 2027 That Combine Luxe Amenities With Rugged Adventure

Visiting the Galapagos can feel like stepping onto another planet. This chain of volcanic islands is a mystical realm of otherworldly lava formations, sweeping oceanic vistas, ancient flora, and endemic animal species not found anywhere else on earth.

This unique archipelago of 20 scattered islands—plus dozens more islets and notable rocks in between—is best explored by a specialty cruise. Sailing through the Galapagos Islands allows travelers the ease of navigating to the destination’s smaller locales, getting up close to rare wildlife, and the constant presence of naturalists who can maximize every moment, from pointing out passing marine life to guided stargazing on deck.

The best Galapagos cruises combine tourism with conservation.

The best Galapagos cruises are intimate voyages aboard specialized ships designed to help preserve the islands’ delicate ecosystems. When the day of intrepid exploring is finished, the ship becomes your floating home, offering travelers a serene space to relax and debrief about the wonders you've just experienced. Here’s a look at the best Galapagos cruises to take in 2027, spanning everything from boutique yachts and all-inclusive cruises to top-of-the-line expedition ships.

This article has been updated with new information since its original publication date.

Ecoventura's Theory is not only luxurious, but it welcomes families (with children ages six and up) with open arms.

For an intimate, curated voyage through the Galapagos, you can’t go wrong with an Ecoventura cruise. The line operates three Relais & Chateaux yachts, Origin, Theory, and Evolve, each of which has just 10 staterooms for a total of 20 guests. Each stateroom offers oversized windows and a sleek, modern design.

Travelers can choose between Ecoventura’s two seven-night itineraries: The “Beaches and Bays” voyage visits San Cristobal, Espanola, Floreana, Santa Cruz, Bartolome, and North Seymour Islands, and the “Volcanic Wonders” sailing calls upon more remote locations like Isabela and Fernandina Islands. (There’s also the option to combine both into a 14-night sailing.)

The line’s expedition guides, who are trained in birdwatching, stargazing, and nature photography, escort travelers to notable locations, like the red sand beach on Rabida Island with its flocks of American Flamingos, and the iconic pinnacle rock of Bartolome Island. There’s also kayaking, zodiac rides, and snorkeling among sea turtles, sea lions, reef fish, and more. Scuba divers can board the line’s 16-passenger luxury vessel, Galapagos Sky, for multi-day dive excursions to seek out whale sharks, hammerheads, and manta rays.

Galápagos sea lions, as seen on a cruise

One of the most luxurious options in the Galapagos, Silversea has brought its lavish, all-inclusive concept to the rugged archipelago aboard its destination-specific ship Silver Origin. The all-suite, all-balcony vessel holds 100 passengers and offers butler service in every suite, plus an in-room bar stocked to your preferences. Each suite is ultra-spacious, but the villa category offers sweeping terraces, vast living spaces and dining areas, and a separate bedroom. Elsewhere on the ship are two restaurants, a lounge, spa, fitness center, and stargazing platform— collectively, a promise that passengers will never be bored.

Silversea’s seven-day Galapagos itineraries all sail round-trip from the island of San Cristobal. Depending on the exact sailing, voyages call upon a wide variety of islands, including Isabela, Fernandina, North Seymour, Santa Cruz, Espanola, and more. With the included excursions, guests can explore the lunar landscapes of Isabela’s ancient lava flows, witness the seabird sanctuaries of Prince Philip's Steps, participate in guided nature hikes, deep-water snorkeling, zodiac cruises, and kayaking. Luxe touches, like free expedition gear and unlimited pours of Champagne on board, push the voyages over the top. Plus, Silver Origin’s specialized features—like a dynamic positioning system and advanced propulsion—are easier on the local ecosystem's fragile marine life.

The National Geographic Gemini hosts some of the best Galapagos cruises for bringing kids along.

Inspire your kids to learn about science and exploration by hopping on board one of Lindblad Expedition's four Galapagos ships: National Geographic Endeavour II, National Geographic Islander II, National Geographic Gemini, and National Geographic Delfina. These journeys, led by National Geographic experts, give kids the chance to become National Geographic Explorers-In-Training. The exclusive, hands-on program is designed to teach kids about geographical exploration and scientific research. The National Geographic Gemini, which launched in 2025, can accommodate up to 48 passengers in 27 suites. More than a dozen suites come with private balconies, and one of those balconies is large enough to accommodate a private hot tub. But don’t fret if that suite is already booked; there’s a whirlpool hot tub on the sundeck that’s open to all guests. There’s also a library, well-stocked bar, and meals made with locally sourced ingredients on board.

andBeyond's 124-foot expedition yacht Galapagos Explorer

With its 124-foot expedition yacht, Galapagos Explorer, andBeyond offers a truly exclusive experience. The yacht has only six rooms to accommodate 12 guests, and it’s also available for a fully private charter. Across the yacht’s four decks are a hot tub, sun deck, swim deck, as well as indoor and outdoor dining rooms and bars. In the five cabins and one larger suite, passengers will find a warm design accented with an oceanic color palette and natural materials like carved wood accents and indigenous textiles—making the ship feel more like a boutique hotel than a cruise. &Beyond’s seven-day itineraries call upon multiple islands either to the east or west, with a mix of popular and more remote locales, like Genovesa, Bartolome, Santa Cruz, Floreana, Espanola, Isabela, and Santa Fe. Snorkeling, kayaking, guided hikes, and island tours are all part of the daily activities with the expedition team, who can personalize each excursion thanks to the small number of guests on board.

The 164-foot superyacht Aqua Mare carries 16 passengers and 16 crew members.

The 164-foot superyacht Aqua Mare is all about bespoke attention. The small vessel carries 16 passengers, with 16 crew members to look after guests’ every need. Within the ship’s elegant interiors are seven cabins with gleaming woodwork, marble-accented bathrooms, and an owner’s suite with multiple bedrooms and living spaces.

Spanning the rest of the yacht’s four decks are a panoramic sundeck, hot tub, and indoor and outdoor dining rooms, where chef Pedro Miguel Schiaffino serves up Peruvian Nikkei-style cuisine. Expect selections like potato llapingachos, tuna crudo, barbecued plantains, and shrimp ceviche created with ingredients sourced from local farmers, fishermen, and other purveyors. The lower-deck swim platform and beach club is the launch point for kayaks, paddle boards, and snorkeling, or lazy days by the water.

Itineraries cover a wide breadth of islands, from the northern reaches of Genovesa to the southernmost Espanola, and Santa Fe, Santa Cruz, and Santiago in between. Western-focused itineraries arc around the far West side of Isabela Island, which allows for rarefied activities. Guests can hike among the penguin colonies and lava rocks of Punta Moreno, as well as the saltwater Darwin Lake located inside of a volcanic crater at Caleta Tagus.

Ecuadorian-owned, family-run expedition line Quasar operates 8-day and 15-day safari-style itineraries that focus on facilitating meaningful wildlife encounters for the small group of guests on board. With these immersive sailings, you might be swimming with sea turtles one day and cruising on a Zodiac boat amid a pod of dolphins the next. The line’s two yachts are designed for intimate trips, carrying a maximum of 32 guests. The 16-passenger Grace yacht has an especially intriguing history: Grace Kelly, who used it for her honeymoon in 1956, and has since been carefully restored to its original opulent glory. Guests can even stay in the revamped Grace Kelly suite, where the iconic actress spent her two-week honeymoon. Both yachts offer modern amenities like oversized hot tubs, al-fresco bars and lounges, sun decks, and more. Everything from meals to shore excursions to the open bar is included in the cruise fare.

Guests also have onboard access to kayaks, paddle boards, and snorkeling equipment for interacting directly with marine life like reef sharks, sea lions, and marine iguanas whenever the mood strikes. With such a small group, tours are immersive and personalized. Travelers can expect daily Zodiac landings across remote sites on islands like Espanola, Genovesa, Fernandina, Isabela, and Bartolome with expert naturalist guides.

While Flora can fit up to 100 passengers on board, excursions are limited to groups of 12 guests or fewer.

Sailing aboard the purpose-built ship Celebrity Flora strikes a perfect balance between relaxing on a luxurious floating resort and chasing the thrill of an adventurous expedition. The all-suite, all-veranda ship offers each guest a personal suite attendant, menus curated by a Michelin-starred chef, and an all-inclusive policy that covers drinks, meals, shore excursions, and even flights. Travelers can also expect a personal touch from crew, with 100 passengers on board and excursions that are limited to groups of 12 guests or fewer. Tours included memorable experiences like walks through lava tunnels, panga boat rides along rocky shorelines teeming with Galapagos penguins and sea lions, guided hikes to see blue-footed boobies, frigate birds, giant tortoises, rare flora, and ancient cacti.

Opportunities to spot diverse wildlife don’t end once travelers return to the ship. Celebrity Flora is outfitted with Sky Suites featuring the line’s signature Infinite Veranda that brings the extraordinary outdoor surroundings directly into your room. The window transforms into an open-air veranda at the touch of a button, allowing travelers to fully immerse themselves in the wondrous landscapes without even leaving their room. Plus, features like solar panels, reverse-osmosis water filtration, and dynamic positioning are gentle on the islands’ precious resources.

How early should I book a Galapagos cruise?

For the widest selection of vessels and sailing dates, aim to book your cruise four to nine months ahead of your intended sailing. More spontaneous travelers may find last-minute deals booking two to eight weeks ahead of their intended departure, though some itineraries will be sold out by then.

Getting to the Galapagos requires some logistical planning. After flying into Quito or Guayaquil, passengers typically spend a night in one of these mainland destinations before flying to the islands to board their ships. Your cruise line will tell you where to be on the islands for your departure, and in some cases, flights from the mainland will be included (or booked for an additional fee).

When is the best time to cruise the Galapagos Islands?

With a consistently mild climate year-round, the Galapagos can be visited at any time, although certain seasons offer exceptional wildlife viewing. December is when the giant tortoises hatch, and July marks the mating season for blue-footed boobies and short-eared owls. In April and May, marine iguanas typically hatch, while sea turtles begin laying their eggs at the start of the year. Given the diverse wildlife and year-round natural phenomena, there's never a "wrong" time to visit the islands.

The Galapagos Islands aren’t a bargain destination. Expect to pay somewhere between $5,000 and $12,000 per traveler, depending on the ship, itinerary, and length of the voyage, though there are options starting in the $3,000s.

What kind of wildlife can I expect to see on a Galapagos cruise?

The Galapagos Islands are renowned for their unique wildlife, including giant tortoises, marine iguanas, blue-footed boobies, and sea lions. The islands’ ecosystems are so diverse that you can see a variety of species in different environments, from volcanic shores to lush highlands.

#6319. ‘Mitt & Ted’ recounts how a political odd couple changed U.S. health care

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The Big Dig podcast host Ian Coss explores how Mitt Romney and Ted Kennedy worked together to reform American health care laws

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

In 1973, U.S. Senator Ted Kennedy often visited the cancer ward at Boston Children’s Hospital, where his eldest son was battling osteosarcoma. Kennedy witnessed other parents on the ward make impossible decisions regarding their child’s care when insurance didn’t cover it. Their stories lit a fire within the senator that burned bright for the rest of his life.

Kennedy spent decades fighting for health care reform, representing his home state of Massachusetts. He even teamed up with a former political rival from across the aisle: Mitt Romney. The story of this unexpected alliance is recounted in Mitt & Ted, the newest season of the GBH News podcast The Big Dig. Over eight episodes, journalist and host Ian Coss explores how their work laid the foundation for the Affordable Care Act, one of the most significant and divisive health care reforms in U.S. history.

We first meet Romney as a young upstart Republican challenger vying to flip Kennedy’s Senate seat in 1994. The race seemed close until a legendary debate. Romney had Kennedy on the defensive until the sitting senator pivoted to the issue near and dear to his heart: health care.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“Kennedy is the elder statesman, in command of the issue,” Coss says. “Romney is like an eager student trying to pass the test.” Using his deep knowledge, Kennedy buries the less experienced Romney. In the election, Kennedy then beat Romney by a landslide, even when many Democrats were ousted by Republican challengers that same year. But the loss may have motivated Romney to keep going.

Several years later, Romney unexpectedly became a champion of health care reform as the newly elected governor of Massachusetts. The state’s health care system was facing the potential loss of about a billion dollars in federal funding, threatening hospitals that served vulnerable populations. Romney’s administration created Romneycare, which was supported by three features: individual and employer mandates, affordable options for low-income people, and a health care exchange where people could compare plans from different providers.

With Senator Kennedy’s help, the groundbreaking law passed in 2006 and expanded health insurance coverage to 98 percent of Massachusetts’ population.

Romneycare gained national attention and kicked off years-long efforts to replicate it on the federal level. Finally, in 2010, President Obama signed the Affordable Care Act, or ACA. Modeled on Romneycare, the law (colloquially called Obamacare) adapted the reforms made in Massachusetts for all 50 states, a challenge since many states had larger shares of uninsured people than Massachusetts had even before Romneycare.

The Democrats in Congress also sought to include a government insurance plan in the reform, similar to Medicaid but available to more people. Republicans were wary of the ACA generally, but a government-provided insurance option was a line they wouldn’t cross. The ACA eventually passed without the public option, but by then the political winds had shifted. If there ever was a chance to secure bipartisan support for the law, it was gone by the time Democrats were willing to compromise on the public option. And as soon as the ACA became law, Republicans started fighting it.

The podcast traces an impressive number of political twists and turns on this health care reform journey. Though I got turned around a few times, I never fully lost the plot thanks to Coss’ well-placed reminders and takeaways.

Beyond the story of Romney and Kennedy, the podcast gives voice to many more people who made the ACA a reality: government workers who went from foes to allies who enlisted unlikely help from the conservative Heritage Foundation; longtime friends in the Massachusetts state legislature who were driven apart by the reform; a father who struggled to afford health care and how he advocated for reform with his church. I teared up more than once listening to the human stories behind these policy changes.

Overall, Mitt & Ted gave me new appreciation for why passing a reform is so difficult, despite how life-changing and life-saving access to health care can be. The series points to moments when stars aligned to make reform possible and suggests that more of those opportunities lie ahead.

“The work of American health care remains very much unfinished,” Coss says. “When the perfect alignment of frustration and opportunity arrives again, that might be what determines whether our leaders actually work together.”
