#6313. The notion of ‘positive masculinity’ is dividing the male studies field

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Researchers’ debate shapes how mental health experts advise men

Does “positive masculinity” exist or reinforce sexist gender norms? Researchers grappling with that question say the answer will help determine how doctors and therapists treat men.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Ryon McDermott set out seven years ago to create a new scale measuring masculinity. McDermott, along with other researchers studying male psyches, was tired of the field’s long-standing assertion that the manlier the man, the worse his outcomes. It was high time to measure masculinity in a positive light.

For almost half a century, the many social science scales that measure gender or masculinity have consistently shown that rigid fealty to Western masculine norms — such as prioritizing work, power-seeking and status — link with poor mental and physical health. Endorsement of such norms also correlates with misogynistic beliefs and violent behaviors, including sexual violence, studies have shown.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

But giving men a talking-to about their many defects rarely lands well. Nor does that negative focus help men thrive. But what approach would help? “We don’t really have a definition of men’s health. If we don’t know what we are going towards, how can we even do this [research]?” says Matt Englar-Carlson, a counseling expert at California State University, Fullerton.

What traits, the researchers wondered, define a healthy man? And could a healthy reframing of manhood improve men’s outcomes, such as by getting them to the doctor or lowering their high rates of social isolation, depression and even death by suicide?

Those questions would cleave the field, though as fights go, this one has been downright nice. McDermott, a psychologist of masculinity at the University of South Alabama in Mobile, would ultimately question positive masculinity’s very existence. Meanwhile, his friends and collaborators at Movember — a nonprofit research organization based in Richmond, Australia that encourages mustache-growing in November to spark conversations around men’s health issues — are poised for a 2027 launch of the Healthy Manhood Index. That scale uses a positive framing and is designed to gauge men’s strengths, while illuminating areas for improvement.

The first gender measurement scale emerged almost a century ago. It positioned femininity and masculinity at opposite poles, with researchers assuming that the most gender-conforming men and women were the healthiest.

That thinking has since unraveled. As women began smashing gender barriers, by doing everything from donning pants to entering the workforce, penalties for women acting more masculine largely disappeared.

Inspired by the feminist movement, researchers began studying the masculine psyche. Yet they largely framed masculinity as a barrier to health. The Male Role Norms Inventory, one of the most popular masculinity scales in use today, exemplifies that focus. Individuals rank statements like: “A man must stand on his own two feet and never depend on other people to help him do things.”

The higher the score on that and more than 60 similar statements appearing in popular masculinity scales used over the past 50 or so years, the worse men’s outcomes, McDermott and his colleagues at Movember reported in July in Men and Masculinities. “Manlier” men often struggle with depression and substance use and engage in sexual aggression. They also tend to avoid asking for help or taking precautionary health measures, such as wearing a mask during the COVID-19 pandemic.

But almost 80 percent of the statements used frame masculinity as a problem to be solved, the team found. That deficit lens biases the findings, argues coauthor and social psychologist Peter Fisher of the Movember Institute of Men’s Health, the organization’s research arm. “If the only tools you have available to you are looking for deficits, you will find deficits,” says Fisher, who is based in Santa Monica, Calif.

That negative framing has also seeped into public discourse, so much so that some people now intuitively link “masculinity” with the word “toxic.”

Yet those most macho of men are the outliers, the small percentage who score highest on masculinity scales, Englar-Carlson says. He suspects that what really matters for health is flexibility around when to behave in certain ways. Stoicism, a typically masculine-coded trait, can be calming in emergencies but scary when a man experiences a mental health crisis and refuses help.

Englar-Carlson and psychologist Mark Kiselica, of Penn State University, Harrisburg, developed the Positive Psychology Positive Masculinity, or PPPM, paradigm in 2010. Public health experts, therapists and others should focus on men’s strengths not deficits, they argued.

The ideas in PPPM are what McDermott began trying to turn into a masculinity scale a few years later. But his efforts sent him into a tailspin.

He and his colleagues began by identifying positive traits that people linked more with men than women. The team generated a list of 79 possible positive male attributes based on findings from focus groups and studies of positive masculinity and positive psychology, such as “having a good sense of humor,” “serving country or community” and “having passion for one’s work.” More than 1,000 individuals then rated those attributes on a scale from 1 for “strongly disagree” to 7 for “strongly agree” along three dimensions: positive, typically expected of men and typically expected of women.

Roughly 40 percent of the attributes, particularly those pertaining to protective behaviors and assertiveness, were seen as both positive and expected more of men than of women, McDermott and his colleagues reported in 2019 in Psychology of Men & Masculinities.

But the study also showed that both men and women scored above the midpoint on almost all the allegedly male attributes. That could mean the supposedly gendered attributes had little to do with gender. And for many measures, such as patience and having good hygiene, women scored higher than men. Could that mean that the study’s list was rebranding attributes from feminism as masculine? The idea didn’t sit well with McDermott.

Then, the team’s research took a dark turn. The researchers had respondents fill out both their new masculinity survey and a scale measuring sexist beliefs. That revealed that the more strongly respondents endorsed masculine ideals, the more likely they were to endorse sexist beliefs, the team’s unpublished work shows. Think about a statement like, “A good man should be strong,” McDermott says. For many people, that translates to “a good woman should be weak.”

“I’ve looked at this across three different samples [of people], and I find the same results each time,” McDermott says. “Whenever you define masculinity, you are inherently defining it against femininity.”

Most attributes are neither male nor female, but human, McDermott has come to believe. And gendering those universal traits merely reinforces sexist stereotypes. The work has left him gutted. “I really thought that there was such thing as positive masculinity,” he says. “But now I believe that it can never truly be positive.”

Fisher is well aware of McDermott’s journey. “He’s been trying to create a positive masculinity scale, or isolate the positive characteristics of masculinity, for a while,” Fisher says. “And he’s been struggling.”

Perhaps McDermott has set too high a bar, Fisher says. Rather than trying to identify and measure masculinity through beliefs, he says, why not focus on men’s actions?

So for the past several years, Fisher and colleagues have been doing just that. They have organized numerous focus groups and tested survey statements with some 12,000 individuals across six countries. Besides addressing the lack of age and cultural diversity used to create most masculinity scales currently in use, Fisher and his team hope that their scale will provide men with a blueprint for what constitutes healthy behavior.

Below are qualities Movember Institute of Men’s Health researchers are evaluating to develop a new masculinity scale. The items are preliminary and may not appear in the final version. The rows show counterproductive behaviors that result from pressures facing men, healthy responses and possible wording for survey statements the men would then rate.

All the statements in the Healthy Manhood Index start with “I” plus a verb, such as “I do,” “I talk” or “I check in,” Fisher says. For instance, men often feel pressure to restrict their emotions, so the healthy response would be for men to open up emotionally. The index might have men rate a statement like: “I share difficult things I’m going through with people I trust.” Crucially, the higher the score on the index, the healthier the man.

Fisher’s goal is to move men toward healthy behaviors without alienating them. “We just want to meet men where they are,” he says.

A debate that could easily become acrimonious has remained almost cloyingly friendly. McDermott refers to Fisher as “brilliant.” Fisher credits McDermott for “letting the data change his mind.”

Researchers in the field recognize that they share the same goals, says psychological researcher Michael Addis of Clark University in Worcester, Mass. They want men to be healthier and to treat others, including women and seemingly less masculine men, with respect. “The question is how do we do that? We either sell them on a new masculinity, or we say ‘…. masculinity is always going to be in some ways a box,’” he says.

Though discussions around how to frame masculinity can feel wonky, the stakes are real, Addis and psychiatrist and behavioral scientist Ethan Hoffmann of Stanford University wrote in 2024 in Psychology of Men & Masculinities.

Consider suicide. Men who strongly endorsed masculine norms were less likely than others to seek help for depression and more likely to die by suicide, researchers reported in 2025 in Psychiatry International.

Theoretically, public health campaigns aimed at men can help. But what form should they take? A positive masculinity campaign may recast a statement like, “real men never ask for help” to “real men know when it’s time to ask for help,” Addis and Hoffman write. But a campaign that rejects gender labels may roll out statements like: “Real men aren’t real: It’s a fiction that could cost you your life.”

Such postgender messaging may feel too abstract for the average guy, Fisher says. Convincing a 65-year-old man to stay on top of his prostate cancer appointments is hard enough without trying to shift his worldview.

McDermott counters that positive masculinity “makes the sex role stuff continue,” enshrining the idea that gender roles and hierarchies constitute a necessary organizing principle for societies.

Reconciliation may be possible, Addis says. Policy makers and public health experts could first rope men in with a more positive masculine approach. Then over time, they could help men question and relinquish gender norms. “I call it dancing with the devil,” or temporarily adopting the gendered approach as a means to a desired end, he says.

However the debate unfurls, researchers are writing their own script on how to fight like real men — or real people. “There’s a lot of men in the psychology of men [field] who have worked really hard to not let our egos get in the way of good work,” Addis says. “It’s sort of like practice what you preach.”

If you or someone you care about may be at risk of suicide, the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline offers free, 24/7 support, information and local resources from trained counselors. Call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org.

#6312. How to make friends at freshman orientation

A group of incoming members of Congress and staff arrive on Capitol Hill for new member orientation on Monday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

What happens when more than 100 members-elect descend on Capitol Hill a week after Election Day?

As Rep.-elect Dan Koh, D-Mass., put it, “It really is like high school — but it’s fun high school.”

Trainings and guest speakers aren’t everyone’s idea of a fun time, but Democrats are feeling good about this year’s new member orientation. Giddy, even.

The incoming freshmen will pose for a class photo on the House steps. They’ll test their luck in a lottery to see who lands the best office space. And everywhere they look, they see signs of the blue wave that swept over the country.

“I think — well, I hope — that we will be doing a lot of exceeding expectations in this caucus. The American people deserve it and expect it,” said Rep.-elect Sam Forstag, D-Mont., as he headed to lunch after an orientation session on Monday.

Forstag is the first Democratic congressman from Montana in 30 years, succeeding retiring GOP Rep. Ryan Zinke. A former smokejumper who parachuted into remote forests to put out wildfires, Forstag won by more than 3 points in a district President Donald Trump carried by double digits in 2024.

“I think there’s a lot of folks who didn’t expect us to,” he said of his win. “Nobody knew who we were this past December when I was still working at the smoke jumper base in Missoula.”

Democrats are still digesting their larger-than-expected wins, which saw them flip more than 40 House seats and oust a number of high-profile incumbents, including National Republican Congressional Committee Chairman Richard Hudson, R-N.C.

“It’s like drinking out of a firehose,” said Rep.-elect Rebecca Cooke, D-Wis., who unseated incumbent GOP Rep. Derrick Van Orden in Wisconsin’s 3rd District.

Cooke and her opponent clashed during the campaign over his use of AI-generated ads that she described as deepfakes. Now, they have to work together to make sure the transition goes smoothly.

“The congressman said that he’s willing to be helpful in that transition. I think it’s important that we make sure that the casework is transferred over, that constituent service is a priority, and that nothing falls through the cracks for people,” she said.

The 120th Congress will be full of history-makers, and a record-breaking number of women are set to serve in the House.

“This is a Congress with the most women ever to be a part of this chamber,” Cooke said. “And a lot of [Democrats], frankly, from the Midwest, and so I’m excited to build that sort of power from the Midwest to make sure that our interests are represented.”

The math isn’t lost on Republicans navigating a freshman class where they have fewer peers than they hoped.

“I thought that it would probably go a little bit different. I think a lot of people did, but it is what it is. You work with what we have,” said Rep.-elect Mark Lamb, R-Ariz.

But just like high school, everyone’s trying to make friends. As incoming members filed into the Capitol Visitor Center on Monday morning, Rep.-elect Cait Conley, D-N.Y., introduced herself to Rep.-elect Sydney Gruters, R-Fla.

Meanwhile, Rep.-elect Claire Valdez, D-N.Y., who describes herself as a “proud democratic socialist,” walked by chatting with Del.-elect Robert White, who will become only the third person in the modern era to hold the title of D.C.’s nonvoting delegate.

“I’m sitting next to a teacher right now; I’m sitting next to the mayor of Scranton … good, nice people,” said Rep.-elect Zack Mullock, D-N.J., who said he was surprised by how many “regular people” he was meeting among the incoming class.

Rep.-elect Brad Lander, D-N.Y., who ousted fellow Democrat Dan Goldman in a Brooklyn-based primary before cruising to victory in the general election, was also making friends.

“I was hanging out with Donavan McKinney yesterday in orientation, and I’m just really excited to meet all the amazing people. Micah Lasher, we were hanging out last night. Jacqui Irwin, so we’re just trying to get to know each other,” he said.

After arriving on Sunday with suitcases in hand, the future freshmen got a chance to set foot inside the House chamber later that day. Lander said he’d been there before to see Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, a friend of his, get sworn in four years ago. But Sunday was his first time on the floor itself.

“It’s obviously a lot different when it’s you,” he said.

Koh agreed, saying “everyone in that room, Republican or Democrat, had a lot of reverence for where they were.”

“I think it was just a good reminder about how despite all the division, that’s what we’re going to focus on — trying to figure out how to get things done for the American people,” he said.

Members-elect were trying their best to navigate their new workplace on Monday, many of them donning backpacks as they came to terms with the realities of their new job.

“We just have to get back to class,” said Rep.-elect Ed Gallrein, R-Ky., to a crowd of reporters trying to flag him down as he left orientation to use the restroom.

They’d have Italian food for lunch, after a session in the CVC auditorium where many of the future members typed notes on their laptops.

“They’ve got a packed agenda for us all week, really helping us figure out how to get started. Build our team, set course, understand where the bathrooms are — large and small. We got a lot to learn,” Lander said.

Scientists reported that an AI-designed protein can activate broken insulin receptors in lab mice, hinting at a potential new treatment for some forms of severe insulin resistance.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A protein designed with the help of artificial intelligence (AI) has successfully switched on faulty insulin receptors in lab mice even when insulin itself couldn't.

The findings hint at a new way to treat certain rare, life-threatening genetic disorders that cause insulin resistance, in which the body's cells don't respond well to the blood-sugar-controlling hormone.

In a study published Wednesday (Nov. 25) in the journal Science Translational Medicine, researchers found that the AI-designed protein, called RF-409, lowered blood sugar and reduced damage to the pancreas in mice with a genetic form of severe insulin resistance. This, in turn, prevented dangerous weight loss that typically comes with the condition.

When blood sugar rises, the pancreas releases insulin, a hormone that binds to proteins called insulin receptors on the surface of cells. This changes the receptors' shape, triggering a series of chemical signals that ultimately help bring blood sugar levels back down.

But mutations in the gene that encodes the insulin receptor can disrupt this process. More than 150 such mutations have been linked to inherited forms of insulin resistance. In one of the most severe forms, called Donohue syndrome, children can experience dangerously high blood sugar after eating, and unusually low blood sugar between meals, as well as poor growth. Most children with the condition die before their first birthday.

"Some [of these] patients produce extremely high levels of insulin, but their receptors cannot respond properly," study co-author Eunhee Choi, a cell biologist at Columbia University, told Live Science. "Simply giving more insulin may not solve the problem."

That's why Choi and her colleagues explored whether they could activate the receptor in another way.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

In 2025, the researchers used computational tools, including AlphaFold2, an AI program that predicts protein structures and how they fit together, to develop proteins that activate insulin receptors in a different way than insulin does. In that previous study, one of those proteins, RF-409, lowered blood sugar in both healthy mice and mice with obesity. In the new research, the team wanted to see whether RF-409 could also activate defective insulin receptors.

First, they ran experiments with laboratory-grown mouse and rat cells and with healthy mice, both with working insulin receptors. This confirmed that RF-409 largely mimicked insulin's effects on cellular signaling and metabolism. In the mice, RF-409 had a nearly 60-fold longer half-life in the bloodstream than insulin, meaning the protein stays in circulation much longer before breaking down.

"Both these features make [the finding] more than just an elegant trick," said Dr. Rajiv Agarwal, a nephrologist at Indiana University School of Medicine who was not involved in the study. Unlike a protein that mimics only some of insulin's effects, RF-409 reproduces most of its normal signaling, "which matters in children who need growth as well as glucose control," he added.

Insulin (orange) plugs into the insulin receptor (blue) to change its shape and trigger signals inside cells. The new protein activates the receptor in a different way.

To test how RF-409 works with defective receptors, the researchers focused on a mutation previously identified in patients with Donohue syndrome; this genetic mutation alters a key part of the receptor's structure, preventing insulin from binding to it. Computer models suggested that RF-409 could bypass the affected region and hold the receptor in the shape needed to transmit signals inside cells.

The researchers genetically engineered mice to carry this mutation. Compared with mice that retained a functioning copy of the insulin receptor gene, these mice had, on average, roughly 2.5 times higher blood sugar and 10 times higher fasting insulin levels (the amount of insulin in blood after a period without food).

When injected with insulin, mice with defective receptors showed no substantial drop in blood sugar. Treatment with RF-409, however, lowered mice's blood sugar by roughly 60% within two hours.

"It is like designing a new key to open a defective lock," said Kalaiarasan Ponnusamy, a computational biologist at SRM Institute of Science and Technology in India who was not involved in the study. "From a computational protein-design perspective, this is a major advance because it demonstrates that entirely new proteins can be engineered to restore receptor function without correcting the underlying genetic mutation."

After 14 days of continuous treatment, five mice given RF-409 had lower blood sugar, maintained their body weight and retained more abdominal fat than five mice given a saline solution, for comparison. The treated mice also showed less pancreatic damage.

"Extending this approach to other disease-causing receptor mutations is a realistic possibility, provided the receptor retains its ability to transmit signals," Ponnusamy said. Some mutations, for instance, prevent insulin receptors from reaching the cell surface or transmitting signals inside cells at all. That means the technique demonstrated in the study is unlikely to work against such mutations.

Identifying which mutations can be treated in this way is now a priority for Choi. The team also plans to investigate how RF-409 affects different tissues in the body and whether it remains safe and effective over longer periods of treatment, she said.

Although Agarwal foresees several hurdles in bringing RF-409 into clinical use; for instance, the immune system's reaction to the protein will have to be carefully studied, and in general, it's challenging to run trials with infants with rare disorders. That said, he remains hopeful that it could help patients whose diseases have no treatments to treat the underlying cause.

"This is the first approach I have seen that addresses the actual defect rather than working around it," he said.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Hung, A., Wang, X., Gao, M., Ng, M., Oliinyk, D., Weaver, R., Zollbrecht, E., Cardoso, S., Ronel, G. S., Paolucci, C., Ye, J., Fan, Q. R., Rhea, E., Mann, M., Baker, D., Accili, D., & Choi, E. (2026). Reprogramming insulin receptor activation with a de novo agonist to overcome severe preclinical insulin resistance. Science Translational Medicine, 18, eaei0487. https://dx.doi.org/10.1126/scitranslmed.aei0487

#6310. On a Ranch in Wyoming, a Stressed-Out Editor Gets in Sync With a Lazy Horse

I used to avoid horses the same way I’d avoid palm readers. While my friends chased $5 readings in Downtown Manhattan, I preferred to keep the velvet curtain closed.

I was convinced that once a fortune teller held my hands in hers, she would trace a life line abruptly cut short or reveal a heart line splintered beyond repair. So I’d sit on the stoop, hands safely secured in the pockets of my jacket. Horses and psychics, I believed, shared the same dark, all-knowing eyes.

The 80,000-acre ranch is nestled between Wyoming's Bighorn Mountains and Paintrock Canyon.

The first time I rode a horse was 10 years ago in Costa Rica, my body clenched for the entirety of the 20-minute sunset beach stroll. “They can sense your fear,” I remember the guide telling me. “Just try to relax.”

Over the next decade I’d continue to receive similar advice—from my mother in a well-intentioned effort to soothe her overthinking eldest daughter, but also from doctors and massage therapists and boyfriends. I am trying, I would say. There was nothing effortless about me, and that was the problem.

So when I found out on the plane to Wyoming that the camp at Ranchlands I was headed to—an 80,000-acre ranch nestled between the Bighorn Mountains and Paintrock Canyon—would have no Wi-Fi, cell service, or nary an outlet to plug into, I sent out panicked slacks and emails apologizing. They tell me there is a hill with a few bars, I tell my manager. I will find it.

The guest accommodations at Paintrock Canyon Ranch

This may come as a surprise, but like most creatives who have converted their personal passions into paychecks, travel editors are sneaky workaholics, adept at turning vacations into deliverables. At customs checkpoints, I’ll still catch myself stumbling when asked if I’m traveling for business or leisure. When the world is your office, is the answer: both? Or neither?

The answer was particularly murky this time around, as I was traveling to Ranchlands for a writing and riding retreat hosted by author Molly Wizenberg. I’d be joined by nine other solo women travelers; labor lawyers, criminologists, educators, and Fortune 500 marketers who I imagined also struggled to relax. After all, their idea of a vacation was to ride five hours a day and sleep in a tent (albeit elegant), all whilst working on novels and memoirs in between.

We introduce ourselves while seated at a long wooden picnic table overlooking a gurgling creek, into which I will plunge each afternoon to wash off the desert dust. All around us, towering limestone walls encircle the camp, a gently sloping field of shin-high sagebrush. Contrasted against the layered prairie grasses, the opaque form and sharp lines of the white canvas tents remind me of a famous painting, but I’m not sure which one. There is something archetypal about this place, and it leaves me with a lingering sense of dejá vu, as if I was remembering a long-forgotten dream.

From the main camp, guests can go hiking, fly fishing, and horseback riding.

Over the next five days, Molly tells us, we will split our time between horseback riding through the surrounding high desert and mountainous terrain and group writing workshops. For the entirety of the trip, each of us will be paired with a horse, a match based on stated riding experience. (Or, your deepest hopes and fears, should you have disclosed these in the pre-arrival form.)

The first time I meet my horse, I’m overwhelmed with the nerves of a blind date. When a cowboy making horseshoe repairs offers me a cigarette, I almost take him up on it. “This is José,” Oliver, an Australian wrangler with a charming snaggletooth grin, tells me as he adjusts the saddle. “He’s a bit lazy, this one.”

As I reach up to pet his coarse black mane, I wait for José to flinch away from my touch, his flaring nostrils surely sniffing out my incompetence. With a horse, there’s no pretending, and no amount of Westernwear could hide my East Coast Puritan roots. While some of my ancestors had made it as far as California, for the most part they sailed across and stayed. Such pioneering ambitions as Manifest Destiny were nowhere to be found in my family tree.

But José doesn't look through me, he just looks at me. And if he does see into the depths of my spur-bearing soul, he doesn’t seem bothered by it. When I climb atop the saddle, he shows no signs of wanting to move. I look down at his long eyelashes, fluttering gently. That's okay, I think to myself. I'm not a morning person either.

“You two are a good match,” says Ella, our wrangler and guide, as the group rides single-file beneath what the ranchers call The Red Wall, an ancient red rock mesa that gives way to sprawling desert. It takes nearly two hours to cross the dusty valley, its rust-colored dirt baking in the sun—it's as though we are climbing out of a shallow clay bowl painted with pastel pigment, waiting to be brought to the kiln.

Our daily rides are approximately five hours long, from 9 a.m. to 2 p.m., though some are shorter. Lunch—which one afternoon included melt-in-your-mouth pork belly and a quinoa salad—is eaten out in the field with the horses, who happily accept the remains of any apple rinds. A short writing exercise follows, and sometimes a cowgirl nap, our backs leaning up against a tree trunk or laying down flat in the tall grasses, hat brims tilted over our eyes. Dinner—fresh fish, meat, and vegetables prepared over an open-fire kitchen—is enjoyed creekside back at camp beneath twinkle lights. By the end of each day, I’m so tired that I fall asleep at 9 p.m. and before the sun has fully set, despite promising myself I’d stay up late enough to see the stars.

Most of the cooking is done over open fire, using local ingredients (including beef from the ranch).

Breakfasts and dinners are communal meals, while lunch is packed and eaten out in the field.

One morning on the trail, the group turns to the topic of AI, and how to make sense of it in a place like this. Our brains, we all agree, feel healthier without the constant distractions of our phones. During the writing workshops interspersed throughout the day, most of us opt to write by hand. My thoughts are clearer, less muddled. There are no extra tabs to open—no research rabbit holes or thesaurus queries to get lost in.

At the beginning of the retreat, Molly asks us each to share one sentence on what writing represents to us. I think of answering “my job,” but instead I say “it’s how I think”—a response that two others echo. Another woman answers, “writing is hard.” We all laugh in agreement, and I wonder why we torture ourselves in this way. Especially now, with the temptation of automation hovering over every email draft and browser.

The bulk of our writing is done in the afternoons, when we bring our notebooks and pens to the “lounge” tent and settle into couches and cowhide chairs to discuss the previous day’s readings before tackling a writing prompt. It’s a welcome break for our shaky thighs and sore tuchuses—and a satisfying tiredness I find myself looking forward to.

Tapas, drinks, and mocktails are served creekside.

Our only assignment for the week? “To Be Absolutely Yourself.” The retreat's title, as Molly explains, means exploring our strangest and most personal obsessions, irrational fears, and inexplicable crushes, with the idea that these idiosyncrasies—such as Sam Anderson’s secret mole that he convinced himself was cancerous for almost a decade—are our most universal experiences. Though some in the group are working on pieces they hope to publish one day, we are reminded on multiple occasions to write without thinking about the end result: not what the poem or essay might turn into, or whether anyone would want to read it. It’s a way of writing that someone who speaks the language of commissioning rates and word counts rarely gets to practice. What is my writing when it’s not a product? I jot down. What is work without a job?

Midway through the week, a smaller group of us embark on an optional ride up into the canyon, weaving between the anemone-like skeletons of burnt juniper trees, sunlight transforming the deep grey charcoal into shimmering shades of silver. José slowly trudges forward, dodging stumps and rocks with careful, decisive footing. Like people, I learn that horses may be better suited for different jobs in line with their personality; some enjoy herding cattle and others are more suited to trail riding. Others, like José, are happiest chewing grass in a meadow.

José is in no rush to get to where we are going, and in accepting that, my thoughts slow down to match his meditative pace. I am not sure if I would be able to sink into this relaxed state if I didn’t have somewhere else to direct my focus: my hands on the reins, the directions transmitted with a quick squeeze of my thighs, and my balance as we climb higher up the canyon wall.

Ranchlands' cattle business uses conservation-focused cattle management

It is counterintuitive to try and go and learn a new skill when you are burned out—but I was coming to realize that sometimes, relaxation takes work. That we write because it is hard, not in spite of it. In an environment like this one, these facts feel obviously simple. But I also know how easy they will be to forget, when the distractions return.

Perhaps that’s why so much of modern travel is now packaged as a retreat. The travel industry, my publication included, has been busy finding new names for this widespread desire toward a similar desire to unplug and reconnect with the physical world: skillcations, dead-zone retreats, analogue travel, cowboy-core, and a growing list of other buzzy trends.

In this way, ranch life has once again emerged as an American frontier. As one guest writes on the Ranchlands’ website testimonial page: “As a professional working in the corporate world, my stay at Ranchlands allowed me to step away from all of the noise in the chaos that is always coming at me. It felt like a reset for my nervous system and the most restful time that I have had in a long time.” Signed, Larissa M.

On our final ride, our wrangler Ella, who grew up working on her mother’s equine therapy farm in North Carolina, explains that the heart of a horse is nine times the size of a human’s, creating an electromagnetic field that pulses with and around that of its rider—which can form a symbiotic relationship between horse and rider that can even lead your heart rates to sync up. Though horses are often associated with bravery and courage, in reality many are quite skittish and easily spooked, by butterflies and birds and the wind and plastic irrigation piping. The same way a horse can calm down an anxious rider, a strong rider can give a nervous horse confidence.

When we turn back toward the ranch José picks up the pace to pass the group, uncharacteristically leading the charge. “He’s a bit sad today,” Oliver tells me. “We left his girlfriend back at the barn.” Her name, he says, is Pistol.

How did I not realize it sooner? The drifting attention, the constant daydreaming, the sudden burst of energy when it was time to go home. José was not a lazy horse, I realized. He was a boy with a big heart and a relaxed nervous system. And he was in love.

Ranchlands' five-night vacations start from $4,150 per person, including accommodation, meals, and activities (closed from mid-October to mid-May).

#6309. Math’s holy grail, the Riemann hypothesis, appears solved with AI’s help

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The proof apparently settles a 167-year-old question related to prime numbers

The Riemann hypothesis reveals a secret order hidden in the prime numbers.

ROBERT BROOK/Science Photo Library/Getty Images

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

A long-sought pinnacle of mathematics has apparently been reached. In a feat that will go down in mathematics history, a human working with AI appears to have solved the most famous puzzle in math, proving the Riemann hypothesis. The problem has foiled repeated and valiant attempts at solution for more than a century.

Now, mathematicians are working to understand the proof, posted by Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, on November 20. The Riemann hypothesis, if true, reveals the secrets of prime numbers. In a statement on his website, Alpöge said he’d developed the proof alongside Anthropic’s AI tool Claude.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

By the next day, independent mathematicians had confirmed the result. “We have full confidence that Alpöge’s proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement,” read a joint statement from Lean Focused Research Organization and Mathlib Initiative.

A proof of the Riemann hypothesis is one of the most sought after achievements in mathematics. “As a mathematical landmark, it really doesn’t get bigger than this. I can’t think of a theorem proven not only in my lifetime, maybe in the history of mathematics that is as important as this,” says mathematician Ken Ono of Axiom Math and the University of Virginia in Charlottesville.

“It’s an historic achievement,” says Bryna Kra, a mathematician at Northwestern University in Evanston, Ill.

Importantly, this was not the work of AI alone, Kra says. First of all, Claude had been trained on the work of thousands of human mathematicians, plus Alpöge was an experienced mathematician himself. He did not just ask for the proof then “push a button and wait,” Kra says.

Over six weeks, he worked back and forth with Claude. As an AI agent, Claude can use outside tools to perform tasks. The precise version of Claude that Alpöge used has not been disclosed, but the AI checked its work using Lean, software that converts mathematical arguments into code in order to confirm that a chain of logic holds up. It also had access to Mathlib, a library of known arguments already converted into Lean.

The result is 250,000 pages of dense, complex math. The world’s mathematicians are still working to translate the proof into a form people can understand. “What’s amazing about this proof is that it involves so many different areas of mathematics,” Ono says. “And I don’t know how a single human being could hold all of the ideas in their mind.”

The Riemann hypothesis, which dates to 1859, is closely linked with prime numbers. Prime numbers seem to be sprinkled randomly along the number line, but the Riemann hypothesis reveals a hidden order. At play is a mathematical enigma called the Riemann zeta function. The zeros of this function — the values that, when plugged into the function, produce a zero — are closely related to prime numbers. The Riemann hypothesis says that certain zeros — of which there are an infinite number — all sit on a particular line on a graph. If that is true, it would reveal how many primes exist below a given number.

Because so much of mathematics involves prime numbers, many other mathematical statements rest on the correctness of the hypothesis. The new proof will have wide implications. “It’s an earthquake throughout mathematics,” Ono says.

Alpöge claims to have solved not only the Riemann hypothesis itself, but a more general form of it, called the generalized Riemann hypothesis, which extends the idea to related functions. Though he guided the AI, Alpöge wrote that “what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater … Claude far outpaced me near the finish line.”

AI has been steadily felling major problems of mathematics, and this is the biggest one yet. But according to cognitive scientist Gary Marcus of New York University, AI’s genius at math will not carry over to more open-ended types of problems in biology, business or robotics. “In short, it’s not at all obvious that whatever Alpöge did has the generality many people are hoping for,” he wrote in a Substack post.

And some mathematicians have pushed back against the dominance of AI, disputing the utility of proofs created with the technology. The Association for Human Mathematics wrote in a November 20 statement on their website that no human being can claim to be responsible for the Riemann hypothesis proof, and that no mathematician can “confirm with full certainty that the proof is correct.”

Kra has been critical of achievements where AI agents worked largely on their own, independent of human intervention. The recent solution, by OpenAI, to a puzzle about the Navier-Stokes equations that describe fluids came about that way. But Alpöge’s approach was different, Kra says. “There is someone to stand behind [the work],” she says. She just hopes that people don’t see this as an end to math. “I think that this is a beginning, this is opening up more questions than it answers. … I think we have to use our imagination and find what’s the next frontier.”

A study claims that ancient "supervolcanoes" hidden under Antarctica may have provided the nutrients that led to an explosion of complex life millions of years later. But not everyone agrees.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists have found the remnants of supermountains in the seabed around Antarctica. They say these ancient peaks may have provided the nutrients that led to an explosion of complex life millions of years later. However, others are more skeptical about these conclusions.

About 600 million years ago, landmasses in the Southern Hemisphere collided to form the supercontinent Gondwana, which included what is now South America, Africa, Arabia, Madagascar, India, Australia and Antarctica. At that time, there was multicellular life, but it was very primitive.

Previous research suggested that the continental collision created massive Himalaya-like mountains in what is now Antarctica. Now, in a new study, published online Sept. 12 in the journal Earth and Planetary Science Letters, scientists say they've found the sediment that accumulated in the oceans when the Gondwanan mountains eroded over millennia.

"The results suggest that the assembly of Gondwana involved multiple major continental collisions, producing an extensive network of mountain belts comparable in scale to the modern Himalayas and Tibetan Plateau," Nathan Daczko, a petrologist at Macquarie University in Australia who was not involved in the research, told Live Science in an email.

"The study highlights just how much geological history remains hidden beneath Antarctica."

Most of Antarctica is trapped beneath an ice sheet, so it is difficult to understand its evolutionary history.

To address this, the team drilled into the seabed at 12 locations around Antarctica, extracting soil samples. They were looking for ancient crystals called detrital zircon. Zircon is a mineral that grows in rocks and is strong enough to remain chemically intact when the rock erodes.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"We can date it very, very precisely, and from the geochemistry, and especially the trace elements, we can determine where the zircon came from," Ian Campbell, a geochemist at the Australian National University and a co-author of the study, told Live Science.

They dated 1,712 zircon grains extracted from marine sediments and compared the abundance of zircons in Antarctica with a global zircon database, across different time scales.

"We have used the zircon record to show that the mountains that formed during the amalgamation of Gondwana were the largest and most extensive in the history of the Earth, and they included some very high mountains like the Himalayas today," Campbell said.

Alan Collins, an earth scientist at the University of Adelaide in Australia, said that he was surprised by the scale of the erosion from these rocks. "It beautifully supports ideas that the mountains that formed as the supercontinent Gondwana amalgamated were amongst the largest on Earth through deep time," he told Live Science in an email.

The formation of Gondwama produced one-fifth of the world's zircons, and the creation of the supercontinent Pangaea around 320 million years ago produced 14%, the study found.

Elias Rugen, a geochemist at the University of Southampton in the U.K. who wasn't involved in the research, was surprised by the "abundance of zircons associated with Gondwana's assembly in the Antarctica samples." "It is remarkable how much information about Antarctica's geological past can be recovered from these tiny minerals, particularly when so much of the continent remains hidden beneath ice," he said.

However, he cautioned against estimating the range's height from the zircon data. "It is really difficult to infer a mountain's height from data like this," he said.

An illustration of what the Pangea supercontinent would have looked like.

The formation and erosion of the Gondwana supermountains had consequences for the rest of the planet and the life on it, the authors said.

"In order to get life, you need nutrients," Campbell said. "At that time, most of the life was in the oceans, so you need to get nutrients into the ocean."

Today, the world's biggest ongoing erosion event is the Himalayas. This massive mountain range is eroding, and sending sediment down rivers and into the ocean. This deep-sea sediment deposit is called the Bengal Fan and is Earth's largest such deposit.

In a similar way, Gondwana's massive mountains also "sent lots of nutrients into the ocean," Campbell said, which "significantly advanced the evolution of life" on Earth.

Soon after the formation of Gondwana, the planet entered the Cambrian period. This era, which lasted from about 541 million to 485 million years ago, saw a dramatic diversification of life on Earth, known as the Cambrian explosion. The period saw the rise of creatures such as chordates (animals with a dorsal nerve, including humans) and arthropods (the ancestors of insects and crustaceans).

The study's authors drew a link between Gondwana's supermountains and this rapid evolution of complex life. While the supermountains don't explain the Cambrian Explosion directly, they "provide the opportunity for it to happen," Campbell said. The paper suggests that these nutrients fed organisms that formed the base of the animal food web.

However, Daczko and Rugen are skeptical. "The methods used in this study cannot directly demonstrate that this particular mountain belt was directly responsible for the rise in oxygen or the Cambrian Explosion," Rugen said. "However, the evidence for a Gondwanan supermountain belt that would inevitably have had a substantial impact on Earth's biogeochemical cycles is growing."

Daczko said he would frame the link between the Gondwana's supermountains and the Cambrian explosion as "an exciting hypothesis rather than an established causal relationship."

However, the study did show that there was much more to discover under the ice in Antarctica.

"The most exciting aspect is the possibility that some of the largest mountain systems in Earth's history are effectively hidden beneath the East Antarctic ice sheet," Daczko said. "Antarctica potentially holds some of the most important remaining evidence for understanding the tectonic and environmental evolution of our planet."

#6306. Redistricting battle could spill into 2028

Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, here at the Capitol in January, wants to see his state's congressional map redrawn. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

The redistricting fights that underscored this year’s battle for the House could continue into the 2028 election cycle, although lessons from last Tuesday will likely shape those efforts.

House Republicans had hoped that new congressional maps in seven states would help them limit losses in the face of an unfavorable political environment. But nearly a week after the election, the GOP appeared on track to flip just three redrawn seats while losing a host of seats in Texas, Florida, North Carolina, Ohio and Alabama that were reconfigured in their favor.

“The question is whether the results have let some air out of the [redistricting] balloon or not,” said Erik Nisbet, a professor at Northwestern University’s School of Communication.

Republicans may question the utility of redrawing more state maps in the 2028 cycle, while Democrats will need to weigh how to spend their political capital. But the new lines approved over the past year could still prove more favorable for Republicans in future elections.

“This was a wave election, and there’s no guarantee that the Democratic generic ballot would be D+13 — which is the reason why redistricting didn’t work for Republicans — in the next cycle,” Nisbet added.

New maps appear possible, if not likely, in at least a few states. Maryland voters last week approved an amendment that would clear the way for new boundaries ahead of the 2028 elections. Democratic Gov. Wes Moore, who easily won a second term last week, said he hopes to see a new map, citing the threat of President Donald Trump continuing to push for friendlier lines in GOP-led states. Maryland Democrats could draw a map that would favor them in all eight of the state’s House seats, including the Eastern Shore district of Rep. Andy Harris, the state’s lone Republican in Congress.

Advocates for a new map in Wisconsin got a boost last week when Democrats flipped both the state House and state Senate, setting up a Democratic trifecta. Gov.-elect David Crowley said he would sign a bill redrawing the state’s congressional map if legislators sent one to his desk.

Republicans in recent years have had a lopsided edge in the congressional delegation for Wisconsin, a perennial battleground state. But Democrats flipped two House seats last week, with Rebecca Cooke and Mitchell Berman unseating GOP Reps. Derrick Van Orden and Bryan Steil, respectively, bringing the state delegation to an even 4-4.

Democrats could also look to redraw the lines in New York and Virginia. Earlier this year, voters in the commonwealth approved a new map that would have given Democrats up to four pickup opportunities, but the Virginia Supreme Court later struck it down on procedural grounds. Even without the new map, Democrats flipped two House seats in Virginia last week and came within 2 points of flipping a third.

Democrats in New York, meanwhile, took initial steps toward mid-decade redistricting earlier this year, but 2028 is the earliest they could hold elections under a new map.

On the Republican side, several states have been mentioned as candidates for new maps in 2028.

Officials in GOP-led Mississippi have held hearings this year on redistricting, which could target Democratic Rep. Bennie Thompson. Republicans are also aiming to redraw the state’s legislative lines ahead of next year’s off-year elections.

It’s not clear whether states that were unsuccessful in redrawing their district lines for 2026 will try again when their legislatures convene next year. Republicans in both South Carolina and Indiana fell short in their push to pass new maps and could decide to revisit the issue. But Democrats flipped a House seat in each state last week, and some Republican incumbents won reelection by narrower margins than usual. Still, Republicans maintained their legislative majorities in both states, though Democrats broke their supermajorities in the South Carolina and Indiana state houses.

An analysis by DecisionDeskHQ offers a potential warning sign for Republicans in the Palmetto and Hoosier states: Under the GOP-drawn maps that were not adopted for 2026, Democrats could have flipped even more seats last week.

Redistricting appears off the table in a handful of states where new maps for 2028 had once been considered possible.

Georgia’s outgoing Republican governor, Brian Kemp, said last week that he would not call a special session to address redistricting before the end of the year, after Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms was elected to succeed him.

There were no House flips in the Peach State in the midterm elections, though several Republicans won by closer-than-anticipated margins.

In New Jersey, Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill told the New Jersey Globe that she also did not “see a path forward for redistricting right now.”

Democrats flipped two House seats in the Garden State last week. Navy veteran Rebecca Bennett defeated Republican Rep. Thomas H. Kean Jr., while Cape May Mayor Zack Mullock scored a surprise win over GOP Rep. Jeff Van Drew.

With their new majorities in Washington, Democrats could propose legislation to ban partisan gerrymandering.

That’s something John Bisognano, the president of the National Democratic Redistricting Committee, anticipates happening, but he said Democrat-led states should be prepared to respond to new maps drawn in Republican-controlled ones.

“If they are going to continue to take those actions, Democrats in states across the country need to be prepared to respond, and we, of course, now have significantly more opportunities than we did before Tuesday to respond to those states,” he said.

#6303. Eagles can prey on adult baboons. Did our ancestors face that threat?

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Outwitting flying predators may have helped human ancestors evolve teamwork and language

Young olive baboons sit on the cliffs of Ennedi Plateau in Chad. New research suggests even adult baboons similar in size to some human ancestors are threatened by birds of prey.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

As if leopards and saber-toothed cats weren’t enough, some ancient human relatives probably also had to contend with predators that swooped down from the skies.Adult male baboon remains found in Africa carry telltale signs of raptor predation. The specimens probably weighed about 22 to 26 kilograms in life. That’s twice the size of the largest primates previously known to be preyed upon by a raptor species and on par with some early human ancestors, researchers report November 18 in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology. Guarding against aerial predators may have pressured humans’ ancient cousins to form tighter social groups and develop vocal strategies that preceded language, the researchers say.

Biologists discovered the baboon bones among the high sandstone cliffs of Ennedi Plateau in northeastern Chad. These baboons (Papio anubis) have developed unique survival strategies, such as scaling 50-meter cliffs and digging for water and food. They share the plateau with multiple birds of prey, and the researchers have identified one as the most likely baboon hunter: the Verreaux’s eagle (Aquila verreauxii).

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Researchers have long studied predation from land carnivores such as big cats and crocodiles as a primary driver of behavioral changes in primates, including human ancestors. While a five-kilogram bird like a Verreaux’s eagle taking down a 22-kilogram monkey may seem unlikely, the raptors appear to have developed specialized hunting techniques.

“It’s pretty brutal, but it’s pretty quick,” says Cat Hobaiter, a primatologist at the University of St Andrews in Scotland. The eagles stab their talons “straight through the eye, straight through the brain, and that’s a very effective control and kill.” The birds may also drag the baboons off the cliffs, a strategy that golden eagles use to hunt large mountain goats and sheep in the Alps. The birds then dismember the prey and carry off pieces to their nests.

Three adult male baboon skulls that Hobaiter and her colleagues studied had clearly visible punctures through the eye sockets. And two specimens also had gashes across the shoulder bones, which appear to have been made by grasping talons. The researchers estimated the weight of the animals based on the size of the head of their femurs, where these upper leg bones attach to the hip.

While the punctures could come from something other than an eagle’s talon, such as a bite or a bullet, the clean circular holes in the skulls match similar damage to smaller monkeys hunted by eagles, Hobaiter says.

“I found the evidence pretty compelling,” says Scott McGraw, an evolutionary biologist at Ohio State University in Columbus who was not involved with the work. The punctures look “remarkably similar” to injuries in monkeys hunted by the African crowned eagle in the Taï Forest of Côte d’Ivoire, McGraw says.

The eagles also use the landscape to their advantage, hugging cliffs to stay hidden and possibly hunting in pairs, Hobaiter says. It’s possible that one eagle could distract the baboons from above while another swoops up from below a cliff to attack, as has been observed against other prey, she says.

While the research team did not witness an eagle attack a baboon, they did observe the monkeys responding to the Verreaux’s eagles’ presence, though not to other raptors in the area.

When the eagles flew down over a ridge, the baboons immediately barked out an alarm call and climbed over the edge of a cliff to safety, Hobaiter says.

The eagles’ ability to hunt large primates suggests that raptors may have also hunted ancient human ancestors, Hobaiter says. In particular, the genus Australopithecus, which lived about 4 million to 2 million years ago and included the famous fossil named Lucy, had similar body sizes to the baboons. A 2.8-million-year-old skull called the Taung child from the species A. africanus even has puncture and scratch marks that McGraw and other researchers argue probably came from a raptor.

The threat from birds of prey paints a more complete picture of how and why our ancestors developed certain behaviors, such as social grouping to protect younger animals. Primates also use a range of vocal alerts to warn the group of danger. They use different sounds or combinations of sounds for different threats, such as a predator on the ground or in the sky.

“Those first steps towards combining information in different ways to be more specific … would have been a really important precursor [of language],” Hobaiter says.

W.S. McGraw and L.R. Berger. Raptors and primate evolution. Evolutionary Anthropology. 2013. doi: 10.1002/evan.21378

Scientists have discovered the earliest-known quasar lurking in the ancient universe — and it's growing at a slower rate than scientists believed possible.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A Euclid space telescope image of the newfound quasar (red dot in the center), which is further away than any known active galactic nucleus found yet.

Astronomers have just discovered the earliest-known quasar — and it's 40 million years older than the previous record holder. The finding, which observed the object at just 630 million years after the Big Bang, could help researchers to better understand how black holes developed in the early universe.

"Finding quasars at ever-increasing distances, at the edge of the observable universe, teaches us something about how the black holes in their centres grew," study co-author Julien Wolf, a researcher at the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy, said in a statement. "The closer to the Big Bang we find them, the faster their black holes must have grown or the more massive they must have been at birth — or both."

The object — estimated to have the mass of 360 million suns — was described in a new study published Tuesday (Nov. 24) in the journal Astronomy and Astrophysics.

A quasar, short for "quasi-stellar radio source," is an incredibly bright core at the center of some galaxies — a region known as the active galactic nucleus (AGN). They form when supermassive black holes, which lurk at the hearts of most galaxies, start to binge on nearby matter. Once enough swirling material accumulates around these black holes, it heats up and glows intensely before falling into the object. What sets quasars apart from other AGNs is their sheer luminosity; they can be brighter than all the stars in a galaxy combined.

Quasars were much more common early in the universe than they are today. They are thought to have peaked in number about 10 billion years ago. Observing them can give scientists important clues as to how galaxies evolve — and how their supermassive black holes develop.

The quasar was discovered during the Euclid Wide Survey's scan of the sky — marked here in light yellow. Dark yellow patches show the target areas of Euclid's Deep Survey, which will repeatedly view smaller parts of the sky.

Because it takes time for light to travel, observing celestial objects that are very far away is tantamount to peering back in time. We see galaxies very near to Earth as they were only a few thousand years ago; conversely, we see galaxies very far away from us as they were billions of years ago, because their light is only now reaching our telescopes. The older the galaxy, the more red its light becomes as it stretches across the universe — a phenomenon called "redshift."

Using data from NASA's James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and the European Space Agency's Euclid Wide Survey, the researchers behind the new study identified a quasar with a redshift of 8.13 — the first such object ever found with a redshift beyond 8. This makes it the oldest quasar yet observed, at approximately 13.1 billion years old. For reference, the universe itself is thought to be 13.8 billion years old.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The scientists named the object Dún Aonghasa, after a prehistoric cliff fort on the Atlantic-facing edge of Inis Mór, an island off the coast of Ireland. The name is meant to reflect the quasar's position at the very edge of our current observational frontier for the cosmos.

According to the researchers, Dún Aonghasa also appears to be growing more slowly than astronomers previously thought possible, given its size. This suggests that its supermassive black hole may have gone through a massive growth spurt, followed by a period of much slower growth in the distant past. The discovery could put new constraints on black hole growth models, which are already being challenged by previous JWST detections of supermassive monsters that seem to have grown too big for their early place in cosmic history.

Future observations from Euclid and JWST could help researchers test this hypothesis and see if it holds for other ancient quasars, the researchers said.

#6300. Massie moves to force Hegseth impeachment vote

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., conducts a news conference outside the Capitol on Monday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., took to the House floor Monday to unveil a resolution that would impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and a vote on the issue could occur by Wednesday.

A draft resolution that Massie read aloud on the House floor on Monday accused Hegseth of eight violations of law or the Constitution, including that he violated the 1973 War Powers Resolution in his prosecution of the Iran war and acted illegally in military campaigns in Venezuela, Yemen, the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean.

Massie's resolution also charges Hegseth with disregarding protection of civilians in wartime and suppressing the free speech of a U.S. senator.

Massie announced his intention to file the resolution as a matter of the privileges of the House.

Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., will now have to rule as to whether the resolution constitutes a proper question of the privileges of the House. There is precedent from prior instances when impeachment was found to be valid as it relates to the House’s constitutionally granted powers.

He must schedule a vote to occur within two legislative days. Assuming that the speaker rules that Massie's resolution is privileged, the House could vote on the resolution itself, or on a motion to table it or refer it to committee.

If the House were to impeach Hegseth under this process, it would mark a historical anomaly. According to the Congressional Research Service, recent attempts to impeach an official as a matter of the privileges of the House have not resulted in approval of the resolution. In cases in which an official has been impeached, the House has nearly always chosen to conduct an investigation first.

In an interview on Oct. 26, Massie put the chances of his resolution being adopted at 50-50.

In comments to reporters outside the Capitol after his floor remarks, Massie said he suspected some Republicans may back his resolution but he indicated he has neither asked for nor received any such assurances from any of them.

He predicted there could be some GOP support in the Senate if Hegseth is impeached and it goes to trial. He noted that if the trial does not start until 2027, any Republicans who might vote to convict Hegseth would presumably be joined by most if not all of a more sizeable Senate Democratic caucus.

Massie's odds of success for his resolution may now be greater than his previous 50-50 prediction given the results of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, which gave Democrats control over both chambers in the next Congress — a vote motivated largely by opposition to the Iran war and its inflationary impact.

The questions now are, first, how many House Republicans will defy President Donald Trump and vote to impeach Hegseth; and, secondly, how many incumbents who lost their reelection bids on Nov. 3, a cohort that is disproportionately Republican, might be absent for the impeachment vote?

Massie said some Republicans who lost their reelection bids may feel freer to vote to impeach Hegseth. And he also said Republicans who were reelected and will have to face voters in 2028 may also think about how their vote on an impeachment resolution would reverberate politically.

"It's going to be everybody's conscience, and then they'll have to live with that vote," Massie said. "And they're going to have to live with that vote two years from now if they're not part of the retirement caucus. And if they were part of the retirement caucus, what do they have to lose?"

Asked why he did not bring articles of impeachment against President Donald Trump, Massie said: "I think the president needs to see one of — this is a metaphor — one of his horses shot out from under him, and then maybe he'll he will see things differently."

If the House does vote on Massie’s resolution, Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who is expected to become the House speaker in the next Congress, said on ABC’s “This Week” on Sunday that he would be a “hard yes” on it.

Hegseth has “got to go,” Jeffries said. “The so-called secretary of Defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe.”

Most if not all House Democrats are expected to agree.

Last week, Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., the ranking member of the Armed Services Committee and its likely chairman in the next Congress, indicated in an interview with The New Republic that he would support Massie’s impeachment resolution, and he predicted it would be adopted.

Referring to Massie’s measure, Smith said, “By every estimation, it will pass and he will be impeached. And off that goes to the Senate. Then the Senate is legally required to spend all of their time dealing with that until it’s done with.”

"Every second Pete Hegseth remains at the top of the Pentagon, our servicemembers are at risk," Rep. Jason Crow, D-Colo., a senior member of the Armed Services Committee, said in a post on X on Sunday.

The letter cited the risks Kelley said the Iran war has posed to the lives of the Defense Department's uniformed and civilian personnel, and the missive noted Hegseth's stripping of workplace rights and protections for the department's civilians.

Massie’s resolution, the House can begin the long overdue bipartisan effort to reclaim its constitutional powers and authority, restore checks and balances, and take responsibility for the lives of military personnel and civilian employees that Mr. Hegseth’s capricious leadership has jeopardized," Kelley wrote.

Massie announced in mid-September his intention to file an impeachment resolution against Hegseth. But Johnson adjourned the House before the vote would have occurred.

Massie’s new resolution is substantially the same as his earlier one, with the same eight articles of impeachment.

The first three of these alleges that Hegseth’s conduct of the Iran war violated the War Powers Resolution.

Massie's measure says Hegseth prosecuted the Iran war without congressional authorization and in the absence of an attack on the United States or an imminent threat.

Further, the measure alleges that Hegseth continued the war despite the House and Senate adopting in June a concurrent war powers resolution calling for the withdrawal of U.S. forces from the fight.

And, the resolution says, Hegseth continued the Iran war after the expiration of the War Powers Resolution’s 60-day termination period and any potential 30-day withdrawal period.

The House has only voted twice to impeach a member of the Cabinet. In 1876, Secretary of War William Belknap was impeached over allegations of corruption, and his abrupt resignation likely contributed to his acquittal in the Senate.

#6297. This man sometimes sees his cat’s eyes on people’s faces

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

By sharing his rare condition, he’s helping scientists study how brains perceive faces

A brain surgery left a man with a big change in how faces appear. Sometimes, his cat’s eyes appear on a family member’s face, and vice versa. He and scientists worked with generative AI tools to create this image of his perception.

AI-generated images co-created by Brad Duchaine and Karl

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

After returning home from a 2024 brain surgery, a man started noticing something strange: Eyes that he had previously seen started showing up on the face he was currently looking at. To his bewilderment, the swapping of features even extended to his pet cat Luna.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

It was unsettling, to say the least. “Looking at her and then looking at somebody else, I might see her giant eyes on a person.”

Scientists have now described Karl’s perception of faces in the December issue of Cortex. His condition, in which echoes of a previously viewed image appear in a new context, is called palinopsia, and it was likely caused by Karl’s brain surgery. Because the echoes appear on faces, they distort how faces look to him, a condition known as prosopometamorphopsia. The new work offers clues about how brains perceive faces, both under normal and unusual conditions.

The researchers’ analyses of the man’s face perceptions are “wonderfully innovative,” says clinical psychiatrist Jan Dirk Blom of Leiden University and Parnassia Psychiatric Institute in the Netherlands, who was not involved in the work. “In this era of big data and complex statistical analyses, we almost forget how informative clinical observations in single patients can be.”

Karl’s unusual perceptions caught the attention of researchers. “His face processing system is disrupted, and it’s disrupted in a specific way,” says Brad Duchaine, a visual neuroscientist at Dartmouth University. “For reasons we don’t understand, items from memory are being pulled up and pasted onto the face that he’s perceiving.”

Duchaine’s lab has been collecting case studies of people who perceive faces differently in an effort to learn about visual perception. Duchaine and his colleagues assessed Karl’s experiences by showing him images of faces and asking him to describe what he saw. This confirmed that he consistently saw distortions in the eye regions of faces, such as the shape, and in faces’ shading and sometimes even texture. As they worked together, Duchaine and Karl used AI-image generators to create pictures of faces that resemble what Karl saw for the cat-human swap.

Karl isn’t the only person with palinopsia that affects faces, Duchaine says. A few other people have contacted him who also see echoes of prior faces. But Karl’s palinopsia seems different. “His were really consistent, very long-lasting. And then the cross-species transfer is something that I’d never heard before,” with one major exception, Duchaine says. A case study from 1986 describes a woman who, after seeing a poodle on a bus, saw poodle heads on every other passenger, too. That woman’s distortions lasted only about half an hour; Karl’s perceptual shifts have been consistently present since his 2024 surgery.

“What is new about the present study is the finding that a cat’s eyes can apparently be transposed from memory banks onto human faces observed in the here and now, and vice versa,” says Blom. “And that we now have a rough idea of the brain areas making this possible.”

During a surgery to correct malformed blood vessels, doctors removed tissue from Karl’s right posterior temporal area, a part of the brain known to be involved in face recognition. Karl’s experiences hint at how the visual system detects and interprets features on faces, Duchaine says. There’s an idea that humans interpret faces holistically, as a single object, he says. Karl’s case shows some of the limits of this idea, because he’s having these effects specific to the eye region, Duchaine says.

“It’s sort of like a filter,” Karl says, describing his experience of palinopsia. “It decides on a style, and then that style is applied to everyone in my reality, including myself.” These filters can change across a day or last several weeks, Karl says. He’s even experienced eye feature swaps from a face he saw in a dream. “And that was then applied to me, looking in a mirror, and then everybody else.”Karl also experiences echoes of environments, he says. For instance, if he has visited an area with lots of potholes in the roads, visual echoes of those potholes can appear in a newer road. A similar thing can happen with shapes, he says: Echoes of square hallways or stairwells can appear in new spots.

Using AI and collaboration to help re-create what Karl sees is an advance, Blom says. And this sort of collaboration between scientist and volunteer is crucial. “In my line of work, clinical psychiatry, we know that everything stands and falls with the descriptions that our patients give us,” he says. “In my opinion, this is patient participation at its best.”

Laura Sanders is the neuroscience writer. She holds a Ph.D. in molecular biology from the University of Southern California.
